Description: The Cook Trail old growth area contains approximately 256 acres of old growth. A moderate 2 mile trail will take you through a forest heavily dominated by E. hemlock. The following trees species 150 years old or greater can be found here: E. hemlock, E. white pine, white oak, N. red oak, tuliptree, chestnut oak, Am. beech, black cherry, cucumber tree, red maple, black birch, yellow birch, black gum, and white ash. Cook Forest is one of the nation's best examples of publicly accessible old-growth forest. It contains some of the oldest and tallest trees in the northeastern U.S. The entire park is 8,500 acres, of which 2,324 have been documented as old-growth. Plan to spend a few days here if you can. Be sure to visit the Forest Cathedral Natural Area too.
Navigation: Address: 113 River Road, Cooksburg, PA 16217
Parking And Admission: Park by River Cabins. Restrooms available. Trail starts across from cabin #12; No charge for park access.
Trails: The Cook Forest trail is 2 mi; there are 27 miles of additional trails through other parts of the forest.
Hours And Camping: The park has two areas of developed campgrounds appropriate for both tents and larger units. There are cabins for rent. Be sure to reserve early since this is a very popular place.
Hunting: Hunting is allowed in 7,000 acres of the 8,500 acre park.
name: Cook Trail - Cook Forest State Park

Description: The Forest Cathedral old-growth area is a registered National Natural Landmark, it is considered Pennsylvania's finest and largest old-growth forest. It was the first forest in the Old-Growth Forest Network, dedicated on April 19th, 2012. Approximately 315 acres of the 448 acre cathedral area is old-growth. The following tree species 150 years old or greater can be found here: E. hemlock, E. white pine, white oak, Am. beech, black cherry, red maple, N. red oak, black birch, yellow birch, cucumber tree, black gum. This forest has no close rival of tall, old, and unique E. white pine in the entire Northeastern United States. This is a very popular area with meandering trails throughout.
Navigation: Address: 113 River Road, Cooksburg, PA 16217
Parking And Admission: There is ample parking. Restrooms available. No charge for park access
Trails: The trail into the Forest Cathedral area starts just behind the Log Cabin Inn environmental center which is located 1 mile up Forest Road from Rt 36. There are 6 miles of trails in the Forest Cathedral area; many of them short enough for family day hikes, and 29 miles of trail throughout the forest.
Hours And Camping: The park has two areas of developed campgrounds appropriate for both tents and larger units. There are cabins for rent. Be sure to reserve early since this is a very popular place.
Hunting: Hunting is allowed in 7,000 acres of the 8,500 acre park.
name: Forest Cathedral Natural Area - Cook Forest State Park

Description: This 353 acre forest is not old-growth yet, but is does have a nice variety of tree species and some impressive specimens. Some that will make you stop in your tracks include, willow oak, loblolly pine, and swamp white oak. The forest also has nice sweet gum, black gum, red maple, beech, and holly. Wear your rubber knee boots if you're going to walk the trail since this flat Eastern Shore forest is very wet, and the trail seems to be the wettest part. Heading off the trail toward the northeast will put you in a drier area with larger trees. This forest is a refuge for the rare Delmarva fox squirrel.
Navigation: Address: 4343 Steele Neck Road, Vienna, MD 21869
Parking And Admission: Parking area is past this on the left, an unmarked circular area with a tree in the center. Parking for 6-8 vehicles. No restroom. No admission charge. Office 1/2 mile further down the road may be open during business hours.
Trails: 2 miles of trails.
Hours And Camping: Open all year. No developed camping area.
name: LeCompte Wildlife Management Area

Description: This 528 acre tract is the largest Piedmont Forest in Maryland. Although it is not true old-growth, the towering hardwood trees and the gently rolling woodland floor will take your breath with their beauty. The dominant species are tulip tree and a mixture of oaks. Wildlife includes abundant deer, fox and woodpeckers. The forest gets its name from the traces of gold mining ruins that are still visible. This forest is adjacent to the Great Falls of the Potomac River. While most visitors to the busy area will be heading toward the river, you will head the opposite direction into the relaxing forest. Begin the blue blazed trail uphill behind the Great Falls Tavern Visitor Center.
Navigation: Address: 11710 MacArthur Boulevard, Potomac, MD, 20854.
Parking And Admission: Parking for over 300 cars and buses. Three-day passes are $5 per vehicle or $3 per person if entering on foot or bike. National Park Service passes are accepted.
Trails: 3.2 mi, with 10 mi. of other trails nearby. Connects with the 184 mi C & O Canal path.
Hours And Camping: Open daylight hours every day except Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day and New Year's Day. No camping in this area, but there is camping available in more northern areas of the park.
name: Gold Mine Tract - C&O Canal National Historic Park

Description: This state forest covers 7,758 total acres of which between 400 and 500 acres are old growth. The oldest trees in the forest are hemlocks, which have been dated to 500 years. Red spruce have been dated to 400, and several other species to over 300. The forest consists of areas of: (1) northern hardwoods and hemlocks, (2) northern red and white oak, black birch and hemlock, (3) red spruce and hemlock, (4) sugar maple, white ash, and yellow birch, (5) white pine, and (6) white pine and hemlock. The forest has been chosen as the logical representative for Franklin County because it is the most prominent old-growth forest icon in the Commonwealth. In addition to the old growth, Mohawk Trail State Forest contains the tallest trees in New England, a section of the original Mohawk Indian Trail, and other historic, cultural, and ecological features.
Navigation: Address: 175 Mohawk Trail/Rte. 2, Charlemont, MA. Directions: From I-91 take Exit 26 in Greenfield and follow Rte. 2 west for 21 miles. The park entrance is on the right, 4 miles west of Charlemont center.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Restrooms. A five-dollar admission for parking is charged for day use in the summer. Walk-in hiking is free.
Trails: 12 miles of trails.
name: Mohawk Trail State Forest

Description: This woodland is part of the historic home site of William Cullen Bryant. Bryant was a poet, and also served as editor and publisher of The New York Evening Post for 50 years. A passionate conservationist and horticulturalist, he used his editorials to rally support for Frederick Law Olmsted's Central Park. He also was a strong abolitionist who helped Abraham Lincoln win presidential election. A self-guided map highlights the Rivulet Trail, where old growth, including ancient specimens of hemlock and a magnificent cherry tree, rise near the Rivulet, a trickling stream immortalized by Bryant's 1823 poem of the same name. The Pine Loop features enormous white pines that reach heights of 150 feet - a stand among the tallest in the Northeast. Some of the trees are named for poets, and some are named for eastern forest activists such as Mary Byrd Davis and Joan Maloof. This gentle trail, winding through a historic old-growth forest, is truly a delight.
Navigation: Address: 207 Bryant Road, Cummington, MA 01026
Parking And Admission: Parking is available at the Homestead with a trail leading across the field to the Rivulet Forest. To park right at the trailhead turn onto W. Cunningham Road and look for the "Rivulet" sign. Free admission, fee charged for house tours.
Trails: Approximately 1 mile long trail through the Rivulet Forest. There are also additional footpaths around the homestead.
Hours And Camping: Open year-round, daily, sunrise to sunset. No camping.
name: The Rivulet at the William Cullen Bryant Homestead

Description: The Heritage Grove is a 37-acre preserve of magnificent old-growth redwoods surrounded by over 800 acres of parkland comprised of younger forest and dry ridges. A sense of awe and tranquility permeates this unique enclave of forest that escaped the timber harvesting of earlier years. Many of the grove's huge redwoods were scheduled to be logged until a citizen's group banded together to raise funds to purchase the grove so that the magnificent trees could be preserved forever. The county matched these funds and made acquisition possible. It is considered to have the largest redwoods in the Santa Cruz Mountains. Trees common to the redwood forest include the coastal redwood. Douglas fir, various varieties of oak and California bay trees. In the lower elevations along moist ravines, many fern varieties are to be found, including the graceful five finger fern, sword fern, lady fern, gold back fern, polypody and woodwardia ferns. Also to be found along the moister slopes in great abundance are trillium, redwood violet, red clintonia and wild strawberry. In the more shady areas, carpets of redwood sorrel cover the redwood floor, and during the spring rainy season beautiful mosses and curious mushroom shapes appear throughout the park in glorious array.
Navigation: Address: 13435 Pescadero Creek Road, Loma Mar 94021
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Restrooms. $6 per vehicle.
Trails: A 4-mi RT trail takes one into the heart of the Heritage Grove. Over 30 miles of trail are accessible from this location.
Hours And Camping: Open all year. 8 am until 5 pm in winter, until 6 or 7 pm in spring and fall, until 8 pm in summer. Horse camps, youth camps and a Sierra Club hut are the only camping in this park. For the general public there is camping nearby in Memorial Park (developed) and Pescadero Creek Park (primitive).
name: Heritage Grove - Sam McDonald County Park

Description: This 200 acre forest is on the grounds of Montpelier, the former home of President James Madison. Sections of the forest are truly old-growth and the towering tulip trees and oaks cast a dense shade. Sounds of bird song will accompany you as you walk the easy trails. While other visitors are touring the stately brick home, you can take the Turkey Foot Loop (0.3 mi), the Poplar Run Loop (0.5 mi), the Spicebush Loop (0.2 mi), or the Mountain Mill Road Trail (0.5 mi) to experience an historic landscape. Some sections of nearby forest are managed, but the Landmark Forest is protected as wilderness.
Navigation: Address: 11407 Constitution Highway, Montpelier Station, VA 22957
Parking And Admission: Ample. Park in visitor's lot and get map at gift shop info desk. Restrooms. Admission fee.
Trails: 1.5 - 2.0 miles of trails.
Hours And Camping: Open daily, 9 am - 5 pm April through October; 9 am - 4 pm November through March. Open all year. No camping area.
name: James Madison Landmark Forest

Description: This 390-acre area along Standing Stone Creek includes virgin white pine and hemlock. Towering above the trail as it winds through 20-foot-high rhododendrons is a hemlock forest bypassed by the loggers at the end of the 19th century. Here are magnificent trees, some over 4 feet DBH and reaching several hundred years old. Other tree species in the area include white oak, red maple, white pine, pignut hickory, black gum and black birch. A mature mixed-oak forest with many large specimens is located on the mountain slope to the southeast. A nature trail leads into the heart of the remnant old-growth forest while winding along Standing Stone Creek, and continuing through a younger forest of oaks, white pine and red maple.
Navigation: Address: Alan Seeger Rd, Jackson, PA 16669
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Restrooms. No admission charge.
Trails: 1 mile, with connections via the Greenwood Spur trail to both the Mid State Trail to the north (approximately 1 mile) and the Standing Stone Trail to the south (approximately 3 miles).
Hours And Camping: Day use only. This forest is open all year. No camping, but camping available at Greenwood Furnace or Penn-Roosevelt State Parks, both close.
name: Alan Seeger Natural Area - Rothrock State Forest

Description: Majestic, magical, inspirational, with trees over 150 feet tall, this site is a sanctuary in every sense of the word. The best of the few remaining examples of pre-settlement forest in the region, this old-growth forest is notable not only for the extreme size of many individual trees but also for the very high number of tree species - at least 23 - of canopy size. Among these is yellow oak (Quercus muehlenbergii), a locally rare species. The preserve totals 181 acres, with almost 40 acres of old-growth forest. Almost every tree was marked for cutting. The property was acquired by Cotton-Hanlon Inc., a company that manages forested lands for timber harvest, with the intent to log it. Saving this old-growth forest involved years of negotiations between Cotton-Hanlon and the Cornell Plantations Natural Areas Committee. Acquired in 1997, the Fischer Old-Growth Forest is named to honor Richard B. Fischer (1919-2005), professor of environmental education, for his delight in natural history and his tenacity and can-do attitude toward environmental protection, which he shared with his many students.
Navigation: Address: 1346 Elmira Road, Newfield, NY
Parking And Admission: Park just north and across the street. Limited parking.
Trails: Trail is1 mile.
Hours And Camping: Day use only. Open all year. No camping.
Hunting: Hunting by permit. Visitor restrictions apply during firearm season. Sign at trailhead.
name: Fischer Old-Growth Forest

Description: Puu Makaala Natural Area Reserve is 18,730 acres in size and was established in 1981 to protect unique native rainforest. Long-term management of this forested watershed provides multiple benefits including protection of the island's water resources, undeveloped open spaces, and culturally significant areas. The reserve provides habitat for rare native plants and animals preserving the biodiversity of Hawai'i for current and future generations. This wet forest contains many large old ohia trees, false sandalwood trees, and towering hapuu tree ferns. Fenced areas are open to the public; fencing is just excluding the animals from the area. Gates and walk-overs allow people to access these areas. The rainforest trails are usually muddy, so waterproof boots are suggested.
Navigation: Address: 194824 Amaumau Road, Volcano, HI 96785.Directions: From Volcano Rd. turn onto Wright Rd. Follow Wright through curves to left and right (where it becomes Amaumau Rd.). Continue until the road ends at a cul-de-sac with three driveways. Follow the center driveway 0.2 mi to the parking area.
Parking And Admission: Parking for five vehicles. No restrooms. No admission charge.
Trails: Over 15 miles of trails.
Hours And Camping: Open all hours. Open all year. No camping area.
Hunting: Currently, No hunting allowed in fenced area.
name: Puu Makaala Natural Area Reserve

Description: This 37-acre grove of old-growth hemlock and pine is one of the few areas in Maryland that have never been logged. Some of the trees are over 300 years old. The coniferous canopy creates a dense shade, and muffles sounds, resulting in a reverential feeling among visitors. Small wood sorrel plants dot the forest floor, and downed wood and snags harbor all kinds of tiny life forms. Although this grove is small, and heavily visited, it is one of the few places in Maryland where one can imagine our nation's original forests. The Youghiogheny River flows along the park's borders, passing through shaded rocky gorges and creating rippling rapids. Tall hemlocks dominate the silent woods. The meandering trails through Swallow Falls guide hikers to some of the most breath-taking scenery in Western Maryland. There are four waterfalls in the park. Muddy Creek Falls is a crashing 53-foot waterfall, a spectacular sight and the tallest single drop waterfall in Maryland. Two other smaller falls occur along the canyon trail on the Youghiogheny itself. Swallow Falls State Park is popular not only for its natural wonder and beauty but for its picnic areas, wildlife like black bear, turkey, bobcat, and white tail deer, and a 65-site campground.
Navigation: Address: Maple Glade Rd, West Oakland, MD 21550. Directions: From U.S. 219 between Deep Creek Lake and Oakland, turn onto Mayhew Inn Rd. Follow to the end (4.3 mi) and turn left at the stop sign. Make a right onto Swallow Falls Rd. In 2 miles you will see a sign for Swallow Falls State Park. Trail begins from parking lot.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Restrooms. Admission charge, year round, various levels.
Trails: 1.1 miles, other trails nearby.
Hours And Camping: Open 8 am till sunset March - Oct.; 10 am till sunset Nov. - Feb. Open all year. Camping area, reservations needed in summer.
name: Youghiogheny Grove Natural Area - Swallow Falls State Park

Description: Many of the magnificent trees in this area are over 300 years old. Diameters of almost four feet are common and many trees tower to 100 feet in height. One hemlock was determined to be 500 years old, but many of the hemlocks have now been killed by the woolly adelgid insect. The area is the meeting ground of the southern and northern hardwood types, creating an extensive variety of trees. In 1868, Colonel R. Bruce Ricketts bought land in northeast Pennsylvania to timber it. Explorations revealed two creek branches that cut through deep gorges in a series of waterfalls then united and flowed through a glen among giant pines, hemlocks and oaks. Col. Ricketts built trails to the area of the waterfalls. The lower glen came to be called Ricketts Glen. The Glens became a registered National Natural Landmark in 1969, and in 1993 became a State Park Natural Area and will be protected and maintained in a natural state. The Natural Area covers 1,261 acres; it is surrounded by more than 10,000 acres of park land. The Evergreen Trail is only 1 mile and easy, the Falls Trail is 7.2 miles, steep and rocky; both are beautiful.
Navigation: Address: 288 State Route 118, Benton, PA 17814
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Restrooms. No admission charge
Trails: 26 miles of trails. The trail starts about 1 mi NE of this address on Rt 118. Look for sign.
Hours And Camping: Open sunrise to sunset. The park is open all year, as is the Evergreen Trail, but the Falls Trail is seasonal. Camping available.
Hunting: No hunting. in the Natural Area, but other areas of the park are open for hunting.
name: Glens Natural Area - Ricketts Glen State Park

Description: Fernbrook Natural Area is an excellent example of a southern Piedmont forest in varying stages of succession. George and Jacintha Paschal donated the 63-acre tract in 1963 as a land gift and requested that it be preserved in its natural state. For the first time since the original virgin timber was cut, the forest is being allowed to "complete" succession into a mature stand and the woodland is evolving to resemble pre-Colonial forest. It is estimated that the land on the first ridge of the preserve was allowed to return to forest at about the time of the Civil War. The resulting upland hardwoods comprise approximately 100-year-old secondary growth forest. Upland hardwoods include red oak, yellow poplar, hickory, black gum, red maple, American beech, and other species with scattered shortleaf and Virginia pine. Bottomland hardwoods include sycamore, ash, hackberry, red maple, black walnut and yellow poplar. With a beautiful mix of many species, and gentle trail, this is a forest that can be enjoyed by everyone.
Navigation: Address: 2893 Burnt Mill Rd, Charlottesville, VA. Directions: From Rt 250 in Charlottesville take Rt 20 (Stony Point Rd)north out of town7.5 miles. Rt 20 will make a very hard right curve (you can't miss it because you have to slow way down). Take a left there, that will be Rt 600 (Watts Passage Rd.). Go 0.6 mi and make a left on Rt 784 (Burnt Mill Rd). Continue 0.8 mi to parking area on the left. You will see a sign for Fernwood Preserve there.
Parking And Admission: Parking for about 5 vehicles. No restroom. No admission charge.
Trails: 2.5 mi of trails.
Hours And Camping: Open dawn to dusk. Open all year. No camping.
name: Fernbrook Natural Area

Description: Hoxie Gorge is a 169-acre natural area maintained by the State University of New York, Cortland for educational, research and recreational purposes since 1965. A portion of the property was the site of a dairy farm from the 1880s to the 1960s, while a portion has remained undisturbed. The natural environments include pristine streams running through the gorge area, mature woodlands and old fields. The McDermott Nature Trail and the Finger Lakes Trail provide access to these areas. As one travels the McDermott Nature Trail near marker #29, the Finger Lakes Trail continues northeast. In this area are old-growth hemlock (Tsuga canadensis) trees on the banks of the gorge, the oldest of which date back to 1736 and another to 1740. In this area are also sweet birch (Betula lenta), red maple (Acer rubrum) and black cherry (Prunus serotina) that date to the late 1800's. Larger mammals in the forest include white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus), eastern coyote (Canis latrans), porcupine (Erethizon dorsatum), and fisher (Martes pennanti).
Navigation: Address: Hoxie Gorge Road, Marathon, NY.  Directions: From Cortland take Port Watson St. east to bridge over Tioughnioga River. Continue on Route 11 south for five miles (four miles south on Route 11 from I-81 exit 10). Turn left on Hoxie Gorge Road. Take the left fork into gorge, drive past houses and look for College signs part way up hill.
Parking And Admission: Parking for about 6 cars. No restrooms. No admission charge.
Trails: 2 miles of trails.
Hours And Camping: Day use only. Open all year. No camping.
name: Hoxie Gorge Nature Preserve

Description: This mature oak-hickory forest surrounds the headwaters of the Governor's Run Watershed. Old maps show this area as being one of the largest forested areas left in the mid-1800s. Although not true old-growth, it has probably not been logged in over a century and a half. Nice black gum, tulip poplar, sycamore and beech may also be seen in this impressively diverse forest. The American Chestnut Land Trust manages over 3,000 acres in Calvert County, but the oldest forest they manage is the one that can be experienced along the 2 mile long East Loop Trail. This is very close to Calvert Cliffs on the Chesapeake Bay.
Navigation: Address: 2650 Scientists Cliff Rd, Prince Fredrick, MD 20678; Directions: Go 4 miles south on Solomons Island Road (Routes 2/4) from the intersection of Hallowing Point Road (Route 231) in Prince Frederick. Turn left on Parkers Creek Road, cross Route 765 and turn right onto Scientists Cliffs Road.
Parking And Admission: The small parking area for this trail is adjacent to the address above. The first part of the trail goes along a field. Limited parking. No restrooms. No admission fee.
Trails: 5. 2 mi, with 13 miles of other trails nearby.
Hours And Camping: Open dusk to dawn. Open all year. No camping.
Hunting: Bow hunting only, sign posted at trailhead during hunts
name: Parkers Creek Preserve - South Side, East Loop

Description: The "Old-Growth Trail" marked with orange trail signs will take visitors into the Tuliptree Cathedral. This may be the tallest publicly owned forest in central New York with tulip-poplars (Liriodendron tulipifera) well over 120 feet tall. In this small area some of the hemlocks and tulip-poplars are estimated to be 300 years old. Green Lakes State Park protects about 1,000 acres of old growth, much of it sugar maple on the hillsides around the lakes. Also interesting are the lakeside white cedar groves. Both Green and Round Lakes are rare meromictic lakes with an unusual green-blue color. The park has a beach area that is very popular in the summer.
Navigation: Address: 7900 Green Lakes Rd, Fayetteville, NY. (May also be listed as Kirkville, NY, 13066). Directions: When entering the park take the first right past the ticket booth. Follow signs to the Rolling Hills Camping Area. The trail to the old-growth starts between campsites 96 and 98. Follow the Orange Trail to the Tuliptree Cathedral.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Restrooms. Admission charge (seasonal) $8. Vehicle entrance fee.
Trails: 2.7 mi; with 7 mi of nearby trails.
Hours And Camping: Open 24 hours. Open all year. Cabins and campsites - open May - Oct. Call or check website for exact dates.
name: Old Growth Trail - Green Lakes State Park

Description: Although it contains the largest area of publicly accessible forest in St. Mary's County - 2,200 acres, few non-hunters know about this forest. The forest is not true old growth yet, but the rolling forest floor and braided streams are shaded by impressive native oaks, hollies, cherries, pine, gum and maple. Hunting may be quite active at times, so be aware that you are sharing the forest and check to see what is in season. Hunting is not allowed on Sundays so that may be the best day to visit. The abundant trails are unmapped and mostly unmarked. After passing the sign board, start down the power line right-of-way and look for a trail to the right. On many days you will be the only visitor and a true sense of solitude may be experienced.
Navigation: Address: 22453 Old Rolling Road, California, MD 20619. Directions: From Rt. 2/4 in California, MD, (heading south) turn left onto Rt. 235. In less than 1 mi. turn right onto Old Rolling Road and continue to the end.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. No restrooms. No admission charge.
Trails: Many trails, but no maps or signage.
Hours And Camping: Open 7am to sunset. Open all year. No camping.
Hunting: Hunting is allowed and may be quite active in season. No hunting on Sundays.
name: Northern Section - St. Mary's River Wildland

Description: While this easy to access hike just off the road to Hana is enjoyable it is NOT a native forest. Tree species such as Eucalyptus robusta have been established here long enough to grow to impressive heights and girths, giving one the feeling of being in an old forest. Unfortunately, there are no native old-growth forests on Maui which are open to the public on a drop-in basis. The state-owned old-growth preserves are all surrounded by miles of private land, and so are inaccessible unless one has permits. Until new land is acquired, or access is provided for one of the existing reserves, this forest will at least serve as a pleasant place to stroll under a tall tree canopy.
Navigation: Directions: Along the road towards Hana, the first parking area on the right after mile marker #9. A large sign identifies the trail.
Parking And Admission: There is parking for 8 to 12 cars, but the lot is often full. No restrooms. No admission fee.
Trails: Nature trail is 0.8 mi loop, sometimes muddy. The ridge trail extends from the top of the nature trail; it is less well maintained the further you get from the parking area.
Hours And Camping: Open all hours. Open all year. No camping.
Hunting: Hunting is allowed and may be quite active in season. No hunting on Sundays.
name: Waikamoi Ridge Trail

County and State: Honolulu, City and County of, HI
Description: From Moanalua Valley Park (NOT Moanalua Gardens): A gated dirt road leads one on a nice walk under the dappled shade of trees. At 2.5 miles up the road the Kulana'ahane trail branches off to the left. The location is well marked with a sign. This side valley contains a more pristine native forest which includes Koa, Kukui, and Ohia trees. Expect stream crossings and some slippery rocks. Eventually the valley trail leads up the ridge. If you make it all the way to the top of the ridge there are gorgeous views to be enjoyed. It is best to plan a full day for this hike since it is over 8 miles roundtrip. Expect some mud and a great time.
Navigation: Address: Moanalua Valley Park: 1857 Ala Aolani Street, Honolulu, Hawaii, 96819. Directions: Access to this park is off of the Moanalua Freeway (A.K.A. the 78). Heading east on the 78, exit at Red Hill. Go straight at the first stop sign at the top of the off ramp (you'll be on Moanalua Rd), then take a left at the second stop sign onto Ala Napunani St. and go under the freeway. Take a left at the stop sign onto Ala Aolani St. You will pass a golf course on your left and then go through a residential area for about 1.5 miles before the road dead-ends into the park's parking lot. If you are headed west on the 78, take exit 2: Moanalua Valley/Salt Lake/Red Hill. The road will split and you want to turn right to Moanalua Valley. You'll then be on Ala Aolani St. You will pass a golf course on your left and then go through a residential area for about 1.5 miles before the road dead-ends into the park's parking lot.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Restroom. No admission charge.
Trails: A single 4-mile trail up the Kamanani Valley forks at 2.5 mi to lead up the Kalana'ahane Valley. Proceed along streambed following trail markers.
Hours And Camping: Open 7 am - 7 pm. Open all year. No camping area.
Hunting: Hunting is allowed and may be quite active in season. No hunting on Sundays.
name: Kulana'ahane Trail

Description: Pfeiffer Big Sur State Park features huge old-growth redwood trees, bay laurel, live oaks, sycamores, cottonwoods, maples, alders and willows - plus open meadows. Wildlife includes black-tail deer, gray squirrels, raccoons, skunks, and birds, such as water ouzels and belted kingfishers. There is a short, family-friendly "Nature Trail" and a few longer trails to choose from.
Navigation: Address: 47555 Highway 1, Big Sur, CA 93920. Directions: Located off Highway 1, 26 miles south of Carmel and two miles south of the hamlet of Big Sur.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Restrooms. No admission charge.
Trails: A family-friendly "Nature Trail" is only 0.3 mi; the Pfeiffer Falls and Valley View trail is 2 mi. (parts of this trail have recently been damaged by storms); a 10 mi. (one way) hike will take you to Sykes Hot Spring.
Hours And Camping: Open 1/2 hour before sunrise to 1/2 hour after sunset. Open all year, but temporary road closures may sometimes be in effect. A large camping area that frequently fills, reservations strongly suggested. A 61-room lodge and restaurant.
name: Pfeiffer Big Sur State Park

Description: The Rockefeller Loop Trail/Bull Creek Flat trail is at the foot of the majestic 10,000-acre Rockefeller Forest. The Rockefeller Forest is the largest remaining contiguous old-growth coastal redwood (Sequoia sempervirens) forest in the world. Trees soaring to immense heights combined with a relatively open under story combine to create a fairy-book forest! The grove has the classic ground cover of redwood needles dusted with a sparse layer of redwood sorrel and dotted with an occasional fern. Walking through these forests is like taking a step back in time. Some of the tallest trees in the world are in this forest, and they may be thousands of years old. When you walk through the forest however, measurements don't seem very important. In 1917, several prominent men traveled to Humboldt County to see these trees. When they found that these trees were not protected, they founded the Save the Redwoods League to preserve examples of these forests. In 1921, the first grove was purchased in what was to become Humboldt Redwoods State Park. The Rockefeller Forest was purchased from the Pacific Lumber Company in 1931. John D. Rockefeller, Jr. had taken a tour of the area with Save the Redwoods League officials and was impressed. The Save the Redwoods League purchased the land with a pair of million-dollar donations from Rockefeller and matching funds from the state. Save the Redwoods is still actively saving forests with the help of generous philanthropists.
Navigation: Directions: From Highway 101 take exit 663 - Honeydew (this is north of Garberville). Follow signs on Honeydew Rd. about 1.5 mi to Rockefeller Forest. Turn right at the sign for Rockefeller Loop Trail. If you are coming from the Avenue of the Giants: four miles north of the park visitor center and just south of the hamlet of Redcrest, turn west on Mattole Road (mile marker 20.6) and drive 1.5 miles to the parking area for the Rockefeller Forest Loop Trail. Park headquarters and the Visitor Center are located on the Avenue of the Giants, State Route 254, between the towns of Weott and Myers Flat. Weott is 228 miles north of San Francisco on Highway 101.
Parking And Admission: Limited parking. No restrooms on the trail. There are restrooms located across the river at California Federation of Women's Clubs Grove Day-Use Area; in the summer accessible by walking over a summer bridge, or it can be driven to (about 5 miles).
Trails: The Rockefeller Loop Trail (0.6 mi; ADA Accessible) is suitable for all ages and all abilities. For those who wish to hike further, the Rockefeller Loop continues onto the 7.5 mi Bull Creek Loop Trail. Altogether there are over 100 miles of trail in Humboldt Redwoods State Park.
Hours And Camping: The park is only open during day-light hours. The only exception being camping in the campgrounds. The trail is open year-round, but the day-use area is closed during the winter months. Over 200 campsites in the park, reservations suggested. No RV hookups. Back country trail camps are also available.
name: Rockefeller Forest - Humboldt Redwoods State Park

Description: This lovely and gentle trail is a delight from the very beginning. Here, all generations may wander through true old-growth forest that includes impressive hemlocks, yellow birch, red maple and red spruce. Smaller beech and balsam fir may be seen as well. Shrubs include hobblebush and mountain maple; colorful fungi and native wildflowers dot the forest floor. One or two soggy places add beauty and diversity, but may involve a wet crossing in the spring. West Canada Lake Wilderness is part of Adirondacks Park. This section of old growth is part of the Squaw Peak to Blue Ridge tract measured in thousands of acres.
Navigation: Address: 4155 Route 30N Lake Pleasant, NY 12108. Directions: From New York State Thruway (I-90), Exit 27 at Amsterdam; north on Route 30 through the villages of Wells, and Speculator. Campground is 12 miles north on Route 30 from Speculator on the left side of the road. From Adirondack Northway (I-87), Exit 23 at Warrensburg; Route 9 north to Route 28 west to Indian Lake Village. Campground is 12 miles south of village of Indian Lake on the right side of Rte. 30. The trail starts right next to campsite #125. It is well marked.
Parking And Admission: Parking for the trail is just north of the campground on Rt 30. Signs will direct you where to park, then walk down the road just a short way to the camping area where the trail begins. Parking for about six cars. Restrooms in the campground. No admission charge.
Trails: After 8 miles the trail connects to the Northville Placid Trail, which continues for many miles.
Hours And Camping: No restricted hours. Campground is seasonal but trail may be accessed all year. Trail is adjacent to a campground which also has cabins for rent.
name: Sucker Brook Trail - West Canada Lake Wilderness

Description: It is not unusual to see cars parked along the roadside at this very popular trailhead. Most folks will be there to climb the mountain, but you will be there to take your time and enjoy the forest. When starting on the trail, right away you will be surrounded by original, unlogged forest. The well-worn trail will take you by impressive sugar maple, hemlock, and yellow birch. The yellow birches are close to 500 years old, and have been called some of the most impressive in New York. There are also beech trees, but the largest of these have been killed by beech-bark disease. Tasteful little bridges will lead you over beautiful streams. This old-growth forest has been described as "two miles wide and 8 miles long," covering approximately 1,400 acres. If you are an off-trail sort of hiker, there are lovely spots to explore and enjoy throughout this forest.
Navigation: Directions: Intersection of Tupper Lake Highway and Bartlett Cary Rd, Middle Saranac Lake, NY. 8.1 mi west of Saranac Lake on Rt. 3; and 7.3 mi east of the junction. of Rts. 3 and 30.
Parking And Admission: A well-marked parking area on Rt 3 has space for about a dozen cars. No restrooms. No Admission charge.
Trails: 5.2 miles RT to top of mountain.
Hours And Camping: Open all year. No camping.
name: Ampersand Mountain

County and State: San Francisco, City and County of, CA
Description: The Oak Woodlands are located in the northeast corner of Golden Gate Park. The coast live oak, Quercus agrifolia,  is really the only indigenous tree in San Francisco County that existed here before European colonization. There are 3 major areas where these old-growth oak woodlands occur: Golden Gate Park, Buena Vista Park, and the Presidio. The grove in Golden Gate Park is the largest of the three. There is good documentation that the trees pre-date the park itself and are hundreds of years old. When Golden Gate Park was started in 1871, approximately fifty acres of wooded oak areas were left as "wilderness." The trees, an historic remnant of an earlier landscape, were eventually cut for fuel, but they resprouted and some of the trees in the woodlands today are from those sprouts. The trees have not yet regained their maximum size. Some of the groves have a scattered overstory of human introduced non-indigenous trees such as the blue gum eucalyptus and the Monterey pine and cypress. Invasive species have changed the nature of the woodland, but aggressive restoration efforts are gradually bringing it closer to its native condition. Do not expect dense forest, but use your time here to celebrate and imagine the original landscape of the Bay area.
Navigation: Address: 501 Stanyan St, San Francisco, CA.  Directions: Various entry points in Golden Gate Park including McLaren Lodge) at the east end and  Arguello Blvd. and Fulton St. at  mid point , and 6th and Fulton St.at the west end.
Parking And Admission: Parking ample. Restrooms adjacent to 'Conservatory of Flowers' near the Arguello Blvd. and Fulton St. entrance. No admission fee.
Trails: The 'Oak Woodlands Trail' extends through the groves almost 1 mile from the east portal at JFK/ East Conservatory Drive to 6th and Fulton at western limit.
Hours And Camping: Open sunrise to sunset. Open all year. No camping.
Phone Number: SFRPD Natural Areas Program, Christopher Campbell, 415-831-6331 and Robert Bakewell, Friends of Oak Woodlands Golden Gate Park 415-710-9617
name: Oak Woodlands of Golden Gate Park

Description: This park includes one of the most-visited old-growth forests in the nation. Immediately behind the Michigan Forest Visitor Center is a paved 1.25 mile trail that leads through a 49 acre remnant of Michigan's original forest. The gentle rolling trail is suitable for all abilities. The forest is dominated by majestic white pines that inspire one to imagine what Michigan was like when it was first settled. In 1927, Karen Michelson Hartwick purchased over 8,000 acres of land here, which included 86 acres of old growth white pine. A short while later she donated the land to the State of Michigan as a memorial park to be named for her husband, who died in World War I. She also specified the forest should never be logged and that a log cabin (the Memorial Building) should be built to honor her husband, Maj. Edward Hartwick, as well as the lumberjacks that worked in the area during the White Pine Logging Era (1840-1910). Today,Hartwick Pines covers 9,672 acres and is one of the largest state parks in the Northern Lower Peninsula -- although very little of it is old-growth. A windstorm in 1940 reduced the old-growth pines area from 86 acres to 49 acres. The Hartwick Pines Logging Museum is open seasonally. Please check the website for hours of operation.
Navigation: Address: 4216 Ranger Road, Grayling, MI 49738. (Northeast of Grayling on M-93, Exit 259 off I-75, well-marked)
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Restrooms. Michigan "Recreation Passport" required, fee varies depending on in-state or out-of-state.
Trails: 20 miles of trails.
Hours And Camping: Park hours: 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. Park and Michigan Forest Visitor Center is open all year. The park includes a campground with 100 modern sites; camping available from April through October.
Hunting: Hunting is not allowed in the "Pines" area, but other areas of the park allow hunting.
name: Hartwick Pines State Park

Description: The forest identified for inclusion in the Old-Growth Forest Network is a contiguous 1,100 acres of mixed conifer and ponderosa pine old growth. Mixed conifer is found on the north and northwest facing slopes, and ponderosa pine on the south and southeast facing slopes. The forest is located in the Hermosa Roadless Area which is being considered in Congress for special designation. The Roadless Area encompasses nearly 142,000 acres and is bisected by Hermosa Creek. The west side of the Hermosa Creek drainage, (nearly half of the area), is being considered for Wilderness designation. The eastern half, which contains the Hermosa Creek Trail, would be retained for multiple use recreation including hiking, mountain biking, horseback riding and motorcycle use. The Hermosa Area contains rugged country and old-growth forests can be found throughout, but these particular stands are located right along the Hermosa Creek Trail, within easy hiking distance from the Lower Hermosa Trailhead.
Navigation: Directions: The Lower Hermosa campground is located 14 miles northwest of Durango. Take Hwy. 550 north from Durango. Turn west at Hermosa onto County Road 201 which becomes Forest Rd. 576 to the campground. The Hermosa Creek Trail begins at the parking lot and follows the creek some 25 miles uphill through the Hermosa Roadless Area to Hermosa Park, near Sig Creek Campground.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. The parking lot is large enough for vehicles and horse trailers. A toilet is in the parking lot adjacent to the Hermosa Creek Trailhead. There is no water available.No admission fee.
Trails: Hermosa Creek Trail is 20 miles long, but the old-growth forest is located along the first 3 miles of the lower end of the trail.
Hours And Camping: No time restrictions. Open all year. Lower Hermosa campground, right next to the trailhead, is free and has 20 campsites; some are for horse use only. There is no water available at this campground. Tables and fire grates are at each site.
Hunting: Hunting is allowed and may be quite active in season. No hunting on Sundays.
name: Hermosa Creek Special Management Area - San Juan National Forest

Description: Whiteoak Canyon is located just off Skyline Drive in Shenandoah National Park. The park covers 200,000 acres, but this is one of the few areas of easily accessible old growth. The very rocky but well-maintained trail gets more beautiful as one drops down along the small Robinson River. A number of waterfalls may be viewed along this trail. Big oaks, maples, and hop-hornbeams abound, but sadly the big old hemlocks are mostly dead - victims of the woolly adelgid insect. The main trail is 4.6 miles roundtrip, but you can choose to take the extended 7.3 mile trail to the bottom of the canyon and back. If you are seeking a handicap accessible trail, the Limberlost trailhead is 0.5 miles to the south. Trail maps are available on the website.
Navigation: Address: milepost 42.7 Skyline Drive, Luray, VA 22835; Trail may also be accessed from eastern side (Rt 600) see park website for directions.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Admission charge. No restrooms.
Trails: 4.6 mi, linked to many more trails.
Hours And Camping: Park is always open. However, portions of Skyline Drive, the only public road through the park, are periodically closed during inclement weather and at night during deer hunting season, mid-November through early January. Visitors can still enter the park on foot to hike even when the Drive is closed. Camping: Yes, and backcountry by permit.
Hunting: No hunting in Shenandoah National Park. Hunting is allowed in adjacent National Forest. For more information see the Lee Ranger District George Washington National Forest.
name: Whiteoak Canyon - Shenandoah National Park

Description: This forest preserve contains gentle, shaded trails, with bridged stream crossings, throughout rolling topography located in the transition zone between the piedmont and the Blue Ridge Mountains. The forest was originally protected to keep the water supply of a nearby mill town clean. The oldest trees are estimated to be 150-200 years old. Visitors will see large oaks, hickories, tulip poplars and many kinds of pine. The Chicopee Woods Nature Preserve is a 1400 acre protected woodland which is overseen by Elachee Nature Science Center, which contains a visitor center and a nature school. Elachee is celebrating more than 35 years of building environmental literacy and promoting a healthy ecological consciousness for Georgians. Chicopee is the largest contiguous conservation easement in North Georgia. The Preserve is also recognized by the National Audubon Society as an Important Bird Area (IBA), an area essential to nesting and migrating birds.
Navigation: Address: 2125 Elachee Dr. Gainesville, GA 30504
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. $1 donation suggested.
Trails: 10 miles of trails. Best short trip would be the Dodd/ Mathis trail loop (1.25 mi.). Intermediate trip: Dunlap trail loop (2.5 mi.). Long trip: East/West Lake Trail loop (4.75 mi.).
Hours And Camping: Monday - Sunday dawn-dusk; open all year.
name: Chicopee Woods Nature Preserve

Description: In a county where chaparral is the dominant land cover, this park with large,ancient trees gives a visitor the feeling of being in the High Sierras. The park covers 1,869 acres. The majority of the park is coniferous forest, but there are also wetlands, ponds, and meadows. Tree species include White Fir, Bigcone, Douglas Fir, Black Oak, Canyon Live Oak, Coast Live Oak, Incense Cedar, and Ponderosa Pine. Many of the trees appear to be old growth, although most of the forest has not been dated and there was likely some selective logging in the past. Two impressively large incense cedars in the Silvercrest picnic area have been dated to be 400 years old, and a ring count on a cut big Cone Douglas fir showed it to be over 300 years old.
Navigation: Address: 19952 State Park Rd, Palomar Mountain, CA 92060. Directions: From Highway 76, either of two roads can be used to reach the park. The one from Rincon Springs (County Road S6) is scenic but rather steep and winding. County Road S7 from Lake Henshaw is longer, but its gentle grade makes it more suitable for heavily loaded vehicles and those pulling trailers. Please note that there are no gas stations on Palomar Mountain.
Parking And Admission: There are three parking areas: Silvercrest, Doane Pond and Boucher Lookout. There are public restrooms at Silvercrest, Doane Pond, Boucher Lookout, Cedar Grove campground, Doane Valley campground. Admission charge is $8.00 per vehicle.
Trails: There are 14 miles of hiking trails. The trails are situated in three main loops that offer a wonderful variety of hikes. The Scott's Cabin loop is mostly forested, it is approximately 4 miles long with an elevation gain and loss of approximately 600'. The French Valley Loop is approximately 3 miles. The terrain is level with big beautiful meadows, creeks and a wide variety of plant communities. It's a great area for bird watching and wildlife viewing. The hike with the best view is the Boucher Loop. It is approximately a 3-mile loop. It takes you up to the highest point in the park at an elevation of 5,400'. On weekends during fire season the Boucher Fire Lookout is manned by volunteers who offer a tour of the tower. On a crystal clear day you can view the Catalina, San Clemente and Coronado Islands.
Hours And Camping: Open 8 am - sunset. Open all year. There is a campground at the park.
name: Palomar Mountain State Park

Description: Deer Springs Trail heads up the side of Mount San Jacinto from just north of Idyllwild. It can be accessed either from the lower end at Idyllwild (5,600 ft) or from the upper end via the Palm Springs aerial tramway (8,500 ft). At its peak the trail tops 10,000 ft. This elevation change results in a wide variety of forest types. At the upper end the gorgeous old-growth trees are mostly Jeffrey pine, Sugar pine, and white fir growing alongside picturesque boulders. At the lower end the oldest pines have died, but many "middle-aged" trees are growing to fill in the gaps. In this zone there are Sugar pines, Coulter pines, western red cedar, and oaks; but perhaps the most beautiful woody plants on the lower end of the trail are the ancient madrones. For those in top physical condition, it can be hiked in one long day. Alternatives are starting at one end or the other for a day hike, or taking two days and camping at one of the wilderness campgrounds.
Navigation: Directions: You can get to this trail either from the lower end - 0.75 mi. north of the town of Idyllwild, CA (25225 Highway 243 Idyllwild, CA 92549) or from the upper end by using the Palm Springs Aerial Tramway
Parking And Admission: Ample parking.
Trails: Deer Springs trail is 9-12 miles depending on route. It connects to 70 miles of other trails and the Pacific Crest Trail.
Hours And Camping: Always open. Open all year, but expect snow in higher elevations in the winter. There is a campground in Idyllwild, and a few backcountry camps (Strawberry Jct and Little Round Valley Camp).
name: Deer Springs Trail - Mount San Jacinto State Wilderness

Description: The Prothonotary Birding Trail guides visitors on a quiet, gentle, stroll through the Cubler Payne Forest along  picturesque Nassawango Creek. There are two distinct forest cover types: upland hardwood and pine; and bottomland cypress and gum. These forest types correspond to the elevation gradient on the property, which is considerable for the local area. Large oaks (white and red) are common on the uplands, as are tulip poplars and sweet gums. The bottomland forest is dominated by bald cypress (near its northern range here) with their characteristic knees sticking above the forest floor; black gum and red maple are also common. The Cubler Payne Forest totals 55 acres. Most of the forest has been cut at least once since European settlers arrived, but portions, including the Prothonotary Birding Trail, are being restored and protected from logging by The Nature Conservancy as future old growth. Increment cores were collected in 2014 to determine the ages of selected trees along the trail, including shortleaf pine (144 years), black oak (147 years), white oak (105 years), water oak (98 years), and bald cypress (181 years). The forest is part of an Audubon Important Birding Area, and neotropical migratory birds such as the Prothonotary Warbler were monitored here for many years. This site is also regionally significant as the northern range limit of two lichen species (Arthonia cinnabarina, Schismatomma rappii), recently discovered by scientists at the New York Botanical Garden. The Cubler Payne Forest is part of The Nature Conservancy's Nassawango Creek Preserve, which protects over 10,000 acres of swamp and upland forest along both sides of Nassawango Creek.
Navigation: Address: 4932 Creek Road, Snow Hill, MD is the address of the private home just north of the parking area. Use this address to navigate, but please respect the privacy of our neighbor. Directions: From Snow Hill Rd (RT 12) turn south on Nassawango Rd. Continue until the intersection of Nassawango and Creek Rd. Turn right on Creek Rd and parking area is immediately on the right. There is a sign by the open field.
Parking And Admission: Limited parking. No restrooms.
Trails: The Prothonotary Warbler Trail is 1 mile in length.
Hours And Camping: Day use only. Open all year. No camping. No charge.
Hunting: No hunting is permitted in the Cubler/Payne Forest
name: Cubler Payne Forest

Description: Visitors to Corkscrew Swamp Sanctuary find a 2.25 mile boardwalk that meanders through pine flatwoods, wet prairie, marsh, and finally into the world's largest (over 700 acres) remaining old-growth Bald Cypress forest. These impressive cypress trees, relatives of the redwood, tower up to 130 feet into the sky and often exceed 20 feet in girth. They are estimated to be at least 700 years old and their massive branches are draped with mosses, lichens, bromeliads and ferns. The forest is the site of the largest nesting colony of federally endangered wood storks in the nation. It is also home to hundreds of alligators, otters, white-tailed deer and red-bellied turtles. A wide variety of wading birds, raptors, and songbirds including the beautiful painted bunting can be seen. Photo opportunities are available at every turn of the boardwalk trail.
Navigation: Address: 375 Sanctuary Road West, Naples, FL 34120
Parking And Admission: Ample parking.
Trails: A 2.25-mile boardwalk meanders through pine flatwoods, wet prairie, around a marsh and finally into the largest old growth Bald Cypress forest in North America.
Hours And Camping: Corkscrew Sanctuary's boardwalk is open daily from 7 a.m.-5:30 p.m. Please note that boardwalk admission closes at 4:30 p.m.
name: Corkscrew Swamp Sanctuary

Description: Zoar Valley Unique area contains some of the last stands of old-growth forest in Western New York, and the Valentine Flats area is a good place to access it. Zoar Valley's most renowned forest stands of "big tree" old growth are found in the bottomland areas. There are groves of large and aging eastern cottonwood, American sycamore, and American elm. An isolated sycamore, now embedded within later successional beech-maple woodlands, has been core dated to 350 years. Species diversity along the canyon bottom is among the highest in the northeast, with more than 30 tree species present. Tree diameters and, especially, heights are superlative. Numerous species exceed 40 inches diameter. The ten tree species occurring here that are the tallest in New York State include tulip poplar, sugar maple, slippery elm, American sycamore, black walnut, cottonwood, red oak, bitternut hickory, yellow birch, basswood, and white ash. On the slopes, trees are generally moderate in size; however, they are exceptionally old. An eastern hemlock with a diameter of only 16 inches has been core dated to 450 to 500 years old. The slope woodlands present an impressive and ancient aesthetic, but few stands can be visited directly. The steep slopes are mostly too dangerous to traverse.
Navigation: Address: 10112 Valentine Flats Rd; Gowanda, NY 14070. Directions: Take Broadway Rd (Route 4) going south out of Gowanda, NY. Turn left onto Point Peter Rd. Follow it for about a mile and make a left on Valentine Flats Rd. Valentine Flats Road dead-ends at the trail head parking area.
Parking And Admission: Parking available for about 10 vehicles. No restrooms. No admissions charge.
Trails: The trail is 2.2 miles and goes from the cliff top down to Cattaraugus Creek. Crossing a wide creek is necessary to visit most of the bottomland groves. Extreme caution should be used when exploring Zoar Valley; numerous accidents have occurred on the steep cliffs. Detailed trail directions may be found in The Sierra Club Guide to Ancient Forests of the Northeast.
Hours And Camping: Open sunrise to sunset; No camping is allowed.
name: Zoar Valley Unique Area

Description: Nestled in the Pierson Hollow area of Carnifex Ferry Battlefield State Park is 30 acres of old-growth forest on the rim of the Gauley River Canyon of West Virginia. At the start of the trail, one passes through late successional stands with yellow poplar and hemlock dominant lower down. Oaks dominate the upper slopes and some pine stands are found on the flats. Dense rhododendron thickets are along the stream and trail. This is one of the nicer virgin areas left in West Virginia. As one continues down the hollow, the trees are older and the canopy is dominated by hemlock and tulip poplar, with an occasional northern red oak. The trees are between 250 and 300 years old; the oldest tree is reported to be 400 years old. There are several generations of coarse woody debris on the forest floor, which were augmented by the heavy snows of super storm Sandy in October 2012, which tore the crown off of many mature trees.
Navigation: Address: 1194 Carnifex Ferry Rd Summersville WV 26651
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Restrooms in Picnic area Open April 1-Oct.31. No Admission Charge.
Trails: Pierson Hollow Trail is 0.6 miles.
Hours And Camping: Hours 6am-10pm. Trails are open year-round. Some facilities are closed November 1-April 1. No camping area.
name: Pierson Hollow - Carnifex Ferry Battlefield State Park

Description: Cathedral State Park is one of the last living commemorations of the vast virgin hemlock forest that once flourished in the Appalachian highlands. Trees up to 90 feet in height and 21 feet in circumference form cloisters in the park. Throughout the woods, eastern hemlock is the dominant species. Over 170 species of vascular flora have been catalogued, including 9 species of fern, 3 species of club moss, over 30 tree species (17 broadleaf) and over 50 species of wildflowers. Cathedral State Park consists of 133 acres, located on Route 50, in Preston County in Northeastern, West Virginia. The region is hilly to mountainous, but the park is located on rather gently sloping ground with an elevation varying from 2,460 to 2,620 feet.
Navigation: Address: Cathedral State Park, 12 Cathedral Park Drive Aurora, WV 26705
Parking And Admission: Ample parking.
Trails: Cathedral offers 6 miles of hiking trails.
Hours And Camping: Day use only; Open all year; No camping.
name: Cathedral State Park

Description: The Gaudineer Scenic Area is a National Natural Landmark located in the Monongahela National Forest. Approximately 50 acres of the Scenic Area is typical of, and considered part of, the virgin red spruce type that originally occupied large portions of the highland areas of West Virginia. The composition of this impressive timber stand consists of virgin and second growth red spruce, yellow birch, beech, red maple, sugar maple, and other hardwood species. Individual trees range up to 40 inches in diameter at breast height and 300 years of age. The remaining 90 acres has had some cutting, mainly salvage of blow-down, with most of the original growth still standing. The total wood volume of the 140 acre tract is estimated at one and a half million board feet.
Navigation: Address: Forest Road 27, Durbin, WV 26264. Directions: The 140 acre Gaudineer Scenic Area is located near Gaudineer Knob of Shavers Mountain in Randolph and Pocahontas Counties in West Virginia. The area is located about 5.5 miles from Durbin, West Virginia. To reach the area, travel west from Durbin on U. S. Route 250 for 4 miles to Forest Service Road 27, then north on FR 27, 1.5 miles to the Scenic Area. The Scenic Area is in the headwaters of Glade Run and Old Road Run, tributaries of Shavers Fork of Cheat River, and West Fork of Greenbrier River, respectively.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Restrooms: One vault toilet. No admission charge.
Trails: 2 Trails, 0.5-mile each.
Hours And Camping: Day use only. Open year-round but Forest Road 27 is not plowed in the winter and snow can be deep at times. Camping nearby, but not right at this site.
name: Gaudineer Scenic Area - Monongahela National Forest

Description: Ferncliff Natural Area is a 100-acre peninsula in the 20,000-acre plus Ohiopyle State Park. Hemlock, tulip poplar, oak, and black birch are some the tree species, with the oldest about 200 years. The peninsula is created by a meander in the Youghiogheny River, which flows north into Pennsylvania from West Virginia and Maryland, carrying seeds from that region. The warmer microclimate inside the river gorge allows these plants to survive. It is a good example of a late successional forest in the Allegheny Mountains, and forever protected. Views of the river and the falls can be seen from the relatively easy trail. This is a very popular ecotourism area.
Navigation: Address: 124 Main Street, Ohiopyle, PA 15470
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Restrooms available at parking areas. No admission charge.
Trails: 2.8 miles for the Ferncliff Peninsula, altogether 79 acres of trail in this park.
Hours And Camping: Open during daylight hours; open all year. Camping area. The campground has about 200 campsites and is open from April to mid-December. The campground has 27 walk-in sites that require a short hike from the vehicle to the campsite. Kentuck Campground also has three sites with walled tents and three multi-tent sites. All campsites have a picnic table, fire ring and parking space, and the campground has a sanitary dumping station and shower houses. Many campsites have electric hookups. Pets are permitted at designated campsites for a fee. Advance reservations are required to ensure campsite availability.
Hunting: Bow hunting only on Ferncliff Peninsula, majority of park open to all Game Commission regulated seasons
name: Ferncliff Peninsula Natural Area - Ohiopyle State Park

Description: Nestled in the heart of Bowling Green, The Wintergarden/St. John's Nature Preserve is 103 acres and includes meadow, short grass prairie, tall grass prairie, old-growth forest, wetland, fields, and pioneer woods. The most dominant tree species are red and white oak and shagbark hickory. The oldest trees in the preserve are 250-300 years old. Some common plant species include cherry, witch hazel, spice bush. Spring wild flowers  include mayapple, wild geranium and Jack-in-the-pulpit. Some unique species in the park include trillium, wind flower, and sweet fern. The meadow is also home to a native population of prickly pear cactus.
Navigation: Address: 615 South Wintergarden Road, Bowling Green, Ohio 43402
Parking And Admission: Approximately 40 parking spots. No admission charge.
Trails: There are a little over 3.25 miles of trails in the preserve. For the most part they are mulch covered in the forest areas while the meadow has a grass/natural ground cover. A few stretches are a sandy composition and left as is to show that the area was part of a prehistoric lakeshore.
Hours And Camping: Park is open dawn until dusk. Open every day of the year. No camping or overnight stays are permitted in the park.
Hunting: Hunting and firearms are banned in the park
name: Wintergarden/St. John's Nature Preserve

Description: Ancient hemlock trees, 200-300 years old with diameters up to 3.5 feet, line the creek along this gentle trail. The scenery here is spectacular with moss carpeting small rocks and boulders, the creek running wide and clear, and virgin hemlocks providing the final magic touch. The Hemlock Natural Area at the center of the Hemlock Trail loop contains outstanding ancient hemlocks. Along the upper loop of the trail are impressive black cherry, yellow birch, beech, maples, and oaks.
Navigation: Directions: Take I-70 & 76 to Somerset or Donegal, PA. From Donegal follow PA 31 east and take a right on Trent Rd. From Somerset follow PA 31 west and take a left on Trent Rd. Once on Trent Rd take a right on Laurel Hill Park Rd. The parking lot is on the right just before you cross a bridge. Park in the lot and walk south over the bridge. The Hemlock Trail is on the right.
Parking And Admission: Parking for the trail is limited, but the picnic area across the road has more parking available. Restrooms available. No admission charge.
Trails: The Hemlock Trail is 1.2 miles.
Hours And Camping: Open dawn to dusk. Open all year. Camping area open April to October.
name: Hemlock Trail - Laurel Hill State Park

Description: This 2,800 acre park features a unique contrast of coast redwood groves and open grassland.  Shaded, fern-filled groves of coast redwoods (Sequoia sempervirens) are found along the canyon bottoms and up the north-facing slopes. Head up the Pioneer Tree trail, just past the gate at the Redwood Grove Picnic Area, for a lovely experience in a quiet forest. Other tree species found in the park are tanoak, madrone, live oak, laurel and Douglas fir. The striking elk clover displays immense leaves with huge cream-colored flowers in early summer. The most common animal in the park is the black-tailed deer. There are also raccoons, striped skunks and gray foxes. Coho salmon and steelhead trout migrate up Lagunitas Creek to spawn. This dedication was made in memory of Betty Setzer, who spent her childhood among California's old-growth redwoods.
Navigation: Address: 8889 Sir Francis Drake Blvd, Lagunitas, CA 94938. Directions: The park is 15 miles / 30 minutes west of San Rafael on Sir Francis Drake Boulevard
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Restrooms. $8 parking fee.
Trails: Pioneer tree trail is 3 miles.
Hours And Camping: Open 8am - sunset. Open all year. There is a popular camping area with services. Also group camping areas and a few rental cabins. Reservations are strongly suggested.
name: Samuel P. Taylor State Park

Description: Although almost all forests in the New River Gorge National River were logged in the past, there is one small eleven-acre patch spared the lumberman's axe at the end of the Stone Cliff Trail. There, you will find a forest consisting of chinquapin oaks, northern red oaks, bitternut hickories, and buckeyes that exhibit old-growth characteristics (large live and dead standing trees, abundant large trunks on the ground, and tip-up root mounds). These large overstory trees are two to three feet in diameter, and are estimated to be 100-200 years old, or greater. One more interesting characteristic of this old-growth forest is the soil, which is high in pH and more characteristic of the limestone country found in Greenbrier Valley to the east.
Navigation:
Directions: From US 19 north of Beckley, take the Glen Jean-Thurmond exit. Take an immediate left, and go 0.5 miles to Glen Jean. Take a right and follow the signs to Thurmond (WV25). Continue for 6.0 miles to a three-way intersection. Bear right and go 1.5 miles on this road. Take a right on the gravel road, just before the bridge crossing over the New River. Continue past the boat launch to the parking area. Park in the open gravel lot beyond the restrooms. Parking is shared between trail users, day use boaters and people staying in the Stone Cliff Campground. The trailhead is at the far (upstream) end of the parking lot.
The Stone Cliff Trail begins beside the picnic area.
Parking And Admission: Parking: Ample. Restrooms: A vault toilet is available at the Stone Cliff Trailhead and Campground. No admission charge.
Trails: The Stone Cliff Trail is a 2.7-mile out-and-back hike or bike ride (5.4 miles round-trip). The rugged trail follows an old road along the banks of the New River. It is fairly level and forested for its entire length. Great views and easy access to the river are available along the trail. The Stone Cliff Old Growth Area is located at the end of the Stone Cliff Trail at the sharp bend in the river. At present no other trails are connected to this one so you return by the same trail. The park has many other trails available.
Hours And Camping: Open 24 hours a day. Open all year. The Stone Cliff Campground, at the trailhead, has free campsites available on a first-come, first-served basis. Other camping opportunities are available throughout the park and the region.
name: Stone Cliff Old Growth - New River Gorge National River

Description: This 1,300-acre preserve contains one of the largest and oldest contiguous forests in Ohio with some of the best back country hiking trails in the state. The large block of contiguous forest is critical for signature deep forest birds such as cerulean and worm-eating warblers. There are many rare plants here and an impressive carpet of flowering spring ephemerals. This forest belongs to the central hardwood region of the Eastern Forest known as "mixed mesophytic," a forest type which extends from southern Ohio into the southern Appalachians and boasts the highest tree diversity in the temperate United States. Mixed mesophytic forests are known to have an impressive number of tree species, none of which particularly dominate over the others. Fort Hill shelters not only true mixed mesophytic forests, but oak hickory, beech maple, and riverine forests. Fort Hill also contains earthen and stone-walled structures built by the native Hopewell Culture around 2,000 years ago. The on-site museum at the park, open only on weekends, houses exhibits on the geology, natural history, and archaeology of the area.
Navigation: Address: 13614 Fort Hill Rd, Hillsboro, OH 45133. Directions: Located one mile west of State Road 41 between the small towns of Cynthiana and Sinking Springs.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking.
Trails: 11 miles of trails; with several options for combining shorter loops.
Hours And Camping: Open during daylight hours. Open year-round. No camping.
Hunting: Special hunts allowed for deer only between November and January.
name: Fort Hill State Memorial

Description: This forest is mature second-growth. The over 2,000-acre reserve contains sugar maple, beech, black cherry, tulip poplar, cucumber magnolia, hop-hornbeam, hemlock, many types of oaks, and more! Birds, chipmunks, snakes, and toads may entertain you on your visit. Bobcats, bears, and fishers live here too, although you are unlikely to see them. Scientists use many of the areas for research, but the Sugar Camp Trail and Porcupine Ridge trail are for education and enjoyment, and portions of these trails include trees in excess of 150 years old.
Navigation: Address: 1847 Route 381,Rector, PA 15677. Directions: Powdermill is 55 miles east of Pittsburgh, off the Donegal interchange of the Pennsylvania Turnpike. For information, call. From the North: At the intersection of Route 30 and Route 711 in Ligonier, PA, take route 711 south 3.3 miles to the Rector/Darlington intersection. There are signs there for Powdermill Nature Reserve and Linn Run State Park. Turn left toward Rector and go 1 mile. At the bottom of the hill, before going over the bridge, turn right on to Route 381 South. Follow Route 381 South for 3.3 miles to the Nature Reserve headquarters.From the PA Turnpike take Exit #91 for Donegal. After exiting the turnpike tollbooth, turn left onto Route 31 heading east. Follow Route 31 East for 2.7 miles. Turn left onto Route 381 North. Follow Route 381 North for 6.4 miles to the Nature Reserve headquarters
Parking And Admission: No admission charge.
Trails: Sugar Camp Trail is directly across from the visitor's center. 1.25 mi in length. This easy trail meanders through a mature, lovely, second-growth forest. From the far end of Sugar Camp Trail, Porcupine Ridge Trail branches off to the south with a spur of moderate difficulty, about 1.25 miles in length, that crosses Powdermill Run and climbs a ridge through the tallest forest on the reserve, crossing an experimental site, and terminating in a scenic overlook (in development). There is also a Black Birch Trail, which starts immediately behind the visitor's center and is a short and easy loop for all ages.
Hours And Camping: Open dawn to dusk. No camping.
name: Powdermill Nature Reserve

Description: Goll Woods is 321 acres with approximately 100 acres of native old-growth hardwoods. The rest of the preserve was once farmed and was replanted with trees in the 1960s. The old-growth area is the least disturbed woodland known to remain in extreme northwestern Ohio and the preserve features some of the largest trees remaining in the state. Goll Woods exemplifies the "Black Swamp" forest which once covered a vast area of the flat post-glacial lake plains southwest of Lake Erie. An outstanding feature of this forest is the abundance of giant bur oaks and exceptionally large white oaks, chinquapin oaks and cottonwoods. Many of these magnificent trees are 200-400 years old and measure 4 feet in diameter. The large ash trees have succumbed to the emerald ash borer. A rich variety of native shrubs and wildflowers occur in the woods including spotted coral-root and three-birds-orchid. The preserve is best visited in the spring before mosquitoes emerge.
Navigation: Address: This address will get you to the area (note-this is not the address of the forest but it will get you close): 5232 County Rd 26, Archibold OH. Directions: Located in Fulton County 1-1/2 miles north of Archbold, then 3 miles west on Township Rd F, and 1/4 mile south on Township Rd 26 to the parking lot. From Archbold in Fulton County, go north on State Rte 66 for 1-1/2 miles to Township Rd F, go west for 3 miles to the junction with Township Rd 26, go south about 1/4 mile to the preserve parking lot located on the east side of the road.
Parking And Admission: The main parking lot is on County Road 26 with 15 spaces. No admission charge.
Trails: Bur Oak Trail: 1 mile; Cottonwood Trail: 1.5 miles; Tuliptree Trail: 1.25 miles; Toadshade Trail: 1.5 miles
Hours And Camping: Open daylight hours, year-round. No camping.
Hunting: There is a seasonal controlled archery deer hunt.
name: Goll Woods State Nature Preserve

Description: Secor Metropark is at the north end of the Oak Openings Region. This region sustains a mosaic of natural communities, making it a place of high biodiversity. The forest in this park is approximately 75-150 years old and covers 159 acres. The tree species include tupelo, silver maple, sycamore, cottonwood, hickory, beech, as well as red, pin, and white oak. This protected natural area is home to a variety of wildlife, including deer, fox, coyotes, reptiles and amphibians, woodpeckers, both migrating and nesting songbirds, raptors, as well as grassland nesting birds. Spring wildflowers such as trillium, wild geranium, wild ginger, bloodroot, and jack-the-pulpit can easily be viewed along the trails in the rich woodlands. A focal point for visitors at Secor Metropark is the National Center for Nature Photography, where educational programs, interpretive displays and photography exhibits are offered.
Navigation: Address: 10001 W. Central Ave., Berkey, OH 43504
Parking And Admission: Ample parking lots are present in many places of the park. No admission charge.
Trails: 12.6 miles of trails.
Hours And Camping: Hours: 7 a.m. until sunset. Open all year. No Camping.
name: Secor Metropark

Description: This 50-acre park supports about 10 acres of forest including a small area considered to be "old-growth". The old-growth forest is dominated by white, red and black oak trees and supports sparse cover of shrub, wildflower, moss, lichen, and mushroom species. Large woody debris, characteristic of old-growth woods, provides habitat for small mammals and other wildlife. The most spectacular elements of the forest are the old red oaks (Quercus borealis var. maximus), some of which are over nine feet in circumference. These oaks tower above all the other trees, forcing the sugar maples, ash, and black cherry into their shade. The oldest tree at DeVeaux Woods State Park is around 315 years old.
Navigation: Address: 3180 DeVeaux Woods Drive, Niagara Falls, NY 14305.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking, no admission charge.
Trails: Just one small trail through the woods.
Hours And Camping: Open year-round, dawn to dusk. No camping.
name: DeVeaux Woods State Park

Description: The 292-acre Reinstein Woods includes several miles of gravel roads used primarily as trails, 19 ponds and wetlands created by a man-made system of dams, and approximately 76 acres of mature Beech-Maple forest that contains an unusually large percentage of black cherry trees. A highlight is the largest forest-grown beech tree in New York State, or "Champion Beech," which is more than 250 years old. Other important habitats include immature forests, conifer plantations, vernal pools, shrub swamp, and wet meadow.
Navigation: Address: 93 Honorine Drive,  Depew, NY 14043
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Nine miles east of downtown Buffalo. Visitors must sign in and sign out at a trailhead kiosk, but there is no admission charge.
Trails: Beech Tree Trail, 0.5 miles long.  3.5 miles of trails in total.
Hours And Camping: Trails open daily, sunrise to sunset. Visitor Center is open Monday through Friday 9 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. and Saturday 1 to 4:30 p.m. No camping.
name: Dr. Victor Reinstein Woods Nature Preserve

Description: Nassawango Creek, Cordrey Tract is part of the Nassawango Preserve which is owned by The Nature Conservancy. This very special forest contains some of the largest bald cypress, holly, and sassafras trees in the State of Maryland. A gentle trail takes one from the parking area to the remote Beaver Dam Creek, and then circles back to the start. Along the way one can appreciate the interesting shapes of the ancient native trees. Amphibians, birds, and fungi, add to the beautiful biodiversity of this forest.
Navigation: Address: 35500 Bear Swamp Rd, Salisbury, MD. Directions: From Snow Hill Road in Salisbury, heading east, turn left onto Johnson Road. Go approximately 10 miles on Johnson Road until it becomes a dirt road (just past Wango Road). Parking area will be on the left (how far?) down this road. Trail starts across the street at a blue post.
Parking And Admission: No admission charge.
Trails: 0.7-mi loop trail.
Hours And Camping: Open every day, year-round, dawn to dusk. No camping.
name: Cordrey Tract - Nassawango Creek Preserve

Description: Glencarlyn Park is in a highly urbanized area, yet it includes examples of mature-old age natural forests, unique water resources, and a great diversity of native flora. In addition to high native plant diversity, the park includes a number of Champion and Significant Tree specimens. The active floodplain and lower slopes are documented as Mesic Mixed Hardwood Forest, with Oak Hickory and Oak Heath forests occupying the drier slopes. The estimated age of the community is 100+ years. It is most likely the second oldest extant growth of natural forest remaining in Arlington, and appears to pre-date the large-scale forest removal associated with the Civil War (Note - the oldest forest remnant is most likely Arlington Woods within Arlington Cemetery). Invasive plant species are a concern, but there are management plans in place to deal with them.
Navigation: Address: 301 S Harrison St, Arlington, VA 22204
Parking And Admission: The closest parking is by the Glencarlyn picnic shelter at the end of the entrance road, and then hiking up the trail.  Restrooms available. No admission charge.
Trails: From the parking lot at the end of the entrance road, near the picnic shelter, begin following the paved Four Mile Run Trail which will eventually switchback around a ravine. Once the ravine is on your right, the old-growth forest will be off to your left on the hillside. This is about 0.3 miles (about an 8-minute walk from the parking area). To get a close up look at the old-growth trees, you will need to go off path a short distance. Alternatively, you can park near the corner of 2nd Street South and South Jefferson Street (a residential area) and enter the forest there. When you see the trail divide, keep to your left (of the ravine) and you will find the old-growth forest to your left on the hillside. The trail goes by the location of the forest.
