The old-growth is just off into the woods actually, not next to the trail itself.
Hours And Camping: Open sunrise to sunset. Open all year. No camping.
name: Glencarlyn Park

Description: The preserve consists of over 200 acres of virgin bottomland hardwood forest complemented by an additional 14 acres of secondary growth forest, field, and pond. The woods consist of sweetgum, sugar maple, tulip tree, shumard oak, and many more species. It is the largest tract of virgin forest located inside any city limits in the United States. The oldest trees are over 400 years old. Among the largest of their species are 3 state champions (Schneck Oak, Biltmore ash & Juneberry) and two county champion trees (Tulip Poplar & Chinquapin Oak). One of the tallest trees in Vanderburgh County is a tulip poplar located within the park. It is 166 feet tall with a 14.4 foot circumference.
Navigation: Address: 551 North Boeke Rd, Evansville, Indiana
Parking And Admission: $3.00 children up to 12 y.o; $5.00 for age 13 and above. Membership is available.
Trails: Over 6 miles of trails.
Hours And Camping: Tues - Saturday 9-5, Sunday 12-5, closed Monday.
name: Wesselman Woods Nature Preserve

Description: Tryon-Weber Woods is an 84-acre forested property owned by Western Pennsylvania Conservancy in Crawford County. Although there are no official trails within Tryon-Weber Woods, the small, rolling woodland can be traversed easily in an afternoon. The property is named for the late Dr. C. A. Tryon (University of Pittsburgh Pymatuning Laboratory of Ecology) who conducted several studies on the ecological interrelationships of the forest, and Dr. Robert G. Weber, who previously owned the property. A 40-acre stand of old-growth beech-maple forest is the highlight of this site.
Navigation: Address: 9935 Greiser Rd, Conneaut Lake, PA. This address will get you close to the area. Directions: From the Meadville I-79 exit head west on RT322.Take RT322 West through the town of Conneaut Lake to RT285W.Take RT285 West 1.8 miles and turn left onto Greiser Rd. (by an old barn). Continue approx. 0.7 miles to a right-of-way/dirt lane on the right (look for a white wooden fence). Park along the lane. Walk west approximately 200 yards to a sign indicating the start of the property. Turn left and follow an old logging road south about 0.25-mile. Keep a sharp eye out for a sudden left turn down into the shallow ravine on your left. Cross the creek and the Tryon-Weber Woods sign will be directly in front of you.
Parking And Admission: Limited parking for 2-3 vehicles along a dirt lane off Greiser Rd.  The parking area is unmaintained. No admission charge.
Trails: There are no designated trails within Tryon-Weber Woods, but the small, rolling woodland can be traversed easily in an afternoon.
Hours And Camping: Tryon-Weber Woods is open year-round.  There are no designated hours.  Camping is not permitted.
Hunting: Hunting is permitted according to PA Game Commission regulations.
name: Tryon-Weber Woods

Description: Hearts Content is a hemlock-white pine-northern hardwood forest type. The old-growth forest is over 122 acres in extent, but the scenic area is most famous for its 20 acres of tall white pine and Eastern hemlock. Many of these trees have diameters of over 40 inches and heights of over 140 feet, and most of the white pine are between 300 and 400 years old. American beech is also plentiful in the forest, but is affected by Beech bark scale. Hay-scented fern covers much of the understory due to overbrowsing by deer. There is a gentle interpretive trail and a nearby picnic area.
Navigation: Address: State Route 2002, Tidioute, PA. Directions: Hearts Content Recreation Area is located 15 miles southwest of Warren, PA. From the Mohawk exit of U.S. Route 6, take Pleasant Drive south for 11 miles. At the hard curve, turn left onto a gravel road; go south for four miles to Hearts Content. The Hearts Content Recreation Area is split by State Route 2002, with the campground on the south side of the road and the scenic area on the north side.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking at the trailhead.
Trails: 1.3 mi Interpretive Old Growth Trail starts at the north end of the east side parking lot and winds about 1 mile through this timber stand before returning to the picnic area. All facilities in the day use area are universally accessible to people with disabilities. Facilities include a picnic area, pavilions, toilet, and interpretive materials.
Hours And Camping: Open April - October during daylight hours. No camping is allowed in the Scenic Area, but the campground across the road is open May 1st to Oct. 20th; Camping Fees: $12.00 per night, $14.00 for a site with shelter and $50.00 for the group site. Campsites are available on a first-come, first served basis only, no reservations.
Hunting: Hunting is allowed outside the recreation area
name: Hearts Content National Scenic Area - Allegheny National Forest

Description: Blanton Forest is a 3,510-acre preserve; approximately 2,000 acres are old-growth, making it the largest such forest remaining in Kentucky. An additional 2,000 acres of forest buffer land is owned and managed by Kentucky Natural Lands Trust. The oldest known tree in the preserve is 338 year old chestnut oak (known from research conducted by Neil Pederson, formerly with Eastern Kentucky University). Blanton Forest has a diverse forest canopy comprising many tree species such as sugar maple, tulip poplar, various oaks, hemlocks, beech and several magnolias. The preserve has several unique natural communities including mountaintop wetlands known as acid seeps and mixed-mesophytic deciduous forest.
Navigation: Address: 4294 State Hwy 840, Wallins Creek, KY 40873. Directions: Harlan County, approximately five miles west of the city of Harlan. From Interstate 75, take exit 29 onto U.S. Hwy 25E at Corbin. Travel south on U.S. 25E to Pineville. Turn left on U.S. Hwy 119 (crossing the Cumberland River) and travel north for 23.5 miles. Turn left on KY 840 at a sign for Camp Blanton. Follow KY 840 for approximately two miles; the parking area for the preserve is adjacent to Camp Blanton.
Parking And Admission: Parking available in lot adjacent to Camp Blanton, 4294 State Hwy 840, Wallins Creek, KY 40873.
Trails: A trail system approximately 4.5 miles in length is open for public use. The main trail consists of two loops leading to points of interest on the south face of Pine Mountain. The first loop is a moderately strenuous trail leading to a large sandstone rock outcrop known as Knobby Rock.From Knobby Rock, visitors gain a spectacular bird's-eye view of the surrounding forest. The more strenuous loop to Sand Cave and the Maze takes visitors higher into the Watts Creek and Big Branch watersheds. Depending on the time of year, visitors can expect to see a wide range of wildlife and plant species within the largest old-growth forest in the Commonwealth. In addition, a shorter half-mile trail leading along Watts Creek offers a scenic but less strenuous alternative route to enjoy the preserve. Designated parking is available in a lot adjacent to Camp Blanton, a private facility. A kiosk and signs direct visitors to the trailhead. The preserve is open year round during daylight hours and is limited to foot travel only.
Hours And Camping: Preserves are open sunrise to sunset.  No camping in the preserve.
Hunting: Collecting, hunting and trapping are prohibited.
name: Blanton Forest State Nature Preserve

Description: The Forest is a protected area high in the White Mountains in Inyo County in eastern California. The Great Basin bristlecone pine (Pinus longaeva) trees grow between 9,800 and 11,000 feet above sea level, in xeric alpine conditions, protected within the Inyo National Forest. The Methuselah Grove in the Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest is the location of the "Methuselah", a Great Basin Bristlecone Pine that is 4,847 years old. For many years, it was the world's oldest known living non-clonal organism, until superseded by the discovery in 2013 of another bristlecone pine in the same area with an age of 5,065 years (germination in 3051 BC). "Methuselah" is not marked in the forest, to ensure added protection from vandals. These trees are all very individualistic, and many are fascinating and beautiful.
Navigation: Address: this will get you within 23 miles: 310 N Main St, Big Pine, CA 93514. Directions: From Big Pine, travel east on Highway 168 for 13 miles. Turn left at the signed junction for White Mountain Road to the Bristlecone Pine Forest and continue 10 miles until the end of the paved road at Schulman Grove. Turn right into the visitor center parking lot.
Parking And Admission: Parking: ample.  Admission: Day Use fee is $3.00 per person to a maximum of $6.00 per car. Children under 18 free,America the Beautiful and Golden Age passes are accepted.
Trails: The Schulman Grove Visitor Center is a good place to get oriented. From there the Discovery Trail is approximately 1 mile and features interpretive signs and rest benches along the trail. Also leaving from the visitor center is the Methuselah Trail, a 4.5-mile loop with some narrow sections. There are numbered posts along the trail and a brochure is available at the start of the trail. If you have a vehicle that will handle 12 miles each way of bumpy gravel road, a visit to the Patriarch Grove is highly recommended. The formal trail there is under a mile, but the high altitudes make for amazing trees and amazing views.
Hours And Camping: Hours: Open on weekends starting in May, then 7 days a week starting in June. Call ahead 760-873-2525 to be sure the road is open.  Camping: Campfires and overnight camping not allowed. But five miles from the grove is the Forest Service Grandview Campground. No reservations accepted. First come. No water on site.
name: Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest - Inyo National Forest

Description: Brigadoon State Nature Preserve is located in Barren County adjacent to the Barren River Reservoir.  With assistance from The Nature Conservancy, 92 acres of mostly mature forest was dedicated into the preserve system on March 14, 1985.  Another 88 acres were dedicated on June 12, 2001.  Today a total of 184 acres are protected.  The rich woodlands contain an impressive array of spring wildflowers, including several species that are considered rare or uncommon.   The preserve also provides a habitat for many resident and migratory birds.  Brigadoon features mature beech, maple and tulip poplar forest.  Owned by the Renfro family from late 1700s until 1960, then owned by one family until acquired as a nature preserve.  The forest has never been commercially logged, only some timber cut for family usage.
Navigation: Directions: From exit 43 on I-65, travel east on the Cumberland Parkway to its junction with US 31E in Glasgow.  Follow US 31E south for 6.5 miles.  Turn left onto Browning School Road and travel approximately 1.5 miles.  Turn left onto Mutter Road.  The parking area is 0.5 mile on the left.
Parking And Admission: Parking area off of Mutter Road provides parking for 5-6 cars.
Trails: A 1-mile hiking trail is open to the public at Brigadoon State Nature Preserve.  The trail is of moderate difficulty and runs through ridge tops, mature forest and scenic ravines.
Hours And Camping: The preserve is open to foot traffic from sunrise to sunset. Camping is not allowed.
name: Brigadoon State Nature Preserve

Description: Vernon-Douglas State Nature Preserve is located within a rugged, steep, forested section of Hardin County. This 730-acre preserve protects one of the most mature second-growth forests in the Knobs physiographic region. Hall Hollow, a north-facing valley in the preserve, supports a rich array of spring wildflowers. A trail system passes through the valley bottom to the dry ridges above Hall Hollow. A spur trail takes hikers onto a narrow point locally known as "the pinnacle," which provides a bird's-eye view of the Younger Creek valley. The forest features mature stands of sugar maple, beech and tulip poplar. Owned by one family from the early 1900s until the 1970s, when it became an Audubon Sanctuary, it is now protected in perpetuity as a state nature preserve.
Navigation: Directions: Hardin County, 9 miles east of Elizabethtown on the Bluegrass Pkwy.  From Elizabethtown, take exit 8, turn right on KY 583 and take an immediate right on Audubon Trace Rd.  From Lexington, take exit 10, turn right on KY 52 and travel 2 miles.  Turn left on US 62 and travel 2.75 miles.  Turn left on KY 583 and travel 2 miles.  Turn right on Audubon Trace Rd.  The preserve parking area is approximately 0.5 mile on the left.
Parking And Admission: Parking lot located off of Audubon Trace Road.  No admission charge,  open sunrise to sunset, 365 days.
Trails: 4.5 miles of trail over uneven terrain, moderate to strenuous. Hiking, nature study, and photography are encouraged but please stay on the trail and leave all living and non-living materials as you find them. Horseback riding and bicycles are prohibited. Help us protect Kentucky's natural heritage by packing out all trash and traveling only by foot.
Hours And Camping: The preserve is open for passive recreation from sunrise to sunset 365 days a year.  Camping is not allowed.
name: Vernon-Douglas State Nature Preserve

Description: Camp Oty'Okwa Old-Growth Forest is a 200-acre forest found within the 737 acres of land owned by Big Brothers Big Sisters of Central Ohio. The forest consists primarily of older growth (80+ years) oak/hickory forst on the ridge tops and mixed mesophytic forest (20-30 different tree species) on the lower slopes and stream valley. Eastern hemlock trees are scattered along the valley sides adding to the overall tree diversity. This forest surrounds an outstanding geologic feature called Split Rocks. Here, perhaps as the result of a past earthquake, the massive Black Hand Sandstone has split into numberous large vertical slabs creating a maze-like feature on the interior. An old guardian chestnut oak growing within the maze is perhaps 200 years old.
Navigation: Address: 24799 Purcell Road, South Bloomingville, Ohio 43152 Directions: Drive approximately 0.25 mile to trailhead on right after turning onto Purcell Road from State Route 374. Directions also: http: //campotyokwa.org/how-do-we-get-there/.
Parking And Admission: Park along Purcell Road in the designated parking area across from the trailhead. Additional parking is available if needed, 100 yards east of trailhead.  No admission charge.
Trails: The trail is no more than 1.5 miles in length.
Hours And Camping: year-round; open daylight hours only.  No camping.
name: Camp Oty'Okwa Old-Growth Forest

Description: Hammon Woods, which is owned by North Central Ohio Land Conservancy, Inc., consists of 172 acres of contiguous forest - 90 acres of which is old-growth. Large old-growth native Ohio hardwoods dominate Hammon Woods with very little infringement from invasive species.  Of the very large old trees, the dominant tree species are White Oak, Sugar Maple, Red Oak, Tulip and Beech.  Healthy spring-fed streams that support at least three species of salamander flow through the forest.  One stream ends in a skunk cabbage marsh with marsh marigold, swamp saxifrage and Pennsylvania bitter-cress.  The woods feature an array of spring ephemerals and several orchids. The age of the oldest trees is about 200 years.  Hammon Woods has rolling hills and the forest type varies based on whether the hills are predominately south or north facing.  The forest types tend to be either a beech-maple climax forest or a white oak forest. This special forest lies in the heart of the Clear Fork Valley Scenic Trail and is thereby connected to 600 acres of nature preserves.   The old-growth forest begins less than half a mile from the public parking area at the Clear Fork Adventure Resort.
Navigation: Address: The Clear Fork Adventure Resort, 342 Resort Drive, Butler, OH, 44822 Directions: Trailhead is next to the parking lot at resort.
Parking And Admission: Parking at Clear Fork Adventure Resort. No admission charge.
Trails: The Clear Fork Valley Scenic Trail has 8 miles of a trail that strings together about 600 acres of nature preserves.  Within that area, old-growth forest is found on 172 contiguous acres along the heart of the trail.  Exposure to old-growth trees begins less than half a mile from the public parking area of the resort.
Hours And Camping: Open year-round except it is closed for a few days each year for deer hunting season.  Trail closings for hunting are conspicuously noted with signage at the trail heads during the time of closure.  Camping is available at The Clear Fork Adventure Resort.
name: Hammon Woods

Description: Flint Ridge is one of the finest remaining examples in Licking County of a mature beech-maple-oak hardwood forest community. It is unclear how old the forest truly is, but historical aerials dating back to the 1940s indicate an intact forest community. Many of the trees in the preserve are over 100 years old. Flint Ridge is approximately 533 acres in size. For more than 14,000 years, American Indian cultures quarried the flint and made it into a variety of  weapons, tools, and other objects.  Over a thousand prehistoric quarry pits are scattered along the ridge. It is believed by many archaeologists that the Hopewell culture traded the highly prized flint for materials from other parts of North America. Today, the forest supports a diverse array of plant and animals species, many of which are considered sensitive and uncommon or rare for the region.
Navigation: Address: 15300 Flint Ridge Rd., Glenford, OH 43739. Directions: From I-70 to Gratiot/State Route 668 exit #141. Go north. When SR 668 meets US 40 in Brownsville, it will jog, i.e., you will turn left on US 40 and then an immediate right on 668 (aka Brownsville Rd.). The park is at the corner of SR 668/Brownsville Rd. and Flint Ridge Rd. From the north out of Newark, take SR. 16 to Brownsville Rd SE. and go south.
Parking And Admission: Park open Mon-Sun: All daylight hours (no fee for hiking trails); Museum: First weekend in May - second weekend in October, Fri-Sun: 10am-4pm.  Admission for Museum: Adult: $3, AAA & Seniors: $2, Student: $1, Ohio History Connection Member: Free, Active Military: Free, Children under 6: Free.
Trails: Quarry Trail: 0.7 mile loop. Creek Trail: 1.0 mile loop. Wheelchair accessible trail: 0.25 mile. Bear Hollow Trail: 1.2 mile loop.
Hours And Camping: Park open year-round dawn to dusk (no fee for hiking trails). No camping available.
name: Flint Ridge Ancient Quarries & Nature Preserve

Description: Crall Woods is a 146-acre forest that is half of Ashland County Park District's Pinehill Park that was acquired in 2005 through the generosity of Two Families. Crall Woods itself is comprised of 50 acres of forest and young woods from the Sauers Family, and the rest is 97 acres of forest from the Crall Family that holds that wondrous 44 acres that are deemed old growth forest. Those 44 acres were part of a much larger farm settled and owned for several generations by the Sutherland Family. Tradition has it that for unknown reasons those 44 acres were treated as someplace special: an untouchable forest where they did not permit grazing or logging. The Crall Family continued this tradition for four generations from the time they purchased the land in 1924 until it became part of the park in 2005. What, if any, logging ever occurred in those 44 acres we will never know, but there were no stumps visible to the Cralls in 1924, and a fallen tulip tree with over 325 rings was counted 3 years ago. Both of those facts speak of a forest untouched for a very long time. The incredibly profuse wildflowers also tend to confirm the story that no grazing ever occurred there. An Ohio State University wildflower study declared it "the best wildflower site in Ohio." Located in the beech-maple forest region, Sugar maple is currently the most dominant species both in the overstory and understory. Other canopy species include yellow poplar, American basswood, and Northern red oak. Sharp differences in species composition between upper canopy (with many shade-intolerant species, like oaks, poplar, and basswood) and lower canopy (maple) indicates that the forest at Crall Wood may be in a transition stage. Geologically, this area was covered by the Wisconson ice sheet about 12,000 years ago. In 1964, John Aughanbaugh conducted a detailed inventory of Crall Woods, and described the old-growth as "...ranking among the best of Ohio's known original forest remnants." He called the entire stand a "naturalist's paradise" and believed that Crall Woods could provide extensive scientific knowledge in forestry, natural history, wildlife, and ecology. In 1974, the National Park Service designated Crall Woods as a National Natural Landmark.
Navigation: Address: 263 Township Road 1601, Greenwich, OH. Directions to trailhead: The entrance to the parking area is less than 500 ft. south (on the left) after turning off of US 224 onto Twp. Rd. 1601. There is an ample parking lot at Crall Woods and the trail head is but a short distance from the parking lot.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. No admission charge.
Trails: Trail is 2 miles long.
Hours And Camping: Open year-round. Open dawn to dusk. No camping.
name: Crall Woods at Pine Hill Park

Description: Established in 1832 as Hot Springs Reservation, the land now known as Hot Springs National Park is under federal jurisdiction to preserve the thermal waters of the hot springs and the associated lands. After the creation of the National Park Service in 1916, the reservation was re-named Hot Springs National Park in 1921. While the boundaries of the park have changed over time, portions of the park have remained protected for more than 175 years. The upland forest communities in those areas remain today as old-growth forest stands, and they are unique for their proximity to the bustling downtown area of the City of Hot Springs. Several trees within two old-growth forest stands of oak/hickory/pine forest within the national park were core-dated in 1983 by the Tree-Ring Laboratory, a facility of the Department of Geosciences at the University of Arkansas. Analysis of the resulting dendrochronology graphs shows that the trees are now approximately 300 years old. These old growth forest stands cover approximately 220 acres and are considered significant old-growth trees for this area and the state. The Arkansas Famous and Historic Tree Program has recognized these old-growth forest stands as Tree Community #37.
Navigation: Address: The Fordyce Bathhouse, the park's visitor center, is located at 369 Central Avenue, Hot Springs, AR 71901. Hiking trail maps are available at the visitor center, as well as on the park's webpage. The Dogwood Trails (Upper and Lower Loops) are accessible from several locations (please see hiking trail maps), and portions of both Dogwood Trails and the Goat Rock Trail (accessible from North Mountain Loop Road) travel through old growth forest on Hot Springs and North Mountains. The old growth forest area on Sugarloaf Mountain is accessed via the Sunset Trail traveling west from the Cedar Glades Road trailhead (please see hiking trail maps).
Parking And Admission: Limited parking  available at the listed trailheads, except for the Lower Dogwood, which has no public parking immediately adjacent to the trailhead. The City of Hot Springs hosts a free public parking garage on Exchange Street, which is 0.15 miles from the Fordyce Bathhouse Visitor Center. No admission charge.
Trails: The Sunset Trail section from Cedar Glades Road to Blacksnake Road is 2.8 miles one way. The Lower Dogwood Loop is 0.7 miles and the Upper Dogwood Loop is 1.0 miles. The Goat Rock Trail is 1.1 miles one way. There are more than 26 miles of trails in the park.
Hours And Camping: Hours: The Fordyce Bathhouse Visitor Center is open daily 9-5 except on Thanksgiving Day, December 25, and January 1; Trails are open sunrise to sunset.  Some roads close at sunset.  Camping:  The Hot Springs National Park campground is located at Gulpha Gorge on AR Hwy 7 Spur (also known as Gorge Road). The campground is open year-round and has 40 sites, each with a picnic table and pedestal grill or fire pit. All campsites have electrical, water, and sewer hookups. Potable water and a dump station are available within the campground. There are flush toilets for campers, but no shower facilities. The park does not take reservations for campsites and fees are collected through a self-registration system at the check-in on a first come, first served basis. Please call the Visitor Center for current rates and additional information.
Hunting: Hunting is not allowed in Hot Springs National Park.
name: Dogwood, Goat Rock, and Sunset Trails - Hot Springs National Park

Description: Many fragments remain of the original forest that covered what is now Dekalb County in metropolitan Atlanta. Some of these forest are formally protected from commercial logging and some are community forests. They are linked by their historical relationship to the "Original Forest of Atlanta," a group of forests that occurs in both DeKalb County and Fulton County, GA. OGFN Network Forests: Dekalb County forests formally protected from commercial logging include Briarlake Forest, Fernbank Forest, Osborne Park, Hidden Acres Nature Preserve, Lullwater Conservation Garden, and Deepdene Park. OGFN Community Forests: Daniel Johnson Nature Preserve and Herbert Taylor Park.
name: Original Forest Of Atlanta - Dekalb County: 1. Briarlake Forest 2. Fernbank Forest 3. Osborne Park 4. Frazer Forest 5. Hidden Acres Nature Preserve. Community Forests: 1. Daniel Johnson Nature Preserve 2. Herbert Taylor Park

Description: Crow's Nest is, simply, a beautiful place and considered highly significant from numerous standpoints. Topography is varied, with the high narrow ridgeline rising 200 feet above two tidally influenced creeks: Potomac and Accokeek. The peninsula is deeply dissected by a series of ravines. Crow's Nest Natural Area Preserve supports 2,200 acres of mature hardwood forest including two forest types that are recognized as globally rare by DCR's Natural Heritage Program. At the southern edge is the Coastal Plain Dry Calcareous Forest, featuring chinquapin oak (Quercus muehlenbergii) with common associates such as chestnut oak (Quercus montana), northern red oak (Quercus rubra), tulip-tree (Liriodendron tulipifera), American beech (Fagus grandifolia), and white ash (Fraxinus americana). In the tidal wetlands the Fresh Tidal Hardwood Swamp is characterized by green ash (Fraxinus pennsylvanica), and red maple (Acer rubum), with occasional additional canopy and subcanopy associates. Crow's Nest supports habitat for about 60 species of neotropical migratory songbirds, nearly 60 percent of which are experiencing population declines, including ten species that are high global priority species of Partners In Flight. There are also nesting bald eagles and great blue herons. These lands and waters that have played important roles in the Native American, Colonial and Civil War histories of Virginia.
Navigation: Address: 81 Raven Road and 2500 Brooke Road. Directions: From I-95, take the Stafford Exit (exit 140). Take Route 630 (Courthouse Road) one mile east to Stafford (intersection of 630 and U.S. 1).  Cross U.S. 1 and continue east on Route 630 for about 2.5 miles. Turn right onto Route 629 (Andrew Chapel Road) and continue for 0.9 mile. Go under railroad overpass at the community of Brooke and turn left onto Route 608 (Brooke Road) and continue for 1.4 miles. Turn right onto gravel Route 609 (Raven Road), cross the bridge over Accokeek Creek, and continue for 0.2 mile. The gate into Crow's Nest Natural Area Preserve will be on the left. To reach the Brooke Road parking lot, continue on Brooke Road for an additional 1.5 miles.  The parking lot will be on the right.
Parking And Admission: A 20-space parking area is open at 2500 Brooke Road, Stafford, VA 22554 that provides access to a half-mile long walking trail along the north shore of Accokeek Creek with two viewpoints of the tidal marsh. This location also provides access to an ADA-accessible launch facility for canoes and kayaks, allowing visitors to experience the Crow's Nest Water Trail.  The second parking lot (18 spaces), accessible from 81 Raven Road, provides access to approximately 8 miles of hiking trails. Parking can be limited on nice days. No admission charge.
Trails: Total trail network is approximately 8.5 miles.  The Accokeek Loop Trail passes through the most diverse forest and is approximately 3 miles in length.
Hours And Camping: Hours: Current hours for the Brooke Road access point are from 8:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. from early November to mid-March and from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. from mid-March to early November.   The Raven Road access point is currently open Thursday-Sunday. No camping.
Hunting: Waterfowl hunts one day a week by lottery; and possible managed deer hunts.
name: Crow's Nest Natural Area Preserve

Description: There are more than 1,000 acres of forest interior in this park. Here is a true sanctuary for many species of birds and rare plants, as well as for humans who wish to reconnect with nature. The park's forest types include oak-hickory terraces, steep ravines, bottomland woods, and a rare shell-marl forest which is rich in calcium-loving plants reminiscent of mountain habitats. Many of the trees in this forest are ancient and, although parts of it were selectively logged before it became parkland, it has the look and the structure of an old-growth forest. Some of the trees are of champion size.
Navigation: Address: 3452 Ferry Place, Indian Head, MD 20640
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Restrooms near the Mt. Aventine Mansion. No admission charge.
Trails: Chapman Wildlands contains several easy trails. Potomac River Trail - This hiking trail doubles as a service road that joins the original Chapman's Landing Road to the Potomac River. The 0.6-mile trail roughly marks the boundary between a dry sandy woodland (to the northeast), and a moister, richer forest (to the southwest). Marsh Trail - This marked trail branches off of the Potomac River Trail, and meanders through a fertile bottomland woods that contrasts the sandier woodland along the Potomac shoreline. The 0.7-mile trail leads to an unusual "scrub-shrub" marsh which is separated from the Potomac River by a narrow spit. Coastal Woodlands Trail - This clearly marked, 1-mile trail joins the Potomac River Trail to make a 1.5-mile loop. The trail runs through various habitats, including a terrace gravel forest and a coastal oak forest, to eventually run along the Potomac shoreline.
Hours And Camping: Open sunrise to sunset. Open all year. No camping.
Hunting: Hunting is allowed in designated areas.
name: Chapman Forest Wildlands - Chapman State Park

Description: Ferncliff Wildflower and Wildlife Preserve has been recognized as a National Natural Landmark because of the old-growth forest that has been maintained here. There are wildflowers galore in spring. This preserve's hillsides offer some of the best examples of River Hills woodland, including tulip trees, beeches, hemlocks, sweet birches, red, chesnut, and white oak, sycamore, sugar and red maple, ironwood, and redbud. In the fall many groves of pawpaw yield succulent, edible fruit. You will also see rhododendron and mountain laurel in abundance.
Navigation: Address: Wildlife Preserve Rd, Drumore, PA 17518. Directions: From Lancaster, follow PA 272 south through Willow Street to the Buck. Continue three miles, then turn right on Chestnut Level Road at Valley View Restaurant. Continue on Chestnut Level Road to River Road.  Left on River Road, first right on Slate Hill Road, right on Harmony Ridge Road, across Furniss Road, to left on Bald Eagle Road. This road leads down a hill; Ferncliff Preserve is at the bottom of the hill on the right. There is a dirt road from Bald Eagle Road to the river (Wildlife Preserve Rd) which permits easy access for hikers. The locked gate at the entrance prevents vehicular traffic.
Parking And Admission: Limited parking. No admission charge.
Trails: 1.4 miles round trip, easy.
Hours And Camping: Open year-round. No camping.
name: Ferncliff Wildflower & Wildlife Preserve

Description: North Bend State Park comprises 2,500 acres.  Within the state park is the Giant Tree Trail/Hollow forest which is about 25 acres in size.  Fifteen of those acres exhibit all the characteristics of an old-growth forest. Four tree species reach height records for West Virginia in the stand. West Virginia's champion white pine is located here.
Navigation: Address: 202 North Bend Park Road, Cairo, WV 26337. Directions: Giant Tree Trail: From the park office and lodge head down hill and bear right at the first two intersections. At the third intersection turn left. Usually this road is gated but it is possible for several cars to park without blocking the road. Walk about 50 yards beyond gate. The trailhead for the Giant Tree Trail is on the left. Nature Trail: Instead of turning left at third intersection continue downhill on road and as you approach the bottom keep a sharp lookout for a trail intersecting the road to left. If you come to the campground road on right and bridge over the river you have gone 100 yards too far.
Parking And Admission: Several larger parking areas are available within a short walk. The biggest is at the lodge. No admission charge.
Trails: Giant Tree Trail (0.5 mile) traverses the top of the hollow. This is not a loop trail. Nature Trail: The entire Nature trail is a 4.2-mile loop trail. A 1-mile section with intermediate access follows the North Fork of the Hughes River and is adjacent to the old growth on the steep slopes above the river and the mouth of the Big Tree Trail hollow. This section is not a loop trail.There are a total of 26 miles of trails in the park plus an access trail to the 72-mile North Bend Rail Trail. A good source for trail information is the West Virginia Trail Inventory page at: http://www.mapwv.gov/trails/. Trail maps are available at the park office.
Hours And Camping: Open year-round. 77 sites available for camping with 50 of them with water/electric available for trailers.
name: Giant Tree Trail/Hollow - North Bend State Park

Description: A tributary of Rock Run stream flows between the Ann Bailey Trail and the Burnside Ridge Trail. In this wilderness area there are 500-1,000 acres of mixed hardwoods. Many oaks in 300-350 year-old range have been found. Ancient trees of many species have been found: white oak, red oak, chestnut oak, black oak, yellow poplar, black gum, pitch pine, white pine, mockernut hickory, black birch, and cucumber tree. Tree size, crown structure, and bark texture all indicate ancient forest. The amount of old-growth is still undetermined. There are clear signs of animal use by black bears, bobcats, deer, turkeys, and owls.
Navigation: Address: Watoga State Park, 4800 Watoga Park Road, Marlinton, WV 24954. Directions: You can reach the park from Seebert, WV on the west side (2 miles from Rt 219) or from Hunterville on the east side (Rt 39). Stop by the Administration building for maps. In the warm months one can drive up to the Ann Bailey Trailhead where there is ample parking.
Parking And Admission: Parking at Ann Bailey trailhead. Ample parking. No admission charge.
Trails: There are 40 miles of trail in this park, but there are no trails directly through the old-growth forest. To get the closest to the old growth, take the Ann Bailey trail. After a 1-mile hike (approx.) on a wide trail through a second-growth forest, you will reach the intersection with Burnside Ridge Trail. The old-growth forest runs along the stream south-west between these two trails. Should you choose to explore off-trail, please use extreme caution in this delicate ecosystem.
Hours And Camping: Full service campground available April - October, 88 sites. Over 30 cabins for rent. Also a lodge and dining room. Lodge and some cabins open year-round. Road to the trailhead closed in winter.
name: Wilderness Area - Watoga State Park

Description: Albright Grove is an excellent example of an old-growth cove hardwood forest. The grove contains some of the oldest and tallest trees in the park. Unfortunately it is almost a three mile hike to get to it. Long, but so worth it! Follow the Maddon Bald trail uphill on a gravel road that goes through a second-growth forest. Follow until you reach the 0.7 mi Albright Grove Loop. Huge eastern hemlock and tulip poplars dominate this protected grove. Hikers will also find buckeye, yellow birch, fraser magnolias, silverbells, basswood, beeches and sugar maples.
Navigation: Directions: Cosby TN: At the junction of 441 and 321 in Gatlinburg (Light 3), head north (east) onto 321/73. Drive 15.4 miles and turn right onto Baxter Road and look for a sign for the Maddron Bald Trailhead on the right. After taking a hard right turn, drive roughly 100 feet down to the trailhead where there is room for a handful of vehicles. The Albright Grove Loop Trail is accessed from the Maddron Bald Trailhead.
Parking And Admission: Parking at the trailhead is limited to a few vehicles. Overnight hikers may choose to park in a more secure location at a nearby business. No admission charge.
Trails: Roundtrip 6.7 mi. The Albright Grove Loop Trail junction is located roughly 2.9 miles from the trailhead. This is where the best old-growth is.
Hours And Camping: Open year-round. More than 100 campsites are available at Cosby Campground on a first-come, first-served basis and 26 campsites are available for advanced reservations. All campsites accommodate tents and, even when all reservation sites are booked, tent campers are likely to find a great site. Back country camping requires a reservation and a permit. Call (865) 436-1297.
name: Albright Grove - Great Smoky Mountains National Park

Description: The entire preserve is 930 acres. The Boyd Tract, which contains the old-growth section, is 165 acres, and about 100 acres of which is old-growth forest. Many of the trees on this property are suspected to be over 400 years old with the oldest estimated currently at 470 years. An increment borer was used to date this particular tree back to 1548. This work was done by a graduate student from UNC Greensboro, and the tree was designated at that time as the oldest known living longleaf pine tree.  There is a well-marked trail that passes by the Old Tree.
Navigation: Address: Weymouth Woods Visitor Center, 1024 Ft. Bragg Road, Southern Pines, NC 28387. Directions: Access to the Boyd Tract is approximately a 4-mile drive from this address. From the park entrance, head east on Fort Bragg Rd for 2 miles. Turn left on E. Connecticut Ave and continue for another 2 miles. Take a right on Den Rd, a private dirt road and continue for a quarter of a mile. On the left side you will see a grassy area and an information kiosk that you can park near to access the trails of the Boyd Tract.
Parking And Admission: There is limited parking space, and only in a grassy area to the side of the road. There is no paved parking lot. No admission charge.
Trails: There are at least 7 miles of marked hiking trails divided among the three tracts of land at Weymouth Woods. The Boyd Tract, where the old-growth forest is located, has 1 mile of marked hiking trail with several more miles of unmarked equestrian trails and service roads that are open for foot traffic as well. The recommended trail at the Boyd Tract is a 1-mile loop called the Round Timber Trail that goes through old-growth open longleaf pine forest, mixed hardwood forest, and an open meadow.
Hours And Camping: The park is open November - February: 8am - 6pm; March - October: 8am - 8pm. All park facilities are closed Christmas Day.  Office hours are 8am - 5pm every day but Christmas Day. There are no overnight facilities and camping is prohibited.
name: Boyd Tract - Weymouth Woods Sandhills Nature Preserve

Description: The highlights of Cathedral Pines natural area are the stands of old-growth conifers dominated by hemlock, along with super-canopy red and white pines. They are found in the area of the Cathedral Pines hiking trail. The oldest known white pine in the area is 368 years old. Many of the white pines are over 9 ft in circumference. The tallest white pines in the state are located here. An active Great Blue Heron rookery is sometimes located in the red and white pines traversed by the hiking trail. Visitors should be careful not to disturb the birds. In the early 1900s, Lucy Rumsey Holt brought her children here - the pines and hemlocks seemed to her a sacred place. She named it Cathedral Woods and persuaded her husband, the president of Holt Lumber Company, to preserve it. Because of her, this stand of virgin timber was never logged. Her descendants have been active in the continued protection of the stand. There is evidence that the Menominee people used this area a thousand years previously.
Navigation: Directions: From the junction of State Highway 32 and County Highway F in Lakewood, go north on Hwy 32  for 1.0 mile to Archibald Lake Road (FR 2121); then south 1.5 miles to Cathedral Lane; then north 0.3 mile to the Cathedral Pines parking area.
Parking And Admission: The parking area holds 5 cars. No admission charge.
Trails: The Cathedral Pines hiking trail is a 0.3-mile loop, and there are other trails in the area.
Hours And Camping: Hours: open year-round, 24 hours.  Closest camping: Boot Lake Campground.
name: Cathedral Pines - Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest

Description: The 23.64-acre Tulip Tree Woods Nature Preserve is surrounded by a 3-foot high historic stone wall and contains an old growth Tulip tree rich woods plant community with spring ephemeral wildflowers (red trillium, white bloodroot). American beech is the dominant understory, joined by flowering dogwood. This forest has been relatively undisturbed for over 200 years.
Navigation: Address: 47 Adams Dam Road, Wilmington, DE 19807. This address will get you to the area. Directions: Tulip Tree Woods Nature Preserve is located behind the Nature Center of the Brandywine Creek State Park, 41 Adams Dam Road, Wilmington, DE 19807. The trailhead is located just adjacent the Nature Center.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking: There is a parking lot outside the Park office/Nature Center.  Admission into the Park is $4.00 per day (in-state), $8.00 per day (out-of-state).
Trails: Trail is 3,400 feet.
Hours And Camping: Hours for the Park are from dawn to dusk.  No camping in the Nature Preserve is permitted, nor is there camping in the Park itself.
Hunting: No hunting is allowed in the Nature Preserve.  Hunting does take place as a management tool within the Park.
name: Tulip Tree Woods Nature Preserve

Description: Of the 230 acres of forest in this tract, approximately 89% is older than 70 years. Forested wetland accounts for 43% of the forest in the tract. The majority of the upland forest is Mesic Coastal Plain Mixed Hardwood Forest. This forest contains mature American beech, tulip poplar, loblolly pine, and various oaks and hickories. Many of these trees were estimated to be at least 140 years of age in 1991. Scattered within this forest are four isolated stands of Coastal Plain Depression Swamp. These forested wetlands are located in depressions ranging from 5.9 to 9.6 acres in size. The depressions are seasonally flooded with ground water. Swamp chestnut oak, black gum, red maple and sweetgum are dominant species commonly occurring in this community. There are also several large examples of river birch growing along Cahoon Branch just downstream from Kenton Road. Barred owls were heard calling and nesting at this site.
Navigation: Address: Across from 2475 Kenton Rd., Dover, DE 19904. Directions: Parking area is near a small bridge over Maidstone Branch. Do not continue on until you cross W. Denney's Rd.
Parking And Admission: There is a small (8 car) parking facility.  No admission charge.
Trails: Trail is 1.75 miles.
Hours And Camping: Hours for the Park are from dawn to dusk.  No camping in the Nature Preserve is permitted.
Hunting: Hunting is normally utilized as a management tool within our Parks, however due to the close proximity to houses, only bow hunting would be permitted and be a part of a managed hunt organized by the State Park staff.
name: Anne M. McClements Woodland Tract of the Fork Branch Nature Preserve

Description: The 23-acre oak-pine forest is bounded on two sides by tidal creeks and swamp floodplain. This mature, undisturbed woodland is one of the few places in the county never cultivated, thereby preserving a rich biological and archaeological record. Part of the trail goes through a floodplain and swamp along a tributary of the Nanticoke River, where signs of beaver can be seen and wood ducks flourish. The preserve has not been logged in this century. Documentary research suggests that the property may have been set aside as a wood lot by the beginning of the nineteenth century. William Neal stipulated in his will, dated March 4, 1834, that his wife was not to permit additional clearing on the property to be inherited by his minor daughter. The land included in the Barnes Woods Nature Preserve was part of this property. The open, upland area of Barnes Woods is an oak-pine mix, typical of vegetation connected with the loamy, sandy soils in this part of Delaware. Among the canopy tree species are white oak, southern red oak, American beech, loblolly pine, and mockernut hickory. The understory includes flowering dogwood, sassafras and American holly.
Navigation: Address: 27268 Woodland Rd, Seaford DE or 100-198 Malihorn Drive, Seaford, DE 1997. Directions: Located 1.5 miles southwest of Seaford, south of County Road 536.
Parking And Admission: Parking is difficult at this location as there are no facilities; however, one can park on the side of the road at the trailhead. No admission charge.
Trails: Trail is 4,000 feet.
Hours And Camping: Hours for the Park are from dawn to dusk.  No camping in the Nature Preserve is permitted.
name: Barnes Woods Nature Preserve

Description: Holly River is West Virginia's second largest state park, containing 8,101 acres of dense forest located in a narrow valley. Surveying and mapping of old-growth areas in the Park is still underway.  The known areas of old-growth are 1) along the Wilderness Trail near the cabin area, and 2) along Potato Knob trail in the southern area of the park. Several known areas of secondary old-growth exist around the Wilderness Trail and Laurel Fork trail (beyond the Crooked Fork footbridge, uphill towards the west), and around the "Giant Trees" area of Potato Knob trail.  Trees to discover here include >200 year-old northern red oaks and chestnut oaks, large old tulip trees, and old black cherry trees. Holly River State Park is also known for a wide range of flora, including wildflowers and ferns.
Navigation: Address: 680 State Park Road, Hacker Valley, WV 26222
Parking And Admission: For Wilderness Trail, park at cabin area parking lot or in parking lot across from park office/restaurant building and walk about .3 of mile to Wilderness Trail trailhead, past the swimming pool area. For Potato Knob Trail, drive back out to Rt. 20 the way you came into the park, turn left and take first left and go about 4 miles. Look for small trail sign for Potato Knob on right of road.
Trails: Old growth forest #1 above on Wilderness Trail starts about 0.2 mile up the hill, mostly on the west (right) side coming up the hill from the cabins.  Old growth continues for another half mile or so before you can turn around and go back downhill when you reach a stream crossing where trail turns to the left.  There are many large northern red oaks and some chestnut oaks along this trail and off the trail to the west up the hill within a few hundred yards. Old-growth forest #2 above on Potato Knob Trail is about 0.3 miles uphill from the access road, and you can turn around where the trail reaches a spur trail to the McClure cemetery where the old growth ends. There are many large chestnut oaks and other species of trees right along and somewhat off this trail. This is the Giant Tree area of the park and it is marked with signs that read "Giant Trees." You can continue on both of these trails for many more miles of hiking. The Park website includes a hiking map you can download:  https://wvstateparks.com/park/holly-river-state-park/.
Hours And Camping: The park is open for camping from April through December with 88 campsites with electrical hookups and bathhouses. Some camp sites are reservable. Several of 10 furnished comfy cabins with electricity and hot showers are now open year-round.  (Call park office for specific times when camping and cabins are available at 304-493-6353.) Recreational opportunities in this park include many miles of hiking, camping, swimming, bicycling and tennis. No ATV riding is allowed in the park.  Amenities include picnic shelters, the Holly River Restaurant (open with varying schedule April to October), rentable Judd Anderson activity building for meetings or other activities, corrals for campers with horses, 10 furnished cabins, picnic tables, and grills.  Also, in the cabin area there is an interesting marked nature trail. (Ask park office for Nature's Rock Garden Trail map which explains the 25 markers.)
name: Wilderness Trail - Holly River State Park

Description: Mature forests of Pinus contorta (Lodgepole pine), Pinus jeffreyi (Jeffrey pine) and Abies concolor (White fir). Scattered about the forest floor you will find a plethora of native wildflowers and fern growth including many varieties of lupine and even some endangered species such as the Bear Valley checkerbloom (Sidalcea malviflora ssp. dolosa). Along with the wonderfully showy wildflower displays, you will see a wide variety of native grasses and sedge species along the lake shoreline and dominating the meadow just East of the lake. Located at 7,600 feet, the forest was thinned in the past when it was owned by another organization. Very impressive trees remain and the landscape feels completely natural. A short spur trail leads to a champion lodgepole pine tree, on Forest Service property.
Navigation: Directions: 1. From Big Bear, CA, take Big Bear Blvd. to Mill Creek Road or Tulip La. At Oak Knoll Lodge (949 Tulip Ln, Big Bear Lake, CA 92315) turn south on Forest Service Road 2N10. After about a mile the pavement ends and becomes an improved dirt road (passenger car accessible). Follow the 2N10 another 2.6 miles to the junction with 2N86 and bear left, following the sign that says "<---Bluff Lake Reserve." In approximately 0.5 mile, look for the sign on the right: "Bluff Lake Reserve 1/2 -->" and turn right on the access road and proceed 0.5 mile to the main parking area. 2. The Reserve may also be reached by hiking the Castle Rock Trail from Big Bear. The trailhead is located directly off Forest Service Road 2N10; start on Mill Creek Road, directly across from Bear Valley Bikes on Hwy 18, and follow this into the mountains 4.25 miles.
Parking And Admission: Limited parking. No admission charge.
Trails: A gentle trail circles the lake, with a spur to the champion lodgepole pine. A 4.25-mile trail leads across Castle Rock and down into the town of Big Bear. There are other trails nearby.
Hours And Camping: Open to visitors seven days a week from 9 am to 6 pm, starting May 1 through November 1. The property is snowed in through winter and spring.No camping allowed.
name: Bluff Lake Reserve

Description: Carpenter's Woods is a 37-acre section of Wissahickon Valley Park. The Wissahickon Valley is an 1,800-acre forested gorge running through Philadelphia's Fairmount Park and continuing through Montgomery County's Ft. Washington State Park. One of the oldest forests in the valley is Carpenter's Woods. The woods are named for a wealthy businessman who had a natural history museum on his estate and associated with the naturalists of his time, including John James Audubon. In 1921, due to the efforts of Caroline Moffett, a conservationist and principal of the nearby Charles W. Henry School, Carpenter's Woods became Philadelphia's first bird sanctuary. It was designated as an Important Bird Area by the National Audubon Society in 2005. Its varied habitat, including its unusual concentration of ancient trees, allows it to host diverse species of breeding birds, including eastern screech-owls and pileated woodpeckers, and makes it a migration hotspot, especially for warblers and thrushes. Among the ancient trees are large white oaks, black oaks, northern red oaks, American beech, black tupelo, tulip-poplar, and sassafras, many of them more than 200 years old. It is true urban old-growth.
Navigation: Address: 655 West Ellet St., Philadelphia, PA (in the West Mt. Airy section of the city) is the closest home address. Directions: The trailhead, where W. Ellet meets Sherman Street, is marked by two stone pillars. There are numerous trailhead entrances, both for Carpenter's Woods and the entire park. See the Friends of Carpenter's Woods website for a map and information https: //www.focw.org/. Also see the Friends of Wissahickon website to obtain a good map of the entire valley: https: //www.fow.org/visit-the-park/maps/
Parking And Admission: Ample parking on the street. No admission charge.
Trails: There are looping trails through Carpenter's Woods that total approximately 1.5 miles. In the entire Wissahickon Valley Park there are over 50 miles of trails.
Hours And Camping: Always open, year-round.
name: Carpenter's Woods - Wissahickon Valley Park

Description: This tract of +/-1,350 acres contains the southwestern portion of the headwatershed of Middlelick Branch of Davis Creek and the entire watersheds of Wall Fork and Hoffman Hollow, both tributary to Middlelick Branch.  The tract is bounded on the north, east, and south by the Kanawha State Forest (KSF) administrative boundary and on the west by Middle Ridge within KSF.  Approximately 65% of this tract is currently covered with secondary old-growth forest, and the remaining 35% will likely meet all secondary old-growth characteristics within two decades.  The dominant old-growth trees are 250+ year old white oaks, chestnut oaks, northern red oaks, and yellow poplar, with significant numbers of 150+ yr old black gum, shagbark hickory, pignut hickory, bitternut hickory, and mockernut hickory.  Some of the white oaks are likely 300+ years old.  Some old eastern hemlocks are scattered in the moister coves and riparian areas.  Much of that portion of the tract that is not now considered old-growth, was severely damaged by wildfire in the middle 1900s, but is now growing rapidly.  There are small stands of a very rare plant association, the shortleaf pine-oak-heath association, scattered on the ridgetops of the tract.  The tract is the summer home to the threatened northern long-eared bat and the endangered Indiana bat.  The northern long-eared bat is known to hibernate in abandoned coal mines within KSF.  The increasingly rare cerulean warbler, an old-growth specialist, is very abundant in this tract.  Bobcat and black bear also frequent the tract.
Navigation: Directions: Middlelick Fork Trailhead to access all three watershed segments of the tract - Exit I-64 at Oakwood Road Exit and turn right on US 119.  At traffic light at top of hill turn left onto Oakwood Road and follow signs to entrance to Kanawha State Forest.  At KSF entrance turn left on Middlelick Road and drive to firing range parking lot.  From this trailhead you may access Middlelick Fork and Wall Fork on the yellow-blazed Mary Ingles Trail to the east or Hoffman Hollow straight ahead on the gated forest access road.
Parking And Admission: Firing range parking lot on Middlelick Road.  No admission charge.
Trails: Wall Fork portion of the Mary Ingles Trail is approximately 4 miles one way.  Other trails skirt the southern and western boundaries of the tract, and the Hoffman Hollow access road is approximately 2.5 miles one way. Additional list of detailed foot-traffic and mountain biking trails available on the official website.
Hours And Camping: Day use hours are 6:00am to 10:00pm, year-round. Camping is available in a 46 unit campground. 21 sites are primitive, while 25 sites offer water and electricity. Campground is open April through December; reservations are available Memorial Day through Labor Day each year; also open on a first-come, first-serve basis after Labor Day. Campsite reservation applications available on the official website. Due to the roads into the park, vehicles longer than 26 feet are not recommended. There is a dump station for RVs, as well as two shower houses with hot showers and laundry facilities.
Hunting: Hunting is permitted; contact the forest officials for details. Hunting is permitted in Kanawha State Forest with the exception of safety zones around popular facilities.
name: Eastern Watershed Tracts of Kanawha State Forest

Description: The Mariposa Grove of Giant Sequoias is the largest grove of giant sequoia trees inside Yosemite National Park, with over 500 mature trees in the grove. Most of these trees are over 2,000 years old. The idea of protecting natural resources and the idea of national parks was rooted in the history of the Mariposa Grove of Giant Sequoias when President Abraham Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant Act in 1864 to protect the Mariposa Grove of Giant Sequoais and Yosemite Valley for all people, for all time. The Mariposa Grove became the first place in the world set aside for preservation and recreational enjoyment.The Washington Tree is the largest tree in the grove, with a volume of 35,950 cubic feet (1,018 m3). The Grizzly Giant is the second largest Giant Sequoia tree in the Mariposa Grove and is one of the 30 largest trees in the world. It is 34,010 cubic feet (963m3)  and stands 210 feet tall. The Mariposa Grove of Giant Sequoias is also home of the Columbia Tree, the tallest tree in the grove at 285 feet tall.
Navigation: Directions: The Mariposa Grove of Giant Sequoias is located near the southern entrance to Yosemite National Park and can be accessed from Highway 41 north from Oakhurst, CA. Enter the south entrance for Yosemite National Park, enter the roundabout and follow signs to the parking area for the Mariposa Grove. Park in the South Entrance Parking Lot, go to the Welcome Plaza and board a free shuttle that will transport you two miles up to the Lower Grove trailhead for the Mariposa Grove of Giant Sequoias. Hike through the Lower Grove to reach the Upper Grove and Wawona Point. For specific directions, visit https://www.nps.gov/yose/planyourvisit/mg.htm
Parking And Admission: Admission fee to enter and recreate inside Yosemite National Park for most personal vehicles is $35 per vehicle and a pass is valid for seven days. Annual passes are available. There is no additional fee to visit the Mariposa Grove of Giant Sequoias.
Trails: There is a network of trails throughout the Mariposa Grove. Mariposa Grove Trail, the longest trail, is from the Lower Grove trailhead to Wawona Point summit. It is 7 miles one way and rated as a strenuous trail. Other trails include the Big Trees Loop, an easy trail accessible for all abilities (0.5 miles), the Grizzly Giant Loop Trail (2 miles round trip, rated as moderate), and the Guardians Loop Trail (6.5 miles round trip, rated as strenuous).
Hours And Camping: The Mariposa Grove is open year-round; however, the Mariposa Grove Road may close due to inclement weather. Access via snowshoeing or cross-country skiing is permitted in the winter. Camping is available in the park; contact Yosemite National Park for specific front country and backcountry camping options.
name: Mariposa Grove of Giant Sequoias - Yosemite National Park

Description: Johnson Woods is one of Ohio's largest and best remaining old-growth forests. Many trees rise 40-50 feet before the first limbs occur and several are more than 400 years old. The largest trees, then and now, are white oaks, red oaks and hickories. The forest is proceeding through a natural succession from an oak-hickory community to a beech-maple community, so the maples and beeches are becoming more prominent members of the forest community. Swamp forest communities, dominated by red maples and pin oaks, are found in the more poorly drained sections of the preserve. In addition to its importance as one of the few old-growth forest stands remaining in Ohio, Johnson Woods is also significant for its size. At 206 acres, Johnson Woods is a self-supporting ecosystem. Its large size makes it less vulnerable to storm damage and threats from disease. Birds, such as the pileated woodpecker, scarlet tanager, Acadian flycatcher, wood thrush, ovenbird and hooded warbler, are found nesting at Johnson Woods along with many other species that are dependent upon larger tracts of forests. The size, age and history of Johnson Woods SNP make it one of the most significant forest communities in Ohio.
Navigation: Address: 13240 Fox Lake Rd, Marshallville, OH 44645. Directions: Located in Wayne County approximately 4 miles north of Orrville on SR 57, then 1 mile east on Fox Lake Road.  Entrance is on the right.
Parking And Admission: Parking: Parking lot (north side of Fox Lake Rd). No admission charge.
Trails: 1.0-mile boardwalk trail system.
Hours And Camping: Hours: year-round; daylight hours. No camping.
Hunting: No open hunting (rarely there are controlled hunts for management purposes).
name: Johnson Woods State Nature Preserve

Description: The Dysart Woods Land Laboratory is 455 acres in total and includes a central tract of 50 acres of old-growth white oak-beech-tuliptree forest surrounded by a mixture of second-growth forest, old-fields, and pastures. The oldest trees exceed 4 feet in diameter and have been dated to well over 400 years old. This is the only known remaining remnant of the Mixed Mesophytic Forest type located in Ohio, and one of only several in the entire central Appalachians. The property is owned and managed by Ohio University, principally for long-term forest research.
Navigation: Address: 62000 Dysart Woods Road, Belmont, OH Directions: Trailhead is approximately 1.0 miles down Dysart Road on left (S-side of road)
Parking And Admission: Parking for 8-10 vehicles located at trailhead.  No admission charge.
Trails: Two trails (red and blue marked) on either side of property connect 1.7-mile loop.
Hours And Camping: Hours:Facility is open to public 24/7/365, dawn to dusk. All pets must be leashed. Nothing may be removed from site. Camping: No camping is available onsite. Camping is available at nearby Barkcamp State Park.
Phone Number: None. All info, brochure, and trail guide at website.
name: Dysart Woods

Description: Approximately 30 acres of mature mixed hardwood woodlands comprised of sugar maple, black oak, red oak, hickory, black cherry and walnut trees.  There are large specimens of tuliptree, white oak, red oak and red maple with amazing canopies!  The meandering path provides a look at many of these species that are close at hand. While the tree ages do not indicate an old growth forest, it is a striking, although modest in size, example of a mature forest and is significant for the region. During spring, wildflowers abound: round-lobed hepatica, Virginia bluebells, Jacob's ladder, trout lily, bellwort, wild blue phlox, etc.It is also great birding habitat too.
Navigation: Address: 17621 Yauger Road, Mount Vernon Ohio for the parking lot for Wolf Run Regional Park and Knox Woods State Nature Preserve.Directions: Parking lot-N 40 23.814' W 82 25.719'.  Knox Woods State Nature Preserve is accessed by traversing Wolf Run Regional Park trails, heading north/northwest from the Wolf Run trailhead.
Parking And Admission: Parking: 17621 Yauger Road, Mount Vernon Ohio- Parking is sufficient and ample. No admission charge.
Trails: There is basically a north loop and a south loop named Shawnee Trail and Mingo Trail. They cover a good part of the 29 acres. There are several foot bridges to cross over the stream. The Knox Woods State Nature Preserve trails tie in with Wolf Run Regional Park trails at coordinates: 40.400617,-82.427117.
Hours And Camping: Preserves are open year around from half an hour before sunrise to half an hour after sunset (dawn to dusk). No camping.
Hunting: This site is not open for public hunting although state law does allow for controlled hunts to be conducted on the site for deer herd management purposes.
name: Knox Woods State Nature Preserve

Description: Walter B. Jacobs Memorial Nature Park is dedicated to helping the citizens of Northwest Louisiana connect with nature by conserving a pine-oak-hickory forest for interpretation and recreation. Native, mature forest exists in most areas of the 160-acre site which also contains about 5 miles of nature trails. The Nature Park is a highly diverse area that is notable for its floristic diversity: over 520 species of plants native to Louisiana can be found here! For a relatively small forest site, this is astounding as it represents nearly 20% of the flora of the entire state of Louisiana. Hiking along the Caddo Trail is highly recommended as one can view natural gradients in habitat and remarkable old-growth trees. The Park also has a wonderful interpretive building with displays that educate about the area's flora and fauna, a rentable pavilion with restrooms, and several knowledgeable naturalists who provide information and interpretation to park visitors. Nature-oriented programs are available on an appointment basis and to school groups. The Walter B. Jacobs Memorial Nature Park is home to a truly exceptional old-growth forest, to stellar environmental educational programs, and is a significant site for the conservation of the natural heritage of the state of Louisiana.
Navigation: Address: 8012 Blanchard Furrh Rd., Shreveport, LA 71107 Directions: Head north on Clyde Fant Memorial Pkwy/Clyde Fant Pkwy; Take Grimmett Dr to N Market St, Turn left onto Havens Rd, Turn right at the 1st cross street onto N Market St, Sharp left to stay on N Market St, Turn right toward Pine Hill Rd, Turn left onto Daugherty Ave, Continue onto Par Rd 4, destination on the right.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. No admission charge Wednesday-Saturday, 8am-5pm and Sunday, 1pm-5pm.
Trails: Total distance of all trails is just under 5 miles. There is a handicapped-accessible trail as well.
Hours And Camping: Open year-round Wednesday through Sundays only. Closed major holidays. 8am-5pm Wed - Sat; 1pm-5pm Sun.
name: Walter B. Jacobs Memorial Nature Park

Description: Briarwood Nature Preserve is a mixed pine and hardwood forest, with native forest as well as restored forest on the site. Further, the Preserve has well-maintained historical elements including the ancestral log cabin home of Caroline Dormon, a botanist, natural historian, and the driving force behind the establishment of Kisatchie National Forest. A native wildflower field is beautiful when in bloom; it intersperses the surrounding forest areas which are dominated by Loblolly pines of +/-120 years of age and older. Several pines on the site are estimated to be at least 300 years old, and very old hardwood trees also diversify the forest. The Curator of the forest is descended from the first caretakers of the site that worked directly with Caroline Dormon; he grew up here and gladly gives visitors fascinating, insightful tours of the Nature Preserve and its historic elements. Restrooms and a small gift shop also on site.
Navigation: Address: 216 Caroline Dorman Rd. Saline, Louisiana. Visitors must go to the visitor center first, where they will be welcomed on a guided tour of the Preserve. Directions from Saline: Take LA 9 South, turn right on Briarwood Road, turn left on Briarwood Preservation Road, this becomes Caroline Dorman Road, destination will be on the left.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. Admission: $5.00 recommended donation/fee for visiting the Preserve.
Trails: The main tour route is about 1 mile, and total trails in the Preserve are approximately 4 miles.
Hours And Camping: Open weekends during March, April, May, October, and November: Saturdays 9:00am - 5:00pm and Sundays from 12:00pm- 5:00pm, or by calling ahead to arrange a visit. Camping is available only for civic and scout groups that are coming to volunteer at the property.
name: Briarwood Nature Preserve

Description: Barataria Preserve is home to 23,000 acres of hardwood forest, swamp, and marsh habitats; these habitats are home to the oldest remaining tracts of forests in Jefferson Parish. More than 400 species of plants can be found in the preserve, and both spring and fall seasons reward visitors with many wildflowers in bloom. Located squarely on the Mississippi Flyway, the preserve is a birder's paradise, where over 200 species of birds have been observed. In the swamp habitats, visitors will see giant old cypress trees. With an active research and citizen science program as well as a fascinating and well-maintained visitor center, Barataria Preserve offers great opportunities for learning about and experiencing firsthand southern Louisiana's native ecosystems.
Navigation: Address: 6588 Barataria Boulevard, Marrero, LA. Rangers at the Visitor's Center can guide you to the accessible trailheads to view.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking is available in the visitor center lots. No admission charge to visit the preserve or to participate in many year-round free programs and walks.
Trails: Trail maps and up-to-date info can be obtained by speaking with a Ranger at the Visitor Center. Bayou Coquille Trail is a 1-mile (round trip) boardwalk and packed gravel trail (wheelchair and stroller accessible). Access via Bayou Coquille Trail Parking area. Highlights include giant live oaks, Bayou Coquille, an American Indian shell mound, the "Monarch of the Swamp" tree, a 600-year old bald cypress tree, seasonal wildflowers, cell phone trail tour and interpretive signage.
Hours And Camping: Barataria Preserve Visitor Center is open Wednesday through Sunday from 9:30am - 4:30pm; closed on federal holidays and during Mardi Gras. Trail access gates are open daily between 9:00am-5:00pm, including federal holidays (except closed during Mardi Gras).
name: Barataria Preserve - Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve

Description: Marshall Forest has one of the last stands of old-growth pine-hardwood timber in northwest Georgia. Once part of the Cherokee Nation's lands, Marshall Forest covers 301 acres of pine-hardwood forest in Floyd County, near Rome in northwest Georgia. Ranging in elevation from 600-900 feet, the site is home to over 300 species of plants and 55 tree species in 3 distinct plant communities: pine-oak, chestnut oak, and mixed hardwood forest. It is thought that periodic ice storms (like the 1993 blizzard) and fires open the canopy for pine growth, preventing domination by a single plant community. The forest is home to Georgia's largest population of the endangered large-flowered skullcap, a perennial herb in the mint family. The site is also home to a wealth of fauna, including frogs, salamanders, at least six species of snake, and dozens of bird species. Marshall Forest was the first National Natural Landmark in Georgia, designated by the U.S. Department of the Interior in 1966.
Navigation: Address: 318 Horseleg Creek Rd SW, Rome, GA is close to trailhead. Directions: From Atlanta (allow 1.5 hours): I-75 North to S.R. 20 at Cartersville (Exit 290, about 40 miles.) Keep eye out for turns to continue on SR 20. Take S.R. 20 West to Rome, about 20-25 miles. Stay on S.R. 20 through Rome (watch for turns), and past the Floyd County Regional Medical Center. At Horseleg Creek Road (stoplight), turn left. (Five Guys Closed and Moe's).  Travel down Horseleg Creek Road about 1.5 miles to Marshall Forest Preserve parking lot (at large Preserve sign) on right. On a blind curve.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking, no admission charge.
Trails: Marshall Forest contains five self-guided walking trails, primarily on the Southwest side of the forest. The trails provide informational aides, including plant identification tags, and twenty stop-and-observe stations, with signs in both Braille and English. The Big Pine Braille Trail, is made specifically for the visually impaired. The trails are not cut over, allowing the undergrowth to spread onto the pathway.
Hours And Camping: Open sunrise to sunset. No camping.
name: Marshall Forest

Description: The 20 hectare (50 acre) Thain Family Forest in the heart of the New York Botanical Garden is the largest remnant of the forest that once covered much of what is now New York City. A canopy of centuries-old oaks, tulip trees, sweetgums, maples, and other native hardwoods rises over dramatic terrain that includes the Bronx River floodplain and gorge, intermittent streams, ephemeral pools, and rocky ridges. The forest, a unique and beautiful urban woodland, has been an important research site, a favorite visitor destination, and an invaluable educational resource since NYBG became its steward in 1895.
Navigation: Directions: Arrive at any Visitor Entrance to the New York Botanical Garden. (Directions to NYBG, including public transportation options, are available on the NYBG website www.nybg.org.) The Thain Family Forest is clearly marked on the visitor maps and within walking distance from all visitor entrances of the Garden.
Parking And Admission: Public transportation is the easiest and recommended way of getting to the Garden as parking may be limited during peak visitation days. Enter via the 2900 Southern Boulevard Main Entrance for onsite parking. Depending on the day, parking is $17-$20 per vehicle. Admission to the Garden per person is, depending on the day, $23-$28 or available via purchasing a Garden membership. NYC residents pay $15 and other discounts may apply; check NYBG website.
Trails: There are well-marked trails through the forest, some with slight incline; some over gravel and natural terrain. A trail across the bridge over the Bronx river is recommended. Maps and staff at NYBG can provide guidance to visitors.
Hours And Camping: New York Botanical Garden is open year-round Tuesday to Sunday, and some holiday Mondays, typically from 10am - 6pm. Closed Thanksgiving and Christmas. No camping available.
name: Thain Family Forest - New York Botanical Garden

Description: Simpson Park is a natural preserve that encompasses over eight acres of tropical hardwood hammock in the center of Miami's urban core, one of the last remnants of the famous Brickell Hammock. The park's unique subtropical flora exemplifies the history and culture of Miami's diverse community. The creation and preservation of Simpson Park Hammock represents the Miami community's trend toward - and commitment to - environmental conservation, restoration, and exhibition of South Florida's flora and fauna for the purpose of public education and public benefit. The park area is also known to have been settled by Native Americans, including the Tequesta people. The majority of the park comprises native trees and undergrowth, with over 162 plant species in Simpson Park. Of these, at least 96 are native species, such as red stopper, spicewood, live oak, strangler fig, Jamaica dogwood, gumbo limbo, false-mastic, and lignum vitae. There are 15 endangered species and 9 threatened species in the park, including wild cinnamon, coffee colubrina, yellow boxwood, silver palm, strongbark, Eugenia confusa, and gulf licaria.
Navigation: Address: 55 SW 17th Rd, Miami, FL 33129
Parking And Admission: Parking on 17th Rd only. Limited to 20 cars. No admission charge.
Trails: 0.60 miles of total trail.
Hours And Camping: Open year-round, from 8:00 am to 5:00 pm. No camping available.
name: Simpson Park Hammock

Description: Long Pine Key occurs on the southwestern most stretch of the Miami rock ridge, a limestone outcropping that forms the eastern boundary of the historic wetlands of the Everglades. The Long Pine Key area encompasses approximately 19,000 acres. The generally higher elevation of the area supports the largest remaining expanse of pine rockland habitat in the United States. Pine rockland is characterized by an open overstory of slash pine (Pinus elliottii) with a diverse understory assemblage of neotropical, temperate and endemic plant species growing on exposed limestone with limited soil. Long Pine Key also features rockland hammock and transverse glade plant communities. Long Pine Key has been managed by the National Park Service since the establishment of Everglades National Park in 1947. Logging is reported to have occurred within pine rocklands during the 1930's or 1940's, prior to the establishment of the park. The area has since recovered and appears much as it would have prior to removal of timber.
Navigation: Address: Homestead Entrance, 40001 State Road 9336, Homestead, FL. From there you are approximately 5.7 miles from the Long Key Pine Campground, where parking is available. The forests of Long Pine Key can be accessed via Main Park Road and Research Road within the park. The Long Pine Key Nature Trail, Pineland Trail and associated fire trails provide access to Long Pine Key on foot, and rangers can provide specific directions and recommendations (based on seasonal conditions).
Parking And Admission: Parking to access Long Pine Key is available at a variety of locations including Long Pine Key Nature Trail trailheads (Long Pine Key Campground and Pine Glades Lake) and Pineland Trail. Admission to Everglades National Park is currently $25.00 for a 7 day vehicle pass.
Trails: Approximately 20 miles of unpaved fire roads found throughout Long Pine Key are available to the general public for hiking. Bicycling is only permitted on Long Pine Key Nature Trail. Pinelands Trail offers paved access to Long Pine Key.
Hours And Camping: Everglades National Park is open 365 days per year. Tent camping is available at Long Pine Key Campground from October 1 to April 30. Facilities include restrooms, showers, water, and a sewer dump station with fresh water fill, but no hookups. More information can be found here: https://www.nps.gov/ever/planyourvisit/longpinecamp.htm.
name: Long Pine Key - Everglades National Park

Description: Coastal forests are iconic to Monroe County, Florida, and this particular mangrove forest is one of the most impressive mangrove forests that can be witnessed in South Florida. Mangrove forests occupy the entire southern land boundary of Everglades National Park from Long Sound in the southeast to Chokoloskee Bay in the northwest. These forests, dominated by closed canopy stands of red (Rhizophora mangle), black (Avicennia germinans) and white (Laguncularia racemosa) mangroves vary greatly in composition and physical structure. At the mouth of Ponce de Leon Bay, towering red mangrove-dominated forests form islands within a complex network of tidal rivers including the Shark and Little Shark Rivers. Stilted roots support trees 75 feet tall and the open understory allows a view deep into the forest. Evidence of direct human influence on this forest is not obvious. Known uses are limited to operation of a tannery in the early 1900s in which the bark of trees was stripped to produce tannic acid. Hurricanes frequently affect the area.
