This mangrove forest is habitat for an abundance of wildlife living in the tall forest canopy all the way down to below the surface of the tidal waters that surround the trees' roots.
Navigation: Directions: Mangrove forests in Everglades National Park reach their greatest development where the Shark River opens into the Gulf of Mexico at Ponce de Leon Bay. The forest can be visited by motorboat or paddlecraft via the Wilderness Waterway, approximately 20 miles NW of the Flamingo Visitor Center. The Everglades National Park also has a webpage (https://www.nps.gov/ever/planyourvisit/canoe-and-kayak-trails.htm) offering full information on how to seek a permitted guide, rent boats or paddlecraft from authorized concessioners within the Park, or obtain detailed guidance on paddle trails in order to view mature coastal forests.
Parking And Admission: Parking to access Shark River/Ponce de Leon Bay mangrove forest is available at the Flamingo Marina. Motor boats and paddlecraft can be launched at this location. Check conditions with the local ranger staff or concessioner. Admission to Everglades National Park is currently $30.00 for a 7-day vehicle pass.
Trails: No trails are available in this area. Access to the forest via motorboat or paddlecraft is available along the Wilderness Waterway and a variety of tidal creeks and rivers.
Hours And Camping: Everglades National Park is open 365 days per year. Primitive camping is available at Cape Sable, south of Shark River/Ponce de Leon Bay. A backcountry permit is required and no facilities are available. More information can be found here: https://www.nps.gov/ever/planyourvisit/backcamp.htm.
name: Shark River/Ponce de Leon Bay Mangrove Forest - Everglades National Park

Description: Hickory Hollow contains 254 acres of mixed pine-hardwood forest, ravines, and swamps. None of the forest is old-growth, but there are some large beeches and oaks. This protected land contains important habitat for migratory songbirds and wild turkey. Cabin swamp is an exceptional quality wetland community that supports a very high diversity of plants including several mountain disjuncts. The dominant community type is Northern Coastal Plain/Piedmont Mesic Mixed Hardwood Forest. A globally rare Coastal Plain Basic Seepage Swamp is a natural community highlight of the preserve. There is also a fine example of Coastal Plain/Piedmont Small-Stream Floodplain Forest in the southern drainage as well as Northern Coastal Plain/Piedmont Oak - Beech/ Heath Forest on the north-facing slopes adjacent to Cabin Swamp.
Navigation: Address: Hickory Hollow Natural Area Preserve, Regina Rd, Lancaster, VA 22503: Directions: From Kilmarnock, follow VA 3 towards Lancaster. Just before you reach Lancaster, turn right onto VA 604. The preserve is on your left.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. No admission charge.
Trails: The recommended trail is the 1.7-mile white loop with an optional 0.4-mile round trip visit to the rare basic seepage swamp on the yellow trail.Several other short trails lead through  254 acres of mature mixed forest and stream habitats. Total distance of all trails in the park is 4 miles.
Hours And Camping: The preserve is open from sunrise to sunset, year-round. No camping.
name: Hickory Hollow Natural Area Preserve

Description: The forest provides habitat for a vast array of plants and animals and protects the quality of the watershed. It also provides places for recreation and relaxation. These ecosystems are complex webs of organisms that include plants, animals, fungi, and bacteria. The park's total size is 3,776 acres and the area within the old growth designation is 777 acres. Common tree species include: scarlet oak, red oak, chestnut oak, white oak, black oak, yellow poplar, eastern hemlock, black gum, red maple, various hickories, sourwood, and dogwood. Both mountain laurel and great laurel are common and often large in size. Jackson Branch, which is entirely within Twin Falls Resort State Park, consistently produces one of the highest average WV Stream Condition Index scores calculated by the WV Department of Environmental Protection from among the thousands of streams sampled. Jackson Branch is one of that agency's reference streams against which all other streams are compared to determine the relative ecological health of the stream and the forest which surrounds it. Twin Falls Resort State Park is completely surrounded by forest, more than 90% of which is corporate owned and actively and aggressively timbered. The visual impact of this juxtaposition of management is not lost on the public and is frequently commented upon in conversations with park rangers. Designation in the Old-Growth Forest Network further enhances the value of this site as both an educational tool and an ecological example. The relatively easy access to this forest provides tremendous opportunities for people to recreate and re-create in a location they will know is among the purest and cleanest places on earth.
Navigation: Address: Twin Falls Resort State Park, 2999 Bear Hole Road, Mullens, WV 25882. Directions: Bear Hole Road, Mullens, WV 25882. Take WV-16 S/Robert C Byrd Dr, WV-121 W and WV-97 W to Black Fork Rd, Take Park Rd 803 , turn left onto Black Fork Road, Continue onto Park Rd 803, turn right onto Park Rd 802, Turn left. Destination is on right.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking is available at all 3 trailheads.  No admission charge.
Trails: Three park trails access the old growth area.  Hemlock Trail is 2 miles long. Cliffside Trail is 3 miles long, and Fall Trail is 1.25 miles long.  There are 14 trails on the park for a total length of 29.5 miles.
Hours And Camping: Hours: open from 6am to 10 pm daily, year-round. Camping: The park has a 47 room mountain top lodge (hotel), 14 cabins, and a 50 site campground. There are two campground bathhouses and a contact center with small store.  Some sites have electric hookups.  All campsites are paved and have a fireplace and picnic table.
Hunting: No hunting except for a lottery permit population control deer hunt that lasts for three days each fall.  Only approximately 15-20 permits are issued.  The number of permits varies depending on deer population trends.
name: Twin Falls Resort State Park

Description: The 1812 Lost Trail Hollow Forest is a 40 acre tract of secondary old-growth, mixed mesophytic forest dominated by (30-40 inch dbh) northern red oak, black oak, and white oak on the drier slopes and ridges, and by (30-40 inch dbh) northern red oak and American beech, and (25-30 inch dbh) tulip poplar and shagbark hickory in the coves.  The largest tree measured thus far is a 48.1-inch dbh white oak.  Oldest trees in the 150-250 age range.  One 36.3-inch dbh fallen Northern Red Oak was cut and the wedge determined to have 152 rings at 4.5 ft. above ground.  This is likely the oldest 40-acre tract anywhere in Beech Fork State Park.  There are no old roadways or skid trails and very few invasive plant species within the tract, indicating that it has had no major human disturbance since approximately the War of 1812.
Navigation: Address: Beech Fork State Park office, 5601 Long Branch Road, Barboursville, WV 25504. Directions: Drive to Moxley Branch Campground and drive south through the campground to the Moxley Branch trailhead.  Follow Lost Trail, crossing a tributary to Beech Fork and turning uphill.  The 1812 Lost Trail Hollow Forest is east of the tributary and all the way to the headwater.  There are no trails within the tract, but both Lost Trail and Mary Davis trail skirt near its border.
Parking And Admission: Multiple parking areas can be used for accessing the area.  Moxley Branch Trail Head (Lost Trail/Mary Davis). No admission charge.
Trails: The Lost Trail (3.5 miles and strenuous) skirts the northwestern boundary of the 1812 Lost Trail Hollow Forest and the Mary Davis Trail (5 miles, difficulty - hard) skirts the southwestern boundary of tract.
Hours And Camping: Park is open year-round with 6 vacation cabins and 275 campsites. 49 full hook up (water, electric, sewer) sites open year around, other campsites (electric, non-electric) open April - October.
Hunting: Hunting is available on the Beech Fork Wildlife Management Area (Adjacent to State Park). Hikers are encouraged to wear blaze orange during hunting seasons.
name: The 1812 Lost Trail Hollow Forest - Beech Fork State Park

Description: Established in 1902, Big Basin Redwoods is California's oldest state park. In the heart of the Santa Cruz Mountains, its biggest attractions - literally - are its ancient coast redwoods. Some of these giants are more than 50 feet around and as tall as the Statue of Liberty. At 1,000 to 1,800 years old, some may predate the Roman Empire. The park also offers spectacular views of the Pacific Ocean, lush waterfalls, and a fascinating natural and cultural history. Home to the largest continuous stand of ancient coast redwoods south of San Francisco, park vegetation consists of old-growth and recovering second-growth redwood forest, with mixed conifer, oaks, chaparral, and riparian habitats.
Navigation: Address: 21600 Big Basin Way, Boulder Creek, CA 95006; Directions: Take CA-9 North/Hwy 9 North; turn Left onto CA-236 S/Big Basin Way.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking at visitor's center. There is a vehicle day-use fee for the day-use area and the campground. Regular sized autos ($10), seniors age 62 or older ($9), bus parking 10-24 passengers ($50), and bus parking for 25+ passengers ($100). There is no fee at the Rancho del Oso Nature and History Center.
Trails: There are 80 miles of trails in the park. Redwood Trail is a 0.6-mile moderately trafficked loop trail that features beautiful wild flowers and is good for all skill levels. The Redwood Trail loop offers easy access to some of the tallest and oldest redwoods anywhere. The main attractions along this trail are Father of the Forest (circumference 66 feet 9 inches, height 250 feet), Mother of the Forest (the tallest tree in Big Basin Forest; circumference 70 feet, height 293 feet) and The Chimney Tree (whose hollow trunk offers a spectacular view up into the sky). Located across the parking lot from the visitor center, the trail is wheelchair- and stroller-accessible.
Hours And Camping: HOURS: 6am-Sunset; CAMPING: Big Basin's 142-site campground rests under the ancient redwoods of the Santa Cruz Mountains. Camping is $35 per night, and a $10 per night fee for additional vehicles. For reservations, please visit www.ReserveCalifornia.com.
name: Big Basin Redwoods State Park

Description: The James River Park System currently totals 562 acres and contains 408 acres under conservation easement, although there are plans to acquire more land, and put more land under easement. The age of the oldest trees is not certain, but 100 rings have been counted on a downed loblolly pine and a downed chestnut oak. There is no old-growth forest in this park; however, the strong protections put in place on this forest ensure that it may recover in time. Tree species include: red and silver maple, white oak, bitternut hickory, hackberry, tulip tree, eastern cottonwood, American sycamore, river birch, black walnut, box elder, sweetbay, beech, and pawpaw. These forests lie along the "founding river" of the United States. Here were Native American fishing villages, the earliest European colonial exploration, a Confederate prisoner of war camp, and early 19th century industrial development. They now provide respite, retreat, and recreation for urban and suburban residents of a city of 250,000 and a region of nearly 1.5 million. They are a crucial contributor to the city's "green infrastructure" and essential to the quality of life and public health for the city of Richmond.
Navigation: Directions: The Pony Pasture/Wetlands unit is the recommended forest area (unit) in the Park. It is located at 7200 Riverside Drive, Richmond, VA 23225. This is off Riverside Drive two miles east of the Huguenot Bridge. Most park unit entrances are within a short walk of city bus service. Addresses of all locations/units can be accessed here: https: //jamesriverpark.org/visit-the-park/
Parking And Admission: Most park unit entrances are within a short walk of city bus service. Although the Pony Pasture unit has a parking lot that holds 150 cars, on some days all the spots are taken. No admission charge.
Trails: The main trail at Pony Pasture is 3 mi. long, it is wide and graveled. It leads to the Wetlands trail which is 2.5 mi. All park units include trail infrastructure which totals 42 miles for the entire park system.
Hours And Camping: The park system is open year-round and is closed daily from dusk until dawn. Boating access to the river is restricted according to water levels. Camping is not available.
name: James River Park System

Description: Vizcaya's Rockland Hammock is located on the grounds of the Vizcaya Museum and Gardens. The forest is approximately 15 acres, almost all of it is old growth, untouched forest. It is the largest remaining portion of the Brickell Hammock, an extensive rockland hammock forest. There are several national champion trees in the forest, and several specimens are over 300 years old. The forest is the only remnant with a dominant and expanding population of Redberry Stopper, an important and critically endangered climax species.
Navigation: 3251 South Miami Avenue. The forest is accessible by two paved paths and a parking lot.
Parking And Admission: Parking is located within the hammock forest and across Miami Avenue. No admission is required to access the forest.
Trails: The forest is accessible by two paved paths and a parking lot.
Hours And Camping: Vizcaya is open 9:30am-5:30pm daily except Tuesdays, Christmas, and New Years Day.
name: Vizcaya’s Rockland Hammock

Description: The Cummins Creek Wilderness features the only old-growth Sitka Spruce forest in the Oregon Wilderness system. Overhung with alder and maple, Cummins and Bob Creeks drain west through this dense rainforest Wilderness, where Sitka spruce sometimes reach nine feet in diameter. Both creeks spill into the Pacific Ocean. Salmon, steelhead, and cutthroat trout spawn in the cool creek waters. Spruce-covered Cummins Ridge, which peaks at almost 2,000 feet, splits the Wilderness in two. Yellow monkey flower, purple aster, white candy flower, and red foxglove brighten summer days, which otherwise tend toward the wet and foggy. Winters rarely see snow.
Navigation: Address: Oregon Coast Hwy, Yachats, OR 97498. Directions: Cummins Creek Wilderness lies between Florence and Yachats on the Oregon Coast, just south of the Cape Perpetua Visitor Center and adjacent to Neptune State Park. There is signage for trailheads along Hwy 101. From Portland: Drive I-5 South to Exit 278 for Donald and Aurora. After exiting, turn right onto Ehlen Road, which becomes Yergen Road, and drive 3.6 miles. At a crossroads, continue straight on McKay Road for 3.4 miles. At the T-junction with Highway 219, turn right, and proceed 3.1 miles, crossing the Willamette River. Turn left onto the Newberg/Dundee Bypass, and go 4.2 miles. Bear right at the merge with Highway 99W, and drive another 3.2 miles. Then turn left onto Highway 18 for Dayton and the Oregon Coast. Keep on Highway 18 for 52.1 miles. Before Highway 101, there’s a junction where cars going north peel off to the right for Neskowin and Tillamook. Drive 0.7 more miles and merge with Highway 101 South. Drive 58.3 miles through Lincoln City and then Newport, cross the Yaquina Bay Bridge, and then pass through the communities of Seal Rock, Waldport, and Yachats. Then, 1.2 miles past the turnoff for the Cape Perpetua Campground and Day Use Area, turn left onto FR 1050 for the Cummins Creek Trailhead. Proceed 0.3 miles up this gravel road to the parking turnaround at the trailhead.
Parking And Admission: No permit is required to park at the Cummins Ridge Trailhead or at Cummins Creek. Parking at the nearby Cape Perpetua Visitor Center requires a $5 fee or recreation pass.
Trails: Only one trail enters the Cummins Creek Wilderness – the Cummins Ridge Trail climbs 5.8 miles through towering stands of Sitka spruce, Western hemlock and Douglas-fir. On the north edge of the Wildnerness, other trails follow Gwynn Creek and connect with Cook’s Ridge Trail and the Cape Perpetua Visitor Center.
Hours And Camping: The nearby Cape Perpetua Visitor Center is open 7 days a week most of the year. Trails are open dawn to dusk every day. Camping is available at nearby Cape Perpetua Campground (https://www.fs.usda.gov/recarea/siuslaw/recreation/recarea/?recid=42273&actid=29)
name: Cummins Creek Wilderness - Siuslaw National Forest

Description: The Cape Perpetua Scenic Area includes 2,700 acres. Much of this area is covered in Douglas-fir, western hemlock, and Sitka spruce forest. While some of this forest near the Visitor Center was logged in the past, the majority of the area has not been. The native forest here has been re-growing since the last fire swept through the area over a century ago. Giant legacy trees that survived past fires, hundreds of years old, are found throughout the area and along the Cook’s Ridge Trail. Also in the area: In the nearby Cape Perpetua Campground, there is a 600-year-old Giant Sitka Spruce known as the Silent Sentinel of the Siuslaw. This tree stands more than 185 feet (56 m) high, and has a 40-foot (12 m) circumference at its base. On September 15, 2007, this ancient spruce was designated an Oregon Heritage Tree by the State of Oregon to recognize its exceptional age and size and ensure its protection.
Navigation: Address: Area is accessed from the Cape Perpetua Visitor Center, 2400 US-101, Yachats, OR 97498. Directions: From Florence, OR head north on US -Route 101 for 22.4 miles. Visitor Center will be on the right. From Cape Perpetua Visitors Center, head east along the Cooks Ridge Trail. After 3.75 miles and 1500ft elevation gain, complete a loop by heading south and then west along the Gwynn Creek Trail, eventually ending up at the ocean along Neptune State Scenic Viewpoint. Head back to the Visitor Center via the Oregon Coast Trail, which was once a wagon trail for early settlers.
Parking And Admission: Recreation Pass or $5 fee required to park at Cape Perpetua Visitor Center, where there is ample parking. https://www.fs.fed.us/visit/passes-permits/
Trails: The Cape Perpetua Scenic Area offers 26 miles of trail, featuring old-growth forests, Native American shell middens, the Devil’s Churn, tidepools and stunning views. Beginning at the Cape Perpetua Visitor Center, where restrooms and parking is available, the recommended old-growth forest trail is a 6.4 mile loop connecting the Discovery Loop, Cook’s Ridge, Gwynn Creek, and Oregon Coast Trails (Moderate-Difficult, with over 1,000 feet of elevation gain).
Hours And Camping: The Cape Perpetua Visitor Center is open 7 days a week most of the year. Trails are open dawn to dusk every day. Camping is available at nearby Cape Perpetua Campground (https://www.fs.usda.gov/recarea/siuslaw/recreation/recarea/?recid=42273&actid=29)
name: Cook's Ridge Trail at Cape Perpetua - Siuslaw National Forest

Description: The Opal Creek Wilderness and the neighboring Bull of the Woods Wilderness comprise the largest contiguous area of low-elevation old growth left in Oregon. Opal Creek’s ancient rainforest is a remnant of the conifer forests that once stretched from the Pacific coast to the crest of the Cascades, and from southeast Alaska to the northwest corner of California. This region, also known as Cascadia, contains trees and other organisms uniquely adapted to the heavy rainfall—70-100 inches per year–including the most diverse moss species of anywhere in the world. The oldest tree at Opal Creek is the Douglas fir and one of the largest known is “Guts Gibbs,” measured at over 270 feet high and 1,000 years old! Growing in its shade are the Western hemlock and the Western red cedar. As a “late successional forest” many of the hemlocks and cedars are beginning to overtake the Douglas firs in height and abundance. Below these giants you will find the Pacific yew. The Pacific yew is an extremely slow-growing shade-tolerant tree; a tree that may appear to be 50 years old could be well over 200! Many plants thrive in this moist temperate rainforest, with 9 months of precipitation and a short 3-month summer drought. The understory is rich with many species of shrubs, ferns, wildflowers, and berries. The forest floor is blanketed with bryophytes like mosses, liverworts, and hornworts, making a lush green carpet that cradles the giant old trees. Bryophytes make up a large percentage of old-growth canopy by growing on tree branches, where they are known as epiphytes (plants that take in nutrients from the air, rain, and debris around them rather than the soil). When it rains, canopy epiphytes absorb and hold up to 30% of the precipitation in the atmosphere. The moisture is released later as occult precipitation. After a rain, you may notice fog lifting from the mountain ridges; this is occult precipitation in action!
Navigation: Address and Directions: (Expect to lose cell service along the way) Roads are clearly marked. Use GPS to get to North Fork Rd., Lyons, OR then follow these directions:1.Turn right (north) onto the North Fork Rd. The Opal Creek trailhead is at the very end of this road, approximately 20 miles and 1 hour of driving time. 2. After 14 miles of pavement you will enter the Willamette National Forest where the road turns to gravel. You are now on Forest Road 2209. 3. After approx 1.5 -2 miles you will see a turn-off on the right towards Three Pools/Shady Cove. Stay to the left on Forest Road 2209. 4.Continue another 4 miles to the Opal Creek/Jawbone Flats parking area and trail head.
Parking And Admission: Parking: limited, please carpool; follow these rules: 1. Parking allowed only along the south shoulder within ¼ mile of the Opal Creek Trailhead and at the designated trailhead parking areas for Henline Falls, Henline Mountain and Nasty Rock Trailheads. 2. 15 minute parking limit at the visitor information kiosk at the 2209/2207 road junction. Admission: All visitors to Opal Creek need a Forest Service parking permit to park at the trailhead. The permit costs $5 per car for a one-day pass or $30 for a full-year pass (the Northwest Forest Pass). Annual and interagency passes are available at most Forest Service offices and outdoor stores, or you can pay per day from a self-serve pay station (cash or check only) at the trailhead. You can purchase annual and interagency passes from the Forest Service online at: https://www.fs.usda.gov/main/willamette/passes-permits/recreation
Trails: Trail to Opal Pool is a 7 mile loop, to Cedar Flats 10 miles RT. Level of Difficulty: moderate to Opal Pool, difficult to Cedar Flats for distance. Dogs are also able to use this trail but must be kept on leash.
Hours And Camping: The area is open year round, weather dependent. There is dispersed camping available in the Opal Creek Wilderness.
Hunting: The Opal Creek Scenic Recreation Area is a no shooting zone. Otherwise all state and federal hunting regulations apply.
name: Opal Creek Wilderness - Willamette National Forest

Description: Three confirmed old growth tracts comprising 171.8 acres have been documented and another 258.2 acres are awaiting confirmation. . The oldest trees in the surveyed stands include a Table Mountain pine established in 1678 and a chestnut oak established in 1718. The 340 year old Table Mt. pine is the longest lived individual of the species known. Trees greater than 30 inches in diameter include chestnut oak, white oak, northern red oak, and black oak. The understory is predominantly comprised of chestnut oak and black oak seedlings, as well as a high dominance of ericaceous vegetation such as great rhododendron, mountain laurel, blueberry, bear oak, and deerberry. Old growth characteristics such as a structurally complex canopy and abundance of tree cavities provide optimal habitat for the largest summer colony of federally threatened Northern long-eared bats in Maryland. The xeric southeast facing upper slope and ridge crest supports an upland oak-pine, formerly oak-American chestnut –pine community.
Navigation:
These directions get you to the summit overlook by car: Take I-68 to Frostburg, Maryland. Get off on Route 36 and head south. At about 4 miles you will see signs on the right for Dans Rock. Take a left on Old Dans Rock Road. Old chestnut/red oak forest can be observed along Dans Rock Rd. approaching the ridge crest when entering the WMA just prior to reaching a tower array along the crest. Continue following Dans Rock Rd. to the ridge crest and into the tower arrays. Near the end of the tower array is a small parking area on the right with a picnic table and metal handrail. Park and follow the metal handrail and staircase that leads to overlook platforms. The crest and upper east facing slope of Dans Mt. south of the tower arrays is all within the Dans Mt. WMA Wildland. 
These directions get you to an old-growth forest area: From I-68 in Cumberland take US Rt. 220 South 13.4 miles to the Dans Mt. WMA campground road entrance (Sign at entrance). If gate is open, follow gravel road past metal building and through both yellow gates up mountain 2.6 miles, then left at the “T” intersection, follow dirt/gravel road for .3 mi., old growth will be on right immediately upslope of pulloff/parking along road. No trail is developed in this or any other old growth stand. Note that along the very sharp bend on the wide road coming up the mountain is another old growth forest stand on either side of the road. If gate is closed at US Rt. 220N, park as to not block gate and hike 2.9 miles in to the site. The gate is generally closed from late March until early September and opened for fall and winter hunting season. You may contact the park to find out if the gate will be open.
Parking And Admission: Parking: Limited parking available at Dans Rock Overlook. Accessibility into Dan’s Mt. WMA is variable by season. Park at lower gate (do not block) and hike in along the road to the site from US Rt 220 N during road closure season, approximately from late March to early September. Contact the Western Region Wildlife office for inquiries regarding gate closure periods and access prior to visiting. Admission: No fees.
Trails: No trails traverse any old growth stands at Dans Mt. WMA; however, one stand is bisected by the main road originating in the campground and another stand is adjacent to a road. A hike along the gated road may be necessary if visiting during a closed gate period.
Hours And Camping: Hours: Open dawn to dusk; Camping: limited seasonal camping is available at the designated campground.
name: Dans Mountain Old Growth – Dans Mountain Wildlife Management Area

Description: Parkinson Forest is 261 acres of woods with approximately 60 acres of old-growth. The old-growth portion is dominated by Sugar Maple (Acer saccharum) with American Beech (Fagus grandifolia), White Oak (Quercus alba), Red Oak (Quercus rubra) and Tulip Tree (Liriodendron tulipfera) having an important presence in the canopy. Several of the White Oaks were cored about 40 years ago and were well over 200 years old at that time.
Navigation:
Bethany College, 31 E Campus Dr, Bethany, WV 26032
Drive along E Campus Dr until you see the trailhead sign.
Parking And Admission: Visitor parking is well marked. There is a large visitor parking lot at the bottom of the hill from the trailhead. There is no admission charge.
Trails: The Waterfall and Sutton Trails form an approximately one mile loop. The reservoir trail is approximately 0.5 miles.
Hours And Camping: Parkinson Forest is open to the public year round. Camping is not available.
name: Parkinson Forest

Description: The 42 acre forest is primarily white pine. Belden is known to be at least 120 years old, with some trees possibly much older. Additional data collection and documentation is under way.
Navigation: ADDRESS: 695 Hopmeadow Street, Simsbury, CT - behind Boy Scout Hall. The trailhead is about 50 ft north of Boy Scout Hall. DIRECTIONS: Entrance is located just east of 7 Beldenwood Road, Simsbury. The forest can be accessed from the east side of Beldenwood Road approximately 500 feet east of the intersection with Firetown Road (marked by a white Town open space marker).
Parking And Admission: Parking: There is ample parking next to Boy Scout Hall and a sign that leads to the forest. Additional parking is available at the library and a paved path leads to the Boy Scout Hall parking area and the trailhead. Parking on Beldenwood Road is on-street only. Admission: No admission fee.
Trails: Total distance is less than 2 miles.
Hours And Camping: Hours: Open daylight hours year round. Trails are not maintained regularly. There are no services (no trash, no water, no restrooms). Belden Forest is located in downtown Simsbury with many shops, restaurants, and municipal services within walking distance. No camping.
name: Belden Forest

Description:
The Sharon Land Trust is a community-based nonprofit organization dedicated to preserving the rural heritage of Sharon, Connecticut. Within Litchfield County, three of Sharon Land Trust’s special properties are dedicated into the Old-Growth Forest Network. Each preserve contains forest land that is protected forever from logging so that it may recover to old-growth status. 

Goodbody Preserve comprises 107 acres with 87 acres in forestland. The average forest age is approximately 100 years with occasional trees to greater than 150 years. Mixed conifer and hardwoods prevail. The preserve captures important ridgeline, hilltop, and terrain features in a highly visible location above Mudge Pond in Sharon. The view of this area is considered one of the finest in northwestern Connecticut. 

Hamlin Farm Preserve includes 278 acres with 228 in forest and wetland. The average forest age is approximately 100 years with occasional trees greater than 150 years. Mixed conifer and hardwoods dominate the forest canopy. This preserve also captures an important ridgeline and terrain feature in a highly visible location. 

Sharon Mountain Preserve includes 159 acres. The average forest age is approximately 100 years. The forest is comprised of mixed hardwoods and a core waterfowl wetland.
Trails: Total trail length of 4.3 miles across all three forests.
name: Sharon Land Trust Forests - Litchfield County

Description: Sharing ownership between the Heritage Conservancy and Doylestown Township, Hart’s Woods, with a total of 34 acres, is a climax oak-beechforest, with mature beech, red oak, black oak and white oak species. Some of the oak species, in particular, feature balding bark. Also found are tuliptrees; hickory species, including shagbark and mockernut; and maple species. Also noteworthy on the Heritage Conservancy acreage: One very large red maple near a small tributary of the Neshaminy Creek that is near the park/conservancy property boundary line. Hart’s Woods has a rich history of preservation. The northern 22 acres was gifted to the Heritage Conservancy by George M Hart in 1958. A decade later, in 1968/69, David Benner, a horticulture instructor at Delaware Valley College in Doylestown, led a long, fierce and ultimately successful effort to have the planned Rts. 611/202 bypass re-routed slightly to the north to avoid destroying a significant portion of the woods. The adjoining 12 acres is part of Doylestown Township’s Central Park. Previously owned by nearby Delaware Valley University, Central Park was purchased by Doylestown Township from a developer in 1991 and dedicated and opened as a park in 1995. Hart’s Woods benefits from the larger contiguous acreage to promote its biodiverse eco-system.
Navigation:
Doylestown Township 12 acres: 330 New Britain Road, Doylestown , PA 18901. Park in parking lot and follow paved pathway up to the forest. Heritage Conservancy 22 acres: 2 Morgan Hill Drive, Doylestown, PA 18901
This home is at the intersection of Morgan Hill Drive and New Britain Road; proceed less than a 10th of a mile westward on New Britain Road and pull off onto the road shoulder opposite a small Heritage Conservancy sign that marks the trail entrance. The Heritage Conservancy trailhead is only 0.2 miles from the parking lot at 330 New Britain Road.
Parking And Admission: Doylestown Township: Ample parking at 330 New Britain Road. Heritage Conservancy: Free Admission. Parking is available along the road shoulder on both sides of New Britain Road; there is roughly 100 yards worth of parking along the north side of the road, and about 20 yards worth of parking along the south side of the road
Trails: Doylestown Township: Main recommended trail is a ½-mile loop trail with multiple entry points that loops around inside the perimeter of the rectangular wooded tract, and a .15-mile spur trail that links up with the loop on the northwest side of the tract. Trails that circle the outside of the woods add roughly 0.8 more miles; with a couple small half-circle trails, including a sensory trail, the total trail mileage is approximately 1.4 miles. Heritage Conservancy: Loop trail about 0.4 miles long; only trail in the woods.
Hours And Camping: Doylestown Township: Open year-round dawn to dusk; no camping. Heritage Conservancy: Open year-round dawn to dusk; no camping.
Hunting: Doylestown Township: No hunting; Heritage Conservancy: No, except for extremely limited bowhunting for deer.
name: Hart's Woods

Description:
Clear Fork Gorge is situated along the north bluff of the Clear Fork of the Mohican River. Out of the total of 29 acres in this Nature Preserve, the 8-acre white pine-hemlock forest community here is one of the best remaining woodlands like this in the state. Huge native white pines and eastern hemlocks grow on the steep sides of the gorge wall. Other tree species include sycamore, beech, ash, tulip, oak and maple. 

The Clear Fork Gorge was declared a National Natural Landmark in 1967. In addition, after passage of the Natural Areas Act in 1970, the Ohio Department of Natural Resources began the task of acquiring and dedicating State Nature Preserves. In 1976, the Natural Areas Act was amended to create the Division of Natural Areas and Preserves. The 29 acres comprising the preserve were transferred from the Division of Parks and Watercraft to the Division of Natural Areas and Preserves in 1997.
Navigation:
Address: ODNR Mohican Park Rd 51, Perrysville, OH. 
Directions: To access the preserve, park at the Mohican fire tower on the south side of State Forest Road 51. The trailhead is located across the street from the fire tower parking area on the north side of State Forest Road 51. When the trail forks, turn right and travel approximately 1/10 of a mile to reach the preserve sign and kiosk. State Forest Road 51 is accessible from State Route 97.
Parking And Admission:
Parking: To access the preserve, park at the Mohican fire tower on the south side of State Forest Road 51. 
Admission: no admission charge.
Trails: An approximately 1/3 mile long trail is present at the preserve which traverses the hillside overlooking the Clear Fork. Visitors will walk through the white pine-hemlock forest community – one of the best examples of this woodland type remaining in Ohio.
Hours And Camping:
Hours: Open year-round. 
Camping: While camping is not permitted within the state nature preserve, a lodge, cabins, campground, and park-and-pack camping are all available within the Mohican-Memorial State Forest and the Mohican State Park. For reservation information, go to the following websites: http://forestry.ohiodnr.gov/mohican and http://parks.ohiodnr.gov/mohican.
name: Clear Fork Gorge State Nature Preserve

Description: Muddy Pond Wilderness Preserve is 322 acres, including a 48-acre Coastal Plain Pond and 273 acres of forestland. The forest at Muddy Pond Wilderness Preserve is an Atlantic Coastal Pine Barrens; the dominant tree species are pitch pine and several types of oak. While it is not yet an old-growth forest, the Atlantic Coastal Pine Barrens are home to rare and diverse flora and fauna. The forest offers habitat for birds of prey, waterfowl, songbirds, amphibians, reptiles, fish, and more. Depending on the time of year, a hiker might spot insects that are unique to this ecosystem, such as the Pine Barrens Bluet and the threatened Water Willow Borer. Or, they may get to see the blossoms of the rare Plymouth gentian or the globally endangered New England boneset. Throughout the forest there are more than 25 verified vernal pools, which give life to an abundance of frogs, toads, salamanders, and insects each spring. Northeast Wilderness Trust is working with Massachusetts Natural Heritage Endangered Species Program to evaluate other potential vernal pools on the land.
Navigation:
200 Bishops Highway, Kingston MA
Look for a small parking lot with a cedar split rail fence and preserve signs on the north side of the road, about a half-mile west of Sacred Heart Elementary School.
Parking And Admission: Parking is located on Bishop’s Highway, a half-mile west of Sacred Heart Elementary School. There are no entrance fees. There is room for about five cars; when the parking lot is full, the Preserve is full and parking along the road is not allowed. This policy helps preserve the wild character of this place.
Trails:
Recommended hike – Pond Loop (a 2.3 mile hike, roundtrip)
Total mileage of all trails – 2.5 miles
Hours And Camping: Muddy Pond Wilderness Preserve is open to the public year-round, from dawn to dusk. Camping is prohibited.
Hunting: Hunting and fishing are not allowed at Muddy Pond Wilderness Preserve
name: Muddy Pond Wilderness Preserve

Description: Within the Giant Forest sequoia grove are some of the finest sequoias in the world, including the largest tree on Earth, the General Sherman Tree. Trails here lead to historic features that include a cabin built into a fallen giant, and to examples of the sequoia’s complex relationship with fire. Named in 1875 by John Muir, the forest covers over 1,800 acres. The rounded tops of mature monarch sequoias dominate the overstory of the grove, with sugar pines, incense cedars, and white firs competing for light below.
Navigation: Address: Giant Forest Museum, Sequoia National Park, 47050 Generals Hwy, Three Rivers, CA 93271 (about 1 hour north of the park’s Ash Mountain entrance at 47050 Generals Hwy, Three Rivers, CA 93271.) Once at the museum, view the hands-on exhibits and browse the Sequoia Parks Conservancy’s bookstore. Here you may also pick up free Junior Ranger books. You may want to check for Ranger programs or ask a ranger questions.
Parking And Admission: There is a park entrance fee. Parking is available throughout the Giant Forest. On busy weekends during the summer parking is limited. A free shuttle is available from Memorial Day to Labor Day to transport visitors from the campgrounds, Wuksachi Lodge and Lodgepole to the General Sherman Tree and the Giant Forest Museum.
Trails: Giant Forest has an extensive network of hiking trails that range from 1-2 hour hikes to half-day or longer explorations of this grove. Descriptions of hiking trails are found at this website: https://www.nps.gov/seki/planyourvisit/gfdayhikesum.htm or pick up a trail map at the Giant Forest Museum. Install the free Sequoia and Kings Canyon mobile app for more trip-planning information. Search for NPS Sequoia & Kings Canyon.
Hours And Camping: The park is open year-round.
name: The Giant Forest - Sequoia National Park

Description: Fall Creek Falls State Park encompasses almost 30,000 acres across the top of the Cumberland Plateau. Within the park is the 16,181-acre Fall Creek Falls State Natural Area. Here old-growth trees are mostly located in the mixed Mesophytic cove forest found in the gorges formed by several creeks which flow into Cane Creek and feed the 256-foot Fall Creek Falls, the highest waterfall in the Eastern US. Estimates of old growth range from 20 to 200 acres (Davis 2003, cited in Riddle & Blozen, Bulletin of the Eastern Native Tree Society, 2007). Tree species include white basswood, American beech, green ash, yellow buckeye, Eastern hemlock, bitternut and shagbark hickory, and tuliptree. According to Riddle & Blozen, the 146.7-ft green ash is the second tallest known while the beeches “may constitute one of the tallest known groves in the southeast”.
Navigation:
Address: 2009 Village Camp Rd, Spencer, TN 38585. 
Directions: When you enter Fall Creek Falls State Park you will need to follow the signs to the main Fall Creek Falls overlook located on the scenic loop in the park. The trailhead is located on the left of the overlook, there is a sign that says “Base of the Falls Trail”
Parking And Admission:
Admission: There is free admission to the park. 
Parking: Parking available at the Visitor Center, Nature Center, and Fall Creek Falls overlook and trailhead.
Trails: There are over 56 miles of hiking trails throughout the park. One can drive and park close to the Fall Creek Falls overlook and trailhead. The trail to the base of the Falls is .35 miles with a natural surface and is moderate to difficult. The Overlook Trail, which overlooks Cane Creek, is .65 miles.
Hours And Camping: Hours: The park is open 24 hours with the road leading to the falls being locked at dark. Camping: There are 10 cabins and 222 RV and tent campsites. Most sites have tables, grills, water and electricity and are served by seven bathhouses. Ninety-two sites have sewer connections. Call 800-250-8611 for camping reservations. There are also two group lodges.
name: Fall Creek Falls Natural Area - Fall Creek Falls State Park

Description: Eagles Nest is a Bald Cypress forest in the midst of the Dragon Run Swamp and is comprised of 39 acres of wetlands and forest. Logging here was stopped over 40 years ago though some segments of the property may not have been logged. In 1976, The Nature Conservancy joined with the Chesapeake Bay Foundation to commission a Smithsonian Institution study of 232 rivers and streams in the Chesapeake Bay watershed. Dragon Run ranked second in terms of ecological significance. The Dragon wilderness covers 12,600 square miles of the Chesapeake Bay region.
Navigation: This area is best reached by taking a tour offered by the Friends of Dragon Run. Tours are given to 12 people a day, 7 days a week, from April 15- May 20th; and the last two weeks in October. Boats and all gear are provided free of charge (a donation is welcomed; $50 suggested). Guides accompany each group. Groups meet at the Food Lion in Saluda, 12532 Tidewater Trail, Saluda, VA 23149. Sign up for tours at www.Dragonrun.org
Parking And Admission: Closest public parking is about 3 miles away. The property is reachable by canoe or kayak. Friends of Dragon Run, in the fall and the spring, guide tours of the Dragon by kayak. Though there is not an admission charge a suggested donation is requested for each person. The Friends of Dragon Run provide the kayaks, paddles, personal floatation devices vests, tour guide and paddle crew for the guided paddle tours.
Trails: .6 miles of land trails and approximately .6 mile of water trails.
Hours And Camping: The property is open seasonally for guided kayak tours and very occasional land tours through the wetlands. Access is via water, and launch areas are generally from property owned and managed by Friends of Dragon Run or The Nature Conservancy. No camping is available.
Hunting: Friends of Dragon Run, Inc. has on occasion leased lands to hunt clubs for hunting to include this property, under restrictions.
name: Eagles Nest on the Dragon Run

Description: Big Island is a Bald Cypress forest and is comprised of 203 acres of wetlands and forest in the midst of the Dragon Run Swamp. Logging was stopped over 50 years ago though some segments of the property may not have ever been logged. One Bald Cypress in particular is estimated to be over one thousand years old and when last measured fifteen years ago (2004) was over 22.5 feet in circumference. In 1976, The Nature Conservancy joined with the Chesapeake Bay Foundation to commission a Smithsonian Institution study of 232 rivers and streams in the Chesapeake Bay watershed. Dragon Run ranked second in terms of ecological significance. The Dragon wilderness covers 12,600 square miles of the Chesapeake Bay region.
Navigation: This area is best reached by taking a tour offered by the Friends of Dragon Run. Tours are given to 12 people a day, 7 days a week, from April 15- May 20th; and the last two weeks in October. Boats and all gear are provided free of charge (a donation is welcomed; $50 suggested). Guides accompany each group. Groups meet at the Food Lion in Saluda, 12532 Tidewater Trail, Saluda, VA 23149. Sign up for tours at www.Dragonrun.org
Parking And Admission: Closest public parking is about 3 miles away. The property is reachable by canoe or kayak. Friends of Dragon Run, in the fall and the spring, guide tours of the Dragon by kayak and occasionally by hiking once on the island. Though there is not an admission charge, a suggested donation is requested for each person. The Friends of Dragon Run provide the kayaks, paddles, personal floatation devices vests, tour guide and paddle crew for the guided paddle tours.
Trails: 1.3 miles of land trails and approximately 1.1 mile of water trails.
Hours And Camping: The island is open seasonally for guided kayak tours and occasional land tours. Access is via water and launch areas are generally from property owned and managed by Friends of Dragon Run. One primitive campsite is available.
Hunting: Friends of Dragon Run, Inc. currently leases lands to hunt clubs for hunting to include this property.
name: Big Island on the Dragon Run

Description: In its 729 acres, Voorhees Nature Preserve offers trails with scenic views of the Rappahannock River, including two overlook spots, and a foot bridge across Owl Hollow Creek. The preserve is adjacent to the Rappahannock River Valley National Wildlife Refuge, which the Nature Conservancy has worked to expand with help from diverse partners. A mature hardwood forest covers the uplands. Flowering wetland plants enliven Owl Hollow marsh, especially during springtime. The diverse terrain and aquatic features support an abundance of wildlife including old growth trees, bald eagles, beavers, foxes, turkeys, diverse flowering plants and an array of amphibians.
Navigation: 648 Bristol Mine Rd, Colonial Beach, VA 22443
Parking And Admission: The parking lot holds eight cars. There is no admission charge
Trails: Over four miles of easy-to-moderate trails. For a current trail map go to: https://www.nature.org/content/dam/tnc/nature/en/documents/voorhees-trail-map-may14.pdf. There is also a trail map posted at the entrance.
Hours And Camping: Voorhees Preserve is open dawn to dusk, year round. No camping.
Hunting: Managed deer hunts are conducted by a hunt club that leases the property.
name: Voorhees Nature Preserve

Description: Within Landis Arboretum are 30 acres of old-growth forest whose trees range from 150-300 years old. Two trails wind through the forest. The Ancient Forest Trail is home to many white and red oaks, yellow birch, sugar maple, eastern hemlock, American beech, black birch, hop hornbeam, American basswood, bitternut hickory, and paper birch. The oldest trees along this trail are eastern hemlocks at 200-300 years old. The Woodland Trail is dominated by eastern hemlock, white and red oaks, yellow birch, sugar maple, American beech, black birch, hop hornbeam, and American basswood. It is notable for its massive, old oaks estimated to be 250-300 years old and is a good example of a northeastern old-growth forest.
Navigation: Address: 174 Lape Rd, Esperance NY 12066
Parking And Admission: Parking is free, and we recommend parking in our main parking lot. Across the street from this parking lot are our offices, located in the farmhouse, our barn and our library and greenhouse.
Trails:
Woodland Trail: Approximately 1 mile loop trail from main parking lot.
Ancient Forest Trail: Approximately 2 miles round trip from the main parking lot
Total distance of all trails: 10 miles
Hours And Camping: Hours: Grounds are open daily from dawn to dusk, year round, free of charge though donations are greatly appreciated.
name: Ancient Forest Trail and Woodland Trail - George Landis Arboretum

Description:
The 913-acre Deer Run Nature Preserve spans the Dummerston, Newfane and Brookline areas of Windham County, Vermont. It is not an old-growth forest, but it is being preserved to become one in the future.

This land is one of the last remaining unfragmented large parcels in the region. It is remarkable for its tall hardwoods, hemlock-filled ravines, stunning views, stone walls and a curious rock structure known as “the monument.” It includes deer wintering yards and a variety of forest types including hardwood savannas and hemlock “cathedrals.” There are several wetlands and vernal pools that host a variety of amphibians including the rare Jefferson Salamander.

The significant features of this land include panoramic views from the highest elevations, topographic benches left behind by a series of glaciations and by more recent flooding events, cliffs created by uplift and continental collisions eons ago, a dramatic and active landslide area, numerous rich forest sites including a cove with incredibly tall trees including shagbark hickories, There are forests of all ages, large maple, oak, ash, hickory, hemlock, and white pine trees, and grasslands that provide nesting sites for numerous bird species and corridors for wildlife and species movement, adaptability, and resiliency.

Two transmission lines cross the preserve, which ecologists and botanists recognize as valuable early-successional/shrub-scrub habitat that these rights-of-way provide.
Navigation:
Address: 940 Camp Arden Road, Dummerston, VT 05301
The fenced parking area and trailhead are just beyond 940 Camp Arden Road on the same side of the street.
Parking And Admission: There is a small parking area (6 cars) at the trailhead. There is no admission charge. Donations are welcome. Maps and donation envelopes are in a mailbox at the trailhead.
Trails: Total distance of all trails: 2.4 miles one way (4.8 out and back) with new trails opening Fall 2022.
Hours And Camping: Open dawn to dusk, year round. No camping.
Hunting: Yes, with written permission. Apply at greenmountainconservancy.org.
name: Deer Run Nature Preserve

Description:
Within the Schoharie Land Trust's 342-acre Paulson Preserve, lies the Paulson Preserve Old-Growth Forest, an 80+-acre forest of mixed hardwoods and conifers including stands of large hemlock trees. The forest is reverting from former farm fields and contains stone walls and an abandoned road that provides public access to the property. There are also active beaver ponds on the property in addition to beaver meadows that contribute to the variety of wildlife and flora present on the land. The relatively undisturbed and remote quality of the preserve allows good opportunities for wildlife observation. Designation of this forest as “old-growth” means it will never be logged or otherwise altered except to allow public access. It will take generations before the forest reaches its climax as truly old-growth, but the Schoharie Land Trusthas started the process with vision and commitment for those who will come after us. The entire Paulson Preserve is open to the public, with access from Rum Hill Road in Jefferson, and from Baldwin Road in Summit.

The Baldwin Road access provides an easy walk along an abandoned town road through second growth woods to a series of beaver ponds. 
 
The Rum Hill Road trailhead, marked “Beaver Trail,” is a more winding downhill trail to the same beaver ponds, but does not connect to the Baldwin Road trail. Woods here are more mature--a mix of maple, beech, pine and various undergrowth shrubs. A stand of large hemlocks can be found at the lower end of the series of beaver ponds.
Navigation:
Rum Hill Road Trailhead Address: 219 Rum Hill Rd, Jefferson, NY 
From Cobleskill, take State Rte. 10 south to Peraglie Road. Turn left on Rum Hill Road to the main entrance of Paulson Preserve. Parking is about one mile at the end of the road. A short distance from the entrance is a sign marked "Beaver Trail."

Baldwin Road Trailhead Address: 283 Baldwin Road, Jefferson, NY
The trailhead is approximately 1 mile from the intersection of State Route 10 and Baldwin Road. Parking is along the road, by a "Schoharie Land Trust" sign. The trail is an abandoned town road.
Parking And Admission: Free parking for 12-18 cars; no admission fee.
Trails:
“Beaver Trail” at Rum Hill Road access: 0.4 miles
Baldwin Road access: 0.2 miles
Total distance of all trails in the preserve: 1.6 miles
Hours And Camping: We neither prohibit nor encourage camping.
name: Paulson Preserve Old-Growth Forest

Description:
Drift Creek Wilderness (5,798 acres) is located in the Oregon Coast Range where towering Douglas fir, western red cedar, Sitka spruce and western hemlock that sometimes reach seven feet in diameter shade the Coast Range’s largest rainforest stand of old growth. At the wilderness’s upper reaches, giant Douglas firs dominate the skyline. Spruces and hemlocks thrive on the flatter, boggier ground near Drift Creek. Western red cedars are also common in this forest and when left alone, as they are in the Drift Creek Wilderness, Pacific Northwest cedars can live to be over a thousand years old. If possible, look up at the cedar crowns, if one has a candelabra crown and a big wide base then it is an old tree, maybe a very old tree. The steep canyons of Drift Creek may give the impression of mountainous county, but the forested hills rise only slightly above 2000 feet. 

Lobaria is a light green and pale algae with a rubbery consistency that grows in the big conifers of the Pacific Northwest. Hikers will see Lobaria lying on the ground only in the old, unlogged portion of the forest. Lobaria captures nitrogen from the atmosphere and then when it blows to the ground and decomposes, transfers that nitrogen to the soil.

Numerous species of mushrooms are hidden and not so hidden in this forest. There are large stumps and massive root structures along the trail that are covered in mosses, lichens and mushrooms. Bring your magnifying glass and your curiosity and explore these fascinating micro-environments. 

Soaked by as much as 120 inches of annual rainfall, moss and ferns as thick as six inches cushion the ground along numerous streams shadowed by overhanging bigleaf maples. 

Roosevelt elk and black bears share this lush territory along with northern spotted owl, woodpeckers, bald eagles, forest wrens, woodpeckers, banana slugs, crayfish, dragonflies, kingfishers, newts, salamanders and many others. In the fall, Drift Creek comes alive with spawning chinook and coho salmon, as well as steelhead and cutthroat trout.
Navigation:
Address: 1130 Forestry Lane, Waldport, OR
Directions: From the south: the Harris Ranch trailhead is located 2 miles north of Highway 34 and is the portal to the southern half of the wilderness area.
Note: The last mile of “road” to the trailhead is extremely full of potholes. Lower clearance vehicles might get into trouble. Drive slow and know that some of the water filled potholes are deep!
Parking And Admission:
Parking: near Harris Ranch trailhead.

Admission: Day use pass required in many areas. Go here to learn more: https://www.fs.usda.gov/main/siuslaw/passes-permits/recreation#passes
Trails: Harris Ranch Trail to Drift Creek is a 5.5 mile moderately trafficked out and back trail located near Waldport, Oregon that features a river and is rated as moderate. The trail is best used from May until October. Dogs are also able to use this trail but must be kept on leash. https://www.alltrails.com/trail/us/oregon/harris-ranch-trail-to-drift-creek
Hours And Camping: Hours: unrestricted. Check website in advance. Camping: allowed - please see guidelines here: https://bit.ly/DriftCreekCamping
name: Drift Creek Wilderness - Siuslaw National Forest

Description:
The initial 2,860 acres of the park was purchased in 1986 in order to preserve several outstanding natural and cultural features. In addition to surrounding one of the world’s largest and deepest springs, the forest holds a number of old growth trees, including virgin bald cypress, some ranging from 400-600 years old, as well as more than a dozen past and current state and national champion trees. The park contains 12 distinct natural communities within the Gulf Coastal Lowlands. Approximately 42% of this area is Upland Hardwood Forest with some of the oldest and most beautiful American beech-southern magnolia climax forest to be found in the South. Approximately 43% of this area is Upland Pine Forest which has previously seen disturbance in the way of fire exclusion, turpentining, logging and agricultural practices. Since 1986, however, park staff have promoted natural growth, prescribed fire and some planting of longleaf pine seedlings. The remaining area is comprised of springs, sinks, river, sloughs, floodplain swamps, and floodplain forests.
After the damage caused during Hurricane Michael and the decimation of the old growth hardwood forests in nearby State Parks like Torreya, Florida Caverns, and Three Rivers, it makes what we have left at Wakulla that much more important to recognize and protect.
Navigation:
465 Wakulla Park Drive Crawfordville, FL 32327

Within the park, the trailhead can be found at the southwest edge of the parking area for the Lodge.
Parking And Admission: There is ample parking. Park Admission is $6 per vehicle for up to 8 people or $4 for a single-occupant vehicle or motorcycle.
Trails: The park has 6.9 miles of trail. The Sally Ward Trail is a 6-mile linear trail and provides. Hikers must hike out and back. A shorter, 0.9-mile loop called the Hammock Spur Trail is also available.
Hours And Camping: The park is open every day of the year from 8am-sunset. There is no camping available, however a 27 guest room, historic Lodge is available for overnight accommodations
name: Legacy Property - Edward Ball Wakulla Springs State Park

Description:
Nestled in beautiful pine flatwoods, the park is the perfect area for nature studies. Of special interest is the endangered red-cockaded woodpecker that nests in the cavities of the park’s mature pine trees. Small grass ponds, bayheads and oak thickets are diverse habitats for the park’s wide variety of wildlife. Deer, fox squirrel, bobcat, gray fox and numerous species of birds are commonly seen. Patient park visitors may be rewarded with a glimpse of white squirrels, a rare color variant of the Eastern gray squirrel. Florida black bears, gopher tortoises, fox squirrels and snowy egrets are other threatened or endangered species that call the park home. Rare plant species, such as wiregrass gentian and ladies tresses (a rare orchid with spiraling fragrant flowers), may be seen in the spring. Colorful wildflowers living in the pine flatwoods, such as meadow-beauty and yellow-eyed grass, depend on fires to survive and flourish.

Pine flatwoods, named for the flat monotonous topography shaped by fire, is the park’s most significant natural community. A prescribed burning program mimics the natural fire cycle and provides healthy ecosystems.
Navigation: 429 State Park Rd, Sopchoppy, FL 32358
Parking And Admission: $4/vehicle. Parking is available at the end of entrance road at the Scenic Drive Parking Area.
Trails:
The Pine Flatwoods Trail leaves from the west end of the Scenic Drive parking area and extends through the central forest of the park. The trail will eventually split, leading North to the Secnic Drive hiking/biking trail or south to the paved portion of the Scenic Drive. Both paths can be walked back to the trailhead parking area along either the Scenic Drive Trail or paved Scenic Drive.

The Pine Flatwoods Trail is at times flooded. The hiking/biking Scenic Loop Trail also begins from the Northeast corner of the Scenic Drive parking area and will take you through the Pine Flatwoods. This trail will loop back around to the paved Scenic Drive, which can be walked back to the parking area.

See the park map for more details. A trail map is posted at the Pine Flatwoods Trailhead.

https://www.floridastateparks.org/sites/default/files/media/file/Ochlockonee_River_0318_web.pdf
Hours And Camping:
8 am until sundown; 365 days a year.

The park is equipped with a 30-site campground with three accessible sites. All 30 sites have 50-amp service, water hookups, fire ring, picnic table and clothesline. A dump station is provided for your convenience. The comfort station located within the campground provides restrooms and hot showers, an outside sink for washing dishes, and water fountains.

One campsite is available for hammock camping (site #14). It can be reserved through ReserveAmerica. It has one three-hammock hanging structure on it. It is the only hammock accessible campsite in our campground due to the live oak canopy.

Maximum RV length = 40 ft.

 Reservations can be made up to 11 months in advance through ReserveAmerica(https://floridastateparks.reserveamerica.com/camping/ochlockonee-river-sp/r/campgroundDetails.do?contractCode=FL&parkId=281059). Book online or call 800-326-3521 (8 a.m. to 8 p.m.) or TDD 888-433-0287
name: Ochlockonee River State Park

Description: Bard College's South Woods Old-Growth Forest is 70-acres of untouched old-growth forest, one of only five remaining virgin forests within several hundred miles of NYC. Follow the 1-mile South Woods Trail, an old carriage road, and you will see ancient hemlocks, old oaks and maples plus young beech and pine trees as the land slopes down to the Hudson River’s edge. The oldest tree on the property has been dated to 1735. According to Jacquetta Haley in 1989, South Woods might be the “oldest oak forest in the Hudson Valley” (Wikipedia; J. Haley 1989).
Navigation: Address: 26 Gardener Way, River Rd, Red Hook, NY 12571
Parking And Admission: The Montgomery Place grounds are open every day from dawn to dusk free of charge. Please park only in the Visitors Center parking lot. See website during COVID for the latest updates. https://www.bard.edu/montgomeryplace/
Trails: South Woods Trail: 1-mile from parking area to Hudson River (2 miles out and back). Historically, there were side trails that shot off main trail. Most of these have become overgrown.
Hours And Camping: The Montgomery Place grounds are open every day from dawn to dusk. No camping. See website during COVID for the latest updates. https://www.bard.edu/montgomeryplace/
name: South Woods Old-Growth Forest - Bard College, Montgomery Place Campus

Description: John Ripley Forbes Big Trees Forest Preserve is a beautiful and unique 30-acre Fulton County Tree, Plant and Wildlife Sanctuary. An oasis in a bustling city, the forest is the perfect setting for a quiet afternoon stroll. It also serves as an outdoor classroom for those looking to take a self-guided nature walk. Grab a trail guide brochure at the entrance to the forest and follow the 15-stop watershed education tour to learn about the positive and negative effects humans have on water quality and the forest community. The forest contains old oaks, beech, and sourwood trees among other hardwoods up to 150 years old, with a 50-foot white oak as the largest.
Navigation:
7645 Roswell Road, Sandy Springs, GA 30350.

 The Forest is located about 4 miles north of I-285 in the northern metro – Atlanta community of Sandy Springs, Georgia, next to the North Fulton County Government Annex building at 7645 Roswell Road.
Parking And Admission: There is ample free parking. Free admission.
Trails: Trail descriptions can be found at http://www.bigtreesforest.com/learn.html
Hours And Camping: The Forest is open sunrise to sunset, seven days each week. Camping is prohibited.
name: Big Trees Forest Preserve Inc

Description: McConnells Mill State Park contains 2,546 acres the vast majority being comprised of forested areas. Much of the forested areas on the steep slopes of the gorge are believed to be old growth or very old secondary growth. The eastern hemlock is the dominant species in much of the park forest, however a mixture of hardwoods including oak, beech and maple are found throughout the mixed Mesophytic forest type. Several trees are known to be at or near state records, including a sugar maple and cucumber magnolia. According to the park resource management plan, written in 1998, some of the older growth hemlock trees are estimated between 154-251 years old at that time and measuring 13 to 23 inches in diameter.
Navigation: Address: For GPS devices, use the following address: 1761 McConnells Mill Road, Portersville, PA 16051.Directions: The park is about 40 miles north of Pittsburgh, via I-79. near the intersection of PA 19 and US 422. From US 422 west, the park entrance is on the left less than one half mile north from the intersection of PA 19.
Parking And Admission: The Kildoo Picnic Area is a large parking area from which most trails in the park can be accessed. Parking areas at Hells Hollow and Breakneck Bridge can reach capacity on most weekends. There is no admission fee to visit the park.
Trails:
The following trails all pass through old-growth forest: Alpha Pass Trail: 1.5 miles, Kildoo Trail: 3 mile loop, Hells Hollow trail: .5 mile, Slippery Rock Gorge Trail: 6.2 miles

11.2 miles of hiking trails total.
Hours And Camping:
Hours: The park is open every day of the year, sunrise to sunset. Day use areas close at dusk.

Camping: No camping is permitted.
Hunting: Approximately 65% of the park is open to hunting in the southern and western areas of the park. Refer to the park guide found at www.visitPAparks.com for a color-coded map.
name: McConnells Mill State Park

Description: This lovely city-owned park is a delight for all the senses. The park covers 425 acres of which 330 acres is forested. Hilly terrain and stream ravines provide habitat for many different tree species. Large hemlocks, oaks, beech, maple, and sycamore (to name a few) create a lovely, shaded setting for the carpets of spring wildflowers below. Sadly, most of the large ash trees have died from the borer and their decaying remains are surrounded by younger ash trees. Although this may not be a ‘virgin’ forest (the oldest trees are approximately 200 years old) it should certainly be considered ‘old-growth.’ The rich soils and good drainage allow for large, healthy tree specimens, and the structure of the forest creates excellent habitat for the many species that live here. There are numerous shallow stream crossings, so wear waterproof boots or be prepared to get your feet wet.
Navigation: Address: 4316 Saint Anthony Road, Coldwater, OH 45828Directions: Head west on OH-219 W/E Main St toward S 2nd St, Turn right onto Burkettsville-St Henry Rd/Burk St Henry Rd. Turn right onto St Anthony Rd. Entrance will be on the right.
Parking And Admission: Two small parking lots are available off Silver Road seven days a week, and additional weekend parking is available in a larger parking lot off Silver Road. Free admission.
Trails:
There are over 11 miles of trails throughout the Park. Three of the most popular trails are the Spangler Trail, Trillium Trail and Outer Trail. Large, mature trees can be seen along these trails. The Spangler Trail, a 1.6 mile loop of moderate difficulty named after original Park donor Paul Spangler takes you from upland forest into the wooded valley, then climbs the steep hemlock-lined ridge and traverses sandstone ledges, an old farm field and upland forest (note: the trail crosses the Run 6 times (no bridges). The Trillium Trail is a 1-mile loop trail that follows the Rathburn Run valley and steep hemlock ridges south of the Run. In spring, masses of large-flowered trillium and other native wildflowers cover the valley floor and hillsides. The 3-mile Outer Trail is one of the most difficult trails in the Park and traverses the hemlock-lined ridges, valley, and side ravines of Rathburn Run (note: the trail crosses the Run 2 times (no bridges).

A trail map can be found at https://www.friendsofwmp.com/trail-map and can be downloaded to your phone.
Hours And Camping: Trails are open dawn-dusk. Camping is not permitted.
name: Wooster Memorial Park

Description: Baker Woods is one of the best remaining old-growth forest remnants in northwest Ohio. Total acreage for this site is 47 acres with approximately 42 of these being old-growth. There are numerous large trees including shagbark and shellbark hickories, bur, swamp white, white and chinquapin oaks, which dominate the forest canopy. This site is legally preserved as a wet oak-maple forest community with some sections dominated by an oak-maple swamp community. Some of the larger trees at this site are estimated to be upwards of 150- 200 years old. Portions of the preserve are wet through most of the year. The best times to visit are in autumn when it is relatively dry and mosquito-free or in early spring as the wildflowers are blooming.
Navigation: Address: 4316 Saint Anthony Road, Coldwater, OH 45828Directions: Head west on OH-219 W/E Main St toward S 2nd St, Turn right onto Burkettsville-St Henry Rd/Burk St Henry Rd. Turn right onto St Anthony Rd. Entrance will be on the right.
Parking And Admission: Parking: For about 6 cars. Admission: None
Trails: 1.3-mile loop hiking trail
Hours And Camping: Hours: Open 1/2 before sunrise to 1/2 hour after sunset. Camping: Camping or staying overnight are not allowed in state nature preserves or natural areas.
Hunting: Public hunting is not permitted in state nature preserves or natural areas. There are lottery deer hunts on select state nature preserves. The preserves included in the lottery hunts changes year to year so please visit the Division's webpage or contact the Division at 614-265-6453.
name: Baker Woods State Nature Preserve

Description:
Although small in size (49 acres with approximately 40 acres being old-growth) and very flat, Gross Memorial Woods is one of the least disturbed old-growth woods in west-central Ohio and one of the few mixed-species swamp forests remaining in this part of the state. The age of largest trees is estimated to be upwards of 150-200 years old.

The woods are characterized by a diversity of tree species, with no one type being dominant. Large bur oaks and basswood occur in the wettest areas, with shagbark hickory, white and red oaks, black walnut, beech and sugar maple on slightly drier ground. The large ash trees have succumbed to the emerald ash borer insect. The forest has a lovely display of spring wildflowers and the brilliant of autumn colors.
Navigation: Address: 19575 Botkins Road, Jackson Center, OH 45334. Directions: From Route 274, Head north on OH-65 N/S Main St toward W Pike for 2 miles, turn left onto Botkins Rd, go 2.9 miles, entrance will be on your right.
Parking And Admission: Parking: limited. Admission: none
Trails: 0.5 mile of hiking trails. Stay on designated trails. Pets are not permitted.
Hours And Camping: Hours: Open 1/2 hour before sunrise to 1/2 hour after sunset. Camping: Camping or staying overnight are not allowed in state nature preserves or natural areas.
Hunting: Public hunting is not permitted in state nature preserves or natural areas. There are lottery deer hunts on select state nature preserves. The preserves included in the lottery hunts changes year to year so please visit the Division's webpage or contact the Division at 614-265-6453.
name: Gross Memorial Woods State Nature Preserve

Description: This mature mixed mesophytic forest woodland has numerous large tulip trees, sugar maple, ash and oak as well as an excellent array of spring wildflowers. The preserve is a total of 103 acres with approximately 90 acres being old-growth. Of these large trees, some of the tulip trees sampled were noted to be 145 years old and one of the larger red oak sampled were 111 years old. The rolling topography of this site is indicative of glacial moraine deposited after the last glacial event.
Navigation: Address: 7661 Lonesome Road, St. Paris, OH 43072. Directions: Located in Champaign County 7 miles west of Urbana on U.S. Route 36. Proceed 1 mile north on Neal Road, 1/2 mile west on Smith Road, and northwest on Lonesome Road to the preserve entrance.
Parking And Admission: Parking: small parking lot. Admission: none
Trails: A nicely maintained 1.5 mile “figure eight” two-loop trail system with gentle topography changes.
Hours And Camping: Hours: Open ½ hour before sunrise to ½ hour after sunset. Camping: Camping or staying overnight are not allowed in state nature preserves or natural areas.
Hunting: Public hunting is not permitted in state nature preserves or natural areas. There are lottery deer hunts on select state nature preserves. The preserves included in the lottery hunts changes year to year so please visit the Division's webpage or contact the Division at 614-265-6453.
name: Davey Woods State Nature Preserve

Description: Located within Hueston Woods State Park, this state nature preserve protects 200 acres of virgin forest! Hueston Woods is a remnant of the beech-maple forest that once stretched in a broad band from southwestern Ohio to its northeastern corner. This forest is dominated by towering beech trees along with varying proportions of sugar maple, red and white oaks, and white ash. In Hueston Woods State Nature Preserve, beech trees form nearly 44 percent of the canopy, sugar maples make up 28 percent and white ashes 19 percent. Many tulip trees here are around 100 years old. Many of the beech trees are over 200 years old and 1 beech tree sampled was found to be approximately 300 years old. During the spring, the forest floor is blanketed with a luxuriant display of wildflowers including dutchman's breeches, squirrel corn, large-flowered and sessile trilliums, may-apple, bloodroot and several species of violets and buttercups. Rolling topography, streams, and well-maintained trails complete the delightful experience of visiting this old-growth forest. Based on the work and writings of Mary Byrd Davis (1936 - 2011), this unique parcel is estimated to be ~ 5% of all remaining old-growth in the state of Ohio.
Navigation: Address: Head toward 5201 Lodge Road, College Corner, Ohio 45003. As you enter Hueston Woods State Park you will be on a Loop Road around the lake. Follow the Loop Road to the Big Woods parking area (south side of the lake). Directions: From North of Dayton: Take I-70 West to St Rt 127 South (Exit #10). Turn left onto 127 South, follow through Eaton to Camden, to St Route 725 West. Turn right onto St. Rt 725. Go approximately 5 miles to St. Rt. 732 South. Turn left onto St Rt 732. Follow St Rt 732 to the park entrance. From Cincinnati: take 1-75 North to I-275 West to US 27 (Colerain Ave). Turn right onto US-27 North. Follow US-27 into Oxford. In the center of town, turn right onto St. Rt 732 North. Follow St. Rt 732 to the park entrance.
Parking And Admission: Parking: Ample parking. 3 parking lots. Big Woods Lot, Brown Road Lot and Blue Heron Lot. Admission: none
Trails: The Big Woods Trail (0.7 MI) is great for viewing large old trees and this is where many of the trees from the sample are located. Total trail length for all trails in the preserve is approximately 3 miles. This trail is part of the American Discovery Trail.
Hours And Camping: Hours: Open ½ hour before sunrise to ½ hour after sunset.Camping: Hueston Woods State Park Campground: The modern campground offers more than 200 electric sites and another 100 non-electric sites. Pets are permitted on any site. Reservations may be made up to six months in advance. Reserve online or by calling (866) 644-6727. Go to: https://ohiodnr.gov/wps/portal/gov/odnr/go-and-do/plan-a-visit/find-a-property/hueston-woods-state-park-campground
Hunting: Public hunting is not permitted in state nature preserves or natural areas. There are lottery deer hunts on select state nature preserves. The preserves included in the lottery hunts changes year to year so please visit the Division's webpage or contact the Division at 614-265-6453.
name: Hueston Woods State Nature Preserve

Description: The first survey of this area of Florida, from 1885, notes the presence of this mangrove forest. Comprised of 285 acres, this beautiful, virgin stand of mangroves on the shore of Perico Bayou has never been disturbed - with the exception of some ditching. The dominant tree species are red mangrove, (Rhizophora mangle) and black mangrove (Avicennia germinans). A trail along the shore allows visitors to experience the ancient mangroves.
Navigation: Site is best accessed from the main trail head at Robinson Preserve located at 1704 99th St NW, Bradenton, FL 34209. Old growth mangrove habitats are located along the shores of Tampa Bay to the north of the trailhead, and Perico Bayou to the west of the trail head. The best representation of easily observable and undisturbed old growth mangrove forest is from the trail leading to the Perico Bayou overlook starting at 27.503593, -82.669079. However, intact and mature mangrove habitats are observable from multiple boardwalks and a 70’ observation tower on the site.
Parking And Admission: Parking is available at multiple locations at Robinson Preserve. Admission: no admission fees.
Trails: Robinson Preserve contains an extensive network of trails.
Hours And Camping: Hours: open daily 365 days a year from sunrise to sunset. Camping: Group camping is available for youth or service groups. Available for groups by reservation only. Group rate: $90/per 25 total occupants. Minimum of 1 adult (over 21) per every 10 children (under 12 years). Please call (941) 742-5923 for more information or to reserve the campground. This is primitive camping with no showers or restrooms.
Hunting: No. Hunting is not permitted within Robinson Preserve. Perico Bayou, consisting of sovereign submerged lands is a location where duck hunting occurs during duck hunting season.
name: Robinson Preserve Old-Growth Mangrove Forest

Description: Because the steep terrain in the Chattahoochee River headwaters area hindered road access, at least 600 acres of this important watershed to Atlanta’s drinking water was never logged. While most of this area has younger or stunted trees growing on steep dry ridges, about 150 acres along the headwater’s tributaries and north facing slopes with gentler slopes survives as old-growth in six distinct areas ranging from 5 to 100 acres. The old-growth canopy in these pockets of larger trees is dominated by tulip trees up to 16 feet in circumference, and white, chestnut, and northern red oaks up to 12 feet in circumference. The estimated age on the larger tulip trees and oaks is well over 200 years. Other tree species present include red hickory, black gum, red maple, Fraser magnolia, and a few white basswoods. Individual large trees can be seen from the Appalachian Trail and Jacks Knob Trail. One notable feature of the headwater’s old-growth stands is the presence of fallen dead chestnuts, a rare sight on the Chattahoochee National Forest. During the 1930s, the Forest Service and timber companies aggressively salvage-logged virtually all the accessible dead and dying chestnuts in the Blue Ridge Mountains. However, the headwaters’ steep terrain prevented the removal of the dead chestnuts so remnant surviving logs are still to be found in some of the old-growth pockets growing on richer soils.
