Another important feature of the headwaters’ old-growth area is it includes the spring source of the Chattahoochee River, which just happens to be located next to a centuries-old giant tulip tree. For more information about some of the old-growth areas in the Chattahoochee River headwaters, see pages 54-56 in the book “Rambling Through Old-Growth Forests Past and Present: A Personal Survey of Surviving Old-Growth Forests on the Blue Ridge Ranger District, Chattahoochee National Forest.”
Navigation: To reach the southbound continuation of the Jacks Knob Trail, walk for about 250 feet down GA 180 East. Just as the road begins to descend, notice the Jacks Knob Trail leaving sharply to the right. A mileage sign and carsonite stake mark the trail.
Parking And Admission: A small off-road trailhead parking area is located at the intersection of GA-180 and the GA-180 Spur that travels up to Brasstown Bald. Free admission
Trails:
Visitors can park at Jack’s Gap on highway 180 and hike the southbound Jack’s Knob Trail 2.4 miles to Chattahoochee Gap. Hikers on the Appalachian Trail will intersect this area at Chattahoochee Gap, where the Appalachian Trail and Jacks Knob Trail intersect. To see the spring that feeds the headwaters of the Chattahoochee, follow the short blue-blazed off-shoot trail southeast from the trail crossings at Chattahoochee Gap. This tiny spring - which is a frequently-used water source for hikers on the Appalachian Trail – is the beginning of the Chattahoochee River that flows through Atlanta and to the Gulf of Mexico. At times the spring may be dry.

Jacks Knob Trail - Blue; Appalachian Trail - White; Chattahoochee Spring Spur Trail – Blue

Because of its remote location, steep terrain, elevation gain and loss, and required bushwhacking, access to the various pockets of old-growth beyond the end of the Chattahoochee Spring trail headwaters is challenging and should only be attempted by experienced hikers. It is further recommended that potential visitors contact info@oldgrowthforest.net for more information about the location of the various pockets of surviving old-growth before they plan their trip.
Hours And Camping: Hikers should be aware that encounters with black bears are common in the area. The use of bear proof food storage containers is highly recommended.
Hunting: The Chattahoochee River headwaters old-growth area is located in the Chattahoochee Wildlife Management Area where special hunting regulations apply. For information on hunting regulations and seasons in the Chattahoochee Wildlife Management Area , see - WMA Regulations: A-C | Georgia Hunting Seasons & Regulations – 2020 | eRegulations
name: Chattahoochee River Headwaters - Mark Trail Wilderness - Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest

County and State: Nantucket Town and County of MA
Description:
The Nantucket Conservation Foundation’s Squam Swamp/Squam Farm forest consists of hardwood mesic forests, forested and shrub swamps, freshwater bogs, shrub swamps, grassy upland areas, and vernal pools. The Squam Swamp/Squam Farm area (two separate NCF properties that connect, totaling 504 acres) are some of the largest areas of mesic forest and wooded swamp on Nantucket island. The oldest known trees are 100-150 years old, regrowing after the island was almost completely deforested in the mid-1800s. While not an old-growth forest, this secondary forest has old-growth characteristics and supports plant and animal life normally associated with old-growth forests.

The upland areas of the forest are dominated by tupelo and sassafras, with some groves of larger white and black oaks and American beech. The wooded swamp areas are dominated by very large diameter red maple. The trees are strongly shaped by the unusually high wind and salt spray effects due to Nantucket’s offshore location. Many of the oldest, largest trees are multi-trunked and some have an almost prostrate growth form in spite of being a meter or more in diameter at the base.

The Squam Swamp walking trail and accompanying interpretive brochure provides an introduction to many of the ecological, geological, and historical features of this property. The 1.8 mile round trip trail is well marked and has numbered posts keyed to the interpretive map. Squam Farm contains an additional 2.4 miles of trails with a number of possible loops; interpretive signs scattered across the property providing similar educational information. Both sites have property welcome kiosks with general information and overview maps at their respective property entrances.
Navigation:
Squam Swamp is located at 69 Wauwinet Road. From the Milestone Rotary, follow Milestone Road ¼ mile and turn left onto Polpis Road. Follow Polpis Road 6 miles and turn left onto Wauwinet Road. Follow Wauwinet Road 1.5 miles and look for the parking area on the right (it is just after you pass Pocomo Road on your left).

Squam Farm is accessed via Squidnet Road off of Quidnet Road. From the Milestone Rotary, follow Milestone Road ¼ mile and turn left onto Polpis Road. Follow Polpis Road 6.25 miles and turn left onto Quidnet Road. Take the first left onto Squidnet Road and follow it approximately 1 mile to the parking area on the right at the end. Visitors should enter through the gate located on the left with the property entrance sign and welcome kiosk.
Parking And Admission: There is ample parking located within the post and rail fencing at the trailheads of both Squam Swamp and Squam Farm. There are no facilities at either site. All NCF properties are open to the public (free of charge) between sunrise and sunset for passive recreational uses.
Trails:
Squam Swamp: the interpretive trail is approximately 1.8 miles in length, round trip. It consists of a single path that proceeds for 0.4 miles and then splits to form a large, circular loop. Along the southern portion of the loop, there is an access path that leads to Squam Farm allowing hikers to access both properties from either trailhead.

Squam Farm: this property contains an additional 2.4 miles of trails with a number of possible loops. The previously mentioned access path to Squam Swamp is located along the northern portion of the property.
Hours And Camping: All NCF properties are open year-round for passive recreation purposes between sunrise and sunset. Camping, overnight parking and motorized vehicle use are prohibited at Squam Farm and Squam Swamp. Because of fragile wetlands, biking is prohibited at Squam Swamp.
Hunting: Hunting is permitted by properly licensed hunters during designated seasons. In the southern portion of the Squam Farm property, there is an occupied dwelling. Hunting is not permitted near this site, which is posted as such.
name: Squam Swamp and Squam Farm Forest

Description: The 2,072-acre White Clay Creek Preserve is in southern Chester County, three miles north of Newark, Delaware. The White Clay Creek Valley, which forms the core of the preserve, varies from steep to gradually falling terrain with some flat bottomlands, all drained by the creek. White Clay Creek Preserve shares boundary with White Clay Creek State Park of Delaware. Because White Clay Creek possesses outstanding scenic, wildlife, recreational, and cultural value, it has been designated by Congress as a National Wild and Scenic River and shall be preserved in free-flowing condition for the benefit and enjoyment of present and future generations. Species most commonly found in wooded acreage are hickory, white ash, black walnut, tulip tree, sycamore, black cherry, and red, white, and pin oak as canopy trees. Understory species include Norway maple, flowering dogwood, ironwood, and slippery elm. Large stands of black walnut are common in the flood plain areas. White Clay Creek Preserve possesses some of the richest woodlands and open marshes in Chester County, with almost 700 known species of plants.
Navigation:
Address: 405 Sharpless Road
Landenberg, PA 19350-0172
Directions: The park is reached via PA 896, 11 miles south of the Forrestville/New London exit of US 1.
Parking And Admission: Four lots total: 1, 2, 3, and office lot. Parking is limited. No Entrance Fee.
Trails:
Trail map can be accessed at : http://elibrary.dcnr.pa.gov/GetDocument?docId=1737199&DocName=WHIT_ParkMap.pdf

Maps can be found here: https://www.dcnr.pa.gov/StateParks/FindAPark/WhiteClayCreekPreserve/Pages/Maps.aspx
Hours And Camping: Hours: Day use areas close at dusk. No camping.
Hunting: Allowed: The new section of White Clay Creek Preserve (formerly the Strawbridge property) will allow the same type of hunting as the rest of the Big Elk Section of the Preserve on the opposite side of Strickersville Road. Specifically, deer hunting only, utilizing archery equipment, shotgun and muzzleloader during all seasons open to deer hunting. All PA Game Commission and State Park Rules & Regulations also apply. Springlawn Trail specifically will be closed during firearms season. Please be advised that hunting season is open and permitted in designated areas within state parks. For your protection, all visitors should take proper precautions such as wearing a fluorescent orange vest and hat while recreating in areas of the park that are open to hunting during your visit. If you have questions please contact the park office.
name: White Clay Creek Preserve

Description: Henry’s Woods, which has never been logged, is the only remaining old-growth forest in the Lehigh Valley. Old-growth eastern hemlock, Pennsylvania’s state tree, and white oak tower more than 130 feet above the forest floor. The 122-acre forest surrounds Bushkill Creek and can best be enjoyed by walking the 1.9 mile trail that loops through the woods.
Navigation: Address: 400 Belfast Rd, Nazareth, PA 18064. Directions: reached from PA 33 at the Belfast Exit, near Nazareth, PA. Off the 33 Belfast exit, head East on Henry road, and turn left on to Belfast Road. The Main parking lot is approximately .75 miles on the left hand side. It is the large triangular shaped parking lot with the large Jacobsburg Environmental Education Center Sign at it’s entrance.
Parking And Admission: Free Admission. Recommended parking at coordinates provided above. Main parking lot has ample parking but fills quickly on weekends. Secondary parking lot has limited parking.
Trails: Henrys’ Woods Trail. Visitors hiking the 1.9 mile loop trail experience the sights, sounds and coolness of the Bushkill creek as it meanders past dramatic slate outcroppings and remnant old growth hemlock and White Oaks.
Hours And Camping: Hours: The center is open every day of the year, sunrise to sunset. Day use areas close at dusk. Camping: none
Hunting: Yes. During established seasons, about 937 acres are open to Hunting, Trapping, Training of dogs. DCNR and Pennsylvania Game Commission rules and regulations apply. Complete information about hunting rules and regulations in Pennsylvania is available from the Pennsylvania Game Commission.
name: Henry's Woods – Jacobsburg State Park

Description:
A dwarf, old-growth white oak forest sits perched at the top of Little Scaly Mountain, four miles southwest of Highlands, North Carolina. The trees here have their roots spread across granite cliffs and show the effects of the harsh environment through their small, gnarled forms. Their stunted forms are resilient toward the intense winds that shear across the mountain bald. These trees have been dated to 400 and 500 years old by Clemson University dendrologists. The Mountain Retreat and Learning Center, an environmentally focused Unitarian Universalist retreat, shares the top of Little Scaly Mountain and offers a space for meetings, retreats, and events. This old-growth forest is approximately 10 acres and is protected and cared for with the help of the Highlands-Cashiers Land Trust. 

The Mountain sites on the Blue Ridge divide, where water flowing from the south-facing cliffs travels to the Atlantic Ocean and water on the northern side flows to the Gulf of Mexico. This area also receives a significant amount of rainfall (over 100 inches in many areas) as saturated air from the Gulf of Mexico meets the cooler, higher elevation mountain sides, creating a temperate rainforest environment.
Navigation:
3872 Dillard Road


Highlands, NC 28741

 Little Scaly Mountain Rd turns off from Dillard Rd and winds up the mountain. The Mountain Retreat and Learning Center is located at the end of this road. Please be aware that cars share this road going both directions, so drive carefully and slowly and yield where needed. This road requires 4WD in winter
Parking And Admission: Limited parking is available for visitors at the Retreat Center Main Office.
Trails: The dwarf forest at the mountain top is dispersed among the retreat center and has no distinct trail. Multiple forest trails leave from the mountain to Glen Falls, Chinquapin Mountain, and Abe’s Creek. Maps are available at the Mountain Office. The forest can be viewed from above by climbing the Lookout Tower on The Mountain’s campus.
Hours And Camping: Daylight hours, year-round. Call before visiting to be aware of special events at the retreat center.
name: The Mountain Retreat and Learning Center

Description:
The Town of Lyme’s 250-acre Johnston Preserve is part of the River to Ridgetop Preserves complex of six contiguous preserves spanning over 1500 acres extending from river to ridgetop and protecting a rare diversity of habitats, including streams, fields, wetlands and several woodland types. The Johnston Preserve itself is a mixed hardwood forest in the 100 year old range which includes oaks; red, white, black, chestnut and pin, as well as tulip poplar, black gum, white ash, red and sugar maple, beech, black and yellow birch and four hickory species. Understory trees include hornbeam, hop-hornbeam and American dogwood. Johnston Preserve has fascinating geologic features, from deep hollows to ridges with dramatic outcroppings and ledges. The white trail gently climbs to breathtaking seasonal overlooks. The yellow trail traverses North Woods Hill, the highest point in Lyme.

Henry Selden Johnston, a lawyer from New York, purchased this abandoned pastureland in various parcels between 1924 and 1932. In 2018, the 250-acre Johnston Preserve was bought from the Johnston family by the Town of Lyme with funding from the Town’s Open Space and Watershed Protection Program and The Nature Conservancy.
Navigation: Closest address: 141-2 Norwich Salem Road, Lyme, CT. Going east, the preserve entrance and parking are a hundred yards past this address, on the south side of Rte 82. It is two miles west from the intersection of Rte. 156 and Rte. 82 and 1.5 miles east of the intersection of Rte. 82 and Rte. 148 at Hadlyme four-corners.
Parking And Admission: Parking is limited to about 10 cars. There is no admission.
Trails:
Recommended Trail: All trails
Total Distance of All Trails in Preserve: 4 miles (3 trails, 2 spurs)
Hours And Camping: Open sunrise to dusk. No camping.
Hunting: Consent to hunt may be granted to licensed hunters by request by mail to the Open Space Coordinator of the Town of Lyme. Contact: openspace@townlyme.org.
name: Johnston Preserve

Description: Approximately 4,500 acres of wilderness and natural open space land. Within the park lands are mature coast live oaks, western sycamores, elderberries and willows, two year-round streams and more than 30 miles of official trails. Some of the oaks are over 200 years old and reach heights of over 50 feet. Many rare and endangered plants and animals make this park their home. This park is designated as a wildlife sanctuary. The Canyon supports chaparral and riparian communities including California scrub oak, coastal chola, coyote brush, lemonade berry, white sage and black willow.

Description: Jakey Hollow Natural Area is a small but unique site in Central Columbia County near Bloomsburg. Several massive old growth white pine and hemlocks will remind the visitor of what Pennsylvania must have been like in the past. The 59-acre area is home to an excellent mixed stand of second growth eastern hemlock, old eastern white pine, hardwoods, with a small area of virgin hemlock. Some of the other tree species at this site include sugar maple, red oak, white oak, American beech, black birch, and black cherry. The shrub layer and herbaceous layer includes mountain laurel, ferns, Solomon’s seal, and purple trillium. The rich variety in plant life attracts and helps sustain multiple wildlife species, especially birds. Barred owls, blue-headed vireo, black-throated green warbler, scarlet tanager, and pileated woodpeckers can be seen here. The invasive Hemlock Wooly Adelgid is a concern in this area.
Navigation:
Address: 2077 Crawford Rd, Bloomsburg, PA 17815


Directions: From Interstate 80 Buckthorn exit, travel north on route 42, turn left to stay on route 42 (Millville Rd), turn right on Mellick Hollow Road, cross bridge and a left on Crawford Rd to parking area on left.
Parking And Admission: Parking is limited to only a few (3) vehicles.
Trails: There is a 0.35-mile trail. One can access it from the parking area.
Hours And Camping: Open year round 24 hours. No camping.
name: Jakey Hollow Natural Area

Description: Worlds End State Park is situated in a narrow S-shaped valley of the Loyalsock Creek, just south of Forksville, Sullivan County. Surrounded by the Loyalsock State Forest, the 780-acre park offers visitors diverse recreational opportunities within a pristine environment. In the eastern half of the park the overlook offers a spectacular view of the Loyalsock Creek gorge from its vista, which is an elevation of 1750 feet. Many wildflowers grow beneath the canopy of maturing ash, sugar maple, and black cherry trees.
Navigation:
Visitor Center: 82 Cabin Bridge Rd, Forksville, PA 18616

The park is along PA 154 and is easily reached from:
North and East: PA US 220 to PA 87 from Dushore
West: I-180 to PA 87 from Williamsport
South: I-80 to I-180 to PA US 220 to PA 42
GPS DD: Lat. 41.4718 Long. -76.58145
Parking And Admission: Parking is available at the outdoor park chapel and Double Run Nature Trailhead along PA 154. Free admission
Trails:
The more than 20 miles of hiking trails of Worlds End State Park are mostly rocky with steep sections that climb the surrounding mountains. Hikers should wear proper footwear and be extra cautious in the winter and spring when trail surfaces can be frozen or icy.

Mature forest can easily be seen at the Double Run Nature Trail.

Trail details available here: https://www.dcnr.pa.gov/StateParks/FindAPark/WorldsEndStatePark/Pages/Hiking.aspx
Hours And Camping: The park is open every day of the year, sunrise to sunset. Day use areas close at dusk. The park office is open specific hours. The beach, overnight areas, and other areas are open specific seasons and hours. Contact the park office for facility seasons and hours.
Hunting: During established seasons, about half of Worlds End State Park is open to: Hunting Trapping Training of dogs DCNR and the Pennsylvania Game Commission rules and regulations apply. Complete information about hunting rules and regulations in Pennsylvania is available from the Pennsylvania Game Commission.
name: Worlds End State Park

Description: The 405-acre Salt Springs State Park is in northeastern Pennsylvania, seven miles north of Montrose in Susquehanna County. Focal points of the park are the towering old growth hemlock trees, many estimated to be more than 300 years old, and the rocky gorge cut by Fall Brook with its three waterfalls.
Navigation:
Silver Creek Rd & Salt Springs Rd


Montrose, PA 18801


From Montrose, follow PA 29 north for six miles to the town of Franklin Forks. Turn left onto Silver Creek Road and follow for one mile to the park entrance.


From New York, take NY 7 to PA 29. At Franklin Forks, turn right onto Silver Creek Road and follow for one mile to the park entrance.

GPS DD: Lat. 41.9119 Long. -75.86553
Parking And Admission:
Free Admission.


Parking is available at the Wheaton House Office and at the Overlook Trailhead on Buckley Road.
Trails:
14.85 miles of trails: The trails pass through old growth forest, overlook the gorge, and meander through various habitats.


Woodland Trail


0.25 mile, easiest hiking, blue blazes


Reached from Hemlock Trail, this trail circles around the east side of the old growth stand. Explore a hemlock almost 300 years old that has fallen across the path. The trail ends at Hardwood Trail.


The Hemlock Grove is also accessible from the Overlook Trail, which leaves from the Overlook Trail Parking along Buckley Road and connects to the Hemlock Trail.


For further trail information: https://www.dcnr.pa.gov/StateParks/FindAPark/SaltSpringsStatePark/Pages/Hiking.aspx
Hours And Camping:
The park is open every day of the year, sunrise to sunset. Day use areas close at dusk.


Rustic tenting sites are privately situated along the banks of Silver Creek. All sites include a fire ring and picnic table. Pets are permitted in the campground.The campground has a restroom with composting toilets.Water is available from an outdoor faucet at the Wheaton House and from a faucet in front of the restrooms in the parking lot. The maximum camping period is 14 consecutive days.


Group camping is available in a large mowed field adjacent to the main campground. There are composting toilets and handpumps for water. The maximum camping period is 14 consecutive days.


The cottages have wooden walls and floors, electric lights and outlets, and a porch. A cottage sleeps five or seven people in a single bunk and a single/double bunk. Rustic restrooms are nearby. Reservations may be made in advance by calling the Friends of Salt Springs Park at 570-967-7275, and are confirmed when full payment is received.
Hunting: The picnic area and the land surrounding the hemlock grove, waterfalls, and farmhouses is a designated Natural Area, which is off limits to hunting. Beyond that, hunting is allowed and must adhere to the rules and regulations of the Pennsylvania Game Commission.
name: Fall Brook Natural Area - Salt Springs State Park

Description: The Keystone Ancient Forest is a great example of the Cross Timbers forest community, featuring 500 year old cedars and 300 year old post oak trees. The same rocky and rough terrain that shapes the gnarled forms of the ancient trees has protected them from logging, development, and farming. The Cross Timbers forest stretches in a band from Kansas through Oklahoma into Texas and is formed by a mosaic of rugged oaks and occasional breaks into prairies and form a geographical point at which the deciduous forests of the East transition to the Western Plains. The 1,360 acre Keystone Ancient forest is owned by the City of Sand Springs and protected through a conservation easement held by The Nature Conservancy. This protected forest provides habitat for deer, mountain lions, bobcats, eagles, migratory birds, and over 80 species of butterflies. Numerous trails take visitors through this varied landscape.
Navigation:
Keystone Ancient Forest


160 Ancient Forest Dr


Sand Springs, OK 74063


From 209th West Avenue (Prue Road) and Highway 64 / 412 exit - Travel north along Prue Road approximately 2 miles. The entrance is directly across from the second cell phone tower and features a large sandstone and black iron gate.
Parking And Admission: FREE and open to the public. Donations are accepted
Trails:
Trails rated as EASY; MODERATE: and DIFFICULT in terms of grade and distance.

Childers Trail is our shortest at 6/10th mile; paved asphalt and ADA accessible. Very kid-friendly and wheelchair accessible and rated EASY

Frank Trail- the backbone of it all. 2.8 miles round trip and made of native soils. MODERATE.

Wilson Trail- a REAL trail for the adventurer. 1.0 mile in length and our only DIFFICULT rated trail

Less Traveled Trail-, 4.1 miles one way to portions of the preserve mostly left alone. MODERATE

Falls Trail - A challenging 3.5 miles one way. Features scenic waterfalls, especially after rainfall, making it a rewarding adventure for experienced hikers.

Fire Road - 8/10th mile; not rated and offers a fun shortcut back to the trailhead.
Hours And Camping: Open year round, but need to monitor Keystone Ancient Forest’s Face Book page and City of Sand Springs (owner) webpage for latest hiking schedule. Mostly select Saturdays from 8:00 a.m. until 2:00 p.m. Camping not permitted.
name: Keystone Ancient Forest

Description:
The Town of Rochester’s Washington Grove is a precious fragment of old-growth forest in which ancient trees grow in an uneven glaciated landscape that makes it seem much larger than its actual 26 acres. It is extraordinary to find such a relatively undisturbed patch of forest within a city limits, one open to all as part of a city park.

Washington Grove is an oak-hickory forest situated on the edge of a kame moraine and containing two glacial kettles. Several oak species are present, but the numerous Black oaks are especially impressive. Burn-intolerant maple, cherry, sassafras, and tulip trees are now widespread in the forest, probably as a result of the suppression of forest fires by settlers 200 years ago in an area transformed by the construction of the original Erie Canal, which ran nearby. In the 1950s, in response to the loss of once-dominant chestnut trees, students from the nearby elementary school planted many sugar maples. As far as is known, the area has never been cleared and although what appear to be the oldest trees have never been cored to determine their age, a dead one, not particularly large, was aged at over 250 years.
Navigation:
Nunda Boulevard entrance: This entrance is at the very end of Nunda Boulevard in Rochester. The closest street address is 8 Nunda Boulevard, Rochester, 14610. You will see stone wall and steps at the trailhead at the end of the boulevard.

Cobbs Hill Reservoir entrance: From Monroe Avenue, turn left into the entrance for Cobbs Hill Reservoir. Follow Reservoir Road (one way only) up the hill to parking spots on the right hand side of the road. The entry to Washington Grove is down an open area of mown grass, the path first leading left and then curving down the slope into the Grove to the right.
Parking And Admission:
For the Nunda Boulevard entrance, parking is available on Nunda Boulevard or on Cobbs Hill Drive, with which it intersects. For the Cobb’s Hill Reservoir entrance, parking is available beside the road and in several other designated spots at the Cobbs Hill reservoir.

There is no admission fee.
Trails: Recommended Trail: Perimeter Trail is .71 miles long. Total Distance of all trails: Approximately 2.5 miles. See https://friendsofwashingtongrove.org/index.php/resources/washington-grove-trails-map/ for a trails map.
Hours And Camping: Open all year round from sunrise to sunset. No camping available. Follow city park rules, including keeping dogs leashed and no biking.
name: Washington Grove

Description: Muskego Park spans 193 acres. The hardwood forest is dominated by old white and red oaks with occasional large sugar maple, black walnut, bitternut and shagbark hickory, butternut, white ash, basswood, black cherry, ironwood, Kentucky coffee tree, and blue ash (a state-threatened species). Most trees on this site are not exceptionally big, likely because the site was grazed at some point in its history. The beautiful forest contains a variety of trees, flowers, and wildlife. The exceptionally rich spring flora contains wild leek, toothwort, bloodroot, several species of trillium, green dragon, and red baneberry. Breeding birds include the state-threatened cerulean warbler.
Navigation: Address: S83 W20370 Janesville Rd, Muskego, WI 53150
Parking And Admission:
Parking: park at Picnic Area #4; main trailhead is behind picnic pavilion

Admission: Fees: $6 (Waukesha County Park Fee)
Trails: See park trail map - the old growth section is mainly concentrated around the Blue and Green Trails (circled in red). The loop, bisecting trail, and two short sections to the wetlands are just less than 2 total miles. The trail is wide with minimal elevation. Trail is easy to traverse, can be muddy.
Hours And Camping: Hours: Sunrise to 10 pm (Year-Round) Camping: located to the west of the State Scientific Area just north of the swimming pond. There are 17 Family Campsites and 3 Group Campsites
name: Muskego Park

Description: Congaree National Park encompasses nearly 27,000 acres, including the largest intact expanse (11,000 acres) of old-growth bottomland hardwood forest remaining in the southeastern United States. There are a variety of forest communities, with dominant tree species ranging from upland pines along the elevated bluffs to bottomland species such as bald cypress and water tupelo within the floodplain. There are at least 25 Champion Trees in the Park, including four over 160’ tall. Champion trees in the park range from pine and oaks on more elevated sites to cypress and tupelo in sloughs and depressions. The old-growth forest forms one of the highest temperate deciduous forest canopies remaining in the world.
Navigation: Address: 100 National Park Road, Hopkins, SC 29061
Parking And Admission: There is no entrance fee. There is ample parking at the Visitor Center.
Trails: There are 20 miles of hiking trails, as well as a 50-mile paddling trail along the Congaree River. Most of the trails start from the Visitor Center. The Oakridge trail (round trip 7 miles) passes through a rich stretch of old-growth forest, traversing a ridge where a variety of large oak trees grow. Maps for all the trails can be found at the Visitor Center.
Hours And Camping: Hours: The Park is open 24 hours/day year-round; the Visitor Center is open from 9:00-5:00 daily, closed on Federal holidays. However, trail maps and brochures, as well as restroom facilities and water, are available in the Visitor Center breezeway 24 hours a day. Camping: Camping in the backcountry is free but requires a permit obtainable at the Visitor Center. There are two campgrounds, for which reservations can be made at Recreation.gov or by calling 1-877-444-6777. Tents and hammocks only. The Longleaf campground has 10 individual and 4 group camping sites, vault toilets, no running water. The Bluff campground has 6 large campsites, no restroom facilities or running water. All campsites have a fire ring and picnic tables.
name: Congaree National Park

Nunda Boulevard entrance: This entrance is at the very end of Nunda Boulevard in Rochester. The closest street address is 8 Nunda Boulevard, Rochester, 14610. You will see stone wall and steps at the trailhead at the end of the boulevard.

Cobbs Hill Reservoir entrance: From Monroe Avenue, turn left into the entrance for Cobbs Hill Reservoir. Follow Reservoir Road (one way only) up the hill to parking spots on the right hand side of the road. The entry to Washington Grove is down an open area of mown grass, the path first leading left and then curving down the slope into the Grove to the right.
Parking And Admission:
For the Nunda Boulevard entrance, parking is available on Nunda Boulevard or on Cobbs Hill Drive, with which it intersects. For the Cobb’s Hill Reservoir entrance, parking is available beside the road and in several other designated spots at the Cobbs Hill reservoir.

There is no admission fee.
Trails: Recommended Trail: Perimeter Trail is .71 miles long. Total Distance of all trails: Approximately 2.5 miles. See https://friendsofwashingtongrove.org/index.php/resources/washington-grove-trails-map/ for a trails map.
Hours And Camping: Open all year round from sunrise to sunset. No camping available. Follow city park rules, including keeping dogs leashed and no biking.

Description:
Olympic National Park is one of the premier areas to see old-growth forest in Washington state. It features a varied landscape from coasts, to mountains, to old-growth forests across the Olympic Peninsula. West of the Olympic Mountains are temperate rain forests, with abundant rainfall and verdant mossy forests. Across Olympic National Park are multiple access points to lowland old-growth forests with towering Douglas fir and western Hemlocks, some up to 1,000 years old. This area has a rich diversity of conifers, also including Sitka Spruce, Grand Fir, Western Redcedar, Western White Pine, and Lodgepole Pine.

The dynamics of an old-growth forest are evident throughout these lowland areas, with decaying, fallen trees often serving as nurse logs for the next generation of seedlings. The constant cycles of growth and decomposition have created a rich layer of soil and abundant rain (sometimes measured in feet) feeds the lush understories of ferns and mosses.
Navigation: There are a number of Visitors Centers, among other access points and lodging options. Open hours for each center vary seasonally. Please see the park’s website for complete information: https://www.nps.gov/olym/planyourvisit/visitorcenters.htm
Parking And Admission:
Olympic National Park requires an entrance fee that is valid for seven consecutive days. Annual Passes and American the Beautiful National Parks Passes are accepted.

Passes can be purchased ahead of time at https://www.recreation.gov/sitepass/74290 or the day-of at any of the entrance gates.

Parking is available at trailheads and Visitors Centers. Summer months are very busy for the park and parking areas may fill up quickly.
Trails:
Olympic National Park offers many chances to hike among old-growth forest. This is a sampling of the most notable trails:

Ancient Groves Nature Trail – Sol Duc River Rd: 0.5 mile loop through ancient Douglas fir and Hemlock

Sol Duc Falls Trail- Sol Duc Road: 2 miles out and back to Sol Duc Falls

Marymere Falls Trails – Lake Crescent: 1.7 miles out and back trail starting at Lake Crescent and ending at a small waterfall

Heart of the Forest trail: 4.8 miles out and back trail leaving from the Heart o’ the Hills campground that meanders through large, old-growth trees

Hoh River Trail: Long out and back trail that runs up to 12 miles each way from the Hoh Rainforest Visitor Center along the Hoh River.

Shady Lane Trail- Staircase Campground: 1.8 miles out and back trail to the Staircase Ranger Station or extend to a 4.5 mile loop trail with the Staircase Rapids Loop. This trail runs alongside the Skokomish river in the Southeastern side of the park.
Hours And Camping:
Open 24 hours a day, year-round. Visitors Center and Hurricane Ridge Road closed Thanksgiving and Christmas.

Campgrounds, some roads, and some visitor facilities have reduced hours from October to May. Weather conditions may affect roads and facilities. Please consult the park’s website for exact operating hours.
Phone Number: Olympic National Park Visitor Center in Port Angeles: (360) 565-3130
name: Olympic National Park

Description: The Rhododendron Preserve protects a rare piece of forest that is almost unchanged from pre-European settlement conditions. The Preserve’s 426 acres holds one of the largest remaining examples of lowland virgin forest (170 acres) in the Puget Sound Basin. About 70 acres of old growth forest lies at its center. Ancient western red cedar and pine trees resistant to blister rust complement the landscape. The Preserve is also home to an impressively big, old growth Douglas fir affectionately called Big Tree.
Navigation:
2401 Seabeck Hwy NW, Bremerton, WA 98312

The entrance to the Preserve is shared with The Mountaineers and crosses private property. We ask visitors to be thoughtful of other users of the property and to drive slowly and cautiously.
Parking And Admission:
Parking is located at The Mountaineers Kitsap Cabin and Kitsap Forest Theater Complex located at 2401 Seabeck Hwy NW, Bremerton. The parking lot can be very busy!

We recommend leaving a note on your car that you are on the Preserve. Free admission.
Trails:
The Big Tree Trail begins at the Kitsap Cabin and is marked with a kiosk. The trail ends at Big Tree. Please stay on the trail. The hike to Big Tree is 1.5 miles, round trip. The Keta Legacy Foundation occasionally offers guided tours through their upcoming tours and events page.

Dogs and pets are not allowed at the Preserve or on the trail.
Hunting: Hunting is prohibited. Picking vegetation, berries, or mushrooms is prohibited.
name: The Rhododendron Preserve

Description:
This beautiful forest is dominated by Red Cedars and Douglas Firs. Some trees are at least 120 years old. Some trees may be older than 178 years, having survived the 1843 eruption and forest fire of Mt. Baker.

The trail leads into a majestic stand of Douglas Fir that regrew after Mt. Baker erupted and started a forest fire in 1843. You can still see the burned snags of the cedar trees that once dominated the area. From south to north, the trail contours the eastern shoreline of Baker Lake, offering glimpses of Mt. Baker.
Navigation: Address: Mt. Baker Ranger District Office, 810 State Route 20, Sedro-Woolley, WA 98284. For the northern trailhead: From the District Office, take Route 20 East. After Birdsview Brewing Company (38302 WA-20, Concrete, WA 98237) go 1.2 miles and at the intersection of Route 20 and Baker Lake Rd (FS Road 11), go left (north) on Baker Lake Rd. Follow this for 26.5 miles all the way to the end. The road is paved until the last 6 miles. Park at the large parking lot with a vault toilet. Access is via the Baker River Trail 606.
Parking And Admission:
Admission: $5/vehicle per day or use a pass: Recreation Passes and Permits — Washington Trails Association or Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest - Recreation Passes & Permits.

Parking can be strained during the busy summer season but is ample most of the time.
Trails: The Baker Lake Trail, sometimes called the East Bank Baker Lake Trail, is 14.5 miles one-way. From the Northern trailhead, it's a 9 miles round trip to Maple Grove and back.
Hours And Camping: There are 3 campgrounds along the eastern shore of Baker Lake, including the Maple Grove Campground with 6 sites open year round, accessible by foot or boat with vault toilets. On the west side of the lake, there are 6 campgrounds.
name: Baker Lake Trail - Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest

Description: North Fork Sauk Trail is 5.5 miles long - the protected portion of this trail that is included in the Network begins only when you have entered the Glacier Peak Wilderness which is about .5-.75 mil from the trailhead. This is a true Pacific northwest old-growth forest. From the very start of the trail there are giant old trees. The dominant tree species is Western Red Cedar, the oldest of which are estimated to be 800-850 years old. The forest composition transitions to include Douglas Fir, Western Hemlock, Red Alder, Big Leaf Maple and Pacific Silver Fir. A wide variety of plants make up the understory including Western lily of the valley, huckleberry, devil’s club, and numerous fern species. There is a rich variety of moss species on tree trunks, hanging from branches, covering large downed logs, on the ground and on rocks. One significant feature of this forest is the presence of various lichen species, including lichens characteristic of old-growth forests.
Navigation: Directions: On the Mountain Loop Highway, drive 16 miles south of Darrington or 26.2 miles east of Verlot to Forest Road 49. Turn east and proceed 6.4 miles to a sign for North Fork Sauk parking lot. Much of the drive is on a gravel road.
Parking And Admission:
Parking: Limited at trailhead: Parking Pass/Entry Fee, https://www.fs.usda.gov/main/r6/passes-permits/recreation; Day pass is $5 – must be purchased in advance. 

Admission: Limited to groups of 12 or fewer.
Trails: The North Fork Sauk trail continues for 5.5 miles, before it climbs up to join the Pacific Crest Trail. The elevation of the trail is from 1800-2800 feet. The largest trees are at the lower elevations.
Hours And Camping:
Hours: No specific hours: Best used from May until November.

Camping: There is a small camping area near the trailhead.
name: North Fork Sauk Trail – Glacier Peak Wilderness - Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest

Description: The Doc Kudish Natural Forest of Paul Smith's College is a 75-acre stand of hemlock-northern hardwood which includes some 30-40-inch diameter hemlock, yellow birch, and sugar maple, and all the structural indicators of old-growth forest. In his Paul Smith’s Flora II (1981) Dr. Kudish describes the western portion of the tract as “first growth” having been maintained as such for educational purposes, so that people can “see today what our forests looked like before 1850.”
Navigation: Closest Address: 505 Keeses Mill Road, Paul Smiths NY 12970
Parking And Admission:
There is a parking area at the St. Regis Mountain trailhead. The forest can be accessed by a half-mile walk from there, down a private road.

There is no admission fee.
Trails:
Park at the St. Regis Mountain trailhead. Walk down the private road for about a half mile at which point the road to the Doc Kudish Natural Forest breaks off to the left, up a hill. At the top of the hill is a locked gate. Walk around it. The forest begins a couple hundred yards past the gate (just past Marvin Pond (AKA Potter Pond). Follow the trail along the western edge of the forest to the Honeymoon and Upper St. Regis lean-tos.

Trail length from the private road to the Honeymoon and Upper St. Regis lean-tos is about a mile (two miles round trip).
Hours And Camping:
Hours: There are no specific hours for this location.

Camping: There are two lean-tos on the Upper St. Regis Lake at the southern end of the forest. They are first come, first served with pit toilets nearby.
name: Doc Kudish Natural Forest – Paul Smith’s College

Description:
Aquidneck Land Trust's Oakland Forest includes a regionally ecologically unique old-growth American beech forest, with trees estimated to be between 200 and 300 years based on tree coring done in 2000. It was conserved by ALT with the support of the community in 2000. In addition to beech, the forest includes old growth tree forms of other species including white oak and red maple. The property was once part of a ‘gentleman’s farm’ owned by the Vanderbilt family in the 1800 and 1900s. There is a row of 100-year-old rhododendrons running through the forested part of the old estate.

The Oakland Forest and Meadow Trail is a 0.6 mile loop trail open dawn to dusk that traverses a 10-acre meadow and 20 acres of the old-growth beech forest. It is an excellent spot for wildlife viewing or a quiet stroll through the forest.

Please note: Because of Oakland’s unique and delicate ecosystem, no dogs, bicycles or motorized vehicles are allowed on the trail.
Navigation: Address: 266 Carriage Drive, Portsmouth, RI 02842
Parking And Admission: The trail can be accessed by a small gravel parking lot (3 spaces) near the end of Carriage Drive in Portsmouth. Overflow parking on Carriage Drive is also permitted. No overnight parking.
Trails:
Oakland Forest and Meadow Trail: 0.6 mile loop trail
Total distance of trails in park: 0.6 miles
Hours And Camping:
Open dawn to dusk.
Parking lot is not plowed in winter but parking on street is permitted.
No camping.
name: Oakland Forest

Description:
Highlands Hammock - with more rare and endemic species than any other Florida State Park - is a place where wilderness and history are preserved. Visitors can walk the trails where the Florida panther and black bear quietly pass beneath the ancient, towering oaks of a magnificent hydric hammock. Deer, alligators and a variety of birds frequent the park.

Encompassing more than 9,000 acres, this park is known for its beautiful old-growth hammock, cypress swamps, the Civilian Conservation Corps Museum and an abundance of wildlife. Nine different nature trails take visitors through lush, jungle-like foliage and deep into the heart of one of the oldest state parks in Florida.
Navigation:
5931 Hammock Road Sebring, FL 33872


U.S. Highway 27, turn west onto County Road 634 (Hammock Road) and travel four miles to park entrance.
Parking And Admission: $6 per vehicle
Trails:
Highlands Hammock is known for its hiking trails, which range in distance from 975 feet to over 3,000 feet. Trail maps are available at the ranger station. Late fall, winter and spring are ideal seasons for exploring the trails. During the summer rainy season, insects are more prevalent and portions of trails are often wet, muddy or overgrown. Wear sturdy footwear suitable for hiking. Carry water and insect repellent.


Visitors might begin by walking the Alexander Blair Big Oak Trail. Named for the park’s chief engineer, this is a short linear trail with a length of 975 feet. Although the “Big Oak” died years ago, the gnarled lower trunk of this giant live oak, whose girth measures 36 feet, is a must see destination. Visitors may continue on to the Hickory Trail via a narrow catwalk. Walk deep into the woods under the expansive canopy and see giant oaks, pignut hickories and air plants.


A magnificent oak marks the entrance to Richard Lieber Memorial Trail. Amble along the boardwalk through hardwood swamp and view the colorful, scattered leaves. See autumn in Florida and observe a flock of white ibis feeding.


Discover how pineland has transitioned into hammock as a result of fire exclusion on the Young Hammock Trail. Stroll along the boardwalk over Charlie Bowlegs Creek and search the tea-colored water for alligators on Cypress Swamp Trail.

 Take a journey back in time to primitive Florida on the Ancient Hammock Trail and finish the loop trails with Fern Garden Trail. Yellow-crowned night herons and alligators may be observed from the Fern Garden boardwalk that runs through marsh.
Hours And Camping:
8 a.m. until sunset, 365 days a year


Campground sites are appropriate for RVers and tent campers.

 Reservations can be made up to 11 months in advance. For reservations, visit the Florida State Parks reservations website or call 800-326-3521 or TDD 888-433-0287.
name: Ancient Hammock Trail - Highlands Hammock State Park

Description: Approximately 4,500 acres of wilderness and natural open space land. Within the park lands are mature coast live oaks, western sycamores, elderberries and willows, two year-round streams and more than 30 miles of official trails. Some of the oaks are over 200 years old and reach heights of over 50 feet. Many rare and endangered plants and animals make this park their home. This park is designated as a wildlife sanctuary. The Canyon supports chaparral and riparian communities including California scrub oak, coastal chola, coyote brush, lemonade berry, white sage and black willow.
Navigation:
Enter and exit the Awma Road parking lot via Alicia Parkway only.

 Address: 28373 Alicia Pkwy, Laguna Niguel, CA 92656
Parking And Admission: Parking Fee: $3 daily Large Parking lot with limited number of spaces
Trails:
Main Trails:


Aliso Creek Trail (3 miles) - Begins at Park Entrance


 (33.550851972761, -117.72086115754006)


Wood Canyon Trail (3 miles) - connects to Aliso Creek at ~1 mi


(33.54118581646656, -117.73764642156868)


Additional Trails with Mature Trees:


Oak Grove Trail (0.75 Miles)


(33.55756330829964, -117.74554659770783)


5 oaks Trail (0.75 miles) (33.56626646087097, -117.74638986494068)


Wood Creek Trail (0.5 miles) (33.56934237249974, -117.74816566007028)


Total distance of all trails in the park: 30+ miles


Trails may be closed for three days or more following rain.


Trail Map: 

 https://ocparks.com/sites/ocparks/files/2021-04/Trail_Map.pdf
Hours And Camping: Park Hours: 7 a.m. to sunset. Note: Parking lot closes at sunset. Camping is not allowed.
name: Aliso and Wood Canyons Wilderness Park

Description: 437-acre preserve with 70 acres of old growth Monterey pine forest dating back to the 1800s and an additional 55 acres of restored forest. Native Monterey pine forest is restricted to approximately 13,000 acres worldwide, with Cambria’s ~3,000 acres being the stand with the lowest tree species diversity. The tree canopy is nearly all Monterey pine with an understory of coast live oak.
Navigation: 2799 Bluff Trail, Cambria, CA 93428
Parking And Admission: In Fiscalini Ranch Preserve there's a Monterey pine forest and some wetlands and marshes – all supporting lots of diverse wildlife. Parking can be found at the south end of Windsor Boulevard in the north part of Cambria (in Seaclift Estates) and at the north end of Windsor Boulevard in the south part of Cambria. To reach the forest, it is fastest to park on the Highway 1 pull out and take the 0.2-mile Creek to Forest Trail.
Trails: 8 miles of trails in total. The Forest Loop and Trenton Trails take you through the heart of the stand on about 2 miles of trail combined. Map located here: https://www.fiscaliniranchpreserve.org/explore/trails/
Hours And Camping: No camping or restrooms. Open sunrise to sunset every day, all year.
name: Fiscalini Ranch

Description: This is not an old-growth forest. But as you make your way back to the rocky areas (less than one mile) you will discover large trees estimated to be over 150 years old. Tulip-poplar, cucumber magnolia, hemlock, white pine, oak, red maple, some ash, some beech. The trail starts out very easy and gets more difficult as you go. Adventurous folks can connect to many miles of rough trails. The area covers 1,526 acres. Many of the original hemlocks have succumbed to the wooly adelgid insect, but hemlocks closer to the parking area were treated in 2006 and most were still living in 20017. A lovely stream accompanies the trail.
Navigation: Address: Sweet Root Trail, Everett, PA 15537
Parking And Admission: Ample parking. No admission charge.
Trails: The Sweet Root Road Trail is approximately 3 miles and connects with many other trails. The OGFN area follows Sweet Root Run – access this by walking along Sweet Root Road (not open to motor vehicles).
Hours And Camping: Open year round 24 hours; no camping.
name: Sweet Root Natural Area

Description: The stand of old growth is 8 acres and is part of a 36.45-acre property. Core samples taken by the service forester determined the stand origin to be around 1838, so many of the large trees are about 180 years old. The dominant trees are white oak. This forest is special because of all the old growth trees.
Navigation: The property is located on Big Creek Road, south of Clearville, PA.
Parking And Admission: The property is open to the public free of charge. Limited parking is available along the lane just before the big field. A pavilion and parking area will be established within walking distance of the old growth stand.
Trails: A trail system is being developed.
Hours And Camping: The property is open year-round. Camping is not permitted.
Hunting: Hunting is allowed in conjunction with the Hunter Access Program through the Pennsylvania Game Commission. See https://www.pgc.pa.gov/HuntTrap/Hunting/HunterAccessProgram/pages/default.aspx
name: Sulzbacher Demonstration Forest

Description: The 21-acre old-growth area has been a dedicated State Natural Landmark since 1983. A number of trees in this old-growth area date to nearly 175 years old, as determined by field studies from the Wooster Tree Ring Lab at the College of Wooster. These are largely white oak (Quercus alba). In addition, there are burr oak (Q. macrocarpa) and sugar maple (Acer saccharum) in this old-growth forest. The Wilderness Center is working in partnership with Dr. Richard Stauffer as part of a larger project being undertaken by Virginia Tech in the establishment of pure American Chestnut (Castanea dentata) within Sigrist Woods as well as several other sites at TWC as well as a number of cooperators in the eastern United States.
Navigation: The Wilderness Center 9877 Alabama Ave SW, Wilmot, OH 44689
Parking And Admission: No admission fee. Plenty of on-site parking.
Trails: A map of the trails can be found here.
Hours And Camping: No camping. Open Weds – Sunday 9-4 pm.
name: Sigrist Forest at The Wilderness Center

Description: The beech-maple forest association in this preserve is considered to be among the least disturbed in central Ohio, although it was logged after settlement. The more mesic northern portion is a maturing beech forest with some sugar maple. The wetter southern area supports an interesting association of white and pin oak, white ash with specimens of red maple, red elm, shagbark and bitternut hickory, hop-hornbeam, American hornbeam and dogwood. Shrubs include spicebush and buttonbush. The seasonable ponds have an excellent population of amphibians. This preserve honors Walter A. Tucker, the founding director of the Columbus and Franklin County Metropolitan Park District and one of the individuals who helped establish the state nature preserve system.
Navigation: Located in Reynoldsburg 1 mile east of Brice Road on Livingston Ave. A trail system is present. Take Interstate 70 to exit 110 to go north on Brice Road, go 0.7 mile. Then take a Right on Livingston Ave, go 1.1 mile. Turn Right (into Metro park it looks like), go 0.6 mile. Turn Left – this should take you to the trailhead.
Parking And Admission: Parking is available at The Nature Center and at The Beech-Maple lodge as well as multiple picnic areas within the park. A map is here.
Trails: Approximately a total of 4.8 miles.
Hours And Camping: Open year round.
name: Blacklick Woods

Description: The Otter Creek Nature Preserve consists of 292 acres on both sides of Otter Creek, which meanders for 3 miles through the Preserve. This is a mature forest of hemlock and mixed-hardwoods including remnants of the American chestnut that once dominated Pennsylvania forests, nearly wiped out from the invasive Asian chestnut blight.
Navigation: Address: Urey Overlook Day Use Area, 1225 Furnace Rd, Airville PA. (Furnace Rd is also PA Rt. 425.) There is a small parking lot there. Directions: From the parking area, take the Mason-Dixon trail which connects Urey Overlook with the Otter Creek Nature Preserve.
Parking And Admission: Parking: The best way to access the Otter Creek Nature Preserve is from the parking area at the Urey Overlook, which is a satellite of the Susquehannock State Park. The lot is small; the parking is free. Admission: Free
Trails: The total distance of all trails within the Preserve is approximately 4 miles. Hike the Mason-Dixon trail down to the Red trail in the Preserve and then follow the Red trail along Otter Creek, then follow the Orange or Yellow trail back to the Urey Overlook parking site -- a total of approximately 4.5 miles. See the trail map here: https://www.lancasterconservancy.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/K.-Otter-Creek-Trails-Map-2019.pdf
Hours And Camping: Camping is available at the Otter Creek Campground, 1101 Furnace Rd, Airville PA. 95 sites, mostly for RVs but also tent camping. Open April 15 - October 15. 717 862 3628 https://campottercreek.com/ (privately owned campground).
name: Otter Creek Nature Preserve

Description: This old-growth forest at the foot of Blue Mountain is located along the Creek Trail loop that starts on higher elevation above the biggest ravine/valley in the 1,025 acres of the Boyd Big Tree Conservation Area. The old-growth area is in a small valley on the western boundary, estimated at 75-100 acres. It has at least ten tree species -- red and white oaks, tulip trees, beech, hickory, and maple, plus understory trees: hemlock (small but old), sassafras, mountain maple, striped maple, birch, and witch hazel. The estimated age of some of the older oaks is that they sprouted circa 1900. There is substantial moisture at ground level, with at least two narrow creeks running straight down the slope, ending in a wider stream. In the spring, the trail at the ravine's bottom has many examples of mosses, club moss, princess pine, and ferns. There is a notable range of fungi and mushrooms in this area, far greater than in other areas of the Big Tree. There is also a population of a native orchid called Rattlesnake Plantain.
Navigation:
401 Fishing Creek Valley Rd, Harrisburg, PA 17112

From the parking lot, follow the pink blazed Pond Loop Trail to the trail intersection at the top of the hill. Turn right on to the blue blazed Creek Trail and follow it along the ridge. Watch for a turn, on the left, that will take you down into the old-growth area. Follow the trail down and then up the slope, where it then loops and intersects with other trails.
Parking And Admission: There is ample parking at the end of the paved entrance at 401 Fishing Creek Road.
Trails: The Creek Trail Loop is 1 mile. It is moderate difficulty. There are a total of 12 miles of trails in the park.
Hours And Camping: Open year-round. No camping.
name: Boyd Big Tree Preserve Conservation Area

Description:
Rockefeller State Park Preserve contains 1775 acres of preserved land, of which about 1450 acres are forest. Much of the mesic woodlands are oak-tulip, a forest community considered imperiled or vulnerable by the New York Natural Heritage Program. These successional forests contain 150-ft tall tulip poplars, the tallest black oak in New York State at 132 ft tall, and countless other over-100-ft trees. This area of the park has likely been regenerating to mature forest since William H. Aspinwall bought it as parcels of farmland in 1860. Since at least 1886, when John D. Rockefeller began acquiring these properties, this land has been preserved and maintained for passive recreation through its private and public ownership. The towering tulips of Big Tree Loop are likely to be untouched since Aspinwall’s time.

The forests, fields, streams, and wetlands of Rockefeller State Park Preserve support a high diversity of native species of resident and migratory birds, mammals, insects, amphibians, reptiles, fish and aquatic species, some of which are in decline and now uncommon in Westchester County. With 202 recorded species of birds and its Important Bird Area designation by the National Audubon Society, the Preserve is a must-visit area for birders. Over 100 species of native wild bees frequent spring and summer wildflowers. In the fall, Monarch butterflies stop to feed and lay eggs during their southward migration. An on-going environmental stewardship is underway to favor native biological diversity.

Thirty miles north of New York City, the property is the former Pocantico Hills and Rockwood Hall country estates of the Rockefeller family. Since 1983, the Rockefeller Family has generously donated over 1771 acres to the State of New York to safeguard these lands for present and future generations. Managed by New York State Office of Parks, Recreation, and Historic Preservation, the Preserve is open to the public year-round, sunrise to sunset.
Navigation:
Address: 125 Phelps Way, Pleasantville, NY 10570

From Route 117 (Phelps Way), turn into the entrance for Rockefeller State Park Preserve and follow the signs to the main parking lot. To access Big Tree Loop from the main parking lot, follow Old Sleepy Hollow Rd Trail southwest of the parking lot. You will cross Sleepy Hollow Rd and the Pocantico River over a steel bridge. Continue up the hill after crossing the bridge, along Eagle Hill Trail, to a 4-way intersection halfway up the hill. Follow the signs “To 13 Bridges” going straight, and at the T junction, turn left onto 13 Bridges Trail and then right onto Witch’s Spring. Turn right onto Spook Rock Trail going uphill. The next junction is the north and south legs of Big Tree Loop.
Parking And Admission:
Parking: At the main parking lot, 125 Phelps Way, Pleasantville, NY 10570, $6.00 per vehicle (Bus permits: $35 for non-profit orgs, $75 for commercial - per visit). Collected: April - October, daily and November - March, weekends & holidays only. This parking lot has 150 spaces, some choose to park on the street when it is full or for easier access to their preferred trails.

Admission is free.
Trails:
Big Tree Loop: 1.18 mile loop

Total distance of all trails in the park: 65 miles
Hours And Camping: Open year round, sunrise to sunset. Camping is prohibited.
Hunting: Bowhunting by permit only, in select areas of the park. For application and information, see https://parks.ny.gov/documents/parks/RockefellerAboutRSPPHuntingProgram.pdf
name: Big Tree Loop - Rockefeller State Park Preserve

Description: The Ice Glen is a glacial ravine in the southeast area of Stockbridge, MA. The sides of the glen are covered with old-stand pine and hemlock. Its north-south orientation protects the glen from much direct sunlight, which in turn has protected the pines from inclement weather. Because of this the pines grow tall and go uncut, and many consider Ice Glen as the most accessible old-growth forest in the state. The crags and crannies of the moss-covered rocks are said to harbor ice and snow into the summer, hence its name “Ice Glen”. At the north end of the glen is a flat rock face with an inscription from the land’s donor, David Dudley Field. At the south end of the glen is reputedly the largest Eastern Hemlock in the state, towering some 132 feet tall, 10.2 feet in girth. It may even be the largest in New England.
Navigation:
Address: Park Street, Stockbridge MA

Directions: From Route 7 (South Street) in Stockbridge, turn onto Park Street. Park in the small parking area at the end of Park Street. After crossing the Goodrich Memorial footbridge at the end of Park Street, proceed over the railroad tracks and up the trail. At the fork (about 1/4 of a mile), take the right and continue over to the glen.
Parking And Admission:
Limited parking is available at the end of Park Street.

Limited parking is also available on Ice Glen Road near the southern entrance to Ice Glen Trail.

There is no admission charge.
Trails:
Length: 1 mile round trip if retracing back through the glen; 2 miles round trip if returning via Ice Glen Road, South Street, and Park Street.

Difficulty: Difficult. Some sections require climbing and holding to navigate boulders.
Hours And Camping:
Open year round. The trail may be dangerous in winter.

There is no camping available.
name: Ice Glen

Description: The SUNY-Fredonia College Lodge Nature Preserve, formerly called the Herbert C. Mackie Memorial Camp, is 173 acres of high-quality forest and wetlands, including a core 14 acres of old-growth forest surrounded by 40 acres of historic woodlot recovering old-growth characteristics. Half of the old-growth is upland Hemlock-Northern Hardwoods forest in which Hemlocks have been dated to 442 years and Beech over 250 years, accompanied by elder Sugar and Red Maples, Black Cherry, Cucumber Magnolia and Basswood. The rest of the old-growth is a rare Rich Hemlock-Hardwood Peat Swamp community with incredible plant diversity and deceptively small trees, including Hemlocks dated to over 330 years old and Black Ash to 192 years old. The Preserve’s habitats support more than 500 species of plants, including several rare and endangered species. There are well developed nature trails throughout the forest. The Muir Trail, the Leopold Trail and the Darwin trail go through the upland old-growth.
Navigation:
8067 Route 380 - Brocton, NY 14716

Specific directions to trailhead: from the parking lot by the Lodge building, find the beginning of the Darwin Trail along the driveway to the east of the utility garages.
Parking And Admission: During the warm seasons, turn into the College Lodge entrance and park in the large parking area just west of the Lodge. In winter, park along the road near the lodge entrance as the driveway and parking lot are closed to visitors during the winter months.
Trails: A hike down the Darwin Trail to its intersection with the Leopold Trail, continuing on Leopold to its intersection with the Muir trail, then following the Muir trail around to its intersection with the Darwin Trail and following that along the marsh until it loops back up to the parking lot accesses much of the old-growth forest, with a total hike of 0.85 miles. The total length of all trails on the property is 4.5 miles.
Hours And Camping: The Preserve is open year-round from sunrise to sunset. Parking facilities are not maintained in the winter (see “Parking & Admission”).
Hunting: Hunting is allowed by permit only.
name: College Lodge Nature Preserve

Description: Plum Lake Hemlock Forest is a near virgin stand of old-growth, nearly 240 acres, on rolling topography between Star Lake and Plum Lake. Canopy trees include hemlock, yellow birch, sugar maple, basswood, and paper birch. Seedlings of birch and red maple are present, but hemlock reproduction is sparse due to overbrowsing by deer, which often use the area as a winter deer yard. The forest contains substantial numbers of snags and coarse woody debris strewn about the forest floor. Shrubs, though not dense, include mountain maple, American fly honeysuckle, and red elderberry. The understory includes a diversity of herbaceous species including Canada mayflower, shining club-moss, creeping-snowberry, bunchberry, American starflower, pipsissewa, lesser rattlesnake-plantain, and Indian-pipe. Nesting birds include red-eyed vireo, black-throated green warbler, blackburnian warbler, northern parula, winter wren, ovenbird, hermit thrush, and veery.
Navigation: From the north junction of State Highway 155 and County Highway N in Sayner, go west on N 2.1 miles, then north 4.2 miles on Razorback Road, then east 1 mile on Rearing Pond Road, then south at the T intersection 0.5 mile to the western boundary. Park along the road and walk southeast into the site. To access the eastern portion, from the south junction of 155 and N in Sayner, go east and north on N 4.8 miles, then southwest on Tramper's Trail (Hook Lake Road) 0.8 miles to a parking area.
Parking And Admission: Small parking area located at the end of Hook Rd in Star Lake, and also at the end of Rearing Pond Rd in Boulder Junction.
Trails: Trampers Trail – 2.8 miles
Hours And Camping: Open year round, though trailhead parking is not plowed on either end of property.
name: Plum Lake Hemlock Forest State Natural Area

Description: 80 acres. Currently the property is a mature Beech-Maple climax forest moving toward "old growth" conditions. The oldest trees on the property are estimated to be 120-140 years old. The forest is uneven aged, with the most mature trees being American beech, sugar maple, Northern red oak, yellow birch, and Eastern hemlock. Evidence of old growth conditions include: forest floor with extensive "pillows & cradles" that indicate long term canopy disturbance, stilt rooted trees identify "nurse" seed bed structures, and large trees with very coarse bark and deformed canopies.
Navigation: 3001 S. 16th Ave., Shelby, trailhead is along 16th Ave. (also called Scenic Dr.) next to Apache Dr. (private road)
Parking And Admission: Parking area is at the trailhead. There is room for about 10 cars. No admission fee.
Trails: Two loops: short loop of 0. 7 miles (begins and ends at trailhead - parking lot), longer outer loop of 1.5 miles (begins and ends at trailhead - parking lot).
Hours And Camping: Trails are open year-round. Dawn to dusk. No camping.
name: Otto Nature Preserve

Description:
The Red Canyon area has been called the "most photographed place in Utah". The brilliant red soil contrasts with the green pines. The Red Canyon Trail System is widely known and very popular and includes diverse habitats of mixed conifer forests and woodlands with 255 acres of old-growth Ponderosa Pine, Douglas Fir and Pinyon Juniper.

Red Canyon is within the Dixie National Forest which is almost 2 million acres across southern Utah and home to wildlife species such as cougar, bobcat, blue grouse, golden eagle, cottontail rabbit, wild turkey, antelope and the Utah prairie dog.
Navigation: Cassidy Trail begins at the Red Canyon Trailhead in Red Canyon. From US 89, drive east 4.5 miles on SR 12. The trailhead is the first trailhead on your left after passing the Red Canyon Visitor Center.
Parking And Admission: Please see directions to trailhead parking in Navigation section.
Trails: There are many trails in the area to view the old-growth mixed conifer-pine forest. Cassidy Trail in Red Canyon is an accessible 5-mile loop.
Hours And Camping:
Camping is available in the Red Canyon Campground. 37 campsites at $21 site.

https://www.fs.usda.gov/recarea/dixie/recreation/camping-cabins/recarea/?recid=24944&actid=29
Hunting: Yes, though this area is dedicated to recreation and education, it is open to hunting, per state law.
name: Red Canyon- Dixie National Forest

Description: The Beartown Woods Natural Area is 27 acres out of the 85,500-acre Michaux State Forest. This area is a relic northern hardwood forest more typical of northern Pennsylvania, New York, and New England. Species found in this forest include sugar maple, yellow birch, American beech, eastern hemlock, and white pine.
Navigation: Browns Spring, Washington Township PA 17268. From Browns Spring, take PA State Rte 16 northwest approximately ½ mile to the Appalachian Trail parking area on the side of the road.
Parking And Admission: The Appalachian Trail parking area on Rte 16 is free but contains only 4 or 5 spots.
Trails: The Appalachian Trail goes through the Beartown Woods Natural Area both north and south of Rte 16.
Hours And Camping: The trails are accessible year round. The nearest camping is campsite #24 of the Michaux State Forest which is near the intersection of Old Forge Rd and South Mountain Road. However, more camping is available in Caledonia State Park, both tenting and RV hook-ups. Details at : https://www.dcnr.pa.gov/StateParks/FindAPark/CaledoniaStatePark/Pages/Stay.aspx
Hunting: Hunting is permitted throughout the state forest during designated seasons for deer, turkeys, grouse and squirrels.
name: Beartown Woods

Description:
The Nature Conservancy’s 427-acre Norton Pool Preserve contains a bog and rare plant species as well as the preserve's crown jewel, its lowland virgin spruce-fir forest. Not only is it the only remaining forest of its kind in New Hampshire, but one of the last few remaining virgin stands in the East. The best way to visit Norton Pool is by water.

Put your boat in at East Inlet, utilizing the public boat launch and paddle up the feeder brook to the Norton Pool Preserve. In the early mornings, moose frequent the pond and feed on underwater vegetation. Look for pitcher plants along the boggy edges and on stumps in the water. Please note that the paddle up the stream that flows into East Inlet can sometimes be blocked by wood debris and may require some amount of portaging. But paddlers need not venture all the way up the stream in order to enjoy a wild forest experience, surrounded on all sides by forested mountains that extend to the international border.

The wonderfully pristine East Inlet is two miles off Route 3 on a well-maintained logging road. East Inlet has a bog/peat bottom and is an ideal spot for canoeing. You can fish from the dam but to get out on the water, use a canoe, kayak, kick boat or john boat. Area lodges rent canoes and kayaks.
Navigation:
From the intersection of US 3 and NH 145 in Pittsburg, head north on US 3 past First and Second Connecticut Lakes for approximately 13.5 miles. Turn right on East Inlet Road. In approximately 2 miles, you will see the entrance and parking area for East Inlet, where you can launch your canoe or kayak.


Canoes and kayaks can be rented locally for about $30/day from local outfitters and in some cases can be delivered to the boat launch. Call ahead to reserve. (Lopstick, North Country Paddle, Tall Timber are a few.)
Parking And Admission: The parking area for East Inlet is on East Inlet Road. You can launch your canoe or kayak from the parking area.
Trails: The approximate paddle distance from East Inlet to the Norton Pool Preserve is about 1.5 miles. Please note that the paddle up the stream that flows into East Inlet can be blocked by wood debris and may require some amount of portaging.
Hours And Camping:
Norton Pool Preserve is open year round, 24 hours/day.

Camping is prohibited.
Hunting: Hunting is permitted. Hunters must follow the NH Fish and Game rules and regulations. East Inlet Fishing Season: 4th Saturday in April to October 15th. Brook Trout ~ 5 fish or 5 lbs whichever is reached first
name: Norton Pool Preserve

Description: This is true old-growth forest with many ancient and impressively large hemlock trees. At four thousand acres, Tionesta contains the largest tract of old-growth forest in Pennsylvania, and the largest between the Adirondacks and Great Smoky Mountains. Dominant tree species in the areas are eastern hemlock, some more than 400 years old, as well as beech, birch, oak, maple, ash, and black cherry. The large beech trees have mostly succumbed to beech bark disease.
Navigation: Navigate to: 2 Scenic Dr. Ludlow PA. From there the road will turn to fairly smooth gravel. Set your odometer. Many small roads fork from this one. Stay on the main road. At 5.4 mi. take a right at the fork. (This is FR 133E but unmarked.) In 1.2 mi more (6.6 mi total) park on the right shoulder of the road and look for the trail sign.
Parking And Admission: Parking is extremely limited. 4-5 cars maximum can fit on the roadside here. It is recommended to park at the nearby Post Office.
Trails: The Tionesta Scenic Area Loop Trails both start at the same place. The small loop is .4 mi and the long loop is 1.4 mi. The North Country National Scenic Trail passes through the forest nearby. That trail is 4,800 miles long.
Hours And Camping: Open year round, 24 hours.
Phone Number: Bradford Ranger District Address: 29 Forest Service Dr., Bradford, PA 16701 Phone: 814-362-4613
name: Tionesta Scenic and Research Natural Area

Description: The 3,500 acre Nordhouse Dunes Wilderness Area was protected by Congress in 1987. Open Dunes and Great Lakes Barrens are found along nearly four miles of Lake Michigan shoreline. Some of the largest swaths of freshwater interdunal wetlands in the world are also present near Lake Michigan. Mixed hardwood forests of maple, beech, and hemlock are interspersed with oak and pine. Streams, small inland lakes, and wetlands are found in low areas between the forested backdunes. This Wilderness Area protects endangered species such as Piping plover, and Pitcher’s thistle and is home to wildlife like bear, deer, and porcupine. While the area was historically logged, the protections afforded by the Wilderness Act of 1964 will continue to allow the forests to grow old and recover their wild character.
Navigation: Trailhead is located at: Nordhouse Dunes Parking Lot, W Nurnberg Rd, Free Soil, MI 49411 or Lake Michigan Recreation Area, 6000 W Forest Trail Rd, Free Soil, MI 4941 - park at the end of the road and head to the beach access. Turn left (south) at the trailhead or along the shoreline and walk a short distance to the Wilderness Area.
Parking And Admission: It is recommended to use the Lake Michigan Rec Area trailhead during peak times (60 parking spaces). Parking is very limited on summer weekends at the Nurnberg Rd trailhead (24 spaces). There is a $5 per day or $15 per week fee at either trailhead. This is national forest land and parking passes may also be purchased.
Trails: There are 13 miles of trails in the Wilderness.
Hours And Camping: The Nordhouse Dunes Wilderness Area is open to dispersed camping year-round. The Wilderness can only be accessed via Nurnberg Trailhead in the winter, as the roads to Lake Michigan Recreation Area are not maintained in the off-season.. Camping is prohibited within 400 feet of the Lake Michigan shoreline, within 100 feet of a designated trail, and within 200 feet of Nordhouse Lake. Visitors are asked to use existing campsites when possible. Campfires or bonfires are not permitted on the beach. Services such as restrooms, water, and trash are only available at the trailheads. Campers should expect to pack water in, and/or treat water from an available source. Visitors are required to pack out all trash. Human waste should be packed out and/or buried at least 6” below the surface. Maximum group size for camping the in the Nordhouse Dunes Wilderness Area is 10 people. Wheels are prohibited in the Wilderness. Campfires must be attended at all times. Glass containers are prohibited.
name: Nordhouse Dunes Wilderness Area - Huron-Manistee National Forests

Description:
Bear Swamp at the Red Lion Preserve is a great example of an Atlantic white cedar forest, with some beech specimens estimated around 150 to 187 years old. Other species include sassafras, white oak, chestnut oak, Southern red oak, American holly, pitch pine, short-leaf pine, black gum, red maple, and black cherry.

The location of Bear Swamp is transitional between the inner coastal plain (with better quality soils) and the outer coastal plain (with very sandy, generally less nutrient rich soils). However, other evidence points towards these beech trees having advanced age, most notable are the abundance and diversity of nonvascular epiphytic organisms on their bark. You can find many trees whose bark is covered with many different species of mosses as well as three types of lichens – crustose, foliose, and fruticose.
Bear Swamp at the Red Lion Preserve is a vast, unspoiled forest that is tremendously important to the surrounding community as it helps to recharge the aquifer that supplies the Delaware River Watershed. The 2,100-acre forest is managed by the New Jersey Natural Lands Trust- an independent agency that "acquires open space primarily by donations of land and easements" in order to "preserve land in its natural state for enjoyment by the public and to protect natural diversity".
Navigation:
360 Hawkins Road, Southampton, NJ

Not a system of improved trails but best access is off of Hawkins Road near the address above on which there is a utility ROW. Walking along the ROW and then heading into the forest may be best.
Parking And Admission: Parking is limited along Hawkins Road. Access to Trust preserves is free.
Trails: There are some rough trails and old woods roads but nothing official.
Hours And Camping: Open for passive recreation such as birding and hiking from dawn to dusk.
name: Bear Swamp at Red Lion Preserve

Description: One of the New Jersey Natural Lands Trusts' model holdings, this preserve is critical for local and migratory wildlife. The wetland forests of the preserve are some of the most extensive in the region. Located less than one mile from the Delaware River, migrating songbirds depend on this forest for stop-over cover on their southward migrations. The unbroken forest habitats also provide desirable nesting sites for interior forest nesting birds including scarlet tanager and ovenbird. The wet woodlands are dotted with countless shallow, seasonal ponds. These vernal ponds possess perfect conditions for frogs and salamanders to breed. Several old abandoned agricultural fields are managed strictly for the benefit of wildlife. Using funding from the Natural Resources Conservation Service’s Wildlife Habitat Incentives Program (WHIP), the Trust has cleared overgrown brush and planted warm season grass to improve habitat for bobwhite quail.
Navigation: There‘s a small grassy parking area with a trailhead directly across the street from 81 Perkintown Road, Pedricktown, NJ 08067. The trails eventually lead to the area of the old growth forest area/forested wetlands.
Parking And Admission: Parking is limited. Access to Trust preserves is free.
Trails: There is a system of mowed and blazed trails constructed by neighbors but nothing official.
Hours And Camping: Open for passive recreation such as birding and hiking from dawn to dusk.
name: Game Branch Preserve

County and State: City and Borough of Skagway, AK
