Description: The trail to Jánwu Sítʼi, also known as the Denver Glacier Trail is a 6.4 mile round trip hike. The trailhead is located 5.5 miles north of Skagway and can be reached easily from the White Pass and Yukon Pass Railroad from May to September. The forest surrounding this trail demonstrates a range of conditions, from lush old-growth spruce and hemlocks trees characteristic of the Tongass National Forest’s temperate rainforests to younger vegetation forming along the retreat of the glacier. At the trailhead hikers pass a 1960s red caboose that has been converted into a basic cabin and is available for rent through the US Forest Service.
Navigation: This trailhead is only accessible via the Denver stop along the White Pass and Yukon Route Railroad. The station to board this train within Skagway is at 201 2nd Ave, Skagway, AK 99840.
Parking And Admission: The trailhead is about 8.8 km (5.5 miles) along the railway tracks from Skagway. It is accessible via the White Pass and Yukon Railroad from May 1 to September 30. Book your train tickets with the White Pass & Yukon Route (roughly $66 round trip). In the off-season people may hike or ski from Skagway, add 8.8 km to the listed hike distance.
Trails: 6.4 miles roundtrip from the train stop to the Jánwu Sítʼi (Mountain Goat Glacier), also known as Denver Glacier, viewpoint. The trail begins from the flag stop at mile 5.8 on the WP&YR railroad. The trail leaves the tracks at the caboose and parallels the east fork of the Skagway River, climbing slowly for 1.5 miles through an immature birch and hemlock forest until you reach a nice view of the Skagway River and the Sawtooth range. From here, the trail begins to climb more steeply for another 1.5 miles, eventually giving way to a large stand of old growth spruce and hemlocks until it turns right and heads up to Lower Elway Falls. From the lower falls you leave the old growth and climb steeply south up the valley through more immature forest that gives way to thick alder. The upper 2.5 miles of the trail receives little use and is often overgrown with alder and fern. The trail dead ends at the end of a box canyon with spectacular views of the hanging seracs of the Denver Glacier and Upper Elway Falls.
Hours And Camping:
Trail is available all hours but access is dependent on the train schedule. Book train tickets at https://wpyr.com/

A USFS primitive cabin that is an old caboose is available for overnight stay at the trailhead. Reserve the cabin at https://www.fs.usda.gov/recarea/tongass/recarea/?recid=78826
name: Jánwu Sítʼi (Mountain Goat Glacier) also known as the Denver Glacier Trail- Tongass National Forest

Description: The Valley Creek Special Interest Area (SIA) is 303 acres and was recognized early on as a unique example of old growth and has been classified as such since the mid-1940s. Dominant trees range in age from 130 to 435 years old and it has several structural characteristics that meet the definition of late-successional Sierra Nevada mixed conifer old growth forest of Douglas-fir and Sugar pine. The old growth Douglas-fir and Sugar pine provide habitat for many local wildlife species, including the sensitive California spotted owl and Northern goshawk. They also provide dwellings for small mammals. Valley Creek, which runs through the Special Interest Area, has been recognized as habitat for the sensitive foothill yellow-legged frog and the Federally Threatened red-legged frog.
Navigation: From the town of La Porte, travel west along the La Porte road 3.5 miles to the junction with Forest Service Road 21N51. Turn right, and drive approximately 1/4 mile to a small trailhead parking area on the left.
Parking And Admission: Trailhead parking is free and open to the public.
Trails:
In 2011, a 2.5-mile hiking trail was completed, providing access for hikers and nature enthusiasts. The trail is gentle with a few moderately steep sections.

https://www.fs.usda.gov/recarea/plumas/recarea/?recid=82796
Hours And Camping:
17 Units are available on a first come, first served basis at Strawberry Campground Plumas National Forest, La Porte Rd, Strawberry Valley, CA 95981 (reservations are not accepted).

https://www.fs.usda.gov/recarea/plumas/recarea/?recid=11223
Hunting: Yes, in the Plumas according to CDFG permit.
name: Valley Creek Botanical Special Interest Area - Plumas National Forest

County and State: City and Borough of Sitka, AK
Description: The Beaver Lake Trail and Herring Cove Trail join as the paths encircle Beaver Lake, which is surrounded by an impressive stand of old-growth trees. The trails route through forests of western hemlock, Sitka spruce, and yellow cedar, and give opportunities to enjoy far-reaching views, muskegs, and waterfalls. The old-growth forest surrounding Beaver Lake can be enjoyed alongside other recreation opportunities such as fishing and picnicking.
Navigation:
You can access Beaver Lake by two trailheads: Beaver Lake Trailhead at the steel bridge at Sawmill Creek Campground off Blue Lake Road and the other is the Herring Cove Trailhead. Blue Lake Road is at times closed to vehicle traffic. Call the City and Borough of Sitka for road updates.

Primary access is from the new Herring Cove Trailhead parking area at the end of Sawmill Creek Road 6 miles east of Sitka. Drive past the Sawmill Cove Industrial Park and past Blue Lake Road to the gate and trailhead parking area.

Access from Blue Lake Road is about 5 miles east of Sitka. At mile 5.5 on Sawmill Creek Road across from the pulp mill, turn left onto the uphill gravel road. Go 1.5 miles along Blue Lake Road to the Sawmill Creek Campground, first right. The trail begins across the bridge over Sawmill Creek on the south side of the open gravel area.

The Herring Cove trailhead is another mile beyond the Industrial Park. Beyond the Sawmill Creek Bridge the road is gravel. The trail head is almost at the end of the road. Take an immediate left after driving through a gate.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking is available at the Herring Cove Trailhead. Free admission.
Trails:
As Beaver Lake is accessible via two trails that loop around the lake, you can pursue a variety of routes:

From Herring Cove to Blue Lake Campground along north side of Beaver Lake 2.82 miles (one-way).

– From Campground around Beaver Lake and back 2.8 miles

– From Campground to Herring Cove and back along south side of Beaver Lake 4.6 miles.

– From Campground to Herring Cove and back along SMC and Blue Lake Roads 6 miles – 3 hrs.

– Big trail loop is easiest hiked beginning at Herring Cove to Beaver Lake. Goes around Beaver Lake and back or on to Herring Cove
Hours And Camping: The recommended season is early spring through late fall. Camping is available at the Sawmill Creek Campground at the Beaver Lake Trailhead along Blue Lake Road. Access begins Mid-may. For campground details: https://www.fs.usda.gov/recarea/tongass/recarea/?recid=79124
name: Beaver Lake Trail- Tongass National Forest

County and State: City and Borough of Sitka, AK
Description: Courtesy of Sitka Trail Works: The trail begins on the east side of the mouth of Salmon Lake stream, the westernmost inlet stream at the head of Silver Bay. The initial section of the trail is narrow and skirts along the base of a small cliff. The trail continues along the eastern shore of the estuary for the first quarter mile and then enters a forest of Sitka Spruce, western hemlock, and Alaska yellow cedar. Salmon Lake is visible to hikers after about a mile.
Navigation: The trailhead is located about 10 miles southeast of Sitka at the southwest end of Silver Bay. Access by sea taxi, boat, or float plane.
Parking And Admission: No parking available. Trail is not accessible via car. Free admission.
Trails:
1.75 miles (one way, to cabin)

• Salmon Lake Cabin – 1.75 miles from mooring buoy

• Cabin to end of maintained trail – 1.9 miles

Trailhead is on the left-hand side of the bay before entering the estuary narrows. Bears are active in this area so practice bear safety and carry bear spray.
Hours And Camping: Trail is available all hours. A USFS cabin is available for overnight stay 1.75 miles in on the trail. Reserve the cabin at: https://www.recreation.gov/camping/campgrounds/233105
name: Salmon Lake Trail- Tongass National Forest

Description: 220 total acres. Although none of the total acreage is technically old-growth, there are trees approaching or over a century old. The forest contains predominantly maples, oaks, black cherry, hemlock, and white pine.
Navigation:
8076 M-25, Pigeon, MI 48755 or 8164-8198 M-25, Pigeon, MI 48755

There are two trailheads at the Preserve.
Parking And Admission: There are two places to park at this preserve. One is located at the Dunn Road gate west of M25 and the other is a gravel parking area on the west side of M25 north of Dunn Road. Parking is ample and there is no fee for admission.
Trails: The trail network at this Preserve is approximately five miles in total length.
Hours And Camping: The Preserve is year round, every day from dawn to dusk. Camping is not allowed at this Preserve.
Hunting: Yes - during state regulated hunting seasons.
name: Sand Point Nature Preserve

Description: The nature preserve is 206 acres and contains a mix of old-growth and younger (50 year old) trees consisting predominantly of oak, maple, and hickory. The park is also significant in that is contains a 1,000 year old Native American earthworks by the Late Woodland native people. It is a National Historic Landmark.
Navigation: 9466 Columbus Pike, Lewes Center, Ohio 43066
Parking And Admission: Oak Covers; free entry to park
Trails: The overlook trails is 2.3 miles that meanders through the forest and passes adjacent to several creeks. The trail will allow access to the native American earthwork, as well as a nineteenth century cemetery. An observation deck permits view of the Olentangy State Scenic River. Well-maintained.
Hours And Camping: Open 365 days a year; 6:30- 8 pm October to March; 6:30 am - 10 pm April -Sept.
name: Edward F. Hutchins Nature Preserve - Highbanks Metro Park

Description:
Sharon Woods is a mixture of forests and fields with old-growth hickory, beech, and oak. There are eight species of oak present, with some dating to 250 years of age. There is an 11-acre lake, as well as seasonal pools. "This is an old-growth forest in the making".

Within the 768-acre park is the Edward Thomas Nature Preserve, named for the renowned naturalist and founder of the Metro Park system.
Navigation: 6911 Cleveland Ave Westerville, OH 43081. From I-270, take the Cleveland Ave North exit. Entrance is about 1⁄2 mile on the left.
Parking And Admission: Parking and admission are free. Follow the main road until it ends by the lake.
Trails: The Edward Thomas trail is 1.1 miles on largely flat terrain.
Hours And Camping:
The park is open 365 days a year. April - September hours are 6:30 am - 10 pm

October - March hours are 6:30-8 pm.
name: Edward S. Thomas Nature Preserve - Sharon Woods

Description: On the entire Eastern Shore a total of 19.4 acres of state land have been identified as "old-growth". This forest, with 14.4 acres, comprises the majority of that acreage. Although the site is small there are beautiful ancient oaks, tuliptrees, beech, holly and pines. The oldest trees are estimated to be over 200 years old.
Navigation: Address of the parking area: 1.2 miles past 632 Wye Island Rd, Queenstown, MD 21658.Directions: From Rte 50 heading West, turn Left onto Carmichael Rd. Turn Right onto Wye Island Rd. Follow Wye Island Rd. to 632 Wye Island Rd. 1.2 miles after 632 Wye Island Rd turn Right to Schoolhouse Nature Trail parking area.
Parking And Admission: Parking is available for up to 5 vehicles. Admission is free.
Trails: Recommended Trail: Schoolhouse Woods Nature Trail – 1.2 miles. This is a flat and easy trail. Wye Island has a total of six miles of trails. Ferry Landing Trail leads beneath a canopy of Osage Orange Trees. The Holly Tree Trail leads to a holly that some say is 400 years old, and others say is “only” 290.
Hours And Camping: Hours: Open year round, dawn to dusk.
name: Schoolhouse Woods - Wye Island Natural Resources Management Area

Description: Holmboe Conifer Forest State Natural Area is small, only 32.15 acres in size. Despite its size, the property is a significant natural area. It features an outstanding example of mature stands of hemlocks, pines and white cedar. There is a rich variety of tree species, old, large trees, and down woody debris scattered on the ground. The terrain is uneven, creating a diversity of forest community types on the glacial ridges and lowland swamps. It is bordered by the Pelican River, near the confluence with the Wisconsin River. Springs are found on the Property near the Pelican River. This forest is special because of the presence of old-growth forest right next to the City of Rhinelander, and because it protects greenspace that is open for use by the public.
Navigation: Directions: From the Intersection of Hwy. 17 South and Hwy. 8 West, head northwest on Hwy 8 toward Boyce Dr. Turn right on to Boyce Dr., and continue 0.3 miles to Riverview Hall. Parking and access to the trailhead is in the back of Riverview Hall (903 Boyce Dr, Rhinelander, WI).
Parking And Admission: There is a small parking area located in the back of Riverview Hall student housing. If you use Google Maps on your phone to navigate, you should be able to simply type in ‘Holmboe Conifer Forest Trailhead’ and it should take you directly to the parking area/trailhead.
Trails: The long loop of the trail is just under 1 mile, and the short loop is about 0.75 miles long.
Hours And Camping: The preserve is open to non-motorized silent sport use year-round. Allowed activities include hiking, snowshoeing, un-groomed cross-country skiing, and wildlife viewing. No camping.
name: Holmboe Conifer Forest State Natural Area

Description: Oden Island Nature Preserve is a 50-acre forested natural area with nearly a mile of frontage on Crooked Lake. A couple of upland ridges occur along the middle of the preserve. These drier upland areas are unique and don’t fit a Michigan Natural Features Inventory classification very well, they are likely a variation of Mesic Northern Forest, but have characteristics of an inland Boreal Forest community type. There are a handful of emergent marsh pockets along the shoreline that comprise important nearshore aquatic habitats. The forests on the preserve are mature and contain many large trees, especially eastern hemlocks, white pine, and some large sugar maples. There have not been any timber harvests since the 1950’s, according to aerial imagery, and it has likely been much longer since any logging, and some trees might even predate the logging boom of the late 1800’s. Thus, portions of the forest in the Oden Island Nature Preserve approach old-growth forest characteristics.
Navigation:
3160 Leeward Dr. Petoskey, MI 49770

Take US31 north from the intersection with M119. Turn east on Pickerel Lake Road and travel 3.5 miles until it takes a sharp turn. Continue northeast on Channel Road 1.5 miles and turn left on Oden Island Road. Continue on this road until you reach Leeward Drive and then turn right and take it to the end of the road to the parking area.
Parking And Admission: A small parking area is available. There is no admission fee.
Trails: 0.7 miles of trails
Hours And Camping: Hours are sunrise to sunset, open year round. No camping available.
name: Oden Island Nature Preserve

Description: Hemlocks Natural Area encompasses 120 acres of virgin hemlock forest in a narrow ravine about one-half mile long within the 96,000 acre Tuscarora State Forest. Many of the hemlocks are believed to be over 225 years old with the largest reaching over 120 feet tall and 50 inches in diameter. A ring count of a wind-thrown hemlock established the age of the older trees at 300 years. Numerous trees are over 24 inches in diameter. The forest is comprised of a variety of tree species including hemlock, yellow birch, black birch, red oak, red maple, and chestnut oak.
Navigation: There is no street address for Hemlocks Natural Area. From Blain, PA take PA State Route 274 west for approximately 10 miles to Big Spring State Park. Just past the park entrance turn left (east) onto Hemlock Rd; a gravel state forest road. Travel 3-4 miles on Hemlock Rd, passing the Hickory Ridge Overlook along the way. There are two trailheads for the Hemlocks Natural Area, one at each end of the ravine. GPS and cell phone signals are weak in the area and should not be relied upon.
Parking And Admission: Parking is limited to a few vehicles at each trailhead. Turn-around space is also limited. No restrooms available. Admission is free.
Trails: Three miles of marked and signed hiking trails traverse the natural area. The trails are rated difficult with downed trees, rocks and roots. Multiple wooden foot bridges criss-cross Patterson Run. Paper maps are available at the trailheads or nearby forest district office.
Hours And Camping: Open year-round. Day use only. Camping not permitted. State forest roads are not maintained in the winter and become impassable with snow and ice. Big Spring State Park has day-use picnic tables and pavilions.
Hunting: Hunting is permitted throughout the state forest during designated seasons.
name: Hemlocks Natural Area- Tuscarora State Forest

Description: The Hemlock Mt and Upper Biscuit Brook Stands are typical of the northern hardwoods hemlock association with sugar maple, yellow birch and hemlock dominant in the canopy and with beech persisting in the understory in the form of small diseased trees or sprouts from formerly larger trees killed off by the beech-bark disease. The Upper Biscuit Brook stand has many large diameter (30-inches and greater) hardwood trees with classic old growth forms and an abundance of old growth indicator epiphytes including the lichen Lobaria pulmonaria and L. quercizans, the moss, Nekera pennata and the leafy liverwort, Porella platyphyloidea.
Navigation:
1. To access the Hemlock Mt. Old Growth Stand go to the Slide Mountain Trailhead Parking Lot, 2099 Oliverea Road, Big Indian, NY: There is no hiking trail leading into or through the Hemlock Mt stand. The stand is reached by crossing the road from the Slide Mt. trailhead parking area and walking away from the road (northwest) and up the slope for a distance of about 0.4 mile to the top of the stand. A small stream runs down through the stand to the roadside and provides an easily followed route.

2. Biscuit Brook Parking Area, 1857 Frost Valley Road, Claryville, NY: The Biscuit Brook stands are accessed directly from the blue-blazed Pine Hill – West Branch Trail starting from the Biscuit Brook parking area on County Route 47. The first area of old growth (Lower Biscuit Brook Old Growth Stand) is reached within about 0.25 miles of the trailhead. The second stand of old growth (Upper Biscuit Brook Old Growth Stand) is reached at a distance of 2.5 miles from the trailhead.
Parking And Admission:
Free parking and admission at both trailheads.

Slide Mt. Trailhead: 25-30 vehicles

Biscuit Brook Trailhead: 7-10 vehicles
Trails:
1. Hemlock Mt. Old-Growth Stand: There is no hiking trail leading into or through the Hemlock Mt stand. The stand is reached by crossing the road from the Slide Mt trailhead parking area and walking away from the road (northwest) and up the slope for a distance of about 0.4 mile to the top of stand. A small stream runs down through the stand to the roadside and provides an easily followed route.

2. The Biscuit Brook stands are accessed directly from the blue-blazed Pine Hill – West Branch Trail starting from the Biscuit Brook parking area on County Route 47. The first area of old growth is reached within about 0.25 miles of the trailhead. Many large trees are observed in this area as well as an exceptionally rich herbaceous flora growing under sugar maple, white ash and basswood which is characteristic of rich mesic forest. The second stand of old growth is reached at a distance of 2.5 miles from the trailhead.
Hours And Camping:
Hours: Open year-round. Note restrictions for camping:

Camping: General information on backcountry camping includes how-to and safety tips and links to rules & regulations.

There are five lean-tos located trailside throughout the area, each supported by a seasonal water source and pit privy. Other designated campsites are marked with a yellow "Camp Here" disc. In addition, primitive camping is allowed. Campsites must be at least 150 feet away from the nearest road, trail, or body of water. Camping for more than three nights or in groups of ten or more requires a permit from a Forest Ranger.

State law also prohibits camping above 3500 feet in elevation from March 22nd to December 21st each year. In a Wilderness Area, group size is limited to a maximum of 12. Larger groups may be accommodated in any of the Forest Preserve's Wild Forest areas such as nearby Balsam Lake Mountain or Willowemoc Wild Forests.
Hunting: Big Indian Wilderness is open to hunting and trapping during appropriate seasons. General information on hunting and general information on trapping includes how-to and safety tips with links to seasons, rules and regulations.
name: Mt. Hemlock and Biscuit Brook Old Growth Stands - Big Indian Wilderness Area

Description: Sanders Park Hardwoods is a 33-acre designated State Natural Area within the 80-acre Sanders Park & Campground, owned by Racine County Parks. The natural area consists of two slightly elevated swells separated by a shallow swale on an ancient terrace of Lake Michigan. Southern dry-mesic forests occupy the two swells with basswood, white oak, black walnut, red oak, and white ash. An elm-ash forest dominates the swale. Dutch elm disease and oak wilt have killed some of the larger canopy trees. The sapling layer is composed of ash, basswood, ironwood, and black cherry. The forest is maturing second-growth with dominant trees over 100 years old. A wildflower guide lists 89 species of flowers and ferns including showy orchis, yellow lady's-slipper, false mermaid, false Solomon's seal, Trillium, sharp-lobed hepatica, spring-beauty, wild geranium, blue cohosh, and the introduced helleborine orchid. Ferns of interest are ostrich, rattlesnake, rusty woodsia, and ebony spleenwort. Breeding birds include great-crested flycatcher, eastern wood pewee, red-eyed vireo, mourning warbler, and indigo bunting. Originally purchased by Racine County in 1930, this area was later dedicated to Edwin Sanders, a local biology teacher. Sanders Park Hardwoods is owned by Racine County and was designated a State Natural Area in 1967.
Navigation: Sanders Park 4809 Wood Rd Mt. Pleasant, WI 53403
Parking And Admission: A large parking lot can be accessed off Wood Road. There is no entry fee.
Trails: There are approximately 6 trailheads of varying length. Total distance is anywhere from .5mi to 2 miles depending on route.
Hours And Camping: Park hours are 6am to 10pm year-round. Camping is available from mid-April to mid-October. The campground has 19 sites. Tent camping is allowed on most sites, RV camping is allowed on certain sites. Site hookups vary from none to water and electric. The campground has bathrooms with showers.
Hunting: Hunting of any kind is not allowed on any County-owned property.
name: Sanders Park Hardwoods State Natural Area

Description: Located in Orange County 15 miles northwest of downtown Durham, Occoneechee Mountain State Natural Area offers a quick escape into nature with trails winding through forests of mountain laurel and rhododendron. Two quiet fishing ponds complement the nearby Eno River, while the summit overlook affords a great sunset view. The rare brown elfin butterfly has called the mountain home since the Ice Age. The dominant tree species are blackjack, chestnut and scarlet oaks and Virginia pine.
Navigation:
625 Virginia Cates Rd, Hillsborough, NC 27278

The main trail is a loop around the entire park area. Both trail heads are clearly visible from the parking area.
Parking And Admission: There is room in the parking lot for at least 30 normal-sized cars. Parking is free, admission to the trails is free.
Trails:
Occoneechee Mountain Loop Trail: 2.20 miles

All other trails branch from that main one, and include: Brown Elfin Knob Trail: .1 mile, Chestnut Oak Trail: .9 mile, and Overlook Trail: .1 mile.
Hours And Camping:
November to February: 8:00am to 6:00pm

March to April: 8:00am to 8:00pm

May to August: 8:00am to 9:00pm

September to October: 8:00am to 8:00pm

Closed Christmas Day

There are no camping facilities at Occoneechee Mountain. The closest state park with camping is Eno River State Park
name: Occoneechee Mountain State Natural Area

Description: 16 acres of the Sylvester Manor Southwestern Woodland is permanently protected, within approximately 40 forested acres on either side of the main entry drive into Sylvester Manor. A 2013 Forest Management Plan identified the Oak/Hickory/Pine woodlands as ‘mature to over mature’, aged 70-120 years. This forest is a remnant of lands held by eleven generations of one family of European descent from 1651 to 2014, following millennia of habitation by indigenous Manhansett people.
Navigation:
The property address and main entrance are at 80 North Ferry Road, Shelter Island, NY 11964. The trailhead is nearby the “Quaker Cemetery” shown on Google Maps.

Using the North Ferry: Travel south on Rt 114 for 1 miles. Turn left through the gates by the Quaker Cemetery and Meeting Area. Park beside the roadway and look for the trailhead just east of the start of the Woodland Walk trail.

Using the South Ferry: Travel north on Rt 114 for 2.9 miles. Turn right through the gates by the Quaker Cemetery and Meeting Area, .2 miles beyond the intersection with Manwaring Road and the main Sylvester Manor entrance at 80 North Ferry Road. Park beside the roadway and look for the trailhead just east of the start of the Woodland Walk trail.
Parking And Admission: Limited parking is available along the driveway entrance to the “Quaker Cemetery.” There is no admission charge. The trails are open to the public dawn to dusk from mid-February through October; closed for Hunting November through mid-February.
Trails: The trail into the Southwestern Woodland branches off the Woodland Walk shown on the map available at the site and online at https://www.sylvestermanor.org/map. Sitewide trails total 3+ miles. The Southwestern Woodland trail branch is approximately one half mile.
Hours And Camping:
The woodland trails are open for your enjoyment 7 days a week, mid-January through October (closed for deer hunting season, November-mid-January). Leashed dogs are welcome. Please pick up after your dog. Bicycles and motorized vehicles are not allowed on the trails at any time. Download our “Sylvester Manor Walking Tour” app in the App store to help you navigate the property.

Click here to view a map of the trail system throughout the entire property.

Camping is prohibited.
Hunting: Hunting is by advance permission and participation in the Sylvester Manor Hunting Program only; contact Sylvester Manor at 631 749-0626.
name: Sylvester Manor Forest

Description: Nolde Forest Environmental Education Center encompasses more than 700 acres of deciduous woodlands and coniferous plantations—some nearing 120 years of regrowth. A network of walking trails makes the center’s streams, ponds, and diverse habitats accessible to both students and visitors, daily from 8AM to Sunset.
Navigation: Address: 10 Sawmill Lane, Cumru Township, Reading, PA 19607. Directions: Nolde Forest is in Berks County, Pennsylvania, on PA 625, one and one-half miles south of PA 724 or three and one-half miles north of PA 568. The park office is located on EE Center Lane. M-F 8AM-4PM
Parking And Admission: Historic Sawmill Parking Area (limited). North Pond Parking Area (limited). Park only in designated parking spaces. Free – 8AM to Sunset
Trails: Visitors are recommended to wear proper footwear as many trails are rocky and steep. Visitors are encouraged to wear blaze orange throughout hunting season. Visitors are asked to follow winter trail etiquette—which includes the use of snowshoes and cross country skis so as to not ruin tracks and create safety issues by “postholing.” Recommended hikes range from one to four miles. Approximately 10 miles of trails.
Hours And Camping: Park Office Hours: M-F 8AM to 4PM. The EEC and EEC Parking Area are open Monday to Friday 8AM – 4PM. Walking trails are open daily 8AM to Sunset. No camping or fires.
Hunting: A permit-only archery deer hunt is held annually. Those interested must apply through the park office.
name: Nolde Forest Environmental Education Center

Description: Mostly contiguous area of old growth with some patches of younger but mature woods. Steep slopes and valleys/ravines. Mixed mesophytic. Many unusually tall trees, some over 140 feet. Tallest over 150 feet is tulip poplar. Erodible very deep soil. Lots of spring flowers. 20 to 40 acres. Bryant, William S. 1987. Structure and Composition of the Old-Growth Forests of Hamilton County, Ohio and Environs. “California Woods Nature Preserve is on a dissected outwash terrace near the junction of the Little Miami and Ohio Rivers. There was a total of 407 trees representing 20 species in the 31 sampling plots. Basal area was highest of any forest sampled at 39.16 m2/ha and density totaled 324 trees/ha.
Navigation: 5400 Kellogg Avenue, Cincinnati OH 45230.
Parking And Admission: Parking is available at the Nature Center.
Trails: There are several trail paths through the California woods Park. Dogs are not allowed.
Hours And Camping: Open 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily. Camping is not permitted.
Hunting: Controlled bow hunting only in specific months late Sept - Feb.
name: California Woods Nature Preserve

Description: Kurtz Woods State Natural Area contains approximately 42 acres of a southern mesic forest, a remnant of the pre-european settlement forest community that once covered much of southeastern Wisconsin. The Preserve hosts over eighty species of trees, shrubs and spring ephemerals and has remained intact for at least 100 years. The trees are predominantly sugar maple and American beech with smaller numbers of basswood, white ash, and black cherry. Many large individual trees are present and create a mature, fairly closed canopy environment. Unique woodland wildflowers found at this property include hepatica, bloodroot, wild leek and spring beauty.
Navigation: Approximately 1211 Dahlia Lane Grafton, WI 53080 (north/main entrance) or approximately 517 West Acacia Drive Grafton, WI 53080 (south entrance). Trail heads are gravel paths are located between two residential houses and are indicated by OWLT signage at the entrance to the woods.
Parking And Admission: Parking exists along the street. Please be courteous of our neighbors. There is no charge for admission.
Trails: 1 mile
Hours And Camping: Open year-round, sunrise to sunset. No camping.
name: Kurtz Woods State Natural Area

Description:
Within the folds of farmland next to Skaneateles Lake, lies the Finger Lakes Land Trust’s 53-acre Bahar Nature Preserve, a hidden forest that calls to visitors yearning for an enchanted retreat. The mature mixed northern hardwood/hemlock forest on the Preserve is part of a larger forest block that fills the Bear Swamp Creek gorge, and extends through the adjacent Carpenter Falls State Unique Area and private lands. Although most evidence of an old mill disappeared many years ago, a trail that has been used for more than a century, referred to by locals as the “Jug Path”, takes hikers along the south rim of the gorge, where they are treated to dramatic views into the 100-foot-deep Bear Swamp Creek ravine. The preserve extends across the creek and up the other slope.

While the forest in the Preserve that is found on the gently-sloping terrain around the rim of the Bear Swamp Creek gorge was logged on and off over the last couple hundred years (most recently in the 1970’s), the forest in the deep gorge was mostly inaccessible because of the steep slopes, and likely harbors a significant area of “old growth”. Eastern hemlock trees dominate the steep slopes, and red oak is dominant elsewhere. Other species include: white pine, American beech, sugar and red maple, white ash, black cherry, American basswood, yellow birch, and tulip tree. Hemlock, red oak, and tulip trees are often over 24" dbh, and some very large oaks are certainly well over 100 years old. In 2006 two trees in the Preserve, an American chestnut and a yellow birch, were winners in the Cayuga County "Big Tree Contest".

All of the forest on the Preserve has much to offer anyone wishing to explore nature. Many large trees entice visitors to crane their necks looking to the canopy far above. Old wild grapevines twist around saplings, grow with the tree, and can be seen gnarled and coiling up a tall maple or ash in search of sunlight. A carpet of mosses and ferns such as shining clubmoss and maidenhair fern add to the lush vegetation. White trillium and Jack-in-the-pulpit are among the wildflowers that add color to the forest floor.

The Bahar Nature Preserve includes 65 feet of Skaneateles lakeshore, which is a fine place to beach a canoe or kayak before hiking up the ridge trail.

The “white trail”, which mostly follows the route of the old “Jug Path” along the south rim of the gorge, runs between the Bahar Nature Preserve and Carpenter Falls State Unique Area for approximately 1.1 miles, with the iconic 90-ft Carpenter Falls at the upstream end. A “red trail” runs 0.5 mile from the FLLT parking area on Appletree Point Road through the Bahar Preserve to the white trail/Jug Path.
Navigation:
Carpenter Falls Unique Area Parking Area Location:

Appletree Point Road, Niles, NY. Slightly east of the intersection with Carver Road.

Bahar Nature Preserve Parking Area Location:

Appletree Point Road, Niles, NY. Approximately 0.8 mile east and north of the Carpenter Falls Unique Area parking area, and 0.3 mile north of the intersection with Plunkie Point Road.

From Skaneateles, follow Rt. 41A south for 10.5 miles; turn left (east) on Appletree Point Rd. and follow for 0.55 mile to Carpenter Falls Unique Area parking area, and 1.35 miles to the Bahar Nature Preserve parking area, both on the left.
Parking And Admission:
Parking at the Bahar Nature Preserve is limited to about 6 vehicles. No fee.

Parking at the Carpenter Falls Unique Area is limited to about 20 vehicles. No fee.
Trails: White Trail, runs 1.1 miles between the west shore of Skaneateles Lake on the FLLT Bahar Nature Preserve and Carpenter Falls on the NYSDEC Carpenter Falls Unique Area. Red Trail runs 0.5 mile from Bahar Nature Preserve parking area to the White Trail (please see the trail map for more details).
Hours And Camping: Open year-round, dawn to dusk. Access road may get limited winter maintenance. No camping allowed.
Hunting: Hunting is not permitted at either the Bahar Nature Preserve or the NYSDEC Carpenter Falls Unique Area.
name: Bahar Nature Preserve

Description:
New York State’s 37-acre Carpenter Falls Unique Area was created for the purposes of recreation and watershed protection. There is a 0.59-mile trail that runs across the length of the property providing scenic views of Bear Swamp Creek and two sets of waterfalls. An ADA accessible, elevated boardwalk and a viewing platform allow all visitors to traverse through the forest to view spectacular Carpenter Falls as it cuts through a notch in the massive overhanging limestone caprock and plunges over 80 feet into a deep pool.

Approximately 2/3rds of the property is dominated by a Northern Hardwood-Hemlock forest type, which is characterized by steep slopes and exposed shale outcroppings towering above Bear Swamp Creek. These gorge areas have likely seen little to no human manipulation since European settlement and contain multiple age classes with very large eastern hemlock and sugar maple dominating. The remaining portions of Unique Area on the more accessible ground host a somewhat younger, transition hardwood forest type with red oak dominating and has an even age structure that shows evidence of previous logging operations.


This trail also connects with the adjacent Bahar Preserve which is managed by the Finger Lake Land Trust and provides access to an additional 1.6 miles of trails and access to a picturesque waterfall.
Navigation:
Address: It has no physical address but the pin on Google Maps suggests an address of 5986-6062 Appletree Point Road

From Skaneateles: Head south on State Route 41A for 11.15 miles and then take a left onto Appletree Point Road. Continue on Appletree Point Road for 0.5 miles. The paved parking area is located on Appletree Point Road near the intersection of Carver Road. Roadside parking is prohibited.
Parking And Admission: Carpenter Falls parking area (20 car capacity, 2 accessible), Access is free.
Trails:
Recommended Trail : Old Jug Trail 0.59 miles, (connects to 1.1 mile trail in Bahar Nature Preserve for a total of 1.69 miles)

Please see the trail map for more details.
Hours And Camping: Open year round from sunrise to sunset. No admission fee. No camping.
Hunting: This property is not suitable for hunting. (However, there is no regulation prohibiting hunting.)
name: Carpenter Falls Unique Area

Description: The 805-acre old growth coastal redwood grove includes a visitor center, self-guided nature trails, and a variety of picnic facilities. It is part of the 5,683-acre Austin Creek State Recreation area. While you can drive into the park, the best way to experience the dramatic effect of the towering redwoods, is to park in the lot at the park entrance and walk in for free. All of the main park features can be found along the Pioneer Nature Trail. This trail is a mile and a half loop, ADA accessible and is mostly flat. The Parson Jones Tree is the tallest tree in the grove, measuring more than 310 feet in height, and the Colonel Armstrong Tree is the oldest, estimated to be over 1,400 years old. The ancient coast redwood is the tallest living thing on our planet and live to be 500-1,000 years old, grow to a diameter of 12-16 feet, and stand from 200-250 feet tall. Coast redwoods are classified as temperate rainforests and need wet and mild climates to survive. The rainfall in Armstrong Redwoods averages 55 inches per year and the trees are often shrouded in fog.
Navigation: 17000 Armstrong Woods Road, Guerneville, CA 95446
Parking And Admission:
$10.00 per vehicle, $9.00 per vehicle for seniors
Free to pedestrians and bicyclists
Bus fee for 10-24 passengers is $50.00
Trails: The Pioneer Nature Trail at the entrance to the forest, and near the visitor center, connects with the Discovery and Armstrong Trails providing a 1-mile loop with ADA access and views of the Colonel Armstrong Tree, Icicle Tree, and Parson Jones Tree.
Hours And Camping: A campground operated by Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods located in Austin Creek State Recreation Area at Bullfrog Pond Campground (3 miles above Armstrong). Austin Creek SRA is accessed through the same entrance as Armstrong Redwoods.
Hunting: Loaded firearms and hunting are not allowed in units of the State Parks System. Possession of loaded firearms or air rifles is prohibited. Exceptions are for hunting in recreation areas that have been designated by the State Park and Recreation Commission.
name: Armstrong Redwoods State Natural Reserve

Description:
Beall Woods State Park includes 329 acres of old-growth forest. It is one of the few places where one can experience the natural hardwood forest of the Eastern Woodland. The forest is sometimes called the “University of Trees” because of the great species diversity. There are sixty-four different tree species in the park, including five kinds of maple, six kinds of hickory, and thirteen kinds of oaks! Joan Maloof highlighted this forest in her book Among the Ancients: Adventures in the Eastern Old-Growth Forests.

The Wabash River valley was once filled with majestic trees. Gradually those forests were all cut out except for this acreage protected by the Beall family. In 1965, after the last member of the family died, the State of Illinois purchased the farm and forest. It is now a State Park, dedicated State Nature Preserve and a National Natural Landmark.
Navigation:
9285 Beall Woods Avenue Mount Carmel IL 62863

The trailhead is located adjacent to the parking lot near the visitors center.
Parking And Admission: One large parking lot is located outside the Visitor Center. Access to the Tuliptree and White Oak trails is directly in front of the Visitor Center.
Trails:
Trails currently open within the Nature Preserve:

Tuliptree - Easy 1-mile upland forest trail. Self-guided tree identification brochure is available at the Visitor Center.

White Oak - Moderately easy 1.25-mile trail (with the exception of three flights of stairs) offering the greatest diversity of vegetation and forest conditions.

Sweet Gum - This .50 mile trail follows Coffee Creek and features an interesting rock cliff.

Schneck - This 1.75-mile trail was dedicated to Dr. Jacob Schneck, a pioneer Mount Carmel physician and botanist.

(The Schneck and Sweet Gum trails are accessed from the north side of the park).
Hours And Camping:
Open sunrise to 10pm, year round.

Sixteen Class C campsites with vehicular access and restrooms, but no showers or electricity, are available. A disposal station is available for camper’s use. Individuals interested in utilizing the group campground are encouraged to call the site headquarters to avoid scheduling conflicts. No reservations are necessary for the campground. Campers are asked to set up at their chosen campsite and park personnel will come by to issue a permit.
name: Beall Woods State Park

Description: Hemlocks Overlook is a 400 acre woodland aligned along Bull Run in southern Fairfax County. There are stands of old-growth eastern hemlocks along steep slopes adjacent to Bull Run, some as old as 250 years. In addition, there are old-growth sycamore and several old-growth stands of tulip poplars. A large canopy of American beech, white oak, red oak, and mountain laurel predominate. Well maintained trails through the steep topography allow visitors access to the old-growth forest areas.
Navigation: 13220 Yates Ford Road, Clifton, Virginia 20124
Parking And Admission: Admission is free. There is a small 8 car parking lot to the right across from the winery and just beyond it, there is a parking lot for approximately 20 vehicles. There are no facilities, however the town of Clifton, Virginia, 3 miles away, has several restaurants.
Trails: A number of trails can take visitors to the primary old-growth areas, and approximately 1 to 1 1/2 miles round trip trail.
Hours And Camping: The park is open dawn to dusk year round.
name: Hemlock Overlook Regional Park

Description: This 1,833-acre park is home to a great forest of coast redwoods as well as evergreens, chaparral, and grasslands. The redwood grove, which is mature second growth from the 1850s is 700 acres. Wildlife within the park includes rare species such as the golden eagle and Alameda striped racer. Deer, raccoons, rabbits, and squirrels are often seen.
Navigation: 7867 Redwood Road, Oakland, CA 94619
Parking And Admission:
Entrance and Parking: 7867 Redwood Road, Oakland, CA 94619

All fees are collected on weekends and major holidays April through October and only at the Redwood Gate entrance | Parking: 5 per vehicle; $4 per trailered vehicle. Buses: $25 per bus | Dogs: $2 per dog. No fee charged for guide/service dogs.
Trails: The largest remaining natural grove of coast redwoods (Sequoia sempervirens) in the East Bay. There are two short hiking/walking trails, .9 (paved) and 2 miles (dirt), and an 8.22 mile bike route. Full map: https://www.ebparks.org/sites/default/files/rredwood_map_2020.pdf
Hours And Camping: Open between 5am and 10pm unless otherwise posted or permitted. Several group overnight camping areas are located within the park. They are available by reservation only; telephone 1-888-EBPARKS or 1-888-327-2757, press option 2, for information. Hiking, jogging, and horseback riding are popular on the park's nearly 40 miles of trails. The East Bay Skyline National Trail and Bay Area Ridge Trail traverses Redwood for part of its 31-mile course. Fishing is not allowed in the park.
name: Reinhardt Redwood Regional Park

Description:
Rowe Woods is part of over 1,016 acres of land owned by the Cincinnati Nature Center that features nearly 14 miles of trails winding through Eastern deciduous forest, fields, streams, ponds and wetlands. The Woods are a mix of oak forest, old growth mesic hardwood forest and old growth bottomland forest. Approximately 96-acres are old-growth forest with some trees dating to nearly 250 years old. Dominant tree species in the old growth oak forest are Shumard oak, chinquapin oak, red oak, sugar maple, American beech, and an abundance of understory trees, shrubs, and wildflowers. Bobcats, mink, pileated woodpeckers, and red bats, among other wildlife, call the old-growth forest home.

The old-growth area was purchased in late 1898 by Carl Krippendorf to preserve the forest. Krippendorf was the son of German immigrants who settled in the Cincinnati area. Carl Krippendorf purchased 97 acres of the land where he spent the summer recuperating from a childhood illness to preserve it from becoming a tobacco field and built a home there.

The walking trails that are open for an admission fee and are free to members of the Cincinnati Nature Center.
Navigation: 4949 Tealtown Road, Milford, OH 45150
Trails: There are 14 miles of trails in total.
Hours And Camping:
Rowe Woods varies - see below:

Rowe Woods Visitor Center 9 am - 5 pm

Monthly hours: January: 8 am–5:30 pm February: 8 am–6 pm March: 8 am–7:30 pm April: 8 am–8 pm May: 7 am–8:30 pm June: 7 am–9 pm July: 7 am–9 pm August: 7 am–8:30 pm September: 8 am–7:30 pm October: 8 am–7 pm November: 8 am–5:30 pm December: 8 am–5 pm
Phone Number:
Olivia Espinoza, Natural Areas Director
oespinoza@cincynature.org
name: Cincinnati Nature Center - Rowe Woods

Description: Shell Ridge is 1,421 acres of protected open space and trails with rolling hills, creeks, coast live, valley, blue and black oaks, and historic structures that include the Borges Ranch and Howe Homestead Park in the City of Walnut Creek, CA. With proceeds of a bond issue authorized by the citizens in 1974, the City bought and preserved the undeveloped Acalanes Ridge, Lime Ridge, Shell Ridge and Sugarloaf Open Spaces. The largest of the four—Shell Ridge—has roughly 1,420 acres of oak woodlands and grassland savannah and 31 miles of trails.
Navigation: Old Borges Ranch, 1035 Castle Rock Road, Walnut Creek, CA 94598
Trails: 31 miles of trails in the park. Visitors are encouraged to park in the lot near the historic Borges Ranch buildings.
Hours And Camping: Park is open during daylight hours only. Camping is not allowed in the park, but is permitted at adjacent Mt. Diablo State Park through the online reservation system https://www.reservecalifornia.com/Web/
Hunting: No hunting is allowed in the park.
name: Walnut Creek Open Space – Shell Ridge

Description: Allerton Park consists of about 1,500 acres of natural areas. The Illinois Natural Areas Inventory (INAI) surveyed Allerton Park in 1976 and 2008 documenting 470 acres of very high (old growth and second old growth) and high (old growth and second old growth; grazed) quality forest on the site. This is the largest area of high-quality forest in the Grand Prairie Natural Division (White, 1978). Allerton Park holds INAI category designations of I (high quality natural communities) and II (specific suitable habitat for endangered or threatened species). Dominant tree species at Allerton Park include White, Black, Northern Red, and Bur Oak, Shagbark, Shellbark, Mockernut and Bitternut Hickory Hackberry, Silver Maple, and American Sycamore.
Navigation:
Allerton Park and Retreat Center

515 Old Timber Rd, Monticello, IL 61856

Once on site there are numerous trailheads that all take you to portions of the oldest forests.
Parking And Admission: Parking for multiple vehicles at all trailheads. No admission charge.
Trails: About 14 miles of trails. The McDonald Family Trails including the Blue and Green trail loops access the oldest most high quality forest.
Hours And Camping: Open year-round dawn to dusk but closed on Christmas and New Years. Camping is not available on site but overnight accommodations are available in the Allerton Mansion and guest houses.
Hunting: Archery Deer Hunting – special permit only https://allerton.illinois.edu/management/
name: Allerton Park – University of Illinois

Description: The 55 acre preserve contains hardwood and understory trees that date to over 100 years old. Red elm, buckeye, and oak are prominent species, while the areas in lower elevations contain sycamore and American beech. The understory consists of spicebush with a significant presence of pawpaw trees. The Preserve grew to its current acreage after an initial donation of 33 acres by Ron and Betty Johnson, Darke County residents. A 1.5 mile trail winds through the forested areas.
Navigation: 5352 Routzong Road, Greenville, OH 45331
Parking And Admission: There is a parking lot off Routzong Road.
Trails: Routzong Preserve has a 1.5 mile trail that is not difficult.
Hours And Camping: Sunrise to sunset daily. Camping is not permitted.
Phone Number: The phone for the parks department is 937 548-0165.
name: Routzong Preserve

Description: Coppess Nature Sanctuary is a 32-acre woodland donated by Frances Carpenter as a legacy to Darke County residents. The Sanctuary offers an example of an Oak-Hickory forest and a glimpse of some of the natural diversity of the Darke County region as it appeared 200 years ago. Five species of oaks dominate, with several white oaks over 40" in diameter. Shagbark and bitternut hickories are scattered throughout the area. Other trees of interest include American beech, American hornbeam, white ash, box elder and sugar maple. The Sanctuary features a 3/4-mile loop trail.
Navigation: 10277 Young Rd, Union City, OH 45390
Parking And Admission: Parking lot off Young Road.
Trails: .75 mile loop trail, not difficult.
Hours And Camping: Sunrise to sunset daily. Camping is not permitted.
Phone Number: The phone for the parks department is 937 548-0165
name: Coppess Nature Sanctuary

Description: The 70-acre Witherell Woods in Palmer Park is the largest old-growth forest in the Tri-County area, and one of only seven forests in the City of Detroit. Witherell Woods contains a true Oak-Beech Climax forest and some of the oaks exceeding 350 years in age were planted by Mother Nature herself. 3 distinct natural communities are present and over 100 different species of native plants, including several species of oak, maple and hickory. Improvements and changes made by People For Palmer Park, the Adopt-a-Park Community Partner with the City of Detroit, are mindful of this, and aim to ensure that the park will become self-sustaining, protected and a treasure to be enjoyed by all for generations to come.
Navigation:
Palmer Park: 910 Merrill Plaisance St. Detroit, MI 48203

The trail system through Witherell Woods can be accessed from multiple parking lots.
Parking And Admission: Large parking lots are available on the north, west, and south side of Palmer Park. Visitors can directly access the trails from the parking lot off of Merrill Plaisance Street near the educational garden and splash pad, and from the west lot of the Detroit Police Department - 12 Precinct off of 7-mile road on the north side of the park.
Hours And Camping: The park is open from 6am-10pm. No camping is available.
name: Witherell Woods - Palmer Park

Description:
Owned by the Northern Connecticut Land Trust, these two preserves totaling 44 acres are in the northwestern border of the unique Bolton Notch/Valley Falls Watershed and are part of only a handful of watersheds in CT that drain in a northerly direction. The remote mixed forest includes many Pitch Pine and hardwood (maple, oak) trees and is surrounded by steep rock outcroppings with great views of Valley Falls Park and Railroad Brook that drains north to Valley Falls Pond. The outcroppings are made up of mostly shiny Bolton Schist with sparkling Ruby Garnets. The property is bisected by the Rails-to-Trails hiking/biking trail developed along the old Manchester to Willimantic railroad bed, which itself offers many miles of open access trails.

The 14-acre Echo Ridge property abuts the 30-acre Webster Preserve providing blazed trails along the ridgeline above Valley Falls Park, with access crossing the Rails-to-Trails from Valley Falls Road, with beautiful overlooks from high above Railroad Brook.

Looking for another hike nearby? Check out Box Mountain Forest, part of OGFN’s Private Forest Registry.
Navigation:
Webster Preserve is located just west of Valley Falls Park (300 Valley Falls Road) and south of Valley Falls Road. Park in the Valley Falls Park lot. Access the Preserve either from Valley Falls Road (sign in tree) or by following the Valley Falls Trail around the west side of the pond and then up the hill. Either route you will be climbing to the Hop River Trail. The upper trails can also be accessed directly from the Rails-to-Trails path, from Manchester to the west or Andover and Bolton from the south.

Echo Ridge is directly adjacent to the Webster Preserve and can be accessed with connecting blazed trails or from the Town of Vernon soccer field at the top of Boulder Crest Lane.
Parking And Admission: Ample free parking is available in the adjacent Valley Falls Park lot.
Trails: Approximately 2-3 miles of connecting trails on the properties. Rail-to-Trails bike path thru the area offers many miles of hiking/biking along a graded railroad bed, and the Connecticut Blue trail system is also accessible from the Valley Falls Park which has 9 miles of trails more easily accessible and traversable (see Town of Vernon, CT website).
Hours And Camping: Open year round for hiking/biking only.
name: Webster Preserve/Echo Ridge

Description: Rising above the west bank of the Arkansas River, River Parks’ Turkey Mountain Urban Wilderness is an untamed oasis in the heart of the city. Encompassing over 600 rugged acres, the park’s thick canopy of native trees watch over winding trails, serene ponds and ancient boulders. Secured to remain a public park in perpetuity, the Wilderness is a one-of-a-kind regional destination that continues to grow in popularity. The landscape creates a sense of being far from city life, with visitors surrounded by a thick canopy of trees including native Post and Blackjack Oak, Hickory, Redbud and other species, with several oaks dating back to the early 1800s.
Navigation: 6851 S Elwood Ave, Tulsa, OK 74132
Parking And Admission: Main parking is free but limited especially during weekends. No charge for admission.
Trails:
A new trail called the Naharkey trail runs through the oldest parts of the forest. It was just put in and has not yet been measured or officially mapped. (A map should be available in March)

Turkey Mountain has 20+ miles of marked trail suitable for Hiking and Mountain Biking.
Hours And Camping: The park is open from 5am to 11pm, daily. No camping is allowed.
name: Turkey Mountain Urban Wilderness

Description:
Exploring the Cross Timbers Trail offers hikers a glimpse to an ancient Western Cross Timber forest that once extended from southern Kansas into North Central Texas. This 3.37 round-trip trail has views of the West Fork of the Trinity River, the Lotus Marsh, and 250+ year old trees. The trail is accessible to hikers from the Cross Timbers parking lot or by hiking on the Riverbottom Trail. Along the trail you’ll see tree species such as Pecan, Bur Oak, eastern Cottonwood, American Elm along the stream, and post oak and blackjack oak in the Western Cross Timbers woods.

The Fort Worth Nature Center & Refuge (FWNC&R) is a 3,621-acre natural area comprised of forests, prairies, and wetlands allowing you to step back in time and experience what the Fort Worth/Dallas Metroplex was like in the early 20th century. With over 20 miles of hiking trails, the park is one of the largest city-owned nature centers in the United States.

The park is located within the Cross Timbers, a complex mosaic of woodlands and grasslands that form a broad ecotone between the eastern deciduous forests and the grasslands of the southern Great Plains; covering about 26,000 square miles. East and West Cross Timbers couch the Fort Worth Prairie on the east and west.
Navigation:
9601 Fossil Ridge Road Fort Worth, TX 76135

From Loop I-820, exit Hwy 199 (Jacksboro Highway) and go west 4 miles. Exit Confederate Park Rd. to the right and stay on service road. At the stop sign, turn right onto Buffalo Road into the Nature Center entrance. Stop by the gate house to pay entrance fee and obtain a day pass and a trail map.
Parking And Admission: $6 Adults (13-64) $2 Children (3-12, under 3 FREE) $3 Seniors (65+) $1 Discount per person (with Military ID-Active/Retired) $1 Dogs (Dogs Free with FONC Membership
Trails:
Cross Timbers Trail loop trail through the ancient forest - 3.37 miles.

Total distance of all trails is 20 miles.
Hours And Camping:
September-April, 8 a.m. - 5 p.m.

May-August, 7 a.m. - 5 p.m.

No camping is allowed.
name: Cross Timbers Trail - Fort Worth Nature Center & Refuge

Description:
St. Francis Woods is an old-growth forest within Independence Grove Forest Preserve in Libertyville, IL. The forest is dominated by red and white oak, with several white oaks dating back between 1737 and 1801. Historic aerials from 1939 show roughly 80 acres of forest which remains intact to this day. Other tree species present include hickories, basswood, black cherry and sugar maple.

Independence Grove Forest Preserve is owned and managed by the Lake County Forest Preserves. Centered around a 115-acre lake, this preserve offers a variety of opportunities for outdoor recreation and nature education. Surrounding prairie and woodlands provide a picturesque backdrop for walking, biking, picnicking, fishing, concerts, playground, volleyball, and other fun activities.
Navigation:
16400 West Buckley Road, Libertyville, IL 60048
Independence Grove Forest Preserve, is north off of Buckley Road (Hwy 137) and east of Milwaukee Avenue (Hwy 21). St. Francis Woods is on the north end of the park. From the entrance go to the northernmost parking area on the left as you pass the welcome building. The trailhead is in the northeastern part of the parking area. St Francis Woods is the forested area north of the lake.
Parking And Admission: Parking is ample and free to Lake County, IL residents. For all others there is a small fee of $6 per car.
Trails:
From the parking lot St. Francis Woods is approximately 1.5 miles. Independence Grove hosts 7.5 miles of walking trails which circle the lake and run through scenic natural areas. Roughly 6.4 miles are available for biking, 3.8 miles for in-line skating, and 0.6 miles for cross-country skiing. Trails here also connect to neighboring communities and provide walk-in access to the preserve.

The preserve’s Lakeside Trail and a short section of the Des Plaines River Trail (DPRT) have gravel surfaces. The Overlook Trail and the South Bay Trail Loop have paved surfaces. The North Bay Trail Loop has a combination of paved and gravel surfaces.
Hours And Camping:
Open year round

Hours: 6:30AM to sunset
No camping
name: St. Francis Woods- Independence Grove Forest Preserve

Description: Although primarily a beech-sugar maple community, Kyle Woods has a striking diversity of woody species and is more complex than similar woodlots in northeastern Ohio. Tree species include American basswood, cucumber magnolia, wild black cherry, black tupelo, beech, tulip trees and several species of oaks and hickories including several white oaks more than 300 years old. Sugarbush is present in the forest. A nearby subdivision that was constructed in the early 2000s has caused some forest distress on that border.
Navigation: 6920 Tippecanoe Road, Canfield, Ohio 44406
Parking And Admission: Pets are not allowed and restrooms are not available. The gate is locked in winter, so visitors should park outside and walk into the woods
Trails: Kyle Woods State Nature Preserve has 0.75 miles of hiking trails.
Hours And Camping: The preserve is open 1/2 hour before sunrise to 1/2 hour after sunset. No camping is allowed.
name: Kyle Woods State Nature Preserve

Description:
Located on the western shore of Pymatuning Reservoir, Pymatuning State Park features two areas that are considered as old-growth forest. The first is the Big-Woods Area, which holds an interior 30-acre section of forest that features multiple towering Tulip trees that have grown upwards of 130 feet and an impressive diversity of northern hardwoods, with many reaching 110 feet or higher. Species of note here include American Beech, Sugar Maple, Yellow Birch, Red Oak, Shagbark Hickory, and American Basswood.

The other section of old-growth exists in the Padanaram area, located at the northern most end of the park. This section of old-growth is located in the interior of a large secondary forest community and is roughly 15-acres in size. The section of old-growth is primarily a Eastern Hemlock/Northern Hardwood forest, with many exceptional examples of Red Maple that are 4-5 feet in diameter, and upwards of 110 feet tall. Species of note here are Eastern Hemlock, Black Cherry, American Beech, Yellow Birch, Swamp White Oak, and Cucumber Magnolia.
Navigation:
Big Woods Area – 6892 Pymatuning Lake Rd Andover, OH 44003

Parking is available at the Poplar Grove picnic shelter. Trailhead is directly across the street from the park water plant. There is a yellow gate at the unnamed trail entrance and signage indicating “Old Growth Forest Area”.

Padanaram Forest – 6960 Padanaram Rd. Andover, OH 44003

Parking is available at the Padanaram Boat Launch area. The unnamed trailhead is located at the Northwest corner of the parking area and is marked with signage indicating “Old Growth Forest Area”.
Parking And Admission: To access the Big Woods area, visitors are able to park in the Poplar Grove picnic area (ample parking) across the street and walk over to access the property. As for the Padanaram area, there is a parking lot there (ample parking) for visitors. There are no admission fees at Ohio State Parks.
Trails:
Big Woods Area – existing unnamed trail/ access road approximately ½ mile in length

Padanaram Forest – existing unnamed trail at northwest corner of parking area is approximately 1/3 mile

Total distance of all trails in Pymatuning State Park (as of 2/10/23) is approximately 5.5 miles
Hours And Camping: Open every day of the year from sunrise to sunset. Day use areas close at dusk A 375 site, Class A campground is available in the State Park. Camping is prohibited in the areas being considered for Old Growth Forest designation.
Hunting: General hunting is allowed in the Padanaram Forest area. Archery deer hunting only is currently permissible in the Big Woods area of the park.
name: Big Woods Area and Padanaram Forest – Pymatuning State Park

Description:
Containing old growth white pine, hemlock, and pitch pine, this 500- acre tract is located 5 miles west of Troxelville along the Swift Run Road in Spring Township, Snyder County. This natural area, within the Bald Eagle State Forest, contains old growth white pine, eastern hemlock, and pitch pine.

The existing old growth was saved from the loggers’ saws in 1902 when a 14,000-acre tract was purchased by the commonwealth and a stop-cutting order was issued. Good access is provided by foot trails.

Hemlock is/was a major component of the old growth forest in areas like the Snyder-Middleswarth and Tall Timbers Natural Areas. The loss of many of these old growth hemlocks, mostly due to the invasive hemlock wooly adelgid, has resulted in increased light to the forest floor and significant flushes of sweet birch seedlings. The state forest staff has cooperated with the Division of Forest Health to treat some high value trees with systemic insecticide like imidacloprid and dinotefuran with mixed results. Because of the nature of the insecticide and the insect, as well as the locations of the stands of hemlock, it is impractical to do this type of treatment on a large-scale basis. The staff has also cooperated with the Division of Forest Health to release predatory beetles that feed on the adelgid. The desire is that these predator insects will assist in controlling the adelgid to the point where hemlock will occupy and maintain its prominence in the forest.
Navigation: Swift Run Road, Spring Township, Snyder County, PA
Parking And Admission: Public access is free. Limited single car parking to 4-5 at the picnic area. Restrooms are located at the Rock Springs State Forest Picnic Area.
Trails: The Snyder-Middleswarth Trail has a long and a short loop, both starting at the Snyder-Middleswarth Picnic Area along Swift Run Road. Swift Run Trail and Tower Trail.
Hours And Camping:
Camping is not permitted.

Public access is 24/7/365. NOTE: state forest roads are not snow plowed or treated during inclement weather.
name: Snyder-Middleswarth Natural Area

Description:
Aman Park is a 331-acre preserve six miles west of the city of Grand Rapids. The park contains a number of natural-surface trails through maturing second-growth forests including dry-mesic forests, southern mesic forests and floodplain forests along Sand Creek. Tree species present include northern red oak, eastern hemlock, red maple, American beech, black cherry, white oak and white pine, with silver maple and sycamore common in the lowlands.

The park is well-known for spring ephemeral display including Virginia bluebells, trout lily, dutchman’s breeches, and trillium.
Navigation:
Aman Park 0 - 1859 Lake Michigan Dr, Grand Rapids, MI 49534

The trailhead is accessed from the northern parking lot.
Parking And Admission: There is parking for several vehicles. No admission fee.
Trails:
Red Trail 1.5 miles

Total distance of all trails is 6.5 miles
Hours And Camping: Open year round from dawn til dusk. No camping is permitted.
name: Aman Park

Description: Redwood National & State Parks is 139,000 acres along 35 miles of California’s northern coast, comprised of Redwood National Park and three state parks - Jedediah Smith, Del Norte Coast, and Prairie Creek. 40,000 acres of the parks' forests are healthy, old-growth redwood forests. Almost twice that amount of forests in the parks are degraded, second-growth forests. The four parks are managed collaboratively between the state and federal agencies.
Navigation:
Elk Meadow Day Use Area

258 Davidson Rd, Orick, CA 95555

The Trillium Falls Trailhead is accessed from the Elk Meadow Parking area at the Elk Meadow Day Use Area - off Davison Road, three miles north of Orick.
Parking And Admission: Parking at Redwood National Park is free and no passes are available or required. Each of the state parks that are part of the Redwood National and State Parks unit charge admission. The Trillium Falls Trailhead is accessed from the Elk Meadow Parking area at the Elk Meadow Day Use Area - just off Davison Road, three miles north of Orick. There is drinking water, information kiosks, flush toilets, picnic tables and plenty of parking for vehicles of any size (busses, RV's, trailers).
Trails: Trillium Falls Trail is a family-friendly, short hike passing old-growth redwoods, maples, trillium flowers, ferns, and huge fir trees with a small waterfall. There are some switchbacks and an elevation gain of 200-feet to reach the falls. Many rangers recommend this as the best little hike in Redwood National and State Parks.
Hours And Camping: Campgrounds: Fees ($35) are required for camping at the four developed campgrounds in the parks. Reservations must be made at least 48 hours in advance by calling 1-800-444-7275 or online at ReserveCalifornia.
Hunting: No hunting is allowed in the park.
name: Redwood National and State Parks

Description: The first old growth forest remnant protected in Kentucky (1969), Lilley Cornett Woods Appalachian Ecological Research Station, is a Registered National Natural Landmark by the U.S. Department of the Interior. The total area of the station is 659 acres with the old growth forest located centrally totaling 252 acres. The oldest trees date to 1669 (white oak), and while never logged, it has been disturbed by livestock grazing the understory prior to 1969. The old growth protects an excellent example of a mixed mesophytic forest with over 530 plant species, 72 of them being woody plant species, and diverse wildlife populations.
Navigation:
91 Lilley Cornett Branch, Hallie, KY 41821

From Kentucky Highway 15 south of Hazard, take Kentucky 7 for 13 miles and turn right onto KY 1103. Follow for 8 miles and the entrance will be on the left side of the road.
Parking And Admission: There is parking at the Visitor’s Center. There is no admission charge.
Trails:
Trails are by guided hike only. Guided hikes are available year-round, with the preference of scheduling your hike in advance. From April 1 to October 31, the visitors center is open and drop in hikes are welcome, but guides may not always be available/on other guided hikes.

There are currently two different guided hikes. The Shop Trail (short trail) is a little over 1.5-mile loop trail that takes approximately 3 hours. The Big Everidge Trail (long trail) is a 2.1-mile loop trail that takes approximately 6 hours.
Hours And Camping:
Guided hikes are available year-round by appointment.

Visitors Center is open and drop in hikes are available April 1 – October 31 from 8:30am – 5pm. Scheduled/appointments are preferred.

November 1-March 31 by appointment only

No Camping
name: Lilley Cornett Woods

Description:
The 1300-acre South Grove Preserve includes a primitive hiking trail that will lead you through a pristine stand of giant sequoias, the earth’s largest living organisms. The South Grove Preserve contains over 1,000 large giant sequoias, with an average age from 1,000 to 3,000 years old. The Agassiz tree is the largest and quite possibly the oldest tree in the park. The largest sequoias in the park are found here in the remote tranquil South Grove Preserve.

Giant sequoias are some of the world’s oldest living organisms. They are outlived only by the 5,000 year-old bristlecone pines in remote mountain ranges of the Great Basin region. The oldest known giant sequoia was 3,200 years old, and many live over 2,000 years. Ideal soil, water, and sunlight conditions in this spot have enabled this species to thrive here. Giant sequoias often grow in groups of two or three because an area of mineral soil opened up with just enough sunlight to enable seeds to take root. They are not able to sprout from roots or stumps as are the coast redwoods.
Navigation: Visitor Center: 1170 East, CA-4, Arnold, CA 95223
Parking And Admission: $10 entrance fee. Parking is available in the Visitor Center Parking Lot.
Trails: South Grove Trail - The first 1.5 miles (2.4 km) of trail is a moderate, steady climb from the parking lot to the start of the loop trail, with a gain of 260 feet (79 m) in elevation. The loop trail passes through a representative portion of the lower part of the grove. Just over one mile (1.6 km) in length, this section of trail first climbs 200 feet (61 m), then gently descends back to the start of the loop.
Hours And Camping:
https://www.parks.ca.gov/?page_id=551 Online reservations are recommended.

Visitors will be able to reserve campsites and lodging six months in advance from the current date. Bookings may extend from the arrival date to the desired departure date – based on availability and the park’s maximum stay rules.
Hunting: LOADED FIREARMS AND HUNTING are not allowed in units of the State Parks System. Possession of loaded firearms or air rifles is prohibited. Exceptions are for hunting in recreation areas that have been designated by the State Park and Recreation Commission.
name: Calaveras Big Trees State Park

Description: The woodlands of Little Mulberry Park, south of Miller Lake, are home to the older hardwood stand with large beech, tulip poplar and white oak tree specimens. Within these older woodlands area, there is moist cove forest with ephemeral ground cover, which is relatively unique to Gwinnett. In the bottom ravine area, there is a dense thicket of red maple and paw paw trees. The Master Plan mentions that park users walking through this area of Little Mulberry Park are afforded a glimpse of how a pre-Columbian forest may have appeared
Navigation:
Auburn Entrance: 3855 Fence Road, Auburn GA 30011

Dacula Entrance: 3900 Hog Mountain Road, Dacula GA 30019

Disc Golf Entrance: 3800 Hog Mountain Road, Dacula GA 30019

Equestrian Entrance:1300 Mineral Springs Road, Dacula GA 30019
Parking And Admission: There is no admission free to Little Mulberry Park. Parking is available at all entrances (limited to equestrian access at the Equestrian Entrance):
Trails:
14.8 miles of trails total:
5.5 miles of multiuse trail
3.6 miles of hiking trail
5.7 miles of equestrian trail

The oldest forest area is located along the Ravine Loop Trail, Woodland Trail, and Beech Tree Trail.
Hours And Camping: Open sunrise to sunset every day unless posted otherwise and no camping is allowed
name: Little Mulberry Park

Description:
Broadly, the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area contains more than 100 miles of trail and 27 miles of the Appalachian Trail. Much of the National Recreation Area is second-growth, though remnants of old-growth forest can be found in this area. This area is formed by the Delaware River cutting through the Blue Mountains within Pennsylvania and the Kittatinny Ridge in New Jersey.

In particular, stretching from N Delaware Dr toward Caledonia Creek is a forest containing mature mixed hardwoods and old-growth oak-dominated forests on the ridge tops and large hemlocks within the ravines.

Hornbecks Creek Trail near Dingmans Ferry, PA offers views of forests and waterfall-fed creeks that converge with the Delaware River. Visit the National Recreation Area website for any closures: https://www.nps.gov/dewa/index.htm
Navigation:
To access the Appalachian Trail to Mount Minsi hike, travel to the parking area near the intersections of Lake Rd and Mountain Rd near the town of Delaware Water Gap (40.980025, -75.1420201).

Hornbecks Creek Trail is along Route 209, Dingmans Ferry, PA 18328. The
mile-long trail to the lower waterfall can be accessed off of US Route 209 between mile markers 10 and 11.
Parking And Admission:
The Appalachian trail can be accessed from a parking area at the northern end of Lake Rd as it turns off of Mountain Rd. [Labeled on Google Maps as Parking for Appalachian Trail to Mount Minsi] This area also allows access to the Lake Lenape trailhead. The Appalachian Trail uses white blazes.

Parking for trails to Mt. Minsi are usually full by 9:00 am on Saturdays and Sundays. Avoid crowded trailheads by hiking early, on weekdays, or choosing a less popular trail. Call park headquarters at (570) 426-2452 for assistance planning your hike or check the park’s Facebook page (https://www.facebook.com/DelWaterGapNPS) on summer weekends for real time updates.

There are no fees to enter the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area and to park at the Appalachian Trail to Mount Minsi trailhead, but fees are collected for use of certain other areas. For more information visit: https://www.nps.gov/dewa/planyourvisit/fees.htm

The lowermost waterfall can be reached from an unpaved parking area off of Route 209 near Chestnut Hill Road. This parking area can be found at the following coordinates: 41.187000, -74.885415. From here, an obvious trail heads into the woods and follows the creek upstream to the waterfall.

The upper parking area for Hornbecks Creek's uppermost waterfalls can be found off of Emery Road at the following coordinates: 41.196111, -74.908831. From this parking area, walk back over the bridge that crosses the creek and head downstream to find the falls. The upper parking area along Emery Road.
Trails:
Mount Minsi via the Appalachian Trail is a 5 mile loop trail.

There are shorter connecting trails throughout the area including a short loop to the Antoine Dutot Homestead and trails that extend south around Lenape Lake toward Caledonia Creek. Hornbecks Creek Trail is a 3.7 miles out and back trail near Dingmans Ferry that follows an old road-bed toward a ladder of waterfalls, ending at Emery Road, where there is an upper parking area. This trail may have snow and ice during winter and is best hiked from March to November.
Hours And Camping: The Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area has camping options that range from backcountry sites for Appalachian Trail hikers to developed campgrounds. Find camping details here: https://www.nps.gov/dewa/planyourvisit/eatingsleeping.htm
Phone Number: Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area Information: (570) 426-2452
name: Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area

Description: The W. C. Coker Old Growth Forest is ~3.7 acres of old growth Eastern Hemlock (Tsuga canadensis) (Canada Hemlock Forest (Typic Subtype)) that represents some of the largest remaining Eastern Hemlock in the Eastern U.S., with several trees > 3.3 feet (100 cm) in diameter and the largest 4.2 feet (131 cm) in diameter (as of February 2021). A subset of the largest trees was cored and the oldest was reliably dated to 1761. However, our largest trees were either hollow or had heartwood that was too degraded to be reliably aged, but we estimate the oldest trees exceed 350 years of age. The hemlocks have been treated every few years since 2004 for the introduced Hemlock Woolly Adelgid (Adelges tsugae), so most of the trees are still healthy. The forest is a remnant of the "primeval forest" that was found on the Highlands Plateau prior to being harvested in the 1930s and 40s. There are also impressive specimens of Northern Red Oak (Quercus rubra), Tulip Poplar (Liriodendron tulipifera), Yellow Birch (Betula alleghaniensis), and Mountain Laurel (Kalmia latifolia). The understory is dominated by Rosebay Rhododendron (Rhododendron maximum). At one time the forest was home to the State-listed Green Salamander (Aneides aeneus), but the species hasn’t been seen in the past 15 years and may be extirpated due to development on the fringes of the forest and over-collecting by herpetologists.
Navigation: 111 Lower Lake Rd., Highlands, NC 28741. This is the primary parking area for day visitors exploring the HBS gardens and trails. Park and follow the boardwalk to the adjacent “Sto” Pavilion on the lake. Continue past the Pavilion on the boardwalk and then take a right on Lower Lake Rd. Travel the paved road about 600 feet (3-minute walk). The road makes a sharp right bend over a creek: to right the trail continues around the lake (Lindenwood Lake Loop) and to the left is the trailhead for the Coker Old Growth Trail. Follow the steps up the path 0.27 miles to the trail’s end at Bowery Road. Turn around to hike back and enjoy the scenery from another perspective.
Parking And Admission: Park at 111 Lower Lake Rd., Highlands, NC 28741. Admission is free.
