Trails: Coker Old Growth Trail is 0.27 miles (0.43 km), one-way. The total length of all the trails at the Highlands Biological Station is 1.34 miles (2.15 km).
Hours And Camping: Open year-round, dawn till dusk. No camping, though picnicking is allowed at various locations on campus. Note that American Black Bears (Ursus americanus) are active in the area, so lock cars (our bears have learned to open car doors) and pack out trash or use one of our bear-proof garbage cans.
name: W. C. Coker Old Growth Forest – Highlands Biological Station

Description:
One of Michigan Nature Association’s most popular sanctuaries, Estivant Pines Nature Sanctuary was originally part of a 2,400-acre tract of land owned by Edward Estivant of Paris, who sold it to Calumet and Hecla Mining Company in 1947. The tract was sold to Universal Oil in 1968, and the area was threatened when Universal Oil cut down 300 acres of forest nearby and began plans for future logging. MNA led a three-year statewide fundraising campaign to purchase 200 acres of Estivant Pines from Universal Oil in 1973. Concerned citizens from the “Save The Pines” committee helped in the fundraising that led to this initial acquisition. Three additional acquisitions occurring between 1989 and 2019 have expanded the sanctuary to 570.5 acres, which protects one of the last old-growth white pine stands in Michigan.


Today Estivant Pines is one of the last and largest preserved tracts of old-growth white pine in Michigan, located south of Copper Harbor near the tip of the Keweenaw Peninsula within a landscape scale forest complex. Many white pines in this sanctuary measure 3-5 feet in diameter and are 250-400 years old. Numerous other co-existing species are also present in an old growth size class include white cedar, yellow birch, balsam fir, red oak and sugar maple. The Montreal River bisects the southernmost eighty acres of the sanctuary.

More than 85 bird species inhabit the old-growth forest, including woodpeckers, hawks, and red crossbills. Despite thin soil and boreal climate, several wildflowers grow, such as asters, clintonia, baneberry, and violets. A wide variety of ferns, like maidenhair, spleenwort, and holly fern, blanket the forest floor.
Navigation: The sanctuary is located in Keweenaw County. Follow US 41 east through Copper Harbor. From US 41, turn right onto 2nd Street at the Community Center and sign for Manganese Lake. Follow 2nd Street (also called Manganese Road) for 1.2 miles and then turn left onto Clark Mine Road. Travel 1.2 miles and turn right onto Burma Road. Travel another 0.5 miles on Burma Rd. to the trailhead and parking area.
Parking And Admission: There is parking for around 15-20 cars at the trailhead. There is no admission fee but visitors are invited to give donations in a donation pipe along the trail or they can donate to MNA at www.michigannature.org
Trails: Two loop trails bring visitors through the towering pines and forest. The 1 mile Cathedral Grove loop passes some of the largest and oldest giant white pines, growing more than 125 feet tall and dating back 300 years. Named after MNA’s founder, the 1.2 mile Bertha Daubendiek trail winds through groves of large pine, maple, and oak. One pine on this loop was determined to have germinated around 1695 after a wildfire swept the ridge. The two trails intersect and can be completed as a 2.5 mile hike.
Hours And Camping: The sanctuary is open during daylight hours. While the sanctuary is technically open year round, it should be noted that the local road, parking spaces and trails are not plowed or cleared in winter. Camping is not allowed.
name: Estivant Pines Nature Sanctuary

Description: Burnwood Old-Growth Forest at the New River Gorge National Park and Preserve is home to multiple overstory tree species, including Eastern hemlock, American beech, red maple, black gum and four species of oak. Many large-diameter trees are present, and 28 of 50 trees that were cored by scientists pre-date the year 1900. Fifteen of these trees date prior to the year 1800, while five date  to c. 1670.  The forest is located within the national park and offers a glimpse into a centuries’ old landscape that once covered much of the New River Gorge.
Navigation: The Burnwood area is located in Lansing, WV, just west of U.S. 19 opposite the Canyon Rim Visitor Center at the northern end of the park. The area includes a maintenance yard, a group camping area and pavilions, and a loop trail that traverses our study site.
Parking And Admission: Parking can be found near the Burnwood Ranger Station Parking area located here: https://goo.gl/maps/8T4QcRhfjtguzx6V8
Trails: The forest is readily accessed via a level 1.3 mile trail.
Hours And Camping: Open year round. There is a group campground adjacent to the trailhead which requires reservations. Link to the campground info: https://www.nps.gov/neri/planyourvisit/burnwood-group-camp-site.htm
name: Burnwood Old Growth Area – New River Gorge National Park and Preserve

Description:
The 172-acre preserve is an excellent example of Appalachian hardwood forest composed of oak-hickory on the southern aspects and ridges, and mixed-mesophytic forest dominated by yellow poplar, sugar maple, and oak elsewhere. 

Fifteen acres are virgin timber, and American beech are likely the oldests in the preserve, but sugar maple, red and white oak, several species of hickory, and other species reach old age across 15 to 20 acres. Many of the largest trees have fallen in the past decades and much coarse woody debris exists. Large windthrown mounds are found across the forest, as are snags, gaps, and a complex structure. The area where the springs join is a lovely spot, but well below the virgin timber in the upper central part of the cove. Spring ephemerals are rich and abundant throughout the cove, and vary tremendously with elevation and topography.
Navigation: It is 6.3 miles from West Union, the County Seat of Doddridge County on Nutter Fork Road.
Parking And Admission: Parking for ten vehicles will be available after July 31th, 2023, off Nutter Fork Road. There is no admission fee, but the West Virginia Land Trust accepts donations.
Trails: Two miles of trails are anticipated by the end of 2023. The main trail follows an abandoned country road to the ridgeline and traverses it for its entirety where it follows the property boundary. A section of trail that crosses the old-growth will connect to each side of the ridge trail. All trails are constructed with native materials to semi-primitive, non-motorized standards, and may challenge hikers due to the topography and undulating terrain.
Hours And Camping: The preserve is open during daylight hours. No camping is available.
Hunting: Bow hunting is allowed by permit only.
name: Marie Hall Jones Ancient Forest Preserve

Description: Flower Creek Dunes Nature Preserve is located on the shoreline of Lake Michigan in the northwest part of Muskegon County, owned and cared for by the Land Conservancy of West Michigan. Established in 2012, the preserve protects outstanding views of Lake Michigan, sand and gravel beach, open dunes, interdunal wetlands, and 64-acres of mesic northern forest. The forest showcases high-quality, second-growth with abundant large dead trees and fallen logs, teaming with fungi, woodpeckers and other forest birds. Notable older hemlocks are present on site, and with careful stewardship from LCWM and community, it will continue to develop important old-growth characteristics. Tree species present include eastern hemlock, American beech, red oak, white pine, sugar maple, and other hardwoods.
Navigation:
8390 Meinert Park Road, Montague, MI

From Meinert Park, walk about a quarter-mile north along the beach to Flower Creek Dunes Nature Preserve. Please respect the private property between Meinert Park and the preserve and walk close to the water’s edge. The preserve is marked with a sign and a stairway that leads up from the beach to the top of the dune. The trail runs north and south along the dune.
Parking And Admission: Parking is available at Meinert Park, located at the west end of Meinert Park Road in Montague. (Note that Muskegon County Parks may charge a fee for parking.) From Meinert Park, walk about a quarter-mile north along the beach to Flower Creek Dunes Nature Preserve. Please respect the private property between Meinert Park and the preserve and walk close to the water’s edge. The preserve is marked with a sign and a stairway that leads up from the beach to the top of the dune.
Trails: Trail length: 1.2 miles (round trip from Meinert Park)
Hours And Camping: Hours are sunrise to sunset. Camping is not allowed.
name: Flower Creek Dunes Nature Preserve

Description:
The 257-acre Beaver Creek Hemlocks Conservation Area is located on Highway 182 in the Town of Sherman, Iron County.

The property protects over 8,160 ft of creek shoreline, 950 ft of bog shoreline, mature & old-growth hemlock- hardwood forest, black-spruce tamarack swamps, vernal ponds, poor fen & wetlands. Major tree species present include eastern hemlock, yellow birch, white cedar and black spruce. No cores have been taken to age these trees exactly, but many of them are very large in diameter and height, indicating they could be very old. Old-growth is very rare in the Northwoods, as less than 1% of its pre-colonization acreage exists intact today. These apex ecosystems are extremely valuable in that they provide a diversified forest structure capable of supporting a greater diversity of plants and animals than younger forests.

Trails and a parking area will be available for low-impact public recreation, including hiking, snowshoeing, backcountry cross country skiing and nature observation. Traditional uses including fishing and hunting are allowed according to established guidelines.
Navigation: From the intersection of Hwy 51 and Hwy 47 in Manitowish, drive south on Hwy 47 for 3.7 miles. Turn right on Hwy 182 and continue for 13.5 miles. A gravel parking lot is on the east side of Hwy 182, across from fire number 387N. Coordinates for the parking lot are 45.991917, -90.170011. Beaver Creek parking area on Google Maps.
Parking And Admission: A small gravel parking area along Hwy 182 can fit 3-4 vehicles.
Trails: Nearly 3 miles of natural surface hiking trails loop through the property. From the parking area follow a ridgeline bordering the cattail marsh surrounding Beaver Creek. After crossing a small wetland via 100 feet of boardwalk, begin exploring the old-growth hemlock-hardwoods. Take the short loop (~1 mile) or make the trip around the long loop (~2.5 miles).
Hours And Camping: The preserve is open to non-motorized silent sport use year-round. Allowed activities include hiking, snowshoeing, ungroomed cross-country skiing, wildlife viewing, hunting and fishing. No camping or campfires are allowed.
Hunting: Hunting is allowed per state hunting regulations.
name: Beaver Creek Hemlocks Conservation Area

Description: The 170-acre Big Pines Natural Area is part of the 2,106-acre Hemenway State Forest. It is one of the finest places in New England to see towering Eastern white pine trees. One champion white pine is 150-feet tall and has a circumference of over 15 feet. Numerous other pines are in the 125-145 foot height range with diameters up to 45 inches. At just 150 to 200 years of age, these giants have not even reached their maximum dimensions yet. Hemlocks 250 to 350 years old also grow here along with sugar maple, red spruce, yellow birch, red oak, and red maple.
Navigation:
Closest address: 1642 Chinook Trail, Tamworth, NH 03886

Parking for the Big Pines Natural Area is along a pull-off of N.H. 113A (Chinook Trail) marked by a large sign on the south side of the road. This location is 2.8-miles west of the junction of NH 113 and NH 113A in Tamworth Village.
Parking And Admission: There is parking for several vehicles along a pull-off on N.H. 113A (Chinook Trail) in Tamworth marked by a large sign on the south side of the road. Deep snow in the winter may limit parking availability. No admission fee is charged.
Trails:
Easy Walker Nature Trail: 0.3 miles with downloadable interpretive guide.

Betty Steele Trail: 1.6 miles

Peg King Spur Trail: 0.6 miles steep climb to summit

Total trail distance: 2.5-miles
Hours And Camping: Big Pines is open year round. Camping or fires are not allowed.
Hunting: Hunting is allowed during hunting season.
Phone Number: (603) 271-2214 for the NH Division of Forests and Lands.
name: Big Pines Natural Area - Hemenway State Forest

Description:
A portion of the preserve protects a significant oak dominated woodland of about 31 acres with towering mature white oak trees. The remainder of the preserve protects about 30 acres of glacial ponds and uplands that are reverting pasturelands and croplands. Approximately 40 acres is being maintained as grassland for nesting birds and an additional 50 acres has been allowed to revert (since the 1970's) to forest.

The oak-hickory uplands and open fields support populations of songbirds, quail, pheasant and several hawk species. Stage's Pond is equally diverse botanically. Aquatic, field, woodland and marsh species abound from April to late October, although the spring season offers the most variety in the form of colorful native wildflowers.
Navigation: 4792 Hagerty Rd, Ashville, OH 43103
Parking And Admission: No admission fee; parking lot on premises.
Trails: Total trails are 3.5 miles. A new accessible trail runs from the parking area and makes a loop through the mature oak woodlands. Entire trail length is 1.2 miles of concrete and boardwalk to allow visitors with any ability to access this beautiful woodlot.
Hours And Camping: Yes, open year round. No camping. No pets.
name: Stage's Pond State Nature Preserve

Description: The Lindy Roosenburg Preserve (70.76 acres) is entirely forested except for a small field bordering the parking area. Forest age ranges from about 40 years (logged in the 1980s) to an estimated 120+ years. Two non-contiguous stands that total approximately 18 acres qualify as old-growth, based on Old Growth Network’s criteria. These are uneven-aged stands that include many large trees with trunks 2.5 to 3 feet in diameter, with straight, tall boles, indicating that they were not open-grown. These large trees are at least 120 years old, and probably considerably older. There are scattered, large blowdowns in varying states of decay, pit and mound topography, a notable lack of invasive species in the understory, and no signs of human disturbance other than foot paths and remnants of boundary fencing. The old-growth stands are surrounded by high-quality forest that is younger and/or less dense.
Navigation: The address is 9686 Sand Ridge Road, Millfield, OH. Parking is located on the north side of Sand Ridge Road, 0.9 mile east of State Highway 13. Sand Ridge Road begins 0.7 mile southeast of the junction of State Highways 13 and 682 in Chauncey. Lindy Roosenburg Preserve is labeled as such on Google Maps.
Parking And Admission: Admission and parking are free, but there is space for only seven cars.
Trails: There are about 1.5 miles of trails in the preserve. To reach the oldest forest that has trail access, follow Peace Tree Trail (0.2 mile, part of which is a steep descent) from the parking lot to a pond, then continue straight on Sheehan Way about 0.1 mile, then turn left onto Magic Is Real Trail. Magic Is Real Trail is 0.58 mile long, about two thirds of it traversing old-growth forest.
Hours And Camping: The preserve will be open dawn to dusk, year round, beginning April 30, 2023. Camping is not permitted.
Hunting: Bow hunting of deer is by written permit only. Hunting of any other animals is prohibited. Guns are prohibited.
name: Lindy Roosenburg Preserve

Description:
The Provincelands Beech Forest, in the Cape Cod National Seashore, offers a glimpse of the original arboreal landscape of the Cape. When the Mayflower landed in the early seventeenth century, much of the Cape was covered in pine-oak forests and groves of hickory, red maple, birch, and beech trees. Over the next two hundred years, settlers cleared almost all of these forests. Due to this forest’s low-lying position, it was spared from logging and is the sole remnant of beech forest on the Cape.

Beech Forest’s gentle trail meanders through forested dunes and skirts the shallow Beech Forest Pond. Bird watching opportunities are abundant, especially in spring and fall. The Province Lands bicycle trail can be accessed from the parking area.
Navigation: Nearest Address: 36 Race Point Road. Turn right off Route 6 at the traffic light onto Race Point Road. Proceed approximately 0.5 mile to the Beech Forest parking area on the left.
Parking And Admission: Park at the trailhead parking area. No admission fee.
Trails: Beech Forest Trail: 1 mile loop, (pond loop 0.75 mile, extension loop 0.25 mile), one hour.
Hours And Camping: Open year-round between 6 AM and midnight.
name: Provincelands Beech Forest - Cape Cod National Seashore

Description: Baker Woodlot & Rachana Rajendra Neotropical Migrant Bird Sanctuary is a high-quality remnant of the forest that once grew before the campus was established. During its 165 years of preservation it has been subject to human disturbance, including road and railroad maintenance on its north and south borders, along with an assortment of management and research programs. Today, the woodlot is protected as a campus natural area and contains a diversity of tree species and ages, a shrub understory of elderberry and spicebush, and carpets of spring ephemerals. The largest trees are northern red oak, tulip poplar, and eastern cottonwood. American beech, black cherry, white oak, and sugar maple are other prominent components of the canopy.
Navigation:
A nearby parking area is located at: 587 Service Rd. East Lansing, MI 48823

Baker Woodlot is located on the south side of Service Drive, trail entrances are located on the east and west sides of the forest.
Parking And Admission:
The woodlot is located on campus and parking options vary depending on the day of the week. Explore your parking options in advanced at https://maps.msu.edu/

Visitor parking in Lot 101 on Service Road just east of Farm Lane. Visitors now use the SPOT ON app or website to pay for parking at www.spoton.msu.edu

Nearby parking is also available along Bogue Street and is restricted and signed for Faculty/Staff, Monday through Friday, 7:00am - 6:00pm; other times it is available for visitors.
Trails: Approximately two miles of trail are available. Visit the Baker Woodlot web page to download a trail map.
Hours And Camping: Hours are dawn to dusk. The perimeter is fenced and four entrances are open year-round. No camping.
name: Baker Woodlot & Rachana Rajendra Neotropical Migrant Bird Sanctuary, Michigan State University

Description: Duncan Park is a 42-acre natural area within the City of Grand Haven containing a rare old-growth hemlock-hardwood forest steeped in local history. Dominant trees present include eastern hemlock and American beech, with black cherry, northern red oak, and sugar maple throughout. An accessible trail provides all visitors with a chance to see magnificent hemlock trees and experience the living legacy of Robert and Martha Duncan.
Navigation:
1113 Sheldon Rd Grand Haven, MI 49417

Follow the entrance drive to the parking area and adjacent trailhead.
Parking And Admission: Parking area provides space for several vehicles. No entry fee.
Hours And Camping: Hours are dawn to dusk, year round. No camping available.
name: Duncan Park

Description: The 80-acre Newton Woods is one of the last remaining old-growth, oak-mixed hardwood stands in Michigan's lower peninsula. Newton Woods exists within the Fred Russ Experimental Forest owned by Michigan State University. Minor management has occurred in the past, including thinnings in 1941 and 1956. 40 acres of the forest was designated as a National Natural Landmark in 1976.
Navigation:
20419 Marcellus Hwy., Decatur, MI 49045

Newton Woods can be accessed through Newton Woods - Russ Forest County Park, a 12-acre roadside park leased to Cass County Parks Department by Michigan State University. Amenities include parking, bathrooms, picnic tables, grills and several shelters that can be rented for special events by calling the Cass County Parks Department at 269- 445-8611. The Parks Department also maintains forest trails that are accessible to the public for use on foot or with non-motorized vehicles.
Parking And Admission: Parking is available at Newton Woods / Russ Forest County Park. There is no admission fee.
Trails: Approximately 2-mile loop
Hours And Camping: Open year-round during daylight hours. No camping is permitted.
name: Newton Woods - Michigan State University Fred Russ Forest

Description:
The 114 acre Scientific and Natural Area (SNA) contains nearly 32 acres of designated old-growth white pine – red pine forest. This old-growth forest is found in two stands, both of which extend beyond the borders of the SNA. The largest of these is 30 acres in size, and extends an additional 18.94 acres on adjoining federally-owned land in the Chippewa National Forest. A 2009 study found the oldest individual trees within the SNA to be red pines 230-240 years old.

The stand on adjoining land within Chippewa National Forest reportedly originated as early as 1745, and includes the "co-champion red pine" of Minnesota's Native Big Tree Registry, measured at 115" in circumference and 120' high.
Navigation:
From Alvwood, 11 miles E on Co Hwy 29, then 2 miles N on Co Hwy 26, then 0.8 mile W on Forest Rd 2240 (Lost 40 Rd). Trailhead can be accessed from the parking lot.

Note: Lost 40 Road (Forest Road 2240), the parking area, and trailhead are administered and maintained by the US Forest Service.
Parking And Admission: There is a parking lot with a loop that can accommodate larger vehicles and school buses. There are also picnic tables and a vault toilet. There is no admission fee.
Trails:
A one-mile self-guided trail winds its way through the majestic pines of the Lost 40.

A 0.2-mile inner loop traverses level ground. This loop highlights the biggest pines. The 0.8-mile outer loop traverses mostly level ground, but with more rolling terrain and steep hills. A 0.4-mile spur trail leads to Moose Brook over rolling terrain.
Hours And Camping:
No camping is allowed within the Scientific and Natural Area. A variety of camping opportunities are available nearby within the adjacent Chippewa National Forest. The SNA is open year-round.

https://www.fs.usda.gov/activity/chippewa/recreation/camping-cabins
Hunting: Yes, see Minnesota Hunting & Trapping Regulations for more information.
Phone Number: Scientific and Natural AreasDNR Northeast Region218-300-7871
name: Lost 40 Scientific and Natural Area

Description: The Scientific and Natural Area is located within Itasca State Park. The 1,600 acre SNA is located along the western side of Lake Itasca and protects roughly two miles of undeveloped shoreline along the lake. A mosaic of eighteen native plant communities occupy the site, dominated by fire-dependent red pine – white pine forest communities. As related by DNR forester Chris Gronewald, the SNA contains 848 acres of designated old-growth forest in 16 stands. Among these, a 1998 inventory documented a 190-year-old red pine stand and 200-year-old white pine stand. Mesic hardwood forests are also well represented in the SNA, composed of sugar and red maple, basswood, aspen and birch. Low-lying areas support a diversity of communities ranging from shrub, tamarack and white cedar swamps, to sedge meadow, marsh and rich fen. Open water habitats add diversity, including two lakes—Bohall Lake and the smaller Snail Lake, and stretches of Boutwell and Nicollet Creeks. Many nameless little spring-fed streams filter into Lake Itasca.
Navigation:
36750 Main Park Drive, Park Rapids, MN 56470

In Itasca State Park, 20 miles N of Park Rapids. Sanctuary can be accessed along Wilderness Drive. The 3 sanctuary trail options are accessed off of Wilderness Drive.
Parking And Admission: Itasca State Park has an entrance fee. To access this SNA, a daily vehicle permit required $7. Parking is available at each of the 3 trailheads.
Trails:
Landmark Trail – A half mile loop on the northern edge of the SNA.

Bohall Wilderness Trailhead – A half mile out to Bohall Lake though the heart of the SNA.

Big Pine Trail – A short (800 feet) hike into the southern end of the SNA.
Hours And Camping: No camping is allowed within the SNA. Open daily from 8am-10pm, year round. Wilderness Drive is closed in the winter months but may be accessed by snowshoe or cross-country ski. Camping and other lodging is available on the east side of Itasca State Park. More information can be found here: https://www.dnr.state.mn.us/state_parks/park.html?id=spk00181#homepage
Hunting: Firearms deer hunting only is allowed in conjunction with Itasca State Park hunts. See Minnesota Hunting & Trapping Regulations for more information. https://www.dnr.state.mn.us/regulations/hunting/index.html. New 2023 hunting regulations now authorize use of non-toxic shot only for deer hunting within both the park and the SNA.
name: Itasca Wilderness Sanctuary Scientific and Natural Area

Description: Pilcher Park is a large and diverse forest complex featuring 52 acres of old-growth mesic upland forests. Other significant features include a Native American burial mound and a reburial site. Pilcher Park is one of northeastern Illinois’ premiere woodlands with outstanding spring wildflower displays and old-growth trees. During a study of the site, one bur oak tree was cored back to 1707. More than 270 native plant species have been documented within Pilcher Park, and at least 11 species of birds with moderate to high sensitivity to habitat fragmentation breed on site.
Navigation:
2501 Highland Park Dr, Joliet, IL 60432

The trailhead is located behind the Nature Center
Parking And Admission: Park entry is free. Gates close at dusk and open at dawn. No charge to visit the nature center and greenhouse on the east side of the park.
Trails: Total distance of all trails is approx. 8 miles. Trail of the Oaks is about .83 miles and is a nice trail through impressive old-growth oaks and maples. The paved interpretive trail is used the most, 1 mile to the greenhouse and 1 mile back, and is straight out the back door of the nature center.
Hours And Camping: The park is open year round from dawn to dusk. We do not allow camping in the park. The nature center is open 7 days a week from 9am to 3pm and the Greenhouse is open 7 days a week 8am to 4:30pm except major holidays.
Hunting: Hunting is not allowed in the park or on any park district property.
name: Pilcher Park Nature Center

Description:
Bear Creek flows through a deep ravine with high rock walls. It is joined by a small tributary stream that has carved an opening through a massive Mansfield sandstone formation and created a natural bridge known as Portland Arch. A few native white pine are mixed with oaks and hickories on the thin mantle of soil on steep slopes. The ground is covered with mosses and lichens, and supports scattered beds of blueberry, huckleberry, and wintergreen. This is the only place in the state where the Canada blueberry is found. The rare native bush honeysuckle is found here as well. Vertical cliff faces have small crevices from which grow bulblet, hayscented, and marginal shield ferns. Several colonies of Forbe’s saxifrage are found in larger pockets of soil. Liverworts cover moist portions of some rocks, and are occasionally joined by the creeping fronds of walking fern. Portland Arch has been recognized for its uniqueness since the first settlers came to western Indiana. A resort and then a Boy Scout camp were located in this area in the past. Now Portland Arch is a National Natural Landmark, as well as a nature preserve.

The Miller-Campbell Memorial Addition is dedicated in memory of Sam Miller and Ron Campbell. Sam was involved in Portland Arch from the beginning, becoming a volunteer steward for 30 years. Ron was the first “field” person for the Division of Nature Preserves, and primary property manager for all the preserves. Portland Arch was among his favorite natural areas.
Navigation:
1599 W Scout Camp Rd., Covington, IN 47932

From Attica go south on US 41 for about 5 miles and then west on CR 650N. Once in Fountain, follow signs to the preserve
Parking And Admission: Two parking lots are available. The north lot provides a trail to the arch. There is no admission charge.
Trails: 1¼ miles of combined, moderate to difficult level trails are accessible from two parking lots, each with adjoining self-guiding trail. The trail from the north parking lot leads to the arch. There is no access to or trail through the Miller-Cambell addition at this time.
name: Portland Arch Nature Preserve

Description:
One of the most beautiful parks in the County Park System, the property is known for stately stands of red and white oak, beech, ash, and birch trees.

 From a high elevation of 240 feet, the parkland slopes down to 110 feet at the lowest level of Doctor’s Creek, which drains to Crosswicks Creek, a tributary of the Delaware River. Because the Clayton woods have not been logged for many decades, they contain some of highest quality hardwood forest in the County. The old growth woods are dominated by American beech, white and red oak, and birch trees and have a diverse and lush understory. Black oak, tulip poplar, and shagbark hickory trees are also plentiful. A small man-made pond at the intersection of forest and fields provides some interesting edge habitat for many species, including beaver, turtles, and wading birds like egrets, heron, and snow geese. The forest and field juncture also provides habitat for quail, pheasant, and wild turkey. Spice bush and greenbriar shrubs and skunk cabbage thrive in wet areas. 


Clayton Park is one of the best spring wildflower sites in the Park System. Look for jack-in-the-pulpit (right), trout lily, spring beauty, wild geranium and the rarer trillium and wild ginger during April and May.
Navigation:
161 Emley’s Hill Road

Imlaystown, NJ 08526
Parking And Admission: Parking for 15 vehicles is on site. There is no admission fee.
Trails:
A favorite spot for all-terrain bicyclists, Clayton Park offers approximately 6 miles of rugged, mostly moderate trails for outdoor enthusiasts. Please obey the rules of protocol for right of way on the trails: bicyclists yield to all other trail users, and pedestrians yield to equestrians. Stay on the marked trails, plan your route and take a trail map with you.

Doctor’s Creek Trail: 1.5 miles

Old Forge Trail: 1.6 miles

Total trail mileage in park: 5.6 miles
Hours And Camping: Open daily 7 a.m to dusk. No camping.
Hunting: Bow hunting deer by permit only. Please visit https://www.monmouthcountyparks.com/page.aspx?Id=2771 for more information on the deer management program.
name: Clayton Park

Description:
Much of TNC’s preserve was once farmland but now protects one of New Jersey’s largest limestone fens. The preserve is home to limestone ridges, dense rolling forests, and vital wetlands. The preserve includes almost the entirety of the Site 546 Natural Heritage Priority Site, which is a shrub and herb dominated wetland surrounded by limestone ridges and mixed hardwood forest.

A tree core obtained from one oak, tree sizes, and mapping suggest the forests at Mackenzie’s Preserve significantly pre-date the earliest available aerial imagery in New Jersey. This is further supported by the high diversity of lichens, including species thought to be restricted to, or at least most likely found in, old growth forests. The presence of several rare plant species, including one State Endangered plant species, at minimum precludes any sort of logging or creation of early successional habitat.

The site contains numerous rare plant species including the state endangered pale-laurel, arborvitae, seaside arrow-grass, bog willow, rhodora, rush aster, bog rosemary and Labrador marsh bedstraw; most of which were discovered by Mackenzie.
Navigation:
1 Linmor Avenue 

Newton, New Jersey
Parking And Admission: The entire Preserve is open to the public from dawn to dusk for passive recreational uses such as hiking, bird watching, and botanizing along unofficial blazed trails. Roadside parking is available at various entry points to the Preserve. As with all Preserves in the NJ Natural Lands Trust’s system, the following uses are prohibited: camping, campfires, use of motorized vehicles, consumption of alcohol, unleashed pets, use of drones, hunting for bear, turkey, small game, or waterfowl. Also prohibited is the collection, harassment, or destruction of plants, fungi, animals, rocks, cultural artifacts, or fossils
Trails: There are not specific trails, but rather pathways created by human treading. Surfaces are not mulched or finished.
Hours And Camping: Dawn to dusk. No camping.
Hunting: At this preserve, deer hunting with bow is permitted during the time frames set forth in New Jersey’s Game Code.
name: Mackenzie's Preserve

Description: The remote backcountry area at Little Moose Mountain encompasses about 750 acres across the ridge of Little Moose Mountain. This Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands site includes several areas of exceptional spruce-fir and northern hardwoods forest. The oldest stands at this site include trees over 300 years old. This site includes Maine’s state record red spruce tree, though this tree is not visible from the trail.
Navigation: From downtown Greenville, head north on Rte. 6/Rte. 15 for 5 miles to North Road. Turn left into the Little Moose Public Lands, and drive 1.7 miles (past the trailhead for Big Moose Mountain). Bear left at the fork and go another 1 mile to the Big Moose Pond trailhead and small parking area on the left.
Parking And Admission: Small parking area at Big Moose Pond trailhead. Admission is free.
Trails:
Park at the Big Moose Pond trailhead parking area. Hike the loop trail past Big Moose Pond and around Little Moose Pond and back to the parking area. (2.7 miles round trip) 



Total distance of all trails in the Little Moose Public Lands: 14 miles



Trail Map: https://www.maine.gov/dacf/parksearch/PropertyGuides/Maps/FullSize/littlemoosemap.pdf
Hours And Camping:
Open year round, but roads become unplowed/groomed snowmobile trails during the winter. Do not drive the roads in the winter.

There are two primitive campsites at Big Moose Pond and three primitive campsites at Little Moose Pond; all are found on the north shores of the ponds and are within 0.5 to 1.5 miles from the trailhead. Walk-in campsites on the ponds are first-come, first-served. All campsites have a table, fire ring, and nearby pit toilet. Before building fires, visitors must get a campfire permit from the Maine Forest Service (MFS). Call the MFS at (207) 287-2791 for permit details.
Hunting: Hunting is permitted, though special rules apply. Do not discharge weapons within 300 feet of any picnic area, camping area, parking area, posted hiking trail or other developed area. Loaded firearms are not permitted at campsites or on hiking trails.
name: Little Moose Mountain

Description: The Donnell Pond Ecological Reserve totals approximately 2000 acres, encompassing the summit and slopes of several small to mid-elevation mountains. Most common forest types include northern hardwood forest, and spruce-fir forest. Much of this Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands Ecological Reserve has evidence of historic timber management. A small stand of spruce- fir forest nested in a saddle on Black Mountain, west of Wizard Pond, has little to no evidence of past timber harvest, with oldest trees aged at roughly 200 years. Wizard Pond is a small waterbody hidden between the summits of Black Mountain.
Navigation:
Black Mountain Road, Franklin, ME

From Rte. 183 (Tunk Lake Rd.) turn west onto Schoodic Beach Rd., then almost immediately bear right onto Black Mountain Road. Watch for the parking area after passing Little Bear Road. The site can be accessed via the Big Chief Trail.
Parking And Admission: Park at the small parking area (3 parking spaces), 2.2 miles down the Black Mountain Road. Admission is free.
Trails:
The Big Chief trail departs from the trailhead 2.2 miles down the Black Mountain Road, at a small trailhead parking area. It climbs steadily for approximately 0.6 miles through mixed woods and transitions into spruce and fir shortly before crossing onto open ledges with extensive views over the southern half of Tunk Lake and on towards the coast. Take Black Mt. Summit Trail for 0.6 miles to Black Mt. Cliff Trail, a 3.0 mile loop, before returning to Black Mt. Summit Trail and heading back to the trailhead. 



https://www.maine.gov/dacf/parksearch/PropertyGuides/Maps/FullSize/donnellpondmap.pdf
Hours And Camping:
Open year round. Be aware that many access roads are not plowed in the winter. 



There are no campsites in the vicinity of this site.
Hunting: Hunting is permitted, though special rules apply. Do not discharge weapons within 300 feet of any picnic area, camping area, parking area, posted hiking trail or other developed area. Loaded firearms are not permitted at campsites or on hiking trails.
name: Black Mountain - Donnell Pond Ecological Reserve

Description:
Wolf Creek Trout Lily Preserve is a conservation area owned by Grady County thru generous private donations, including the previous owners, Flint River Timber Company, and a grant from the Georgia Land Conservation Program. 

Established in 2009 through the efforts of volunteers from the Magnolia Chapter (Tallahassee) of the Florida Native Plant Society (including some Georgians). The Preserve is destined to remain forever undisturbed from human development, protecting the many acres and literally tens of millions of beautiful yellow and maroon dimpled trout lilies and thousands of maroon spotted trillium. The bloom in February forms an expansive carpet covering approximately 15 acres on a gently sloping hillside. This is considered the largest extent of these trout lilies known anywhere in the world.

The preserve consists of diverse beech-magnolia and floodplain forest bisected by Wolf Creek. Wolf Creek is a tributary of Tired Creek which flows into the Ochlocknee River. Over 200 species of plants have been identified on the Preserve. 
Other ephemeral blooms include Spring Coralroot, Bloodroot, Southern Twayblade Orchid, Jack-in-the-Pulpit, Green Dragon.

A few noted trees include Sparkleberry, American Holly, Water Oak, Shumard Oak, Magnolia, Beech, Spruce Pine, Hop Hornbeam and Ironwood

Approximate older growth around 80 plus years, trout lilies have been there hundreds of years.
Navigation:
Wolf Creek Road, Cairo, GA 39828

The gate will be clearly marked on your left as you drive down the road. Pull through to parking area.
Parking And Admission: Parking is available in a grassy field just inside the gate. Parking is limited and sometimes folks park on the road outside during peak bloom season, when visitors are many and parking places are few! There is no charge to visit the Preserve, though donations are appreciated.
Trails: There are three major trails that are prepared and marked. Two trails meander through and around the trout lily bloom on a northern slope. The loop is approximately 1 mile. Another trail on the back side of the parking area wanders through a wooded area with trillium, which is approximately .5 miles in length.
Hours And Camping: The Preserve is open to the public at specified times and dates during the trout lily bloom season. (Information may be found on their website and the relevant Facebook page.) Outside of the bloom season, the gates are kept locked to protect the property. Individuals or groups may request a tour or access to the site by contacting Margaret Tyson. Access is always free of charge, though donations are appreciated. Camping is not allowed. Pets are not allowed.
name: Wolf Creek Trout Lily Preserve

Description:
Located in north Garland, Texas, only 14 miles from downtown Dallas, this old-growth hardwood bottomland forest and native prairie areas along Spring Creek are a haven of towering trees and unusual wildflowers. Scientists, conservationists, and naturalists have studied this forest community and determined it is one the few remaining old growth forests in the Blackland Prairie eco-zone of north central Texas. The Spring Creek Forest Preserve is protected as a biological treasure used for scientific studies and natural enjoyment.

The Spring Creek Forest Preserve is owned by Dallas County, Texas with maintenance provided by the City of Garland under the direction of the Society for the Preservation of Spring Creek Forest.

The Preserve consists of three parcels of land totaling 100 acres of the larger Spring Creek Greenbelt. Old growth forest coverage varies from one third to two thirds of each tract with the balance in regenerative forest and prairie grass communities. 

From counting the growth rings on some of the fallen trees, the tree age has been determined to be 125- 130 years old. The dominant species are Shumard Oak, Chinkapin Oak, Bur Oak and Pecan. Other species include American Elm, Slippery Elm, American Ash, Green Ash, Hackberry and Black Walnut. The forest community varies from slope to floodplain bottomland to creek side communities. One of the unusual features of the Spring Creek Forest is the occurrence of Chinkapin Oak among the dominant species in both the bottomland and the slope communities.
Navigation:
There are 3 potential access points:



Spring Creek Forest Preserve

1770 Holford Road, Garland, TX 75044



Spring Creek Park Preserve

1787 Holford Road, Garland, TX 75044



Halff Park

4695 Ranger Drive, Garland, TX 75044
Parking And Admission:
Admission is free. 

Parking is ample. Three locations: 

1770 Holford Road, Garland, TX 75044

1787 Holford Road, Garland, TX 75044

Halff Park, 4695 Ranger Drive, Garland, TX 75044 (3 hour limit on school days).
Trails:

Hours And Camping:
Camping is prohibited.

Park Hours: 6:00 a.m. until 10:00 p.m.
name: Spring Creek Forest Preserve- Spring Creek Greenbelt- City of Garland

Description: Norris Woods is a 75-acre nature preserve protected by the St. Charles Park District. The preserve provides a buffer to the Fox River and protects a high-quality, dry-mesic forest with many old-growth red and white oak trees from 100-150 years old. During the springtime, visitors can view a rich display of spring wildflowers. Along the river are small local mesic communities dominated by sugar maple, while floodplain communities support willow and silver maple. Other notable plants include twinleaf, cancer-root, shinleaf, poke milkweed, ferns, and blue ash. The area's rich diversity of plant life provides excellent habitat for many woodland animals. Sightings have included squirrels, woodchuck, American toad, and 41 species of nesting birds. Several threatened and endangered species have also been recorded. Norris Woods has been recognized as one of the highest quality natural areas in the region, 62 acres of which were dedicated as a State Nature Preserve in 1978.
Navigation: The forest is located near the intersection of Third Ave & Johnor Ave, St. Charles, IL 60174
Parking And Admission: A small parking lot is available and there is no admission charge.
Trails: A gravel trail is present and is 0.66 miles.
Hours And Camping: Hours are dawn until dusk. No camping is permitted.
name: Norris Woods Nature Preserve

Description:
This 126 acre gem of a park is located on the Apalachicola River bluffs below Jim Woodruff Dam and Lake Seminole. Spring fed streams emerge at the bottom of ravines, trickling from below ground. Slope forests host alluring wildflowers, some very rare. Every season has special gifts to be discovered by the appreciative nature enthusiast.

In 2002 the Apalachicola boat landing in Chattahoochee was expanded through a grant from the Florida Communities Trust to create protected lands known as the Chattahoochee Landing Park and the Angus Gholson Nature Park (called Chattahoochee Nature Park in the grant documents), resulting in a combined area of approx. 130 acres, 84 acres of which are old-growth forest exceeding 100 years of age. 

Diversity of habitats is the most outstanding feature: upland slope forest with calcareous subgrade, upland ericaceous river escarpments, and wide riverine floodplain. Steep ravines from natural seepage spring runs create a forest more reminiscent of Appalachian forest communities than typical northern Florida pinelands. An ongoing survey of plant species records more than 400 species to date. Dominant overstory tree species include Mixed Pine, Oak / Hickory, Beech / Magnolia, and Mesic Hardwood Floodplain.
Navigation: Drive to the terminus of Park Street by turning left off of Morgan Avenue in Chattahoochee. Parking is available for about fifteen vehicles. There are two trail entrances, minimally marked, down the slope from the parking area. Detailed signage is present though not all trails shown on the map are currently accessible due to damage from Hurricane Michael.
Parking And Admission: Admission is free of cost, as is parking. Space is present for about 15 vehicles.
Trails: Several trail loops of varying distance are available to the public for discovery. Trails encourage single-file walking on fairly rough terrain in order to minimize damage to sensitive plant species and erosion-prone slopes. Several seating opportunities have been created in particularly scenic areas to encourage observation, quiet reflection, and "forest bathing".
Hours And Camping: The park is open year-round from dawn 'til dusk. Camping is not allowed, though there is a campground nearby at Chattahoochee Landing.
name: Angus Gholson Nature Park

Description:
Five distinct woodland areas are mature or old-growth forest areas. Species include white oak, red oak, American beech, tulip-poplar, blackgum, flowering dogwood, along with others less dominant. Most of the trees age between 100 and 300 years of age in Browns Woods (17 acres), Chandler Farm Woods (53 acres), Old Quarry Woods (44 acres), Duck Ponds Woods, (46 acres) and Negandank Woods (12 acres). 
A William Penn tulip poplar grows in the Chandler's Woods, which means the tree was likely growing upon Penn's arrival in the region.
Navigation: 5105 Kennett Place, Wilmington, DE 19375
Parking And Admission:
$22 daily admission; plentiful parking

Visitors: March to December 10am to 5pm

Members: All year, sunrise to sunset
Trails: Browns Woods and Chandler's Woods both have trails that allow one into the Old-Growth area.
Hours And Camping:
10 am to 5 pm

No camping
name: Winterthur Museum, Garden & Libaray- Old-Growth Forest Areas

Description:
Early explorers to the "Bootheel" region of southeast Missouri discovered a unique landscape where the Ozark hills dropped off abruptly into flat flood plains covered with giant trees. The forest trees that took root here grew to enormous proportions in the fertile earth. Today, nature-seekers to "swampeast" Missouri will find a forested island, known as Big Oak Tree State Park, in the midst of a vast agricultural area. The park features the state park system's only cypress swamp.

The big oak tree that the citizens fought to save was located in an 80-acre tract of virgin bottomland hardwood forest, which is now designated as a National Natural Landmark. It stood its ground there for nearly 400 years before dying in 1952 and was cut down. Today, trees in the park are unsurpassed in the state for their size, with a canopy averaging 120 feet and with several trees more than 130 feet tall. Two trees qualify as state champions in their species. Ninety percent of the park is designated as a Missouri natural area because of its rarity and value in preserving this significant representation of Missouri's natural heritage.

In addition to the towering hickories and majestic oaks, the rich soils provide habitat for green ash, eastern cottonwood, American elm, black willow, persimmon, baldcypress and patches of giant cane. An undergrowth of woody vines, such as poison ivy, Virginia creeper, wild grape and peppervine, covers much of the area. The park protects 12 species of rare plants and animals, 250 kinds of plants and 25 mammal, 31 reptile and seven amphibian species.

A boardwalk winds its way through the park past some of the park's largest trees. A walk on the boardwalk also gives visitors a chance to view many common mammals, such as deer, raccoons, squirrels and opossums that call the park home, along with the rare swamp rabbit. Amid the lofty trees live more than 150 species of birds, giving the park a national reputation among bird watchers. Several of the birds are considered rare in the state, including the prothonotary warbler, cerulean warbler, red-shouldered hawk, Mississippi kite and fish crow.
Navigation:
13640 S. Highway 102

East Prairie, MO 63845-8768



From East Prairie, head east on Highway 80. Turn right (south) onto Highway 102 and go approximately 10 miles south from the junction of Highway 80 and 102. Turn right (west) onto Highway RB. Follow signs into the park and drive to one of the trailheads.
Parking And Admission: There is no fee for admission. Ample parking is available.
Trails: A boardwalk winds its way through the park past some of the park's largest trees.
Hours And Camping: Park grounds are open 6 a.m. to sunset, year-round. No camping is provided.
name: Big Oak Tree State Park

Description:
Hach-Otis Sanctuary is an 130-acre forested tract overlooking the beautiful Chagrin State Scenic River valley. Primarily a beech-maple-oak mixed mesophytic forest with deep ravines of eastern hemlock, Hach-Otis is home to some unusual plants including trailing arbutus, pink moccasin flower and red trillium. There are a few young American chestnut trees along the bluffs. Many of the ancient beech trees have completely hollow trunks and provide "apartments" for a number of different species of animals. Squirrels can be heard barking among the treetops, and pileated woodpeckers, great horned and barred owls, white-tailed deer, foxes and raccoons are some of the other animals found within the preserve. The steep eroding clay banks high above the Chagrin State Scenic River are ideal nesting spots for bank swallows and noisy kingfishers.

Bluffs overlook the Chagrin State Scenic River re-cutting an old valley that was completely filled with glacial drift during the last ice age. The ridges stand more that 150 feet above the streambed of the ever-changing river. The unstable hillsides of glacial clays and sands perched above shale are constantly being eroded by the meandering arm of the river.
Navigation:
37142 Skyline Dr. 

Willoughby Hills, OH 44094
Parking And Admission: A small, gated parking area is located at the trailhead. No admission fee.
Trails: Approximately 1.25 miles of trails traverse the Preserve.
Hours And Camping: Preserve is open daily 8 am to 4 pm.
name: Hach-Otis State Nature Preserve

Description: Cudahy Nature Preserve is a Southern Mesic Forest consisting of northern and southern uplands separated by a small perennial stream and adjacent riparian wetlands. Detailed plant inventories have discovered 198 native species of plants including 54 species of native trees and shrubs. Approximately 75% of the woodland would be of an age class that would be considered old growth forest and the oldest trees are likely 200+ years of age. As is typical with this type of forest, the dominant canopy trees consist of sugar maple, red oak, American basswood with smaller populations of eastern white oak, American beech, and bitternut hickory. Given the Preserve’s proximity to Lake Michigan, it also acts as an important stopover site for migratory birds, with 121 species seen to date.
Navigation: The park is located at 501 E. College Ave., Oak Creek, WI. The trailhead is located off of the parking lot.
Parking And Admission: Parking is located on the north end of the park and the entrance is on the south side of College Avenue. The parking lot can accommodate 10 vehicles, and there is no admission fee.
Trails: One-mile of the Forked Aster Hiking Trail System is located within the park with the trailhead located at the parking lot.
Hours And Camping: The park is open from sunrise to 10:00 PM daily. There is no camping available at this site.
name: Cudahy Woods State Natural Area

Description:
Newly re-named State Park in 2021. 
This is an approximately 20-acre stand of Eastern hemlocks and other hardwoods in the southern end of the 201-acre property that comprises the McKeever Center – Clear Creek State Forest. There is a steep ravine in this area and McKutcheon Run bisects this tract of land.

There is a newly constructed trail that will allow views of the hemlocks and older trees in this area.
Navigation:
55 McKeever Lane

Sandy Lake, Pennsylvania 16415
Parking And Admission: Free parking. No admission fee.
Trails: Multiple trails throughout the 200 acres, Most are about a mile in length.
name: McKeever Center- Clear Creek State Forest

Description:
The forested areas of the park are approximately 140 acres of mixed deciduous forest. Some knowledgeable volunteers estimate the oldest trees to be between 170 and 210 years old. Some volunteers suggest that some of the trees may be as old as 260 years. These trees are not far from the main loop of the park trails (“Edge Hill Trail”). 

The forest has a great mix of native trees, plants, fungi, and fauna. The trail system was created in a way to ebb and flow with the landscape and natural boundaries around it.
Navigation: 1253 Bushy Run Road – Jeanette, PA 15644
Parking And Admission: Two main parking lots on Route 993. Both parking lots are large. There is no fee for accessing the trails, forest, and battlefield. $5 general admission applies to guided museum tours of the property
Trails: The main trails in the park are gravel, but get steep in some places. We area working with PHMC on accessibility options that do not interfere with the natural landscape. Approximately four miles of trails.
Hours And Camping:
8am to Dusk.

Park grounds are open 365 days a year.

Scout troops are permitted to camp with prior reservation.
Hunting: No hunting, fishing, or trapping permitted.
name: Bushy Run Battlefield

Description: This nature preserve is a fine example of the many landforms associated with the Valparaiso Moraine. The Valparaiso Moraine runs for several hundred miles from southern Wisconsin through northern Illinois and northwest Indiana into west-central Michigan. The moraine was formed by the southern edge of the Lake Michigan Lobe of Wisconsinan glaciations. The nature preserve contains a combination of rolling upland ridges, steep hills and numerous shallow ponds. Mature beech-maple forest is found on some of the uplands and ravines. Buttonbush and black willow surround a number of the ponds. Several upland areas are in various stages of succession. The Moraine Nature Preserve is one of the few large, unfragmented blocks of forest left in Northwest Indiana.
Navigation:
Valparaiso, IN 46383

From Valparaiso, go north on SR 49 to CR 600 N, turn right and then immediately left on CR 200 E. Take CR 200 E north to the “T” intersection. Turn right on CR 750 N (Meska Road), the entrance to the preserve. Parking is located along this road and straight ahead to a 10 vehicle gravel parking lot.
Parking And Admission: There is a 10-vehicle gravel parking lot at the main trailhead for Moraine Nature Preserve. There is also a 2-vehicle parking area as you enter Moraine Nature Preserve along the entrance road. There is no fee or admission charge to visit Moraine Nature Preserve.
Trails: Two trails can be accessed from the central parking lot. Both trails are approximately 1.5 miles in length. The east trail is rated easy. The north trail is moderate in difficulty due to tripping hazards, elevation changes and a portion of the trail occurs on the entrance road.
Hours And Camping: Moraine Nature Preserve is open year-round from dawn to dusk. Camping is not allowed.
Hunting: Hunting is not allowed at Moraine Nature Preserve. However, management hunts of white-tail deer have occurred on specific parcels under specific requirements.
name: Moraine Nature Preserve

Description: Kennesaw Mountain NBP, which is located on a portion of the ancestral homelands of the Cherokee people, preserves a Civil War battleground of the Atlanta Campaign. The forests of Kennesaw Mountain have remained largely undisturbed since the conclusion of the Civil War and are now protected by the policies of the National Park Service. These forests are primarily loblolly pine and mixed hardwoods such as oak, hickory, and beech, once common throughout the Piedmont. Many miles of trails wind through the park and are beloved by locals for recreation.
Navigation: 900 Kennesaw Mountain Dr, Kennesaw, GA 30152
Parking And Admission:
Environmental Loop: Parking available at the Visitor’s Center.

Hardage Mill: Parking available on Burnt Hickory Road.



There is a $5 entrance free for private vehicles. Annual passes and Interagency America the Beautiful passes are also accepted.
Trails:
Environmental Loop: 1.35 miles 

 Hardage Mill Trail (Burnt Hickory to Dallas Highway): 2.20 miles 

 Total trail distance: over 40 miles.
Hours And Camping: Kennesaw Mountain NBP is open from 6:30 AM - 8:30 PM during Daylight Saving Time (March - November) and 6:30 AM - 6:30 PM Standard Time (December - February) These hours apply to all trails and parking lots.* *Cheatham Hill Parking Lot opens at 7:30 am
name: Kennesaw Mountain National Battlefield Park

Description:
The Forrest H. Dutlinger Natural Area is a protected area in Clinton County, Pennsylvania, United States that includes a 158-acre old-growth forest of eastern hemlock, American beech, black cherry, sugar maple, and northern red oak.

This 1,521-acre tract is surrounded by the Hammersley Wild Area in northern Clinton County. Its main feature is a 158-acre stand of old growth timber, but it is also an important reptile and amphibian protection area.

The forest community is characterized by oak-heath
association, including mountain laurel thickets,
huckleberry, and blueberry.

Some of the largest hemlocks in the natural area exceed four feet in diameter. District staff take measures to protect them
from the hemlock woolly adelgid.
Navigation: Trail head into the forest off Route 144.
Parking And Admission: By late 2023, or summer 2024, DCNR will be adding a trail head off the Trout Run Ridge Trail.Now there are about 3 spaces for cars and a few more may be added.
Trails: Vehicle access to the area can be found at its southeastern corner where an improved dirt road dead ends off of Route 144. The area can also be accessed via several trails, including from Trout Run Ridge and Beech Bottom Trail.
Hours And Camping: Camping primitive back-pack hiking is allowed. At the top of beech bottom. Campsites are on the map of Hammersley. FTF maps. There are rattlesnakes.
name: Forrest H. Dutlinger Natural Area

Description: According to Forest Service legacy date the forest nominated for the Network dates to 1885. The total acreage for the area is 1620. The upper drier slopes are composed of mainly Chestnut oak. The coves especially along the Belfast Trail include cove hardwoods such as Northern red oak, White oak, yellow poplar, and hickory. The canopy along the Belfast Trail is composed of tall straight cove hardwoods. The drier slopes offer a contrast of gnarly Chestnut oak.
Navigation: Take 1-81 to exit #180. Take US 11 south 3.5 miles to SR 130. Turn left on SR 130 and proceed 3.2 miles to Arnolds Valley Road (CR 759). Turn right and travel 3.2 miles. Turn left on Petites Gap Road (CR 781). Travel 1.3 miles to the trailhead.
Parking And Admission: There is no charge. Currently parking is limited but the Forest Service has acquired some property to enlarge the parking area.
Trails: The Belfast Trail crosses into the James River Face Wilderness at 0.7 miles. The grade is easy to moderate. It reaches the cove hardwoods near the Devils Marbleyard just past 1.0 miles.
Hours And Camping: Primitive camping is allowed along the Belfast Trail. There are no facilities.
Phone Number: U.S. Forest Service, Glenwood and Pedlar
name: Belfast Trail - James River Face Wilderness - Jefferson National Forest

Description:
St. Phillips Island is a 4-mile-long, 4,680-acre undeveloped barrier island off the coast of Beaufort, South Carolina. This former private island can only be accessed by boat and is a true hidden gem of the Lowcountry. For nearly 40 years, it was owned by billionaire conservationist Ted Turner, who purchased St. Phillips in 1979 to preserve its integrity as an unspoiled natural environment and protect it from development. In 2017, the State of South Carolina purchased the island, which is now operated in conjunction with nearby Hunting Island State Park. 

The old growth forest on St. Phillips Island includes towering live oaks and magnificent magnolias, in addition to many other common maritime forest species. The old growth forest on the island helped to earn the designation of National Natural Landmark by the National Park Service. Four miles of trails provide access to the forest, freshwater ponds, saltwater creeks, and about one mile of pristine beach.
Navigation: St. Phillips Island is managed by Hunting Island State Park, located at 2555 Sea Island Parkway, St. Helena Island, SC 29920. Public day tours are provided by Coastal Expeditions at 1928 Sea Island Parkway, St. Helena Island, SC 29920.
Parking And Admission: The island is accessible by water with approved tour groups only. Visitors may register for a day tour with Coastal Expeditions Beaufort (1928 Sea Island Parkway, St. Helena Island, SC 29920) and take their ferry to the island for $65/adult, $35/child, infants free of cost. The ferry ride includes a presentation on the history and ecology of the island and surrounding marshes by an experienced naturalist. Once on the island, a guided tram ride will take you across the island to the picnic area near the Turner House, from where many trails (and the beach) are accessible. Overnight rentals of the Turner House are available to book through Hunting Island State Park.
Trails:
There is a network of trails to explore on the island winding through various habitats.



Recommended trail: Long Pond Trail & Marshview Trail, 2.2 miles 

Total length: 3.8 miles

Including park road: 7.2 miles
Hours And Camping: Open year round to approved tour groups. No camping opportunities yet, but check back in the future!
name: St. Phillips Island

Description:
Considered the birthplace of the conservation movement, Aldo Leopold famously championed protections for the Gila Wilderness Area in western New Mexico. In 1924, the Gila Wilderness became the first designated wilderness area in the world. 

Spanning more than a half a million acres within the Gila National Forest, the vast Gila Wilderness is rugged and diverse. The Gila’s ecosystems are influenced by the arid climate and the convergence of the Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts and rocky mountain and sierra madre mountain ranges. 

Forests in the Wilderness vary from bottomland riparian forests in the canyons with willow, sycamore and walnut, to oak woodlands and pinyon-juniper scrub, ponderosa and aspen parklands, mixed conifer forests and high-elevation subalpine spruce forests. 

Evidence of its earliest inhabitants dates back to the Paleoindians (9500-6000 BC) followed by Cochise Culture, Mogollon Culture and eventually the Apache. Indian removal, conflict, settler disputes, fire suppression, and exploitation through mining, logging and grazing, and over-hunting/predator loss all continue to shape and influence the Gila landscape. 

Old-growth takes many different forms across the variety of forest types in the Gila Wilderness, from scattered old trees, clumps, and patches of old-growth trees within a diverse mosaic, to continuous, large stands of old-growth found at higher elevations in mixed-conifer forests. The amount of old-growth is unknown.
Parking And Admission: Parking is available at numerous trailheads. Parking is also available at the Gila Visitor Center. There is no entrance fee for the Gila Wilderness Area.
Trails: Off the path of turkey creek is an area known as McKenna park, and dry tank lake. Only a part of turkey creek trail is in the wilderness
Hours And Camping: The Wilderness is open year round. Camping is permitted within the Wilderness and several US Forest Service campgrounds are available within the surrounding Gila National Forest. For more information visit: https://www.fs.usda.gov/recmain/gila/recreation
Hunting: Hunting is permitted. For more information visit: https://www.fs.usda.gov/activity/gila/recreation/hunting
name: Gila Wilderness Area - Gila National Forest

Description:
The 82 acre preserve is an excellent example of Appalachian ‘hardwood forest’ comprised of oak-hickory on the southern aspects and ridges, and mixed-mesophytic forest dominated by yellow poplar, sugar maple, and oak elsewhere. Twenty-five acres are ‘late successional’ and are developing a more complex structure. timber. White and Chestnut oaks are approximately about 120-130 years old. 

Some fraction of the largest trees have fallen over past decades, and much course woody debris exists. The soils are loamy to clay-loam, not particularly light, but rich and mesic across the uplands but becoming drier at the bottom along Little Falls Road. 

Many blowdown and wind-thrown mounds are found across the older forest, as are snags, gaps, and an increasingly complex structure. The area traversed by the upper half of the Elizabeth’s Loop Trail is the best example of mesic, Appalachian cove / mixed-mesophytic forest. The spring ephemerals are rich and abundant throughout the cove as well as on the upper half of the Hollenhorst Trail.
Navigation:
Little Falls Road

Morgantown, West Virginia

Directions: From I-79 N or S, take the Goshen Rd. exit, exit 146. Turn west on Goshen Rd. (a right from the N, a left from the S), and proceed to the Smithtown Rd. junction. At the junction, beware of the truck traffic. Make a left, heading S on Smithtown Rd., then a quick right on Little Falls Rd., so you’re only on Smithtown Rd. for a jag, a 100 feet or so. Take Little Falls Rd. slowly ~0.4 miles, and take a right on the steep gravel access road (there is an inconspicuous wooden sign at the bottom of the access road, and no other right turns off Little Falls in the vicinity). The parking lot is a few 100 feet ahead
Parking And Admission: Parking for 20 vehicles. No admission fee, but the West Virginia Land Trust accepts donations.
Trails: All trails are constructed or native materials to semi-primitive, non-motorized standards, and may challenge beginner hikers.
Hours And Camping: Dawn to dusk. No camping.
name: Elizabeth's Woods

Description:
The Curtis Gates Lloyd Recreation and Wildlife Area- the 600 acre property, about 40 acres of old-growth forest occur in 2 remnant stands on the non-hunted portion of the area, which are collectively known as the Lloyd Woods. Dalton and Brewer (1997) described these woods as the best uncut forest in the Bluegrass Region in north-central Kentucky.

Large old-growth trees include tulip poplar, (species) oak, shagbark hickory, black walnut.
Navigation: One-half mile southeast of Crittenden; from I-75 take Crittenden exit, follow US 25 south to left turn across railroad tracks to area.
Parking And Admission: 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Mon-Fri. for main administration building only.
Trails: Dogs must be on leash.
Hours And Camping:
8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Mon-Fri. for main administration building only. 

No camping on premises but there are campgrounds nearby.
Hunting: Not open to hunting. Trap range and fishing range at mouth of the Old-Growth Forest. Public use of the trap range; clubhouse there.
name: Lloyd Old-Growth Woods - Curtis Gates Lloyd Wildlife Management Area

Description:
Spring wildflowers include Dutchman's breeches, red trillium, nodding trillium, spring beauty, blue phlox, Solomon's seal violets, doll's eyes, Mayapples, geraniums, waterleaf and many, many more—too many to count! Of course, there are other plants to admire while at the preserve. Queen of the prairie is the most striking of flowers, and restoration has brought back the Michigan lily, swamp goldenrod, cup plant and several species of sedge. Skunk cabbage, golden ragwort, marsh marigold, jewelweed, and blue-eyed Mary cover the forest floor. Above, the canopy is created by beech, maple, tulip, black cherry, black walnut, red elm, and bur oak on 28 acres of old-growth forest.

Flying across the sky or nesting in a standing dead tree could be a number of different species of birds: Barred Owls, Great Crested Flycatchers and migrant species like cerulean warblers, blue-gray gnatcatchers, ovenbirds, scarlet tanagers, Baltimore Orioles, red-eyed vireos, wood thrush, and Acadian flycatchers.

Easy to moderate terrain, two looped trails through the preserve and the beauty of nature will make for a great day of hiking. Watch out for stinging nettle, the most prominent plant in the woods during the summer months.

Description: Shrader-Weaver, a National Natural Landmark, contains a pioneer homestead, open fields, and woods. A 28-acre old-growth upland forest is beech-maple dominated. Large specimens of tulip, black cherry, black walnut, red elm, and bur oak are also present. The diverse shrub layer includes pawpaw, Virginia creeper, and spicebush. There is also a rich variety of spring wildflowers. The old field area is now being invaded by woody species. It illustrates the successional trend to a forest community. Hayes Regional Arboretum and Earlham College have planted black walnut in this area using seedlings from selected trees having superior qualities.
Navigation: From Bentonville, travel east on C.R. 700 N for one mile and turn right (south) on C.R. 450 W. Travel 1.75 miles to a marked parking lot on the right hand side.
Parking And Admission: A small parking lot is available. There is no admission fee.
Trails: There are 2 self-guided trails in this preserve; one goes through the old-growth upland forest (approx 1.5 miles) and the other through the old field and lowland forest (approx .5 miles).
Hours And Camping:
Open dawn until dusk.

No camping.
name: Shrader-Weaver Woods Nature Preserve

Description: Victor Baltzell donated this 37-acre property to the State in memory of his wife Alice Lenhart Baltzell. The woods is a mesic and wet-mesic flatwoods typical of the central till plain, yet, unique in that it has an old-growth aspect due to the lack of trees removed during the Baltzell tenure on the property. The area is dominated by oaks and hickories, but the presence of such species as bur oak, swamp white oak, pin oak, red maple, sycamore, and cottonwood attest to its wetness at times.
Navigation:
466-988 E 200 N,

Decatur, IN 46733



From Decatur, take US 27 south for about 3.5 miles to CR 200N. Turn left and travel about 0.5 mile to the preserve which runs alongside the south side of the road for about 0.25 mile.
Parking And Admission: A small parking area is available. There is no admission fee.
Trails: The trail is ¾ of a mile long.
Hours And Camping: Open dawn to dusk, no camping.
name: Baltzell-Lenhart Woods Nature Preserve

Description: The 2,768- acre Quinault Recreation Area is veiled by a canopy of ancient Sitka spruce, Douglas fir, western red cedar, and western hemlocks this area showcases the ancient temperate rainforest of the Olympic Peninsula. Towering giant trees cloak the fern and moss laden forest floor in an ecosystem that contains more biomass per acre than any other forest type. Home to the historic Lake Quinault Lodge, various campgrounds, and a vast network of trails spanning Quinault National Recreational Trail System, Colonel Bob Wilderness and the West Fork Humptulips River, the Quinault area provides a wide array of recreation opportunities for all.
Navigation: From Aberdeen, WA travel north on US Highway 101 for 45 miles to the junction of South Shore Road. Turn right (east) and drive 1.4 miles to Quinault Rain Forest Trailhead on right side of South Shore Road.
Parking And Admission: A large parking area is available off of S. Shore Rd. A $5 daily vehicle permit is required.
Trails: The Rain Forest Nature Trail is a ½ mile interpretive trail that provides an excellent opportunity to view the temperate rainforest. Overlooking Willaby Gorge, the trail follows Willaby Creek, a typical rainforest stream. Experience stands of ancient large trees and view interpretive signs along the trail that describe aspects of old-growth forest ecology. The trail also connects you to the Quinault Recreation Area Trail System which offers approximately 10 miles of trails.
Hours And Camping:
Open year-round.

There are several camping options nearby which are open from May to September. Falls Creek Campground includes 21 tent, RV and trailer sites, as well as 10 walk-in tent sites. Reservations can be made in advance. Gatton Creek Campground has 5 first come, first served walk-in sites. Willaby Campground includes 19 tent, RV and trailer sites, as well as 2 walk-in tent sites.
name: Quinault Lake Rain Forest - Olympic National Forest

Description:
The 86-acre property includes an amazing old-growth forest and two rare prairies and is full of birds and wildlife. The preserve overlooks over a mile of shoreline on Admiralty Inlet, benefiting marine species like salmon that migrate along its shores. In addition, the two rare prairies (less than 1 percent of Whidbey Island’s prairies remain) both feature golden paintbrush populations, making the preserve one of only 11 sites in the world where this endangered prairie plant occurs naturally.

What you may marvel at the most are the trees! The branches of the old-growth Douglas fir trees twist and turn making their way under and around each other. At over 4 feet in diameter and 250 years old, these trees have weathered many coastal storms. In addition to fir, the forest contains grand fir, western hemlock, Pacific yew, Sitka spruce and red alder trees with most trees over 145 years old. There are lots of snags, providing perfect nesting and feeding areas for all kinds of raptors, owls and songbirds.

There’s a loop trail on the property that is open to the public for walking and nature enjoyment, and a small parking area off Engle Road.
Navigation:
797-813 S Engle Rd, Coupeville, WA 98239

• From Hwy 20 in Coupeville, go south on Main St.

• Follow the road for 2.4 miles the parking lot is on the left.
Parking And Admission: There is free parking at the preserve and no admission charge. Parking is located on the east side of Engle Road across the street from the trail system.
Trails: There are two loop trails on the property. The perimeter loop is 1.5 miles and includes the native prairie and old growth forest. There is also a 1-mile northern loop option the focuses on the prairie habitat.
Hours And Camping: Open year round. Dawn to dusk. No camping.
name: Admiralty Inlet Natural Area Preserve
Cave Creek Canyon - Chiricuhua Wilderness - Coronado National Forest

Description:
Marys Peak, at 4,097 feet, is the highest point in Oregon’s Coast Range and the most prominent peak to the west of Corvallis. On a clear day, from the Summit Parking Lot at the top of the peak, you can see both the Pacific Ocean to the west and many of the Cascade peaks to the east across the Willamette Valley.

At approximately 964 acres, Marys Peak has been designated a Scenic Botanical Area because of its rich, unique scenery and plants. The open meadows offer a range of wildflowers throughout the spring and summer. Wildflower displays in the meadow and rock gardens change throughout the late spring and summer months. The rich rolling meadows of Marys Peak are fringed by a unique Noble fir forest. 

Noble fir occurs only rarely in the Oregon Coast Range and almost never forms extensive stands. These stands do include areas of Douglas-fir and western hemlock, but noble fir on Marys Peak is unique in the size of the population, the extent of the
stand, and the absence of competing Pacific silver fir. These huge trees form a closed canopy high above a dense carpet of Oregon woodsorrel and other herbaceous flowering plant species.
Navigation:
Marys Peak Observation Point Parking Lot

NF-3010, Philomath, OR 97370
Parking And Admission: Parking is available at the trailhead. Day Use Fee Area ($5 a vehicle) or valid Recreation Pass required. Fee can be paid at the Marys Peak Day Use Area.
Trails:
The 1.6 mile Meadowedge Trail is recommended.



Other hiking options include East Ridge Trail, North Ridge Trail, Summit Trail, and Tie Trail. When there's snow, cross country skiing, snowshoeing and other non-motorized winter recreation are available, although the road to the day use area is not maintained for winter travel and caution is advised.
Hours And Camping:
Marys Peak is open year-round. Camping is available at the nearby Marys Peak Campground 



NOTE: The roads to Marys Peak from Highway 34 are not maintained for winter travel. Always watch out for potentially dangerous conditions from heavy rains, slides, falling trees and debris, high winds and heavy snowfall when traveling in the Coast Range. Snow may limit driving access to trailheads. North Ridge trail is accessed from Highway 20 which is at a lower elevation and less affected by winter weather. In all cases, even if you can reach a trailhead, trail access may be limited by snow. Conditions change quickly. Please check weather before heading out.
name: Marys Peak - Siuslaw National Forest

Description:
In a verdant floodplain valley between the Patagonia and Santa Rita Mountains of southeastern Arizona, within the watershed of Sonoita Creek, lies some of the richest of the remaining riparian (streamside) habitat in the region. One of a few remaining permanent streams, it provides for a wide array of diverse species from endangered fishes to butterflies and birds.
This site contains the first two miles of permanent flow of Sonoita Creek and the floodplains adjacent to the stream. The site contains very high biodiversity values that are primarily focused on the riparian habitats along Sonoita Creek. As the first project for The Nature Conservancy in Arizona, it contains much of the biological diversity associated with these habitat types. The watershed is mostly undeveloped, and the natural processes of flooding are mostly intact and functioning.
The 873-acre preserve protects a magnificent example of the rare Fremont cottonwood-Goodding willow riparian forest. Some of the trees are among the largest (more than 100 feet tall) and oldest (130 years old) Fremont cottonwood trees in this country. This is one of the few remaining sites in Arizona where this once-common forest type still persists. Arizona black walnut, velvet mesquite, velvet ash, netleaf hackberry and various willows are found in slightly different habitats throughout the preserve. Here are remnant wetlands, or cienegas, a once-common feature of the Sonoita Creek floodplain and the most endangered natural community in Arizona. A significant number of rare and sensitive plant species are found in the Sonoita Creek watershed, including Huachuca water umbel, Santa Cruz striped agave and the Santa Cruz beehive cactus.
