Today, the preserve is visited by thousands of people every year seeking to see and experience some facet of its rich natural diversity. The preserve has been
actively engaged in hydrologic research and monitoring and is the site of some of the first community-based activities seeking to build understanding and support for conservation in southern Arizona. It has been a platform for promoting the work of TNC and a site of several innovative environmental education activities.
Navigation:
Visitor Center

150 Blue Heaven Road

Patagonia, AZ 85624
Parking And Admission:
General Public: $8 per person.

TNC Members and Cochise County Residents: $5 per person

Ages 17 and under: Free

Annual pass to Ramsey Canyon Preserve and Patagonia Sonoita Creek Preserve: $55
Trails:
Creek Trail – 0.89 miles (plus ~0.15 miles to access trail).

Total trail system - ~8.73 miles

Link to preserve trail map:

nature.org/content/dam/tnc/nature/en/documents/PSCP_Trail_Map_2023.pdf
Hours And Camping: April-September: Wednesday-Sunday, 6:30 a.m.-4 p.m.; October-March: Wednesday-Sunday, 7:30 a.m.-4 p.m. Closed: Mondays and Tuesdays all year and on Thanksgiving, the day after Thanksgiving, and Christmas and New Years days.
name: Patagonia-Sonoita Creek Preserve

Description:
Designated in 1978, Wolsfeld Woods was among the first of Minnesota's Scientific and Natural Areas. It was acquired to protect one the best remaining examples of the Big Woods forest community in the state. The site's hilly topography can be credited at least in part with the survival of the forest here. Early homesteaders found it impractical to till for farming, opting instead to establish a maple syrup operation that continued from the 1880s into the 1940s.

Mature maple-basswood forest dominates the SNA, with some of the state's largest individual sugar maple trees. The site also hosts areas of oak forest and emergent marsh. Permanent and intermittent streams have carved meandering valleys through the rolling terrain.

All but the northwest corner of 35-acre Wolsfeld Lake lies within the SNA. Researchers have used lakebed sediments (including pollen) to reconstruct the area's environmental history. Studies by U of MN researcher Eric Grimm and colleagues indicate that 12,000 years ago this site was characterized by spruce forest. As the climate grew warmer and drier, conifers were gradually replaced by deciduous forest and then by prairie. Prairie persisted until about 5000 years ago, when a return to cooler/wetter climate fostered a transition to oak savanna and oak forest. This, in turn, was replaced by maple-basswood forest within the last 500 years.
Navigation:
2060 County Road 6,

Long Lake, MN 55356



The trailhead is located in the northeast corner of Trinity Lutheran Church parking lot.
Parking And Admission: No admission fee. Parking is available in the northeast corner of Trinity Lutheran Church parking lot.
Trails: A trail network of approximately 2-3 miles can be found within the Scientific and Natural Area, trails from the parking area and south of Wolsfeld Lake provide good access to old-growth viewing.
Hours And Camping: Restrictions on camping and campfires help protect native plant communities. In many instances, public camping facilities are available nearby. See where camping and campfires are allowed at Minnesota State Parks.
name: Wolsfeld Woods SNA

Description:
On the boundary between the prairie and the "Big Woods", this 835-acre park offers a diversity of landscapes. Situated on the shore of Upper and Lower Sakatah lakes, this wooded park offers camping, biking, hiking, fishing and canoeing. Sakatah Singing Hills State Trail runs through the park, providing access to 39 mi of biking and snowmobiling trails with approx 3 mi of the trail within park boundaries. The park has 5 miles of trail for hiking.

The park was established in 1963 by an act of the Minnesota Legislature. The parklands include 3.5 miles of shoreline along Sakatah Lake. The rolling topography of the park features rich, mixed hardwood forest and dry upland prairie. The Cannon River area formed the boundary between the “Big
Woods” of the Minnesota and Mississippi River Valleys, and the southern oak barrens south of the park. Sakatah Lake, a natural widening of the Cannon
River, provides visitors with opportunities for many forms of outdoor recreation and nature study including hiking, biking, birding, fishing, and other activities. 

Located just a few miles east of Minnesota's Prairie Region, frequent fires shaped this old growth forest. As a result, ancient oaks are the most common trees, and prairie plants grow along the area's roadsides and railroad lines.
Navigation: 50499 Sakatah Lake State Park Rd, Waterville, MN 56096
Parking And Admission: A $7 vehicle permit is required for entry which can be purchased online or at the park gatehouse. More information about permits can be found at: https://www.dnr.state.mn.us/state_parks/permit.html
Trails:
There is a total of eight miles of trail within Sakatah Lake State Park providing visitors with a variety of trail experiences. The trails provide opportunities for:

• Eight miles of hiking with varying degrees of difficulty, including three miles on the Sakatah Singing Hills Trail.

• Three miles of paved bike trail via the Sakatah Singing Hills State Trail.

• One-quarter mile of accessible trail within the park and 3 miles on the Sakatah Singing Hills State Trail is considered accessible.

• Five miles of groomed cross-country ski trails.

• Three miles of snowmobile trail via the Sakatah Singing Hills Trail.

• Snowshoeing is allowed anywhere off of groomed ski trails.
Hours And Camping:
The park is open daily from 8 a.m. until 10 p.m. Camping is available within the park including 52 drive in sites for car/tent and rv camping. Bike-in sites are also available. More information can be found at:

https://www.dnr.state.mn.us/state_parks/park.html?id=spk00256#overnight_facilities
name: Sakatah Lake State Park

Description:
Townsend Woods was designated an SNA to preserve a high quality remnant of Big Woods sugar maple forest, a native plant community ranked as imperiled in Minnesota.

This small but important site is associated with the Emmons-Faribault moraine: an area of rolling topography formed beneath and at the margins of stagnant glacial ice. Irregular knobs and ridges, dotted by lakes and wetlands, offered a barrier to fire that allowed the forest to develop and persist here. Through the years, the old-growth stand within the SNA also managed to escape the impacts of gravel mining, clear-cut logging and conversion to cropland. Aside from small-scale maple sugaring and some selective cutting of elm, it is essentially undisturbed.

The forest has an open aspect, with young maples in the understory but few shrubs. Large red oak and sugar maple dominate in the canopy, joined by basswood, elm and ironwood. Hollows among the hills host a small pond as well as ephemeral pools found in spring and during periods of above average rainfall. A steep ridge with north/northeast-facing slopes bi-sects the site, below which a small creek runs through a cattail marsh.
Navigation: From Morristown 0.75 mile W on MN Hwy 60, then 3.6 miles NW Co Rd 99, then 0.5 mile N on LeSueur Ave. Park in lot on East side of the road. Hike corridor 0.5 mile East, North, then East to site.
Parking And Admission: A small parking area is available. There is no fee for admission.
Trails: Reaching the woods requires a half-mile long trek in from the parking lot. The site has no maintained trails.
Hours And Camping: Restrictions on camping and campfires help protect native plant communities. In many instances, public camping facilities are available nearby. See where camping and campfires are allowed at Minnesota State Parks.
name: Townsend Woods Scientific & Natural Area

Navigation:
1023 Sandy Flash Drive South

Media, PA 19063
Hours And Camping: The park is open every day of the year, sunrise to sunset, including the restrooms in picnic area number 7 and number 17. Day use areas close at dusk. Camping for qualified groups is allowed with a reservation. Rest rooms are available, but no showers.
Hunting: Archery full season on north side only by registered hunters. Shotgun full park first two Thursdays of season only by registered hunters.
name: Ridley Creek State Park

Description:
Spanning across 130 acres, Solon Woods State Nature Preserve is renowned for its mature mixed hardwood forest with large specimens of bur, red, white and swamp white oaks and beech and tuliptree. There are not large stands of the oldest trees, and they are scattered among the property. 
Amongst the old-growth forest are several vernal pools that provide important breeding habitat for frogs and salamanders. Spring peepers and wood frogs are abundant.

Despite its location in an urban landscape the preserve remains a sanctuary for wildlife. An excellent birding location offering a variety of bird species throughout the year. In spring, the forest floor comes alive with a carpet of spring wildflowers such as yellow trout lily, wild geranium, cut-leaved toothwort, spring beauty, bloodroot and squirrel-corn.

The property is owned by the City but managed by the Ohio State Nature Preserves division.
Navigation:
34227 Russell Drive

Solon, OH
Parking And Admission: Park at end of Russell Drive near entrance sign. No actual parking areas, but they are considering a secondary area on the eastern side of the parcel.
Trails: Not much of a trail - a poorly maintained trail exists that was built 15-20 years prior to 2024 by an Eagle Scout.
Hours And Camping: Open 1/2 hour before sunrise, 1/2 after sunset, 365 days a year. Pets are not permitted. No camping is allowed and there are no restrooms present.
name: Solon Woods State Nature Preserve

Description:
Protected in 1992, Pyatt Lake represents not only an undisturbed landscape with unique habitat and geologic features but also the Conservancy’s first land preservation effort. Many diverse groups, from local artists to school children, came together to shield this land from the threat of impending development. Prior to Pyatt’s protection, the beauty and value of this property were recognized by both developers and conservationists. Luckily, the property had been identified as one of the most botanically diverse privately owned properties in Grand Traverse County and was one of three remaining examples of a “Wooded Dune and Swale Complex” habitat in northern Michigan. As a result, a compelling argument for Pyatt’s regional significance and preservation was successfully made. Over the years Pyatt Lake Preserve has been expanded eight times, bringing it to 159 acres.

Approximately 107 acres of forested natural communities are protected within the preserve include Rich Conifer Swamp, Northern Hardwood Swamp, Hardwood-Conifer Swamp, Dry Mesic Northern Forest, and Mesic Northern Forest. Tree species present include northern white cedar, red and white pine, hemlock, paper birch, sugar maple, red maple, American beech, yellow and paper birch, tamarack and red and white oak.
Navigation:
Pyatt Rd, Traverse City, MI 49686 



Pyatt Lake Nature Preserve is located just 20 minutes from Traverse

City. Take Peninsula Dr. north approximately 10 miles. Just past Bowers Harbor Marina, turn left on Neahtawanta Rd. Follow Neahtawanta Rd. 1/2 mile to Pyatt Rd. Turn right on Pyatt Rd. The parking area is 1/4 mile down Pyatt Rd.



An alternative parking area is available on the west side of Peninsula Dr, 1/2 mile north of the intersection of Peninsula Dr. and Neahtawanta Rd.
Parking And Admission: Access to the Preserve is via the main parking lot off of Pyatt Road. Pyatt Road is an unmaintained seasonal road which is not plowed in the winter. A turnaround at the end of Pyatt Road also serves as an overflow for larger vehicles. An alternative parking area is available on the west side of Peninsula Dr, 1/2 mile north of the intersection of Peninsula Dr. and Neahtawanta Rd. There is no admission fee.
Trails: The western loop trail is .7 miles. Total trail length is 1.2 miles. A trail map is available on the preserve website and trail entrance.
Hours And Camping: The preserve is open dawn until dusk, year round. Note that Pyatt Road is an unmaintained seasonal road which is not plowed in the winter. No camping is permitted.
Hunting: Yes, however it is limited to deer with a bow. Please see the hunting rules on the preserve webpage in addition to observing all state laws and regulations.
name: Pyatt Lake: The Bill Carls Nature Preserve

Description: Locally known as the Valley of the Giants, this impressive area of older forest is accessed via the North Country National Scenic Trail. The trail follows a transition of forest types from upland red oak, to unique natural stands of old eastern white pine and red pine, to eastern hemlock and white cedar along twenty-two creek. The Valley of the Giants is approximately 60 acres located within the Traverse City Forest Management Unit of the Pere Marquette State Forest.
Navigation: From the intersection of Garfield and River Road southeast of Traverse City, go east on River Road for 1 block to Arbutus Hill Road. Continue straight onto Brown Bridge Road (formerly River Road). Continue east for 0.7 miles, then bear right at the fork onto Scharmen Road. At 3.6 miles, watch for the North Country Trail blue blazes to cross Scharmen Road. Continue east and at 3.9 miles, find the blue blazes crossing the road for a second time (right after mailbox number 6985). Pull into the two-track on the left and park off to the side in the grass/snow. This is right where Scharmen Road turns south and becomes Hodge Road.
Parking And Admission: There is a small parking area on the north side of Scharmen road with space for roughly 8 cars. There is no admission fee.
Trails: An easy to moderate 2.5 mile out and back along the North Country Trail showcases the area well. Head east on the trail from the parking area following the blue blazes to a bridge across twenty-two creek. A bench and trail log box also mark this location.
Hours And Camping: Several state forest campgrounds are located in the area. Sheck’s Place State Forest Campground is located roughly a mile away. Other camping options are available in the area.
Hunting: Hunting is permitted per MI DNR regulations.
name: Valley of the Giants - Pere Marquette State Forest

Description:
The Frohring Forest area is located in a conservation easement area of approximately 221.3 acres within the larger James H. Barrow Biological Field Station, owned, and operated by Hiram College. The core of the Frohring Forest includes over 100 acres of old-growth beech-maple forest, one of largest remaining uncut
beech-maple forests in Ohio. This old-growth forest is surrounded by approximately 103 acres of other forested areas such as early- to mid-successional beech-maple forests, early- to mid-successional mixed hardwood forests, and floodplain forest. 
Additionally, the area contains a portion of Silver Creek and its tributaries and associated floodplain/high-quality wetlands; Silver Creek is recognized as one of the last remaining cold-water streams in the Mahoning River watershed. The remaining land within the conservation easement area includes emergent wetlands, two ponds, old-field habitat with scrub-shrub, meadow, and landscaped and maintained areas.
Navigation: The visitor’s entrance of the Field Station at 11305 Wheeler Rd, Garrettsville OH, 44231.
Parking And Admission: Free parking; no admission fee.
Hours And Camping: Dawn to dusk, open daily.
name: Frohring Forest

Description:
The 405.16-acre Humbug Marsh Unit is a major part of the conservation crescent of the lower Detroit River - including Humbug mainland, Calf Island, Gibraltar Bay and Sugar Island - and a hotspot of biodiversity in an urban landscape. Sitting south of the Refuge Gateway, Humbug Marsh is mostly forested with some areas that were clear-cut in December 1998. In 2004, the property was purchased by the refuge after a group of local supporters stopped development that would have forever changed the face of the river and surrounding lands. The parcel represents the last mile of undeveloped shoreline along the U.S. mainland of the Detroit River and contains important habitat for many rare fish and wildlife species. Humbug Marsh was designated as Michigan's first Wetland of International Importance in 2010 by the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands.

This wet mesic flatwoods habitat is underlain by poorly drained stiff clay that can hold water for prolonged periods. Shagbark hickory, oak, ash and elm trees dominate the landscape in a mosaicked fashion across the unit with rough-leaved dogwood and goldenrod species present in early successional habitats. The coastal wetland is dominated by bulrushes, native and naturalized grasses, cattail and invasive phragmites. An ever-changing habitat that is dependent on Great Lake water levels, Humbug Marsh is a major repository of species and preservation of ecosystem processes.
Navigation:
5437 West Jefferson Avenue, Trenton, MI 48183

After driving through the Refuge Gateway main entrance along W. Jefferson Ave., stay right/south, park in the lot in front of the John D. Dingell Jr. Visitor Center. Follow the sidewalk to the right/southwest of the facility and continue over the small bridge that passes over Monguagon Drain. This is the start of the trailhead for both the Green Trail and Orange Trail. The Green Trail leads to the Old Growth Forest area of the Humbug Marsh Unit.
Parking And Admission:
Parking lot by the John D. Dingell Jr. Visitor Center at the Refuge Gateway: 24 standard parking spaces



Overflow parking lot near the John D. Dingell Jr. Visitor Center at the Refuge Gateway: 49 standard parking spaces and 6 bus parking spaces.



No admission charge.
Trails:
Green Trail

Open season: Open year round. Walking, snow shoeing and cross-country skiing. Not open to biking or horseback riding.

Length: Approximately 2.25 miles from the visitor center and back

Location of trail: Humbug Marsh Unit, look for #8 on the wayfinding signs

Surface: Dirt with wooden planks over wet areas

Difficulty: Fairly easy with benches for resting and enjoying the views. The trail can become extremely muddy during spring and after rain events.

Information: This trail gets you into the heart of the Humbug Marsh Unit, where you can try wrapping your arms around old oak trees that are more than 300 years old and enjoy the views of the lower Detroit River and northern Lake Erie. The trail is flat, with the exception of getting onto the berm along the Handler Drain.
Hours And Camping: The grounds are open for self-guided visitation seven days a week during daylight hours year-round. The John D. Dingell Jr. Visitor Center at the Refuge Gateway is open Thursday – Sunday year-round. The hours are as follow Thursday - Sunday 10:00 a.m. - 4:00 p.m. There is no camping.
Hunting: There is no hunting allowed in the area of the old growth, north of the Handler Drain.
name: Humbug Marsh Unit - Detroit River International Wildlife Refuge

Description: Sylvania Wilderness encompasses approximately 18,400 acres. This large, primarily undisturbed area includes 34 named lakes, islands, rolling hills, marshes, bogs, wetlands and secluded old growth forests. Sylvania is a northern hardwood forests where dominant tree species include sugar maple, white pine, eastern hemlock, yellow birch, white birch and red pine. The specific acreage of “old-growth” within Sylvania is undocumented however, the majority of the 18,400 acres is relatively untouched old-growth forest.
Navigation:
Sylvania Rd, Watersmeet, MI 49969. 



To reach Sylvania entrance station and recreation area: From Watersmeet, travel approximately 4 miles west on U.S. 2 to County Road 535, then drive south on CR 535 approximately 4 miles south to the Sylvania Recreation Area.
Parking And Admission: Two main parking areas (Clark Lake and Crooked Lake) are established for the wilderness, each of these provide trailheads and carry in canoe launches. Multiple smaller parking areas (or maybe pull-offs are the better word) are present on the perimeter of the wilderness area. A parking fee is established where users can either pay $5 daily fees or a $30 annual pass.
Trails:
The Clark Lake Loop is 8.4 miles and provides access to the natural beauty of the Sylvania Wilderness. This trail can be used as an out-and-back to shorten the length. Approximately 26 miles of hiking trails are present within Sylvania Wilderness. 

Individuals interested in renting equipment or guided trips should contact Sylvania Outfitters (Sylvania Outfitters - Your Adventure Starts Here).
Hours And Camping: Sylvania Wilderness is open year-round with reservations mandatory from May 15th – September 30th (Recreation.gov - Camping, Cabins, RVs, Permits, Passes & More). Nearly 100 campsites are present within Sylvania Wilderness with 48 being at Clark Lake Campground. Clark Lake Campground is the only area within Sylvania with flush toilets, the remainder are vault toilets. Clark Lake campground does not provide electricity or water hook ups at the sites. The more rustic options are the 50 wilderness campsites which are dispersed throughout the wilderness, some are more challenging to get to with multiple portages between lakes. Clark Lake and Crooked Lake landings provide handpump drinking water, otherwise, all water must be carried in.
Hunting: Hunting is allowed within Sylvania Wilderness. Individuals interested in hunting within Sylvania must follow all Michigan Department of Natural Resources hunting regulations (michigan.gov/dnr/-/media/Project/Websites/dnr/Documents/LED/digests/hunting_digest.pdf?rev=54c4fa4e30514aa8b2af49e36ad82ca6)
name: Sylvania Wilderness - Ottawa National Forest

Description: Sturgeon River Gorge Wilderness is a 14,500-acre parcel of land that includes rocky outcrops, steep terrain, rushing rivers, marshes, bogs, wetlands and secluded old growth forests. Dominant species within the wilderness include Eastern Hemlock, Red and White Pine, Aspen, Sugar Maple, Paper Birch and Basswood. The wilderness also includes the Sturgeon River, a federally recognized Wild and Scenic stream. The area around and within the Sturgeon River Gorge Wilderness experienced heavy logging prior to the wilderness designation in 1987. Therefore, limited stands of old-growth are currently present.
Navigation:
Federal Forest Road 2217, Pelkie, MI 49958



From Sidnaw, MI, travel east on M 28 approximately ¼ mile to FR 2200, turn left onto FR 2200. There are several locations to enter the wilderness, it is recommended that you use the campground or approved trailhead. To access the campground travel north on FR 2200 approximately 5 miles. To access the southernmost trailhead travel north on FR 2200 approximately 3 miles to FR 2224, the trailhead is on the right on FR 2224.
Parking And Admission: Limited parking is available on the western perimeter trailhead, no admission or parking fees are required for this area. FR 2237 has multiple single car pull outs that may be utilized for day use.
Trails: There are very few established trails within the Sturgeon River Gorge Wilderness additionally these trails and remnants of logging roads may be difficult to find and follow due to an overgrown understory. Many hikers utilize the North Country National Scenic Trail which follows the northern and eastern boundaries for roughly 8 miles.
Hours And Camping: Sturgeon River Gorge Wilderness is open year-round with no entry fee required. Camping is allowed within the wilderness; however, no designated campsites are established, and no trace camping practices are required. Additionally, on the southeast perimeter of the wilderness there is a 9-site campground (Sturgeon River Campground). The campground is open from May 10th until October 31st and no reservations or fees are required.
Hunting: Hunting is allowed within Sturgeon River Gorge Wilderness. Individuals interested in hunting within Sylvania must follow all Michigan Department of Natural Resources hunting regulations (michigan.gov/dnr/-/media/Project/Websites/dnr/Documents/LED/digests/hunting_digest.pdf?rev=54c4fa4e30514aa8b2af49e36ad82ca6)
name: Sturgeon River Gorge Wilderness - Ottawa National Forest

Description: McCormick Wilderness encompasses approximately 16,850 acres. This large area encompasses diverse habitat locally known as the Peshekee highlands which is very hilly habitat with lakes, islands, rocky outcroppings marshes bogs and secluded old growth forest. Dominant tree species includes Eastern Hemlock, Red and White Pine, Aspen, Sugar Maple, Paper Birch and Basswood. Within the McCormick Wilderness is also the McCormick Research Natural Area (RNA) which is an experimental forest that allows research on the most unaltered area within the McCormick Wilderness. The area around and within the McCormick Wilderness experienced heavy logging prior to the wilderness designation in 1987. Therefore, limited stands of “old-growth” are currently present.
Navigation:
Huron Rd (or Peshekee Grade), MI, 49861



From Marquette Mi., Take Big Bay Road to Triple A Road to Ford Road to the boundary of the wilderness. From Ishpeming take US41 west to MCR 607 and go north. From Michigamme or points west take M28 to US41 and then turn left on MCR 607.
Parking And Admission: Limited parking areas are located at each of the trailheads. Drinking water is not available anywhere in the wilderness so users must carry in water. No admission charge is required for parking or usage of the McCormick Wilderness.
Trails: Multiple networks of hiking trails are present within the McCormick Wilderness. The hiking is recommended for experienced hikers who are familiar with reading a map and compass. The topography often obscures GPS signal and phone service is not found in most of the wilderness. Limited traffic on trails also makes staying on trail difficult in certain sections.
Hours And Camping: McCormick Wilderness is open year-round with no reservations necessary. Camping is allowed within the wilderness and must follow standard leave no trace procedures. Fires are permitted however, camping stoves are recommended for remote area camping. The goal of this area is to leave it as close to a natural state as possible.
Hunting: Hunting is allowed within the McCormick Wilderness. Individuals interested in hunting must follow all Michigan Department of Natural Resources hunting regulations (michigan.gov/dnr/-/media/Project/Websites/dnr/Documents/LED/digests/hunting_digest.pdf?rev=54c4fa4e30514aa8b2af49e36ad82ca6)
name: McCormick Wilderness - Ottawa National Forest

Description:
Shorakapok Preserve lies in the center of New York City’s 196-acre Inwood Hill Park, situated at the northernmost tip of Manhattan. Shorakapok Preserve is the only remaining natural forest on the island. The majority of the preserve is a thick deciduous, secondary forest, containing mature red oak and some of the largest tulip trees in the City. The forest is also home to some unique and impressive geological features such as glacial potholes and caves which were used by the Lenape (Delawares) Native American tribe as shelter from prehistoric times through the seventeenth century.
Within the preserve, there is a rich, moist valley between two rock ridges called The Clove. During the early spring, the valley is covered in wildflowers, which are able to thrive before the thick canopy is filled. Some of these wildflowers include downy yellow violet, bloodroot and Dutchman’s breeches. The forest is also home to over 150 species of birds, including hairy woodpeckers and black-capped chickadees.
Navigation:
By Subway: Take the 1/9 train to 215th street and walk north to 218th. Take a left on 218th to the end, and you will reach the park.

Or take the A train to 207th street and turn west onto Seaman Ave and walk north into the park.

By Bus: Take Bx7, Bx12, Bx20, M100 to 207th street.

By Car: From Westside Highway, take the Dyckman St exit. Follow the exit as it merges with Broadway. Drive north on Broadway to 218th street. The entrance to the Park is on the end of the street.

From FDR/East River Drive, go north to the end. The end of the highway is at Dyckman St. Bear left on Dyckman St. Take Dyckman west to Broadway and take a right on Broadway. Proceed north to 218th St and make a left turn and park at the end of the street.
Parking And Admission: Public transit is recommended, but limited street parking is available. There is no admission charge for Inwood Hill Park.
Trails: The Inwood Hill Park orange trail was designated a National Recreation Trail in 2022. It is 1.3 miles long. There are a total of 4.2 miles of trails within the park.
Hours And Camping: Open year round, dawn to dusk. No camping.
name: Forever Wild Forests of New York City: Shorakapok Preserve - Inwood Hill Park

Description:
The parki has approximately 430 acres of forest in various stages of growth. The older growth trees grow closer to the shoreline and along the Duck Run ravine area. This property was most likely logged around the turn of the century.

There is a notable mature forest with very large trees. The tree canopy is species rich, with some very large oaks and a sugar maple on the edge of the Duck Run Ravine. Tree species included red maple, sugar maple, black cherry, Eastern hemlock, northern red oak, black oak, American hop-hornbeam, tulip poplar, sassafras, pignut hickory, bitternut hickory, black locust, and basswood. Pumpkin ash is a rare tree species found in the park.An enormous sassafras was noted in this area. Several plant species of conservation concern include a black oak woodland/savannah, Great Lakes region sand barren ecosystems, forested wetlands.

Erie Bluffs lies along the Lake Erie shoreline in western Erie County, twelve miles west of the city of Erie. The park has a mile of shoreline, 90-foot bluffs overlooking Lake Erie.
Navigation: Main Parking Lot, 11122 West Lake Road, Lake City, PA 16423.
Parking And Admission: Parking located at the Elk Creek Access and Erie Bluffs State Park main parking lot. There is no charge. Parking area is ample for the demand. To visit the Timber and West Overlook Trail, park in the main parking lot outside the gates and hike in. There are no facilities at this entrance but there are restrooms at 10990 West Lake Road.
Trails: Duck Run
Hours And Camping: No camping. The park is open year round.
Hunting: The park is open to hunting during the designated seasons set by the PA Game Commission.
name: Erie Bluffs State Park

Description:
Mettler's Woods is one of three patches of virgin woods remaining in New Jersey, and one of the last uncut, unburned oak-hickory forests in the country. The 65-acre forest is a National Natural Landmark and lies within the larger 500-acre William L. Hutcheson Memorial Forest Center, which is managed by Rutgers University, Department of Ecology, Evolution and Natural Resources.

The forest, predominantly oak and hickory with red maple and American beech, is managed as a living laboratory, with experiments on forest renewal, forest succession, and similar research topics. The old-growth forest has stood for hundreds of years, serving as sanctuary for biodiversity in our rapidly urbanizing landscape.
Navigation: 2150 Amwell Road (Route 514), Franklin Township, NJ
Parking And Admission: Visits are by appointment only, however there are regularly scheduled tours on weekends (please refer to website). Parking is limited and is located at 2150 Amwell Road, Somerset, NJ 08873. There is no admission charge.
Trails: The old growth trail is approximately 1 mi / 1.6 km. The mowed path around the old fields is approximately 0.6 mi / 0.9 km.
Hours And Camping: By appointment only through Rutgers; there are regular weekend tours scheduled.
name: Mettler's Woods - Hutcheson Memorial Forest Center

Description:
This is a 120-year old second growth forest with stands of Dry Oak – Heath Forest, Red Oak – Mixed Hardwood Forest, Northern Hardwood Forest, Aspen/Grey (Paper) Birch Forest, Hemlock (White Pine) Forest, and Red Maple Forests. Less than 200-acres of the Wild Area received silvicultural treatments in 1980’s and early 2000’s before its official designation as a Wild Area. 

Square Timber is named because the first timber was hewn into square timbers. Hewing logs was a learned and sought-after trade. The area is famous for a log loading record on January 30, 1905 when 51 cars (average is 22 cars loaded per day) were loaded with 711 logs totaling 170,000 board feet in six-hours, fifty-nine minutes. Just six months later, the mill was dissembled and moved to a new location
Navigation:
State Route 120 is the highway paralleling the Wild Area; with Stillhouse Road as the northern boundary; Ridge Road as the eastern boundary; and Grove Hill Road (rough road) as the southern boundary.



No physical street address exists for the Square Timber Wild Area.



The ridge tops off Ridge Road provide the best access overview of this steep, rugged, and unforgiving area.



Intersection of Stillhouse Road and Ridge Road…41.445, -78.115

Intersection of Brooks Run Road and Ridge Road…41.42, -78.112

Intersection of Grove Hill Road (rough road) and Ridge Road…41.391, -78.122
Parking And Admission: No admission fee; each trailhead can accommodate two to three cars.
Hours And Camping: Overnight camping is limited to primitive backpack type along one of the four (4) hiking trails.
Hunting: Hunting with permits is allowed during designated hunting seasons only.
name: Square Timber Wild Area

Description:
This state nature preserve, located on the Sandusky State Scenic River, was acquired as a Scenic River area. In addition to the large wooded riverine corridor with an excellent floodplain community containing large oaks, sycamore, ash, tulip and cottonwoods, the area also has an impressive amount of relief.

This woods contain numerous large American beech trees as well as a diversity of spring wildflowers including sharp-lobed hepatica, Dutchman's-breeches, squirrel-corn, three trillium species, trout-lily and marsh marigold. The display of marsh marigolds and skunk cabbage found in the floodplain in early May. 

The site is named in honor of former state budget director, Howard Collier.
Navigation: 1655 W Township Road 38. Tiffin, OH 44883
Parking And Admission: Free admission. Parking is free.
Trails: Earthen and boardwalk trails. The trail follows the ridgetop and then drops dramatically over the hillside to the Sandusky River floodplain.
Hours And Camping: Dawn to dusk. No camping.
name: Howard Collier State Nature Preserve

Description:
The forest at Mill Run is a mixed mesophytic and bottomland forest that features sugar maple, red, white, and scarlet oaks, American beech, shagbark hickory, black cherry and yellow birch Eastern hemlock dominate the stream valley.

Maturing mixed mesophytic forest dominates the steeper southwestern corner of the unit. Maturing bottomland woods occur along the stream valley where the Eastern hemlocks do not grow. 

In the spring, wildflowers, which prefer the acidic environment of the hemlock forest floor (trillium, hepaticas, geranium, jack-in-the-pulpit, lady's slippers and other orchids) are abundant. Various species of club moss are also present.
Navigation: 79 Mill Run Rd, Friendsville, MD 21531
Parking And Admission: Limited parking spaces at end of road.
Trails: There are no trails at this time.
Hours And Camping: Campground is open May 1 - Sept 7. 30 sites, non-electric.
name: Mill Run Natural Area

Description:
Klondike Ridge Natural Area features a mixed mesophytic forest type. The deciduous forest is unusual due to its diverse habitat. Portions of this area were not timbered, likely due to the steepness of the slope. Sections of mature woods are preserved, while other areas have remained relatively undisturbed over the past decades and are maturing.

Within the mixed mesophytic woodlands, white, black, and Northern red oaks are dominant. American beech is abundant on the north-facing slopes. Chestnut oak, scarlet oak, and pignut hickory are abundant near the ridge top. 

Other species include white ash, shagbark hickory, black cherry, sugar maple, tulip poplar, flowering dogwood, and common spicebush. Most of the larger trees are oaks, American beech, and sugar maple.
Navigation: 497 Flanigan Rd, Confluence, PA 15424
Parking And Admission: Parking lot next to natural area and is free of charge.
Trails: There are no trails at this time.
Hours And Camping: Camping April - October; many sites, some with electric available.
name: Klondike Ridge Natural Area

Description: This 191- acre nature preserve is located within the central portion of Bald Head Island and is bounded by the Cape Fear River and the Atlantic Ocean. The forest is dominated by live oak and laurel oak, with a thick understory consisting of American holly, yaupon, wild olive, and cat briar. Cabbage palmetto also appears throughout the forest. The Timmons Oak, a beloved live oak in the forest, is believed to be over 300 years old.
Navigation: Bald Head Island may be accessed by private ferry from Deep Point Marina in Southport or private boat. Cars are not allowed on the island, but bicycles and golf carts may be rented, and maps are available to direct visitors to Bald Head Woods. Trail heads to access the site are located along Federal Road, Bald Head Island, NC 28461.
Parking And Admission: Cars are not permitted on Bald Head Island, but bicycles & golf carts can be rented. Parking to access trail heads is accommodated at each trail head marked by a wooden parking platform that can fit a max of 2 golf carts.
Trails:
Loop trail: 0.41 miles

Middle trail: 0.63 miles

East trail: 0.54 miles

Creek trail: 0.67 miles



Loop, Middle, and East can be completed as a hike through on the south side of Federal Road. The Creek trail is standalone on the north side of Federal Road. Combined the trail system is 2.25 miles.
Hours And Camping: Bald Head Woods is open year-round. Camping is not permitted on Bald Head Island.
Hunting: Hunting is not permitted on Bald Head Island.
name: Bald Head Woods Coastal Preserve

Description:
Spring Hammock Preserve covers about 1500 acres and shelters hydric hammocks, floodplain forests, pine flatwoods, and upland mixed hardwoods. Various hiking and biking trails offer encounters with old-growth oaks, cypress, sweetgums, and magnolias. This preserve protects some of the oldest and most impressive cypress trees still standing in Florida. 

Big Tree Park has a wooden walkway that guides you through the flooded hammock and ends up at a tree known as the Senator. The Senator was an impressive old growth Bald Cypress that was utilized as a landmark by Native Americans and early settlers. It is very unfortunate but January of 2012 this tree was killed due to an arsonist, but the remains are still present and admirable.
Navigation:
2985 Osprey Trail
Longwood, FL 32750

Directions to trails available on-site.
Parking And Admission: No admission fee, there is parking at main address in navigation section.
Trails: There are 3.5 miles of trail. Recommended trail is the 2 mile out-and back Osprey Trail (unpaved). There is also the 2.5 miles of paved Cross Seminole Trail that goes through Spring Hammock. Check the website for trail conditions, as this area is a floodplain and hydric forest and may have occasional inundated areas.
Hours And Camping:
Open year-round, sunrise to sunset. 



No camping allowed on site, though camping areas are available in the vicinity.
Hunting: Hunting is not allowed on the Preserve.
name: Spring Hammock Preserve

Description:
At Gunpowder Falls/Walker Run confluence grow large, old Eastern hemlocks with similar, large circumferences and heights, and older yellow birches that lack large circumferences but have great height. Small to medium examples of the same species grow along the waterways and on the hillsides. 

The old-growth area is approximately six acres and runs along the Gunpowder Falls from 250 feet west of Walker Run to 650 feet east of Walker Run to 300 feet north of the Gunpowder Falls. The older growth area becomes narrow towards the east and there is a clear demarcation where a previous cutting of the forest occurred. All the trees north of the cut are uniform in size. The trees of varying sizes nearer to the Gunpowder Falls, and particularly the largest trees, were spared. 

Non-woody vegetation is a mix of native and non-native wildflowers: vinca groundcover, along with bulbous buttercup, Dame’s rocket, day lilies, and other non-native species. At the same time, you also find stands of Canada mayflower, marsh violets, hooked buttercup, false Solomon’s seal, yellow avens, mayapple, and other desirable natives. 

Prettyboy Reservoir CWMA hunting access is managed by the Wildlife and Heritage Service. The Wildlife and Heritage Service conserves and enhances diverse wildlife populations and associated habitats while providing for public enjoyment of the State’s wildlife resources through hunting and other wildlife-dependent recreation. 

Prettyboy Reservoir CWMA provides habitat for upland and forest wildlife species, primarily white-tailed deer, wild turkeys, rabbits, squirrels, and songbirds.
Navigation: 20598 Gunpower Road, Freedland, MD
Parking And Admission: Prettyboy Reservoir is located primarily in northwestern Baltimore County with a small portion extending into northeastern Carroll County. Numerous public roads provide access points to this area.
name: Prettyboy Reservoir Co-op WMA-Hemlock Gorge

Description:
Straddling both the Pere Marquette and White River watersheds, Richmond Woods Nature Preserve protects a pristine sphagnum bog and a high-quality sedge meadow wetland. Those wetlands protect water quality and are also home to the American Bittern, a bird in the heron family that is classified as special concern in Michigan. Red-headed woodpecker and red-shouldered hawk, two other special concern birds, inhabit the preserve’s forests. Adjacent to U.S. Forest Service land, Richmond Woods Nature Preserve helps protect a large expanse of Michigan’s iconic forest and wetland habitats. 

The Land Conservancy of West Michigan is using prescribed fire and planting to restore oak savanna and open oak forest conditions on the preserve.

Forested parts of the preserve include an 85 acre dry-mesic northern forest of red oak, black oak and white oak, white pine and red maple, and a 13 acre hardwood conifer swamp dominated by white pine with yellow birch and red maple as minor components.
Navigation:
Approximate Street Address: 8000 N. Centerline Road, Bitely, MI 49309





The trailhead is located adjacent to the parking area.
Parking And Admission: A signed small gravel parking lot is available. There is no admission charge.
Trails: The preserve includes two loop trails, one on the east side of Center Line road and one on the west side. The total trail distance is 1.4 miles. The trails are natural surfaces which may impact accessibility.
Hours And Camping: The preserve is open dawn until dusk. Camping is not permitted on the preserve. US Forest Service campgrounds are located in the vicinity.
Hunting: Hunting is limited to archery only through the Hunter Access Program. See website for more details.
name: Richmond Woods Nature Preserve

Description:
Most of the forest can be classified as mixed-mesophytic, regardless of age. The younger stands in the north are dominated by yellow poplar and red maple, and the older stands in the center and south have much more canopy species diversity. This forest type is the most geographically extensive forest community and is best characterized as ‘mature’ second-growth mixed-mesophytic forest. In these older sections of the forest, various species of oak, maple, hickory, and beech dominate. 

While the property is mostly second and some third-growth forest, it has an area of older forest that is increasingly comparable to old-growth, particularly along the eastern portion of the property
Parking And Admission: Parking for three to four vehicles is available along S. Ruffner/ Hampton Rd. while two vehicles are able to park at the end of Adrian Rd. There is no admission fee.
Trails: 4 miles of trails exist on the preserve: ‘Fern Dolly Trail,’ ‘Big Beech Trail,’ ‘Eagle Scout Trail,’ and ‘Ferrell Family Trail.’ There is a historic cemetery from 1900 at the end of the ‘Ferrell’ trail while ‘Big Beech,’ along the property’s eastern boundary, contains some of the preserve’s largest trees. There are also two picnic tables, a metal bench, and two pedestrian bridges
Hours And Camping: The preserve is open during daylight hours. No camping is available
name: Wallace Hartman Nature Preserve

Description: The preserve of 124 acres encompasses nearly 30 acres of outstanding cove hardwood and oak-hickory forests. While likely not virgin forest, they have high natural value, with no signs of recent disturbances. Many of the large American beech and white oaks in the cove are over 13 feet in circumference. A few trees exceed 56 inches in diameter. An 80-acre buffer zone of second growth forest and ridgetop meadows secures this primeval forest. There are over 80 species of spring flowering plants and many neotropical migrant birds.
Parking And Admission:
Turn east at end of exit ramp, towards Clendenin. At the Park & Ride parking lot immediately East of the interstate interchange turn, left onto Rt. 119 north.

Follow Rt. 119 North for 8 miles, reaching top of hill. Turn left onto Ambler Ridge Road, at old Huffman Country Store. Travel 3.4 miles onto paved Ambler Ridge Road, reaching local mailbox address of 1702 Ambler Ridge Road on the right.

Turn left onto gravel Paxton Ridge Road, at a blue house which is located at the intersection across from 1702 Ambler Ridge Road.

Follow Paxton Ridge Road for 3.1 miles to preserve on the right.

Trailhead into preserve is marked by old locked pipe gate with TNC preserve signs on trees. Park along edge of state road.

Follow old road in to first large field and watch for trailhead sign at woods’ edge on your left. Trail is sparsely marked, but woods are welcoming for an exploratory walk.
Hours And Camping: Dawn to dusk daily.
name: Hungry Beech Preserve

Description:
The LaRue County Environmental Education and Research Center is a total of 200 acres and is the former Pearman Family property. The property can be broken into six habitat types including a mature old-growth forest. It is best known for its old growth wooded area that contains trees well over 150 years of age. The dominant wooded section is broken into two conjoined sections designated as the 30-acre Woods #1 and the 50-acre Woods #2.

In Woods #1, 19 tree species are present with white oak being the predominant species. In Woods #2, 14 species were noted, with the dominant species as white oak.
Navigation:
LaRue County Environmental Education and Research Center

State highway 1794 (635 Leafdale Road)

Hodgenville, KY 42748
Parking And Admission: Parking for 10 cars on a gravel lot. Free admission for nature lovers.
name: Pearman Forest Preserve

Description: Stout Woods is a 35.2 acre property that is entirely old growth. There is no evidence that it was ever logged for timber or grazed. As such, Stout is of exceptional quality. The property is a botanically diverse mesic woodland with an overstory largely composed of sizable oaks (white and northern red). Large hickories, sugar maples, and American beeches are seen in abundance as well. The trees have not been officially dated, but the largest trees in Stout Woods are likely to be around 200 years old. The most recent tree inventory data we have is from 1985, and the largest tree that data mentions is a 34.3 DBH white oak. Given white oak’s growth rate of 5, and accounting for the 40 years since that measurement was taken, that tree is likely to be approximately 211 years old.
Navigation:
3499-3325 N County Rd 300 W, New Castle, IN 47362.

After parking in the gravel lot, follow the tree line and walk east down the grassy lane to access the trailhead.
Parking And Admission: A small gravel parking area is located off of North County Road 300 West. The parking area fits 3-4 cars maximum. No admission is charged for parking or preserve entry.
Trails: The hiking trail in the woods is approximately half a mile of varied terrain. Predominantly a footpath, there are some boardwalks and foot bridges located over wet areas. The grassy lane that leads from the parking area to the wood’s entry is roughly a quarter of a mile walk. In total, the trail is about three quarters of a mile long.
Hours And Camping: Stout Memorial Woodland is open year round from dawn until dusk. No camping is permitted.
name: Stout Memorial Woodland

Description: In the southwest portion of the park, a 27-acre state dedicated nature preserve protects a beech-maple climax woodland showcasing a spectacular spring ephemeral display of large-flowered trillium. The preserve was the first non-state owned public land to be dedicated by the Indiana Department of Natural Resources.
Navigation: Park’s main entrance: 56960 Timothy Road, New Carlisle, IN. After entering the park and passing the gatehouse, continue along the road until you come to the first intersection. Turn right. Continue along the road to the Hardwoods Picnic Area. Turn right into the parking lot. Cross the road to get to the Runnels Shelter. The trail head is behind the shelter.
Parking And Admission: Gate fees are collected on weekends at certain times of year. Please check the park website for current information: www.sjcparks.org.
Trails: The best trails for viewing the nature preserve are the Big Tree Trail (0.49 miles), the Lower Big Tree Trail (0.35 miles) and the Hardwoods Loop (0.3 miles.) A trail map is available on the park website: www.sjcparks.org.
Hours And Camping: Park hours vary according to time of year. Please check the park website for current information: www.sjcparks.org. Camping is not permitted in the St. Joseph County Parks.
Hunting: Controlled deer hunts are conducted annually to manage deer populations and protect the plant community. The entire park is closed to the public during these activities.
name: Bendix Woods Nature Preserve

Description:
On the west rim of Pine Creek Gorge, also known as the Pennsylvania Grand Canyon, the 368-acre Colton Point State Park resonates with the rustic charm of the Civilian Conservation Corps era of the 1930s.

The rugged overlooks offer great views of the canyon. Leonard Harrison State Park is visible on the other side of the canyon.

The park area was logged by Henry Colton from 1879-1880. As with some other logging operations of the time, some trees were not harvested.

Several acres of old growth hemlock and white pine exist between overlook areas, picnicking areas and hiking trails. This area also demonstrates a relatively healthy native plant community with mountain laurel and other woody and herbaceous species. Scattered old growth can be observed throughout the entire Pennsylvania Grand Canyon area, many in areas that are difficult to access.
Navigation: 927 Colton Road, Wellsboro, PA
Trails: Turkey Trail: A difficult down and back trail descends 1.5 miles to the floor of the canyon. The highlight is a 70-foot cascading waterfall less than 0.5 mile down. The lowest parts of the trail run along a series of waterfalls.There is no bridge across Pine Creek at the bottom.
Hours And Camping: Park is open from dawn to dusk daily. Day uses close at dusk. The campground is open from the beginning of May until the third Sunday in October. Campsites at Colton Point are not reservable but are available first-come, first-served. Non-flush toilets, water, picnic tables, and fire rings are provided. There is no sanitary dump station
Hunting: 100 acres available for hunting with permits only.
name: Colton Point State Park

Description:
The Bark Cabin Natural Area encompasses 82 acres in the eastern section of the Tiadaghton State Forest, enclosed by state forest, private land, and a natural gas right-of-way. The Bark Cabin Natural Area was established to protect a small grove of old growth hemlocks, mostly found within a 7-acre area within the Natural Area.

The predominant forest composition has a coniferous component; hemlock (white pine) forest, dry hemlock (white pine)-oak forest, hemlock (white pine) northern hardwood forest, and hemlock (white pine) -red oak mixed hardwood forest account for 20 of the 32 completed plots. 

Bark Cabin’s shape is generally three-sided with rolling terrain and an increasingly deeper drainage from its south to east boundary. The west side is bordered by private land. Between the private land border and the Mid-State Trail resides the small tract of old growth hemlocks. 

To the north is a neighboring right-of-way clearing for natural gas line that also acts as a boundary. The central part of the natural area is large hardwood timber with a scattered hemlock/white pine understory.

The age of the stand is approximately 150 years old, with some hemlock trees approximately 210 years of age.
Navigation: Hacketts Road, Waterville, PA 17776
Parking And Admission: A small parking turnout near the trailhead that's large enough to fit one vehicle. The road is also a narrow road with no additional parking turnouts.
Trails: The distance from the parking area on Hacketts Road to the Bark Cabin Natural Area old growth is 0.85 miles. Proceed north on the Mid State Trail (orange blazes) for 0.85 miles. The walk would be categorized as moderate and will take most people approximately 20 minutes to reach the old growth.
Hours And Camping: No camping. Open dawn to dusk.
name: Bark Cabin Natural Area - Tiadaghton State Forest

Description:
This 412-acre preserve is dedicated in memory of Juliette Hoiles DeStaebler (1903-1950), a former owner of the property. It consists of a mile long, steep-sided bluff situated in a bend of the White River. The principal natural features of the property include cliffs and rockshelters of Mansfield sandstone running the length of the bluff, and mesic and dry-mesic forest communities. Mesic upland forest areas are dominated by sugar maple, American beech, tulip poplar, and basswood, while dry-mesic forest areas are dominated by scarlet oak, white oak, post oak, black oak, chestnut oak, and pignut hickory. The various habitats support a diversity of plant species, in particular a wide variety of ferns. Additionally this stretch of the White River is considered significant for its healthy mussel populations and several rare fish species. Bald Eagles frequent this stretch of river and are common visitors to the property.

William Barnes, the first director of the Division of Nature Preserves, wrote in a 1969 article in Outdoor Indiana that “The scenic quality of this unique area must not be overlooked. One may stand on several promontories about 100 feet above the river. The view of the bend to the east is spectacular with churches and buildings in Shoals standing out in relief against the backdrop of distant hills. The view to the north reveals the tree-bordered river adjoining farmed bottomland with high hills beyond.”

The nature preserve was acquired through the assistance of the Indiana Chapter of The Nature Conservancy and the Indiana Heritage Trust.
Navigation:
Spout Springs Rd. Shoals, IN 47581



US 50/150 runs through Shoals. Take US 50 into town. Immediately past the White River Bridge on the southeast corner, turn left (south) onto Water Street (C.R. 63). Continue south to Spout Springs Road (this is the first right you can take) and turn right. Travel to the parking lot on the left side of the road.
Parking And Admission: There is no parking fee. Parking space is limited.
Trails: The gravel road that runs north from the gate provides an easy 3-mile round trip hike with views of both the river and sandstone bluffs. A moderately rugged 2.5-mile loop trail also runs through the preserve.
Hours And Camping: Open dawn to dusk, no camping.
Hunting: Special deer management hunts may apply.
name: Bluffs of Beaver Bend Nature Preserve

Description:
Bristol Woods Park is the most natural of all the Kenosha County Parks. This 200-acre park boasts over 4 miles of hiking trails through mature oak-hickory woodlands, vernal pools, and evidence of a glacial past and more recent agricultural past with overgrown apple orchards. Trees found in the park include mature red oak, white oak and burr oak, as well quaking aspens, black cherry, shagbark hickory, and sugar maples. 

Visitors can also stop by the Pringle Nature Center which is a regional resource where people of all ages can experience nature, environmental education, conservation and stewardship and in doing so, be inspired to become responsible stewards of the environment or visit the aerial adventure park in the northwest part of the park.
Navigation:
9800 160th Avenue, Bristol, WI 53104



The red trail is located just off the main parking lot just north of the Pringle Nature Center.
Parking And Admission: Ample parking is available near the Pringle Nature Center and trailhead, including ADA accessible parking. Cell service is generally available. There is no fee for admission.
Trails: The red trail is a 1.86 miles long loop. A self guided interpretive trail can be downloaded ahead of the visit or can be accessed via QR code on the trail. The park contains a total of 4.28 miles of trail. https://www.pringlenc.org/selfguided
Hours And Camping: The park is open daily from 7am-10pm. No camping is available.
name: Bristol Woods County Park

Description:
The Dolan Nature Sanctuary is 127 acres in size and is largely comprised of wetlands, floodplain forest, mixed hardwoods, and abandoned agricultural fields, which have undergone restoration efforts toward an oak savanna. The property has frontage on two designated trout streams, the Coldwater River and Tyler Creek with the oldest forest located within the floodplain. The floodplain forest contains a series of oxbow ponds and wetland pools amongst the mature trees and is known for a population of Virginia bluebells which provide a striking blooming display in the spring. The forested corridor along the Coldwater River provides excellent habitat for neo-tropical migrants, forest birds, amphibians, and reptiles. The oak
barrens restoration consists of close to 30 acres and provides habitat for grassland bird species.
Navigation: 10350 Baker Ave SE, Alto, MI 49302
Parking And Admission: Free admission. There is a small dirt parking lot no west side of Baker Ave.
Trails: There are trails on the property. The best place to access the trails is from the parking area. A portion of the North Country Trail is present on the property and runs from Baker Ave. on the west boundary to Taylor Creek near the eastern boundary and which follows the north bank of the Coldwater River. There is also a trail loop which runs through additional portions of the property which joins the North County Trail along the Coldwater River frontage.
name: Dolan Nature Sanctuary

Description: Owned and protected by the Finger Lakes Land Trust (FLLT), the Wesley Hill Nature Preserve comprises 435 acres (six tracts acquired by FLLT between 1999 and 2024), including the immense Briggs Gully, some of which forms the southern boundary, and several other gullies that wind through the preserve. Diverse stands of mature forest, including about 10 acres thought to be original old-growth forest, and another 200-220 acres of late-successional forest, host a wide array of native plants and wildlife. Sweeping views of the hills surrounding Honeoye Lake’s southern end, and 5.6 miles of hiking trails, make this site truly special for visitors. There are particularly large red and white oak, eastern hemlock, and eastern white pine trees on this Preserve.
Navigation:
Public Parking Area is located at 6280 Gulick Road, Naples, NY

From Honeoye, take Rt. 20A east to East Lake Road. Follow East Lake Rd. south for a short distance and then turn left on County Rd. 33. Continue a short distance and turn right on Pinewood Hill Rd. Follow Pinewood Hill, then Gulick Road south toward Cumming Nature Center, for a total of 6.4 miles to preserve entrance, on right.

PLEASE NOTE: The Finger Lakes Land Trust owns only a PORTION of Briggs Gully. Please respect private property by staying on trails within the preserve boundaries.
Parking And Admission: There is a small parking area at the trailhead on Gulick Road. There is a 2nd public access point just west of the snow-plow turn-around on Wesley Road. Admission is free.
Trails:
Recommended Trail: Red Trail loop (2.7 miles), through mature forest, including beautiful stands of eastern hemlocks, traversing gorges typical of the Finger Lakes region, and passing by the old Wenrich cabin and a small, pretty pond in a meadow.

Total Trails: 5.6 miles
Hours And Camping: Open hours are dawn to dusk. Camping is prohibited.
Hunting: Hunting is prohibited on the red, orange, and green trails. Bow hunting is allowed only in designated areas around the blue and yellow trails and only during hunting season. For complete information and to create an account and apply for permits, go to: https://fllt.huntmanagement.net/home
name: Wesley Hill Nature Preserve

Description: Approx 40 acres of mixed second growth. Includes: Ash, Aspen, Bass Wood, Beech, Birch, Cedar, Black Cherry, Dogwood, Elm, Hemlock, Iron Wood, Maple, Nine Bark, Oak, Pine. The property has thousands of feet of Bear Creek frontage.
Navigation:
12555 Coates Highway Bretrhen, MI 49619

US-31 North, East on Coates Highway to Driveway (Spirit of the Woods Road)
Parking And Admission: Ample parking is available.
Hours And Camping: Property is open to all public dawn to dusk, 365 days a year.
name: Spirit of the Woods

Description: Protected in 2003, Arcadia Dunes is Grand-Traverse Regional Land Conservancy’s largest nature preserve, at 3927 acres, and includes 20 miles of trail that winds through dunes, forests and many other landscapes. Adjacent working farms have also been permanently protected, ensuring the longevity of this area’s rich agricultural heritage. The property’s incredibly diverse matrix of secondary hardwood forest, coastal dunes, and open fields provides a wide range of wildlife habitat. It also offers thoughtfully designed recreation opportunities and experiences, from hiking and birding to mountain biking and hunting.
Navigation:
Arcadia Dunes: The C.S. Mott Nature Preserve

Gilbert Road, Arcadia, MI 49613
Parking And Admission: No admission fee.
Trails: A total of 15 miles of trail is available.
Hours And Camping: The preserve is open dawn until dusk, year round. No camping is permitted. Public and private campgrounds are located nearby.
Hunting: Hunting is permitted in certain zones of the property per State of Michigan rules and regulations and GTRLC’s hunting rules and zone map found on the preserve’s website.
name: Arcadia Dunes: The C.S. Mott Nature Preserve

Description: Bole Woods is a National Natural Landmark and a highly mature beech-red maple forest in beautiful condition. A trail of 1.2 miles runs through the oldest areas.There is a significant amount of fallen woody debris, magnificent height red maples, as well as chestnut oaks, American beech and western red cedar.
Navigation: 9550 Sperry Road, Kirtland Ohio, 44094
Parking And Admission: Admission is $20. Plenty of free parking. Memberships available to provide unlimited admissions.
Trails:
To access the trail to Bole Woods, a visitor must walk down the visitor center driveway and across Sperry Road to the trailhead. Maps are available. 

On the trail, there is some minor terrain change, but generally easy to naviagate.
Hours And Camping:
Tuesday-Sunday: 9 am - 5 pm

Monday: Closed to the public; member-only access is provided using the member gate.

Members have dawn-to-dusk access to the Holden Arboretum.
name: Bole Woods at Holden Arboretum

Description:
Stebbins Gulch is the crown jewel of the Holden Arboretum's extensive natural areas and one of the most unspoiled natural preserves in Northeast Ohio. It is a deep ravine environment with its microclimate and multiple forest zones. It displays one of Northeast Ohio's most complete sequences of exposed rocks, spanning 30 million years of marine sedimentation and five named geologic units.

Stebbins Gulch encompasses a total of 825 acres, of which 222 acres is old-growth forest. Chestnut oaks here exceed 400 years old and beech trees are older than 250 years old. These natural areas are primarily beech-maple forests.
Navigation: 9550 Sperry Road, Kirktland, OH
Parking And Admission: By appointment or arranged group tour only by registration.
name: Stebbins Gulch at Holden Arboretum

Description: Alley Pond Park Preserve is host to freshwater and saltwater wetlands, tidal flats, meadows, and forests, creating a diverse ecosystem and supporting abundant bird life. Numerous trails wind through native hardwood (oak-hickory) forest and glacial-formed kettle ponds. The north end of the park boasts splendid salt marsh views. And don’t miss the Alley Pond Giant! With a height of 133.8 feet and a circumference of 18.6 feet, this tulip tree may be the tallest and the oldest living organism in the city. It is estimated to be between 350 and 450 years of age.
Navigation:
By Bus: Take the Q27 or Q88 bus lines to the stop at the intersection of Springfield Blvd and 75th Ave. Enter the Park at 75th Ave and continue eastward on the paved paths, past the playground and public restrooms into the forest.

By Car: Take the Long Island Expressway or Grand Central Parkway to the exit for Springfield Blvd, then navigate to the NYC Parks parking lot on 76th Ave.
Parking And Admission: Free admission and free parking at NYC Parks parking lot on 76 th Ave.
Trails:
Alley Pond Tulip Tree Trail:

This 1 mile trail runs along the western wide of the Park and ends at the famous tree, the Alley Pond Giant. With a height of 133.8 feet and a circumference of 18.6 feet, this tulip tree may be the tallest and the oldest living organism in the city. It is estimated to be between 350 and 450 years of age. It was a sapling in the 17th century, when the Dutch West India Company sent a group of Walloon families to Manhattan. It was a well-established young tree when General George Washington passed close by in 1790 on a tour of Long Island.



Total distance of all trails: 18.75 miles of Official Trail

For more trail information, please visit https://www.nycgovparks.org/park-features/hiking/alley-pond-park
Hours And Camping:
Open year-round, 6:00 a.m. - 10:00 p.m

Camping not permitted.
name: Forever Wild Forests of New York City: Alley Pond Park Preserve

Description:
This site's ridges, slopes, cliffs and valleys support one of the largest blocks of essentially undisturbed old-growth northern hardwood forest in Minnesota.

At the heart of the SNA is the 240-acre Scherer Conservation Unit, donated to the state for this purpose by local landowner Lloyd Scherer and his family. Scherer had purchased the land in three parcels in the late 1960s and 70s, understanding the value and rarity of its undisturbed forest. In the following years he spent countless hours walking the site in all seasons, becoming intimately familiar with the forest and the wildlife that inhabited it: wolves, pine marten, deer, red fox. He was determined that it would not be lost to logging or development.

The Scherer family gift spurred protection of additional land at the site. Soon after its designation, the SNA tripled in size when acreage to the east and south was acquired with the help of the Trust for Public Land.

This is a rugged landscape, with parts of two ridges of the Sawtooth Mountain Range. Eagle Mountain and Raven Ridge rise over a thousand feet above Lake Superior, about two miles to the southeast. The Minnesota Biological Survey has documented ten native plant communities on the 720-acre SNA, including 276 acres of old-growth northern hardwood forest and upland white cedar forest. Individual trees as of 2025 include a 221-year-old white cedar, 143-year-old yellow birch and 131-year-old white spruce (based on cores taken in 1998).

As one can see on the detail map, upland areas of the SNA are dominated by sugar maple forest, aspen-birch forest (balsam fir subtype) and white cedar – yellow birch forest. North and northwest-facing slopes of both ridges host upland white cedar forest, while the steeper, rocky slopes of Eagle Mountain support scrub talus (rocky slope at base of a cliff) and mafic (igneous rock rich in iron and magnesium) cliff communities. Lower elevations are occupied by lowland white cedar forest, black spruce swamp and part of a large beaver complex that extends onto adjacent land.

For a real sense of this SNA (and of Lloyd Scherer), see the essay, Tales From Lutsen Woods from Paul Gruchow's book Worlds within a World: Reflections on Visits to Minnesota Scientific and Natural Area Preserves, © 1999, Minnesota Department of Natural Resources.
Navigation:
Directions (east side): From Lutsen, 1.4 miles north on County Highway 4 (Caribou Trail), then about 300 feet west on Homestead Road. Park on the northside road shoulder prior to where the road narrows. Take the snowmobile trail southwest into the site.



Directions (west side): From Lutsen, 1.5 miles southwest on MN Highway 61, then 0.75 mile north on County Highway 5 (Ski Hill Road). Park on eastside then take the ski trail east into the site.
Parking And Admission: See navigation details for parking information. There is no admission charge.
Trails: The SNA is crossed by the Lutsen Access snowmobile trail and a cross-country ski trail.
Hours And Camping: No camping is allowed within the Scientific and Natural Area. A variety of camping opportunities are available nearby within the adjacent Superior National Forest and nearby Minnesota State Parks. The SNA is open year-round.
Hunting: All hunting allowed (only deer hunting within Scherer Conservation Unit), see regulations for details. Non-toxic ammunition is required.
name: Lutsen Scientific & Natural Area

Description:
Established in 1979 to preserve an outstanding example of the North Shore Highlands Biocultural Region, the 9,346 acres of Tettegouche State Park contain a unique combination of natural features: rugged, semi-mountainous terrain, one mile of Lake Superior shoreline, six inland lakes, cascading rivers and waterfalls, and an undisturbed northern hardwood forest. Tettegouche offers a great sense of the North Shore: the spectacular overlooks at Shovel Point; rocky, steep cliffs and inland bluffs; the cascading 60 ft. High Falls of the Baptism River; and the historic Tettegouche Camp where visitors can stay the night. Tettegouche State Park is a hiker's paradise with miles of trails that overlook the Sawtooth Mountains and wind down to inland lakes accessible only by foot.

The park is also known for rock climbing opportunities and quality birdwatching in the spring, summer, and especially the fall.

The wide variety of plant communities in the park supports more than 40 species of mammals. Most commonly seen are white-tailed deer, snowshoe hare, red squirrel and beaver. Less commonly observed are moose, black bear, red fox, and river otter. Occasionally, coyote, fisher pine marten, northern flying squirrel, and even the timber wolf are seen.

Northeastern Minnesota is recognized as one of the better areas in the nation to find rare birds. Diversity of habitat, geography and proximity to Lake Superior combine to produce a variety of bird life at Tettegouche. In all, 140 species have been identified. Kinglets, spruce grouse, and many northern warblers nest in bogs and coniferous forests in the summer. In fall, hawk migration along the shore of Lake Superior numbers in the tens of thousands. Winter is an excellent time to see northern owls, woodpeckers, finches, and unusual water birds. The park is home to peregrine falcons.
Navigation:
This visitor center is located at:

5702 MN-61, 

Silver Bay, MN 55614



The trailhead is located at the end of the entrance drive on the west side of Highway 61 located just south of the visitor center.
Parking And Admission:
A $7 day pass is required per vehicle. A $35 annual pass is also available. Passes can be purchased at the Tettegouche State Park Visitor Center at 5702 MN-61, 

Silver Bay, MN 55614
Trails:
From the Trailhead Parking Lot hike to Raven Rock and back to experience a portion of the old-growth forest (3 mile loop, moderate difficulty). 



The park includes 23 miles of moderate to difficult trails. Snowshoeing, snowmobiling and cross-country ski trails are also available. The hikes feature the high cliffs along Lake Superior's shoreline, the Baptism River, three scenic waterfalls or the loops that wind around interior lakes.



About twelve miles of the Superior Hiking Trail (SHT) pass through the park. These trails will treat you to many spectacular views of Lake Superior, inland lakes and northern hardwood forests with remnant red and white pine.
Hours And Camping: The park is open daily from 8 a.m. until 10 p.m., year round. Several types of camping are available within the park including reservable drive-in sites, backpack sites, walk-in sites and rustic cabins.
Hunting: Hunting is prohibited in Minnesota state parks unless authorized by the Commissioner of the Department of Natural Resources.
name: Tettegouche State Park

Description:
Waterfalls cascade through a volcanic canyon surrounded by majestic forest in this North Country wilderness park. Park trails are steep and challenging, but reward hikers with spectacular views as they carve through a forest of fir, cedar, spruce and northern hardwoods.

This is a rugged, wilderness park where bears, wolves, moose and deer share the trails with hikers. The park is home to many species of birds and small animals, including snowshoe hare, red squirrels, Canada jays, sharp-shinned hawks and beaver. 

The 3,400-acre George H. Crosby Manitou State Park was the first park in the system to be designed primarily for backpackers, and it remains a backpack-only park today.
Navigation:
7616 Co Hwy 7, Finland, MN 55603

The park entrance drive is located off of Cramer Road. The Benson Lake Loop Trailhead is located at the end of the entrance drive.
Parking And Admission: A $7 day pass is required per vehicle. A $35 annual pass is also available. Passes can be purchased at the park kiosk or the Tettegouche State Park Visitor Center at 5702 MN-61, Silver Bay, MN 55614
Trails:
The Misquah Trail (Overlook) 1 mile one-way

From the parking lot, hike the Yellow Birch Trail to the Misquah Trail. Take that north about 0.2 miles, then go east to the spur trail for a spectacular view of Lake Superior and the Sawtooth Mountains. The trail contains steep terrain, bare dirt and rock. The trail passes through a portion of the old-growth forests within the Yellow Birch Natural Area, which is listed in the Natural Area Registry of the Minnesota Scientific and Natural Areas Program. The Registry is a way to recognize natural features of statewide ecological and geological significance on any public land in Minnesota.



The park contains a total of 24 miles of rugged backcountry trails with great wildlife viewing, old-growth forests and scenic waterfalls. About five miles of the Superior Hiking Trail run through the park.
Hours And Camping: The park is open daily from 8 a.m. until 10 p.m., year round. 20 backpack sites are available.
Hunting: Hunting is prohibited in Minnesota state parks unless authorized by the Commissioner of the Department of Natural Resources.
name: George H. Crosby Manitou State Park

Description:
The largest of the state parks at Lake Tahoe, Ed Z’berg Sugar Pine Point is 2,000 acres of mixed conifer, aspen and cedar forests set behind nearly two miles of lake frontage. 150 of this 2,000 acres is old-growth forest. The approximate age of the oldest trees here is 400-500 years old. 

The park lies within the traditional territory and ancestral homeland of the Waší·šiw (Wa she shu), recognized today as the Washoe Tribe of Nevada and California. The Washoe people have been the original stewards of this land since time immemorial. Lake Tahoe’s name is a mispronunciation of the Wá∙šiw name for lake, Dáʔaw’ (dah ow). 
The California Gold Rush and Nevada Silver Rush of the mid-1800s brought a flood of Euro-American settlers, drastically disrupting the Wá∙šiw People’s way of life and devastating the environment. Logging, mining, overfishing, unchecked development, and grazing stripped the land of its old-growth forests, native plants and animals, and vital habitats.

The logging era gave rise to elegant hotels and family resorts around the lake, including the Bellevue Hotel and Sunshine Post Office, here at Sugar Pine Point State Park.

In 1901 the Hellman-Ehrman family purchased the property and began building their summer home, Pine Lodge. Construction was completed in 1903 and for the next 62 years the family spent their summers recreating on the west shore of Lake Tahoe.
Navigation:
7360 CA-89, Tahoma, CA 96142



The park is located on the west shore of Lake Tahoe, ten miles south of Tahoe City on Highway 89
Parking And Admission:
Day Use facilities, including the historic Hellman-Ehrman Estate (Pine Lodge), picnic area, beach and pier are 3/4 mile south from the campground. Parking is $10 per vehicle or free if you are camping at dukMéʔem wáťa Campground. Fees are required year round and due by self-payment when the kiosk is unstaffed.



Tahoe Regional Annual Pass is $75
Trails:
Dolder Nature Trail

To reach this 1.5 mile loop trail, start on the paved Rod Beaudry Trail. The Dolder Trail begins at approximately 1/4 mile and is the first dirt path to the right. The trail leads through mixed forest and circles the Edwin L. Z’Berg Natural Preserve. Along the way it passes the world’s highest — in elevation — operating maritime navigational light, and gives excellent views of the lake. 



There are an additional 20+ miles of trails in the park, some which lead into adjacent Forest Service-managed lands in the Desolation Wilderness containing old growth trees. Wilderness Permits are required.
Hours And Camping:
Sugar Pine Point State Park Hours: - Sunrise-Sunset.



The campground has 175 sites and is open throughout the year, conditions permitting. During the winter months, the entry road and parking spaces are cleared of snow. No showers are available in winter. For camping reservations for 2025, call Reserve California at 1-800-444-PARK (7275) or visit www.reservecalifornia.com. Reservations can be made 6 months in advance of the date you would like to arrive. The Lake Tahoe area is a popular destination and reservations are recommended.



dukMéʔem wáťa Campground has a paved accessible trail, seven accessible campsites and two accessible restrooms. Picnic areas and the visitor and campfire centers are accessible.
name: Sugar Pine Point State Park

Description:
Van Cortlandt Park, in the northwest Bronx, is a natural showcase featuring the last vestiges of New York City’s native woodlands and wetlands. Founded in 1888, its 1,146 acres abound with sites that are important to the region and nation. 

Over half of Van Cortlandt Park, 640 acres, is designated a Forever Wild Preserve, a program established by the NYC Parks to protect New York City’s most ecologically valuable lands.
