Many areas in the forest were planted as part of the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) efforts and includes red pine, tamarack, white pine and spruce in these areas. 

The park is dominated by mixed hardwood and evergreen forests with the largest species being white pine, sycamore, Norway spruce and a few others. The CCC pine and tamarack plantations are almost 100 years old and many of the other trees are as old as 120 years.
Navigation: The park is along PA 144, 18 miles south of Galeton and 26 miles north of Renovo.
Parking And Admission: No admission charge.
Trails:
There are sevearl park trails and several connect into other larger regional loop trails such as the Susquehannock Trail. Maps provide further information on the trail head locations.

The Beaver Haven Trail offers a variety of habitats and highlights the CCC plantations along with the riparian Sycamores and huge White pine and spruce of the campgrounds. This trail is an easy walk, but is not ADA accessible
Hours And Camping: The park is open every day of the year, sunrise to sunset. Day use areas close at dusk. The park office is open specific hours. The beach, overnight areas, and other areas are open specific seasons and hours. Contact the park office for facility seasons and hours.
Hunting: Yes, permitted in the allowed season.
name: Ole Bull State Park

Description: This 3,800-acre forest is one of the Nation’s most impressive remnants of old-growth forest. The forest contains magnificent examples of more than 100 tree species, many over 400-years-old, and tulip poplars that are more than 20 feet in circumference and 100 feet tall. There are virgin stands of sycamore, basswood, oak and yellow poplar.
Navigation:
Address: 5410 Joyce Kilmer Rd, Robbinsville, NC 28771 

Directions: From Robbinsville, take Highway 129 North for 1½ miles to the junction with Highway 143 West (Massey Branch Road). Turn left on Highway 143 and travel approx 5 miles to a stop sign. Turn right onto Kilmer Road. Drive for approx 7.3 miles and bear to the right at the junction of Santeetlah Gap and the Cherohala Skyway. Continue for another 2½ miles to the entrance of the Joyce Kilmer Memorial Forest.Turn left, into the entrance, and drive another 0.5 miles to the parking area.
Parking And Admission:
Parking: ample parking near the trailhead.

Admission: no admission fee.
Trails: The Joyce Kilmer National Recreation Trail is a two-mile round-trip figure-eight trail that leads to a memorial plaque and also through Poplar Cove, a grove of the Forest’s largest trees. There are many more trails in the Joyce Kilmer - Slick Rock Wilderness, totalling over 20 miles.
Hours And Camping:
Hours: The Joyce Kilmer Memorial Forest is open year-round. A restroom and picnic tables are located in the parking area near the trailhead. 

Camping: There are two campgrounds around ½ mile from the trailhead. Horse Cove Campground, open from April to October, has 18 sites. For groups, the Rattler Ford Group Campground, open April through October, has four sites, each site accommodating 25. To make required reservations, call the Cheoah Ranger District at 828-479-6431. Back-country camping is allowed anywhere in the Wilderness, using Leave No Trace principles.
Hunting: Yes, hunting is allowed at regulated times.
name: Joyce Kilmer Memorial Forest - Nantahala National Forest

Description: Between the elevations of 5000 and 5400 feet, on the Big Creek Trail in the Bitterroot Mountains, there exists an old growth larch and engelmann spruce forest (among a few more varieties) that is situated in a protected bowl type valley. There are large specimens of both species in this valley, but there is also a massive build up of lichens, dead and down trees, and dead but standing wildlife trees. The valley is situated about 7 miles down the Big Creek Trail and is part of the Selway-Bitterroot Wilderness area. The lower sections of this trail have been burnt by wildfires in the past, but this upper valley has no evidence of fire or logging.
Navigation: From Lolo, MT, continue south on Hwy 93 for 22.5 miles. Turn right on to Bell Crossing W, then right on Curlew Orchard Road. Curlew Orchard turns into Big Creek Rd and the trailhead is 4.7 miles from the turnoff of Hwy 93.
Parking And Admission: Big Creek Trailhead has adequate free parking for both cars and trailers. It offers access to Big Creek Trail #11 and the Selway-Bitterroot Wilderness. Facilities include a picnic table, vault toilet, hitching rails and a stock ramp.
Trails: Big Creek Trail is 9.7 one-way miles to Big Creek Lake, but hikers can enjoy a variety of old-growth forest types starting after 1.5 miles as you enter Wilderness Boundary. The most impressive old-growth can be found between 2.7 and 5.2 miles.
Hours And Camping: Open year-round, depending on snow conditions. The best times to visit are May-Oct. The nearest campground is Charles Waters campground.
name: Big Creek Trail - Selway Bitterroot Wilderness -Bitterroot National Forest

Description:
The Castle in the Clouds Conservation Area is located in the Ossipee Mountains of Moultonborough and Tuftonboro and is conserved and stewarded by the Lakes Region Conservation Trust (LRCT).

The conserved property encompasses 5,246 acres, over 800 of which are old-growth forests. There are 21 delimited old-growth areas that range from 1 acre to 238 acres. These are scattered across the property, although most reside in the upper elevations from 1800 feet to approximately 2600 feet. The most common old-growth forest type is Red Oak Rocky Ridge, followed by Dry Red Oak-White Pine Forest and Northern Hardwood Forest. At least two of the old-growth areas, the Rich Red Oak Rocky Woods and the Circumneutral Red Cedar Rocky Ridge are state recognized rare natural communities. The oldest known tree ages are 385 years for eastern hemlock, 315 years for white pine, and 360 years for white oak.

The property was first settled in 1790 by the Lee family. By 1861, at least eight farms occupied the area, but the agricultural era was limited to the lower, more productive slopes. Building lumber and firewood was harvested from the forests that immediately surrounded the early settlements. The upland forests were effectively protected when the land was purchased in the 1880s by Benjamin Franklin Shaw, whom Mount Shaw is named after. Shaw created Ossipee Mountain Park and a luxury hotel, which provided a place where visitors could take in the splendid views, have picnics, and take walks through the woods. Shaw created a bridle path to the summit of Mt. Shaw and laid out the scenic Brook Walk, which are still popular trails today. Two decades after Shaw’s death, Thomas Gustave Plant, one of the most successful shoe manufacturers in the 
country, purchased the property in 1911and acquired an additional fifty parcels until his estate included close to 6,300 acres. Over the next few years, Plant constructed Lucknow Mansion (the “Castle in the Clouds”), an 18-hole golf course, many outbuildings, extensive stone walls, and over 40 miles of carriage roads. After Plant’s significant financial troubles and death in 1941, the property was put up for auction to satisfy multiple mortgages, foreclosures, taxes, and unpaid bills.Eventually the property fell into the hands of Plant’s friend, land developer, and lumber magnate, Fred Charles Tobey, who extensively logged some sections of the property (mostly of old-growth timber) in the early 1940s for the war effort. Anything not cut was left alone and exists as untouched forest to this day. In 1956 the property was sold to Richard S. Robie, who eventually turned the property into the “Castle in the Clouds” tourist attraction, which was opened to the public in 1959.

The Lakes Region Conservation Trust purchased this property for conservation and recreation in 2002 and currently maintains 30 miles of trails, including much of the historic carriage road system, providing opportunities for hiking, cross-country skiing, and snowmobiling. LRCT subsequently established the Castle Preservation Society (CPS) in 2006 to own and steward the historic buildings on the property, including Lucknow Mansion (also known as the Castle) and 135 acres of its surrounding grounds. In late 2024, Lucknow and the surrounding 5,000+ acre conservation areas were listed as a National Historic Landmark.
Navigation:
LRCT maintains two trailhead parking areas that are free and open to the public for accessing the trails during daylight hours: one at the end of Ossipee Park Road (458 Ossipee Park Rd, Moultonborough, NH 03254) and one on Route 171 (455 Old Mountain Rd, Moultonborough, NH 03254). 



From the Ossipee Park Rd. trailhead, proceed east across the Shannon Pond dam to access trails on the eastern portion of the property. To access trails on the northern portion of the property, proceed north towards Cold Spring Rd. or the entrance of the Mt. Roberts Trail. 



From the Rt. 171 trailhead, proceed north, crossing Rt. 171, to enter the Shannon Brook Trail. The Shannon Brook Trail, Connector Trail, and Turtleback Mountain Trail are part of NH Snowmobile Corridor 15.
Parking And Admission:
LRCT maintains two trailhead parking areas that are ample, free and open to the public for accessing the trails during daylight hours: one at the end of Ossipee Park Road (458 Ossipee Park Rd, Moultonborough, NH 03254) and one on Route 171 (455 Old Mountain Rd, Moultonborough, NH 03254. 



There are two designated ADA accessible parking spots in close proximity to the recommended parking area, along the shore of Shannon Pond. Cell service is spotty at both parking areas due to the area’s topography.
Trails:
The easiest old-growth patch visible by the general public is the one below the scenic vista along Pamela’s Terrace (the “scenic road”). When the road is open in the summer, visitors can park at the vista and look out over an old-growth dry oak-pine forest. Visitors can also meander down through it right from the Castle’s parking area, although no trail is present. 

The Mount Roberts Trail is a 2.5-mile well-used, scenic trail that directly traverses a large old-growth forest patch. The start of this patch is approximately one mile from the parking area at the end of Old Mountain Rd. This patch includes a Red Oak Rocky Ridge and Dry Red Oak-White Pine Forest. The trail is rated as “strenuous” due to the elevation gain and rocky tread surface. 

The Bald Knob Trail is a 0.75-mile scenic, wide trail that also crosses through a Rich Red Oak Rocky Woods in an old-growth condition near the summit of Bald Knob. The Bald Knob Trail is rated as “easy”, but requires a ~2-mile hike with substantial elevation gain to reach the summit. This substantial old-growth forest patch continues below the summit of Bald Knob.

The Upper Bridle Path is a .75-mile singletrack trail that brings users through an old-growth patch on a ridge at ~2000 ft between Faraway and Turtleback Mountain. The trail is rated as moderate and requires a ~1 mile hike from the parking area with moderate elevation gain to reach the beginning of the old-growth forest area. This is primarily a beech forest.

The Brook Walk is a 0.5-mile out-and-back trail that follows Shannon Brook. Although this is not an old-growth forest viewing experience, opportunities exist to see 7 spectacular waterfalls in a relatively short distance, on a trail that is accessible to most user groups.

Many other trails exist on the property, 30 miles of which are sanctioned and maintained by LRCT.
Hours And Camping: This conserved area is open year-round to the public, during daylight hours, for low-impact recreational uses such as hiking, snowshoeing, and cross-country skiing. Camping and fires are prohibited.
Hunting: Hunting is permitted from the beginning of muzzleloader season through April 30th on most of the Castle in the Clouds Conservation Area property. Due to Castle business and events, hunting is prohibited inside a buffer area around the Castle grounds. More information and a map of the buffer area can be found here.
name: Castle in the Clouds Conservation Area

Description:
One of the finest examples of an ancient forest in New Hampshire is along Snyder Brook in Randolph, NH. Here in the White Mountain National Forest are gorgeous waterfalls and towering trees. This 36-acre tract is the only remaining original old-growth forest on the Northern Presidential Range.

As you walk toward Snyder Brook the change from second-growth hardwood forest to old growth hemlock and spruce is abrupt and dramatic. These ancient trees towering up to 90 feet in height, spanning up to 10 feet in circumference and with a measured age of 370 years give us a picture of what much of this area would have looked like before the extensive cutting began. 

The big trees include some state and county champion hemlock, white pine, and red spruce. Large specimens of sugar maple, yellow birch, and beech are also present. This forest, a Hemlock-Spruce-Northern Hardwood type, was never logged and is an easy hike from the Appalachia Trailhead on US Route 2 in Randolph.
Navigation:
US Route 2, Randolph, NH



Park at the Appalachia Trailhead parking lot on US Route 2 in Randolph, NH. The trail begins at the Appalachia Trailhead kiosk on the east end of the parking lot.
Parking And Admission: Parking is available at the Appalachia parking lot on US Route 2 in Randolph. From Gorham, head west on US-2 for 5.4 miles past the split with NH-16 and the parking area will be on the left. This popular trailhead fills quickly. Parking is permitted along US-2, but ensure your vehicle is completely off the road.
Trails:
Fallsway Trail: 1.6 miles round trip

Total trails: 1.6 miles



From the Appalachia Trailhead kiosk on the east end of the parking lot, walk east a few hundred yards along the Presidential Rail Trail to the start of the Fallsway Trail. Cross under a powerline and enter the forest. Soon you will realize that you are standing amongst giants. This forest is what much of the original forest looked like before the extensive logging over a century ago. Continue uphill past Gordon and Salroc Falls until you come to Tama Falls. 



You can return the same way along the Fallsway Path or during low water, cross over Snyder Brook and take the Brookbank Path down to the rail trail. Yellow blazes mark both paths. The round-trip hike or snowshoe is 1.6 miles with a 400-foot elevation change.
Hours And Camping:
Open year round, 24 hrs/day

Snyder Brook Scenic Area is part of the USFS Forest Protection Area. Camping is permitted within Snyder Brook Scenic Area only at the designated Valley Way tentsite. Visit https://www.fs.usda.gov/activity/whitemountain/recreation/camping-cabins/?recid=74405&actid=34 for camping regulations.
Hunting: Hunting is allowed on all White Mountain National Forest Lands including Wilderness areas pursuant to state regulations. State hunting licenses are required to hunt on National Forest land.
name: Snyder Brook Scenic Area - White Mountain National Forest

Description:
The 218-acre older-growth forest within the larger 592 acre Preserve s a Central Appalachian Dry-mesic Chestnut Oak – Northern Red Oak Forest. Red oak (Quercus rubra) and chestnut oak (Quercus montana) dominate the canopy, with smaller components of black oak (Quercus velutina), mockernut hickory (Carya tomentosa), and sassafras (Sassafras albidum). This older-growth area was never cleared for agriculture and remains relatively free of invasive plants.

Red oaks measured 44.7” and 43.4” diameter in 2026 and estimated to date to the later part of the nineteenth century 

Hunterdon's older-growth forest area provides habitat for forest-interior migratory songbirds such as veery, wood thrush, ovenbird, and scarlet tanager, as well as red-bellied woodpecker and barred owls.
Navigation: Sanatorium Road, Lebanon, New Jersey
Parking And Admission: There is a small parking area that can accommodate approximately five vehicles located off of Sanatorium Road (40.69857, -74.92096). There is also some roadside parking available along Sanatorium Road.
Hours And Camping:
The entire Preserve is open to the public from dawn to dusk for passive recreational uses such as hiking, bird watching, and botanizing along unofficial trails. Camping is not permitted.



As with all Preserves in the NJ Natural Lands Trust’s system, the following uses are prohibited:campfires, use of motorized vehicles, consumption of alcohol, unleashed pets, use of drones, hunting for bear, turkey, small game, or waterfowl. Also prohibited is the collection, harassment, or destruction of plants, fungi, animals, rocks, cultural artifacts, or fossils.
Hunting: Bow hunting only with permit from the NJ Natural Lands Trust.
name: Hagedorn Preserve

Description:
Gorges State Park hosts 8,000 acres of temperate rainforest including waterfalls and incredible Southern Appalachian biodiversity. At least 250 - 500 acres of Gorges is old growth, likely protected from historic logging by the steep terrain. While the trees have not been dated via trunk cores, it is believed the oldest parts of the forest are estimated to have remained undisturbed by humans since at least European settlement of the area. 
Gorges State Park sits along the blue ridge escarpment, the topological termination point between the Appalachian Mountains and the lower elevation piedmont. It is host to 125 protected species including the charismatic Oconee Bells (Shortia galacifolia), Green Salamander (Aneides aeneus), and a variety of other rare ferns, mosses, and vertebrate creatures. Gorges SP hosts extensive natural communities such as Montane Oak-Hickory Forest, Chestnut Oak Forest, and Acidic Cove Forest, and widespread Pine-Oak/Heath Forest. Rich Cove Forest and Spray Cliff Forest, uncommon natural communities, also occur in small patches within the park. Other attractions to Gorges are numerous waterfalls, hiking down to Lake Jocassee, and travelers of the Carolina Foothills Trail pass through the park on their 70-mile trek.

Description:
This 235-acre Illinois Nature Preserve exists within the 565-acre Edward L. Ryerson Conservation Area, which supports some of Illinois' most pristine woodlands and several state threatened and endangered species. This protected land includes one of the best examples of a northern flatwoods forest, a rare northern Illinois landscape, and most of the floodplain forest left in northeastern Illinois.

The Nature Preserve contains four distinct forest communities that are representative of the Morainal Section of the Northeastern Morainal Natural Division. The wet floodplain forest is located along the Des Plaines River. Silver maple and bur oak are characteristic species. The mesic sugar maple forest is on the better-drained terrace soil. The drier uplands are dominated by oaks and hickories with younger sugar maples common in the understory. Finally, a wet flatwood is located on a poorly drained upland area. Many showy marsh and meadow plant species occur here: gentian, great blue lobelia, and cardinal flower. The area also provides valuable wetland habitat for several species of bird, waterfowl, and other wildlife.

According to a 2008 study, the oldest cored trees include a walnut which was estimated to have germinated in 1812, a bur oak in 1815, and a sugar maple in 1828. Each of these trees were established in understory conditions and released into canopy gaps in the mid to late 1800s.
Navigation:
21950 North Riverwoods Road, Riverwoods,IL 60015 



Ryerson is located in Riverwoods, Lake County, IL, in the southeastern portion of Vernon Township, due west of I-94. Ryerson is generally bordered by Half day Road to the north, Riverwoods Road to the east, Deerfield Road to the south, and Milwaukee Avenue to the west. The entrance to the preserve is located along Riverwoods Road.
Parking And Admission: Two large parking lots are available near the Ryerson Welcome Center and Brushwood Center. There is no admission fee.
Trails:
The preserve is home to 6.5 miles of trail.

Hours: 6:30AM to sunset

No camping
name: Ryerson Nature Preserve – Edward L. Ryerson Conservation Area

Description:
A fire in 1926, destroyed nearly 75 percent of the original grove and left two small remnants. The Lower Grove, approximately 2 acres, has 4 picnic sites available under the towering trees.
The Upper Grove, approximately 20 acres accessible via a trail system following an old logging road, has been left undeveloped. Feel free to explore this grove on foot. Estimating the age of these giants, which range from 4 to 12 feet in diameter and reach heights of 150 feet, is difficult due to heart rot which hollows out the center of the tree; therefore, an
accurate count of the rings cannot be made. Through cutting windfalls and increment borings of healthy trees, the average age has been estimated at 800 years, with a few hearty survivors achieving the 2000-3000 year old status.
Navigation:
The Grove of Ancient Cedars is near the Washington-Idaho border and may be accessed via gravel forest roads from either state. The route from the Idaho side is suitable for all vehicles. The route from the Washington side includes some potentially rough stretches and is suitable for vehicles with high clearance. Best check with USFS staff before you go, especially early in the season.



From the west/Metaline Falls, drive north on WA 31 about 2 miles and turn right on Sullivan Lake Road. At Sullivan Lake, turn east on FR 22 and drive 21 miles over Pass Creek Pass; part of this route may be rough. Turn south at Granite Pass toward Nordman, Idaho. Go 1.7 miles on FR 302 to reach the Stagger Inn Day Use Area / Roosevelt Grove of Ancient Cedars.



From the east/Newport, Washington, drive east on U.S. 2 about 6 miles and turn north on Idaho 57, which turns into Nordman Road. About 37 miles from U.S. 2, the road becomes a good gravel road, FR 302 (a.k.a. Nordman Metaline Road). Drive another 9 miles until you see a sign for the turnoff to the Stagger Inn Day Use Area / Roosevelt Grove of Ancient Cedars.
Parking And Admission: Parking at the trailhead, also called Stagger Inn Day Use Area. No fee.
Trails:
An easy 2.5-mile loop, departing from the south end of the parking area, takes in Granite Falls and the Upper Grove, which covers about 20 acres. First, take the little spur trail to see Lower Granite Falls, then return to the main trail, where you’ll soon reach a junction. Turn left toward the overlook. The trail ascends to a wonderful viewing platform, where you can see the falls from a higher angle.



The trail continues to ascend through some switchbacks, passes Upper Granite Falls, and then intersects Trail 301. Turn left and hike 0.8 mile until you see a sign for trail 301A, Cedar Grove Trail. After wandering around that lollipop loop through the grove, return to the parking area via Trail 301.



An easy 0.3-mile loop through the lower cedar grove starts at the north end of the parking area. It’s not shown on the trailhead map and isn’t signed, but the trail is very clear.



Total trails length 3 miles.
Hours And Camping: Hours are from dusk to dawn. No camping. Vault toilet.
name: Roosevelt Grove Of Ancient Cedars and Granite Falls Scenic Area - Idaho Panhandle National Forests

Description:
The Hanna Flats Cedar Grove includes a 1/4-mile interpretive nature trail highlighting the valuable features of this old-growth forest. The trail takes you beneath immense trees that have survived generations of homesteading, logging, firestorms and centuries of nature’s wrath. In addition to the cedars, the grove also contains numerous other trees, shrubs and plants. Eight different species of trees, ten species of shrubs and over a dozen plant species have been identified in the grove. 

Estimating the age of these giants, which range from 4 to 12 feet in diameter and reach heights of 150 feet, is difficult due to heart rot which hollows out the center of the tree; therefore, an accurate count of the rings cannot be made. Through cutting windfalls and increment borings of healthy trees, the average age has been estimated at 800 years, with a few hearty survivors achieving the 2000-3000 year old status

This grove of western red cedar and western white pine trees provides habitat for birds that require old growth forests. Species present include Varied Thrush, Pacific Wren, Cassin’s Vireo, Pileated Woodpecker, Ruffed Grouse, and Northern Goshawk. Hanna Flats is stop N16 on the Idaho Birding Trail.
Navigation:
Near Intersection of National Forest Rd 313 and Intersection of Idaho State Highway 53 on the south side of the Hanna Flats landing strip. 



From Priest River, drive north on ID 57 for about 30 miles, turn left/west on ; turn onto FR 313 and drive ~1.5 mi to the trailhead.
Parking And Admission: Small parking area for about 5 cars, ADA accessible for wheelchairs and strollers. Free admission. Vault toilet.
Trails: Hanna Flats Cedar Grove Interpretive Trail- 0.4 mile loop.
Hours And Camping: Open dusk to dawn. No camping.
name: Hanna Flats Cedar Grove - Idaho Panhandle National Forests

Description:
The Old Salmon River Trail is a family-friendly trail through a gorgeous old-growth forest not far from Portland. The trail follows the path of the Salmon River through massive Douglas Firs, western redcedars, and western hemlock. Bigleaf maples drip with moss, snags host cavity-nesting birds, and downed logs melt into the forest floor. 

Eager hikers can continue on through the “keyhole” (an area excluded from Wilderness protections that Oregon Wild is working to include within the Wilderness boundary), and beyond, up the Salmon River trail to experience more old-growth forests as one gains elevation.
Navigation:
From Sandy, OR - follow US Hwy 26 17.3 miles east. Then turn south on Salmon River Road (Forest Road 2618) following it 2.6 miles to the first trailhead access.



Other access points lie further along Salmon River Road on the pullout areas on the right-hand shoulder. The southern end of the trail is 2.4 miles past the first along Salmon River Road and is just before a bridge across the river.
Parking And Admission: The Old Salmon River Trailhead parking is near the trailhead. Admission: $5.00 per vehicle per day. A valid Recreation Pass required – go to https://www.fs.usda.gov/main/mthood/passes-permits
Trails: Salmon River Trail is 6.2 miles round-trip. Shorter options are also available.
Hours And Camping: Open year-round. No camping. Restrooms at trailhead.
name: Old Salmon River Trail - Mt. Hood National Forest

Description:
Zurich Bog is a large, locally acidic wetland/fen trapped between large drumlins in central New York State. Such wetlands were never common in this portion of the Great Lakes plain but have become increasingly rare since European settlement due to drainage, filling, and pollution. The full property occupies 660 acres dominated by wetlands and swamp forest, but a small, 20 to 30-acre drumlin in the center of the wetland area is home to an unlogged persistent forest. Sugar maples, American beech. black cherry, paper and white birch, and tuliptree dominate the deciduous forest on the higher portions of the 40’ high drumlin. There is an unlogged eastern hemlock forest at the southern and downslope end, with some white pine. The crest of the drumlin contains the telltale characteristics of persistent forest: large tip-ups, fallen decaying trees, and pit and mound topography. At its northernmost point, the loop approaches a floating moor, botanically, a graminoid fen. 

On September 7, 1973, Zurich Bog was designated as a National Natural Landmark. Over the past 7 decades, research has been conducted under the stewardship of BSPS by students and faculty from many of the local colleges and universities. This work continues today in both the old-growth forest and the wetlands/bogs that surround it.
Navigation: 3855 Arcadia Zurich Norris Rd, Lyons, NY 14489
Parking And Admission: There is a grassy parking area at the trailhead, which is marked by a large glacial erratic boulder with the National Natural Landmark plaque.
Trails: There is a short quarter-mile access trail to a moderate, locally rugged, 2-mile loop trail that encircles the drumlin and crosses its southern section. Hikers circle the forest and then walk through it.
Hours And Camping: The site is open to the public from dusk to dawn. There is a sign-in book at a kiosk about 300 meters into the property. We do ask that any groups larger than 6 please call the Property Manager ahead of a visit. If you have never been to the bog before it is recommended you call also. Jimmy may be able to make suggestions on what to look for at the seasonal time of your visit.
Hunting: Yes, by permit, deer only during season, for forest and botanical management.
name: Zurich Bog

Description: Located in Ashe County 25 miles northeast of Boone, Mount Jefferson State Natural Area surrounds a natural landmark that offers vistas as far as Tennessee from its overlooks and Luther Rock. The mountain, first spotted from the Blue Ridge Parkway, rises abruptly from the surrounding landscape. Over 700 plants call the park home, including the Dutchman's pipevine, which is visited by the beautiful swallowtail butterfly and its distinct black-and-orange-spiked caterpillar. Northern red oaks, white oaks, yellow birch, and skeletons of American chestnuts are prevalent.

Description:
The Martin-Beland-Miller Memorial Woods was donated to MNA by Otto Miller and Mary E. Frolich Miller in 1996. The sanctuary honors the last names of Otto Miller’s ancestors who had owned the property beginning in 1839. After the initial ownership by John C. Martin—the brother of Otto Miller’s great-great-grandfather — the property was eventually transferred to Otto Miller’s grandfather, Fred Beland, and then Otto Miller’s parents, James and Florence (Beland) Miller.

The Millers prided themselves in the stewardship of the property in the family’s 160 years of ownership; the land was never pastured, and only light timber harvest was ever conducted. The only known timber removal was in 1910, when Fred Beland cut timber exceeding 21 inches to build a nearby house. 

The sanctuary is a fragment of southern mesic forest which has been exposed to very light past disturbance. Mesic southern forests are dominated by American beech and sugar maples and found on flat to rolling topography with predominantly loam soils. Natural disturbances in these forests are characterized by gap-phase dynamics; mesic southern forests experience frequent, small windthrow gaps, which allow for the regeneration of the shade-tolerant, canopy species. These forests tend to be multi-generational, with old-growth conditions that last for many centuries.
Navigation: The sanctuary is located at the end of Martin Street. From Ford Highway turn east onto Tangent Rd. and then east on Martin Street. To get to the sanctuary, visitors traveling the trail from the Indian Creek Camp and Conference Center should cross the bridge over the ditch and walk toward the sanctuary sign. The trail by the sign will take visitors through the nicest parts of the sanctuary.
Parking And Admission: Parking located at Indian Creek Camp and Conference Center or at the end of Martin Road. If parking at the end of Martin Road be aware that the parking area can get wet and muddy after rain leading to cars getting stuck.
Trails: Short trail - around .33 miles.
Hours And Camping: Dawn to dusk.
name: Martin-Beland-Miller Memorial Woods Plant Preserve

Description:
The Magney-Snively Natural Area is a critical ecological asset within the City of Duluth. Encompassing nearly 1,800 acres, this natural area north of Bardon’s Peak is well-known for its old growth hardwood forest. This forest was the original justification for setting this land aside for protection: “A far-sighted person can see that forested areas of northern Minnesota are fast-dwindling, and that in not more than 10 years a stand of timber of this size will be almost a novelty… I should like to see this wood land left in its natural state…” - Samuel Snively, Mayor of Duluth, Minnesota, 1921 (Dierkins & Nelson, 2017). It is also recognized as one of the best examples of large, contiguous Maple-Basswood (Bluebead Lily) forest in Minnesota.

In addition to the old growth hardwoods, the area also contains a diverse landscape of wetlands, streams, uplands, and bedrock outcrops, making Magney-Snively Natural Area perhaps the most ecologically significant and high-quality natural area in an urban setting within Minnesota. The natural area encompasses the headwaters portions of two of Duluth’s fourteen Minnesota Department of Natural Resources (MNDNR)-designated trout streams: Stewart Creek and Sargent Creek. These streams have naturally-reproducing, native Brook Trout populations that are dependent on stable cold water and suitable habitat.
Navigation:
W Skyline Pkwy, Duluth, MN 55810



The trailhead is located in the northeastern part of the natural area off of the skyline parkway.
Parking And Admission: Parking is available at the trailhead. There is no admission fee.
Trails:
Two areas of old-growth can be accessed via trail. The area just south of the trailhead can be accessed via the Skyline Parkway, multi-use pathway and superior hiking trail. The area in the southwest part of the preserve can be accessed via the Skyline Parkway and cross-country ski trail. Note that the Skyline Parkway is open to traffic March-October and closes to traffic in the winter.



There are snowmobile trails-approx. 2 miles, ski trails-approx. 7 miles (equestrian use in summer), and hiking trails (Superior Hiking Trail-approx. 4 miles) and a multiuse trail-approx 2 miles (DWP trail/old railroad).
Hours And Camping: Open year round. No camping is permitted.
name: Magney-Snively Designated Natural Area

Description:
The Pioneer Mothers Memorial Forest is an 88-acre block of remnant old-growth Central Hardwood forest, which includes cathedral stands of mature black walnut (Juglans nigra), yellow-poplar (Liriodendron tulipifera), white oak (Quercus alba), and white ash (Fraxinus americana).Many of the biggest trees are currently 30 to 40 inches at breast height. This is one of the few remaining unharvested tracts of Central Hardwoods in the region. There are also many spring wildflower species including trillium, jack-in-the-pulpit, wild ginger, and eastern bluebells.

The topography is hilly and rugged, due in part to the presence of several sinkholes. Pioneer Mothers is in the heart of the southern Indiana karst topography. The soil is a residual, unglaciated loam and silt loam derived from the weathering of a sandstone stratum overlying limestone. In the lower areas, the soil is derived from weathered limestone with accumulations of eroded overlying sandstone colluvium. 

Pioneer Mothers Memorial Forest is also a designated National Natural Landmark and a Research Natural Area. Researchers have used the site for decades to study old-growth forest ecology, tree growth patterns, and biodiversity in Central Hardwood ecosystems. The forest serves as a kind of living laboratory that continues to provide valuable data. To ensure its natural state no bikes, no horses, no camping, and no plant collecting are allowed.
Navigation: 100 SW 1st St, Paoli, IN 47454 – from here head south on State Road 37 and travel 1.7 miles to the parking area for Pioneer Mothers Memorial Forest.
Parking And Admission: Limited parking is available at the trailhead off Hwy 150. A larger parking area is available at the Hwy 37 trailhead. The trail, part of which is paved, runs between the two trailheads.
Trails: Pioneer Mothers Trail is 1.3 miles, and open to hiking only. While sections are relatively flat, there is steeper terrain to get to the old-growth forest area.
Hours And Camping: Open dawn to dusk. Camping is prohibited.
name: Pioneer Mothers Memorial Forest - Hoosier National Forest

Description: This old-growth woods is a portion of the forest which originally covered southwestern Indiana. The larger upland section supports oak-hickory forest, with white oak and black oak as dominant trees. There are also large specimens of white ash, red oak, and sassafras, along with pignut, small-fruited and shagbark hickories. The bottomland has sweetgum, tulip, river birch, sycamore, wild black cherry, and mixed oaks. The strong southern influences on this woods are particularly evident in the bottomland area. Hemmer is one of the best examples of a woods with southern affinities in the preserve system. Because of the outstanding natural communities present here, the woods has been registered as a National Natural Landmark.
Navigation:
CR 1050E, Oakland City, IN 47660



Parking and trail: From Buckskin on SR 57 take CR 900S about 2.5 miles east to CR 1050E, the 4th intersection after the railroad tracks. Then go 0.5 mile north to a marked parking lot. An easy 0.7 mile self-guided nature trail circles through the upland forest.
Parking And Admission: Free admission. There is limited parking in gravel lot.
Trails: 0.7 miles dirt loop trail.
Hours And Camping: Dawn to dusk. No camping.
name: Hemmer Woods Nature Preserve

Description:
Andrews contains one of Florida’s largest remaining unaltered contiguous upland hardwood hammock forests, representing xeric and mesic vegetative communities in close proximity. Of the estimated 20,000 to 25,000 acres of upland hardwood forest that once existed along the lower Suwannee, the last remaining tract is located within AWMA. Impressively, the old-growth upland hardwood forest at Andrews shows little evidence of human disturbance.


Of the total 3,582 acres, 2,329 are upland hardwood forest, 541 acres are upland mixed woodland, and 37.6 acres are restoration upland mixed woodland. The forest canopy is dominated by sand laurel oak and pignut hickory, with abundant magnolia and sweetgum. The subcanopy includes young trees of these species, along with red bay, American holly, and eastern hophornbeam. The shrub layer features sparkleberry, horse-sugar, red bay, and occasional saw palmetto.
Navigation:
NW 160th St, Old Town, FL 32680 

From US 19 in Fanning Springs, travel south approximately 2.5 miles. Turn right on NW 160th Street, the road leads straight into the WMA. If arriving by boat, tie up at the river dock.
Parking And Admission:
There is a small parking lot with 1 ADA parking spot and access to the ADA hunting blind off Old Fanning road and 1 ADA parking spot by the river pavilion and 1 ADA parking spot by the kiosk by the office and check station. There is a small parking area near the intersection of Old Fanning Rd, Dick Slough Rd and Randall Rd with no ADA parking. The cell service is mostly good throughout Andrews but sometimes is poor in the southwestern portion.



Persons engaged in recreational activities other than hunting must possess a daily-use permit or a management area permit. Permits may be purchased at designated entry points of the management area. A daily-use permit is $3 per person, $6 per noncommercial vehicle, $75 per group of 25 to 100 people and $150 for groups of 101 people or more. Cash and personal checks are acceptable methods of payment.
Trails: Persimmon Trail- 1.1 miles, Bluff Oak trail 2.2 miles, and Maple Loop Trail 1.7 miles (ADA accommodation can be requested). Trails are not paved and users can expect some elevation changes, but mostly uneven ground from roots and wildlife disturbance.
Hours And Camping: Camping is prohibited at Andrews WMA. Open to public access year round, except during periods open to hunting, when only persons participating in the hunts are allowed. During non-hunting periods, a daily use permit or management area permit is required to access the area and persons may enter ½ hour before sunrise and must exit no later than ½ hour after sunset.
Hunting: Hunting is allowed by permit at Andrews WMA. Open to public access year round, except during periods open to hunting, when only persons participating in the hunts are allowed. Learn more about hunting permitting and regulations at https://myfwc.com/recreation/lead/andrews/planning-your-visit/
name: Andrews Wildlife Management Area

Description:
San Felasco Hammock Preserve State Park is 7,353 acres, with 2,940 of those being classified as Upland Hardwood Forest and 690 acres classified as Bottomland Forest. It is estimated that 2030 acres of Upland Hardwood Forest and Bottomland Forest are old-growth or have old-growth characteristics. According to Dunn 1982, some selective logging occurred within the Upland Hardwood Forest and Bottomland Forest between 1937 and the late 1960s based on available aerial photography. These areas have been excluded from the acreage figures. A protected area totaling 4,467 acres is designated as a Wilderness Zone within the State Park and includes the majority of the old growth forest.

Many large diameter live oak, swamp chestnut oaks, and spruce pines occur on site, but no systematic coring or aging of the trees has been done.

The Florida Natural Areas Inventory (FNAI) has designated a portion of the Upland Hardwood Forest as a Reference Natural Community Site and conducted floristic research on site (attached).

The park’s Unit Management Plan provides descriptions of the Upland Hardwood Forest (p.26) and Bottomland Forest (p.30) (attached).

Willian Dunn conducted a floristic inventory and analysis of San Felasco Hammock in 1982 (attached). 

The original proposal to acquire San Felasco Hammock was developed in the early 1970s by a core group of faculty from the University of Florida and other local preservationists with the Alachua Audubon Society.
Navigation:

North Trailhead (Equestrian & Mountain Bike Trailhead)

This is the northern entrance of the park, which was a later addition to the original park.
Parking And Admission:
$4 per vehicle. Please use the honor box - correct change is required. $2 Pedestrians, bicyclists, extra passengers. Trailhead parking is a limestone parking lot that supports ~20 vehicles on the south side of Millhopper Rd. Most of the hiking trails (Old Spanish Way, Spring Grove, Sandhill Cutoff, and Hammock Cutoff) are located north of Millhopper Rd. A crosswalk from the parking lot to the north side of the road connects the parking area to the trailhead. When the parking lot reaches capacity during peak times. 



There is one designated/paved handicap parking space in the limestone parking lot. 



Cell service is available from the parking lot and most of the trails in this area. 



Park Admission is $2.00/pedestrian or $4.00/vehicle (1-8 people). The park is fully cashless, and visitors pay either via QR code at the trailhead, or they can pay online ahead of time at https://reserve.floridastateparks.org/Web/Memberships/CustomerMembershipPasses.aspx
Trails:
From parking area trailhead north on Spring Grove/Old Spanish Way Trail then west at Hammock Cutoff = 1.5 miles (see Old Growth SFH Map). Approximately 0.9 miles are within the Old Growth Upland Hardwood Forest.



Total Distance of All Trails:

Mountain Bike: 32.5

Hiking: 12.4
Hours And Camping:
Open year-round, 8:00 AM – sunset daily. The trailhead does not close gates, unless closing for emergency situations (tropical storms, hurricanes, etc.)



San Felasco Hammock does not have camping available. The two closest State Parks that have camping are O’Leno State Park to the north, and Paynes Prairie Preserve State Park to the south.
name: San Felasco Hammock Preserve State Park

Description:
The park includes approximately 2,300 acres of natural communities and 68 developed or disturbed acres. Longleaf pine sandhill is the dominant natural forest with 1768 acres included within the park. Of that, 350 acres are considered to be old growth longleaf pine as documented in Johnson et al (2018). Selective coring of the largest longleaf pines exhibiting old growth characteristics resulted in numerous individuals over 200 years of age, with a maximum estimated age of nearly 400 years. The sandhill community at Gold Head is dominated by an overstory of longleaf pines (Pinus palustris) with an open midstory with scattered turkey oaks (Quercus laevis). Although fire-tolerant, individual turkey oaks do not typically reach an advanced age in areas with a natural fire regime.

Floristic studies at the park include White and Judd (1985) and the Florida Natural Areas Inventory Reference Natural Community data (FNAI Reference Communities). The Gold Head sandhills are typical of the Trail Ridge region of NE Florida. Groundcover is dominated by pyrogenic grasses including wiregrass (Aristida stricta), lopsided Indiangrass (Sorghastrum secundum), pineywoods dropseed (Sporobolus junceus) and numerous herbaceous species. Johnson et al (2018) detailed the old growth characteristics of the site, including flat-topped longleaf pines with twisted limbs, evidence of red heart fungus, and box-cut turpentine scars. The park has historical records of red-cockaded woodpeckers which rely on old growth longleaf pines for nest sites. Southeastern kestrels breed onsite and utilize old longleaf snags for nest cavities, and Southern fox squirrels are often seen. Bachman’s sparrows nest in the open sandhills.

The park also contains the largest steephead ravine system in northeast Florida. Steephead ravines are a unique geological formation more common in the panhandle of Florida in the vicinity of the Apalachicola River.
Navigation:
6239 State Road 21, Keystone Heights FL 32656



The Old Growth Longleaf Stand can be accessed on foot via the Florida National Scenic Trail which crosses the park entrance drive at the Mike Roess Gold Head Branch State Park Ranger Station. Follow the trail NE and then SE. The first 3500’ pass through the best examples of old growth. The first 4200’ of the park entrance drive also passes through the Old Growth Longleaf Stand providing accessibility for vehicles.
Parking And Admission: Limited parking is available at the Park Ranger Station. ADA accessible parking is available. Admission fees are: $5 per vehicle (two to eight people). $4 single-occupant vehicle and motorcycles. $2 pedestrian, bicyclist, additional passengers. Cell service is typically available.
Trails:
Florida National Scenic Trail from Ranger Station towards Devil’s Washbasin (3500 feet). 



There are a total of 7.5 miles of hiking trails within the park, 6.3 miles of which are designated as part of the Florida National Scenic Trail.
Hours And Camping: The park is open from 8AM until sundown, 365 days a year. The park has 73 campsites divided between three full-service campgrounds. There are two primitive hike-in campsites associated with the Florida National Scenic Trail with up to six people per site. Three primitive group campsites, allowing up to 25 people per site, are available for organized groups.
Hunting: Hunting is not permitted. Fishing is allowed in Big and Little Lake Johnson.
name: Mike Roess Gold Head Branch State Park

Description:
Sitting in hundreds of protected acreage are several old-growth forests. The first is fifteen acres of Mesic Southern Forest. This forest sits atop a glacial moraine consisting of a high ridgeline flanked by rich conifer wetlands. It is a land of massive American beech (Fagus grandifolia) and sugar maple (Acer saccharum) trees. 

The second old growth forest is fifteen acres of dry-mesic southern forest. This forest is dominated by large oak (Quercus species) and hickory (Carya species) trees. Fire frequents this landscape, promoting oak regeneration and an open lower canopy.
Navigation:
701 West Cloverdale Road, Hastings, Michigan 49058



Upon reaching the entrance on Cloverdale Road, follow the paved driveway around past the Maintenance Building and Education Building to reach the parking area. Trailhead for all trails is between the Visitor Center and Education Building.
Parking And Admission: Parking is ample, and access to parking and trails is free of charge. Restrooms are available inside the South Entrance of the Visitor Center, accessible dawn to dusk. ADA accessible parking spots are available, as is cell service in the parking lot.
Trails:
Red Trail (Oak forest): 1.9 miles

Blue Trail (Oak and Beech Maple forest): 1.5 miles

Total trails: 9 miles
Hours And Camping: Access to parking and trails is free of charge year-round, dawn to dusk. Exceptions to this may take place during deer hunting season as the Institute may host hunters in the fall months to help manage deer populations. Camping is not allowed or available, however housing options are available on site for a rental charge. Restrooms are available inside the South Entrance of the Visitor Center, accessible dawn to dusk.
Hunting: Possession and/or discharge of firearms, weapons, fireworks, and/or explosives are prohibited with the exception of bows and firearms used strictly for the Quality Deer Management program. To use bows and/or rifles as part of PCCI’s Quality Deer Management program, one must be selected for participation into the program, and one must obtain an authorized permission slip to hunt the property.
name: Pierce Cedar Creek Institute

Description:
DeLeon Spring State Park is 625 acres, with an OGFN recognized old-growth area of 5-10 acres. 

The oldest bald cypress tree, Old Methuselah, is estimated to be over 500 years old. It’s d.b.h measures 108” and is located on the north side of the park. There is a new boardwalk that was constructed in 2025 that allows visitors to view the tree without causing erosion and trampling of vegetation, that leads visitors to view the tree that escaped the cypress timbering era. You may see younger but still impressive live oaks even in the parking lot, but there’s a nice mix of large trees out on the trails, including cypresses, a variety of pines, live oaks, and red maples, among others. This area would be considered as a tropical hardwood hammock forest type. There are 262.82 acres of Hydric Hammock Forest among other natural communities including Xeric Hammock, Cypress Swamps, Depression Marsh, Upland Mixed Forest, Mesic Flatwoods, Shell Mound and even an Aquatic Cave. Some of these areas are not in public use areas.
Navigation:
601 Ponce DeLeon Blvd., DeLeon Springs, FL 32130

Take the first right after the Ranger Station to locate the trails. The trails are on the right side of the road.
Parking And Admission: $4 for a vehicle with a single passenger, $6 for a vehicle with multiple passengers up to 8 people. ADA parking is available. Cell service is available. Park is busy on weekends in the summertime and may experience capacity closures.
Trails: The trails in DeLeon State Park all spur off the main paved Nature Trail, most of the mature forest is along the nature trail and out to the spur where Old Methuselah resides. This main loop is paved and there are maps present for visitors on different parts of the trail. There are two short spurs off the nature trail, one of which is a boardwalk to “Old Methuselah”, and the other to “Monkey Island”, which goes out into a shallow swamp along a raised footpath. Old Methuselah boardwalk trail is ADA accessible. More experienced hikers may want to check out the longer, 4-mile Wild Persimmon trail, which also begins on the main nature trail.
Hours And Camping:
8 a.m. until sunset, 365 days a year.

No camping facilities available.
name: De Leon Springs State Park

Description:
The Trout Brook Valley Old-Growth Forest Reserve (OGFR) encompasses 236 acres, with 39 acres in the Town of Weston and 197 acres in the Town of Easton. The forest is estimated to be 90–100 years old or older, although the age of the oldest individual trees has not been confirmed. The extent of formally verified old-growth forest within the reserve has not yet been determined, but aerial photographs from 1934 show that most of the area was already forested, with few visible stone walls, suggesting relatively limited historical agricultural use.

Dominant tree species include red oak, chestnut oak, and sugar maple, with eastern hemlock prominent in the southern portion. The forest also features dense mountain laurel thickets, highbush blueberry shrubs, and a variety of lichens and mosses.

The preserve supports a diverse assemblage of forest-associated bird species, including barred owl, northern goshawk, pileated woodpecker, brown creeper, winter wren, wood thrush, worm-eating warbler, Louisiana waterthrush, and scarlet tanager. These species, together with the forest’s vegetation and historical continuity, contribute to its conservation value.
Navigation:
Drive to the end of Bradley Road in Weston, CT 06883 



From the Merritt Parkway (Rte 15), take exit 21 for CT-57 toward Westport/Weston. Turn left onto CT-57 N/Weston Rd, then turn right onto Lyons Plain Rd. In about 3.5 miles, turn left onto Davis Hill Road and then quickly bear right onto Valley Forge Road. In about a mile, turn right onto Bradley Hill Rd. and continue to the Trout Brook Valley Preserve parking area on your left.



From the parking lot, enter the White Trail behind the kiosk and follow it a short distance to the Red Trail. Turn onto the Red Trail, cross Hawleys Brook, and continue into the Trout Brook Valley Old-Growth Forest Reserve.
Parking And Admission: Parking can be found at the end of Bradley Road in Weston, Connecticut. There is parking for approximately 12 passenger vehicles. No buses, RVs, or other large vehicles. No admission charge is required. Donations are accepted at https://www.aspetucklandtrust.org/donate-membership to support the protection of this special resource. Cell phone service available but can be “spotty”. This location is not ADA accessible.
Trails:
Use the Trout Brook Valley Preserve Trail Map.



The Old-Growth Forest Reserve (OGFR) lies between the western boundary of the Trout Brook Valley Preserve and the western branch of Hawley's Brook all the way to the southwestern edge of Jump Hill Preserve. To reach the heart of the OGFR from the Bradley Road Parking Area trailhead, there are several loop hike options. The Red and Orange trails include more challenging sections. Lavender and Green are easier.
Hours And Camping: The preserve is open year-round from dawn to dusk. No camping is permitted in this preserve.
Hunting: Hunting is permitted on a limited basis within approximately 300 acres of the 1,009-acre Trout Brook Valley Conservation Area. Much of the Old-Growth Forest Reserve (OGFR) falls within the designated hunting area, with the exception of the 39-acre portion located in the Town of Weston.
name: Trout Brook Valley Old-Growth Forest Reserve - Trout Brook Valley Preserve

Description:
This 18-acre Scientific and Natural Area hosts a magnificent old growth pine forest near the eastern tip of Minnesota Point, the 7-mile long sandbar that shelters the Duluth Harbor and Superior Bay from the open waters of Lake Superior. Large red and white pines are anchored in the sandy soil of beach ridges. Many are between 120 and 200 years old, their crowns rising higher than 100 feet.

It's an old forest on a geologically young sandbar which is itself a significant natural feature. Ideas about the origins of this baymouth bar system (which includes 3-mile long Wisconsin Point) are still evolving. Dr. Andy Breckenridge, University of WI-Superior, theorizes that it may have formed during a period of rising lake levels less than 1200 years ago, when sediments carried in longshore currents were deposited along a pre-existing beach ridge.

The SNA is comprised of two parcels, each of which is surrounded by other public lands. One of these spans the .3-mile width of the Point, its north side exposed to the wind and waves of Lake Superior and its south (bay) side more protected. Bands of vegetation correspond to the increasingly stable conditions as one moves inland from the water's edge. Wave-washed shoreline and open beach transition to beachgrass dune, then to juniper dune shrubland, and finally, to the pine forest on the interior. Rare plants that occupy these specialized habitats include beach heather, slender hair grass, and American beach grass (listed as threatened in Minnesota, and at the western edge of the species' natural range here).

Together with the adjacent St. Louis River estuary, this is a hot spot for birders and outdoor enthusiasts. During spring and fall the Point serves as a critical stopover area for migratory birds funneling along the North Shore to rest and refuel. The SNA's old growth forest also offers summer breeding habitat for up to 16 species of northern forest birds. The flowers of spring blooming cherries, currants, and blueberries can be seen buzzing with yellow-banded bumble bees and other bees.

As visitors enter the cool, shady forest of the SNA with its towering red and white pines, the benefits of its preservation are abundantly clear. There is nowhere else in Minnesota quite like it.
Navigation: In Duluth, from I-35 4.8 miles SE on Lake Ave (becomes Minnesota Ave after the aerial lift bridge). Park in the public lot on W just before Sky Harbor Seaplane Base. Hike trail NE of hangars and runway 0.75 mile to site.
Parking And Admission: Parking is available at the trailhead and parking area for Park Point Beach. Plenty of spots are available. No admission fee.
Trails:
The trailhead is located at the end of the parking lot on the north side of the airport building. The Park Point Nature Trail runs through both parcels and adjacent city-owned land, an out-and-back 2-mile roundtrip to the far edge of the SNA. The trail extends further beyond the property boundary onto adjacent city and federal lands to the end of the point for an approximately 4-mile roundtrip.



A detailed property map can be found here:

https://files.dnr.state.mn.us/destinations/snas/detail_maps/02000.pdf
Hours And Camping: No camping is allowed within the Scientific and Natural Area. The SNA is open year-round.
name: Minnesota Point Pine Forest State Natural Area

Description: Approximately 50 acres of exceptional old-growth forest, located within the 165 acre nature preserve. The mixed-mesophytic forest includes species such as black oak, white oak, black cherry, shagbark hickory, sugar maple, red maple, American beech and white pine. In addition, a rich understory of ferns, native phlox, white violet, golden ragwort, Dame’s rocket, and mayapple.
Navigation:
1740 Vernonview Drive Mount Vernon, Ohio 43050

Lat. 40.42166 Long -82.45542

Trailhead is located SW of Pavilion off parking lot.
Parking And Admission: Admission is free. There is a larger parking area near Vernonview entrance and smaller parking area near Upper Gilchrist Road entrance at 12185 Upper Gilchrist Road, Mount Vernon Ohio, 43050.
Trails: There are two natural surface loop trails with a connector that are in total about four miles in length. Trail map is available at https://knoxcountyparks.org/. Select “Parks and Trails.
Hours And Camping: The park is open every day of the year, sunrise to sunset. Day use areas close at dusk. No camping available.
Hunting: The Park District manages a controlled bow hunt with the explicit goal of limiting browsing pressure on the understory.
name: The Woodlands

Description:
McDowell Nature Preserve in southwest Mecklenburg County protects over 1,140 acres of forested, rolling terrain along the banks of Lake Wylie. Over 90% of the nature preserve is undeveloped, which offers many wildlife and hiking opportunities. The preserve also offers an accessible trail, two playgrounds, picnic shelters, nature center and a campground.

All of McDowell is considered mature forest; the oldest trees are between 170-190 years. It can be described as a mature Dry-Mesic Oak-Hickory Forest community in very good condition dominated by a mixture of oaks and hickories such as White Oak, Red Oak, Black Oak, Mockernut Hickory, Sweet Pignut Hickory, and Pignut Hickory.Rare plants that may occur in Dry-Mesic Oak-Hickory Forest are Piedmont indigo-bush, Nestronia, Indian physic and Biltmore carrion-flower. McDowell has been deemed by the Secretary of the N.C. Department of Natural and Cultural Resources to qualify as an outstanding natural area under statutory criteria for nature preserve dedication. McDowell Nature Preserve is rated at the highest level for NCNHP’s Biodiversity and Wildlife Habitat Assessment scale
Navigation:
15222 York Road, Charlotte, NC 28278



Traveling on I-77: Take Exit 90 onto Carowinds Boulevard. Go west approximately 2 miles to the intersection of S. Tryon St. & Hwy. 49. Turn left on Highway 49 and travel 4 miles. McDowell Nature Preserve entrance is on the right.
Parking And Admission: There are 15 parking lots throughout the Preserve. The closest to Chestnut Trail is near the McDowell Campground. Free to visit from sunrise to sunset. There is ADA parking throughout the preserve (Call Nature Center to ask about an accessible all-terrain chair).
Trails:
OGFN visitors should seek the Chestnut Trail (1.11 miles). This moderate to difficult trail has occasional steep inclines. This trail circles around a natural valley divided by a small creek and passes beneath the canopy of a mature hardwood forest. Some of this forest was affected by a tornado in 2004. The forest floor is carpeted in wildflowers during early spring. Watch for Witch Hazel blooming during late autumn and winter.



McDowell Nature Preserve has 8 miles of trails offering hikers and nature enthusiasts the opportunity to explore a variety of terrain while enjoying scenic views of the lake, forests, and streams. Some of these trails include Chestnut Trail (1.11 miles), Four Seasons Trail (0.4 miles), Piedmont Prairie Trail (1.1 miles), and Kingfisher Trail (1.11 miles).
Hours And Camping: The Preserve is open daily sunup to sundown. McDowell Campground offers 56 camping sites. Sites include: 13 RV sites, 26 Drive-To tent sites, 10 primitive tent sites, and six Tent sites with Decks. All sites can sleep up to six persons each. For more information or to make a reservation, please call 980.314.2267 or visit www.parkandrec.com.
Hunting: Fishing is allowed on Lake Wylie, but all anglers must purchase a valid North Carolina fishing license. No hunting is permitted.
name: McDowell Nature Preserve - Chestnut Loop Trail
